Introduction

The Apple Watch is one of those devices that many people buy with enthusiasm, but it can also raise questions from the very first minute. It is not a phone. It is not exactly a traditional watch. It is not just a fitness band. And it is certainly not a magical device that solves your life simply because it has an Apple logo on the back. We already know how this works: technology promises a great deal, and then you find yourself facing a tiny screen, three hidden settings, and a user trying to work out whether they have pressed the Digital Crown, the side button, or their own patience.

This course has been created by Canal TifloAcosta with a very specific purpose: to guide a blind person from the moment they receive an Apple Watch until they can use it in a practical, safe, and independent way with VoiceOver.

The idea is not to create a catalogue of features or a collection of technical terms. The idea is much simpler and much more useful: to explain what you have in your hand, how to turn it on, how to pair it with the iPhone, how to activate VoiceOver, how to configure it, how to use it in daily life, and how to make the most of important areas such as notifications, calls, messages, physical activity, workouts, health, sleep, personal safety, and alerts.

This course is especially intended for blind people who use an iPhone with VoiceOver and want to start using the Apple Watch from scratch. It may also be useful for people who already have an Apple Watch but feel they barely use it beyond checking the time or receiving the occasional notification. And, of course, it may also help relatives, trainers, support professionals, and anyone who assists blind users in learning technology.

The starting point will be very basic: a person buys an Apple Watch, takes it out of the box, and is not quite sure what to do next. From there, we will move forward step by step. First, we will identify the watch physically.

Then we will see how to put it on, charge it, and turn it on.

  • Next, we will activate VoiceOver.
  • After that, we will pair it with the iPhone.
  • Then we will review the most important settings.

And once the watch is ready, we will move on to what really matters: how to use it. Because the Apple Watch starts to make sense when it stops being a nice object on your wrist and begins to solve small everyday situations. Answering a call without taking out your iPhone. Reading a notification. Setting a timer. Finding your phone at home. Starting a workout. Checking your heart rate. Reviewing how you slept. Receiving an important alert. Using a vibration on your wrist as a discreet warning. Paying with Apple Pay, if you use it. Asking Siri for something. Going home with more information and less dependence.

This course will also pay particular attention to health and physical exercise. Not as decoration, but as a central part of the Apple Watch. Many people buy this watch precisely because they want to move more, monitor their activity better, record workouts, keep an eye on certain health metrics, or have safety features such as Fall Detection or Emergency SOS. For that reason, these topics have their own section and are not hidden at the end as if they were extra padding.

We will also keep in mind that not all users have the same needs. There will be sections dedicated to sounds, vibrations, haptic feedback, non-visual alerts, and use of the watch by people who, in addition to blindness, may also have hearing loss or deafblindness. In those cases, we need to be especially clear: the Apple Watch can offer interesting possibilities, but not every feature will be equally useful for everyone. Technology helps, but it does not perform miracles. That job is still reserved for advertising brochures.

How to use this course

This course is designed to be read and practised in parts. It is not advisable to try to do everything in a single afternoon. Although, naturally, there is always someone willing to pair the watch, configure health, change the watch face, try Apple Pay, start a workout, and activate Emergency SOS before having a snack. Better not.

The most practical way to follow the course is this:

  • First, read the introduction and the full table of contents so you know what the course includes.
  • Follow the first modules in order, especially if the Apple Watch is new.
  • Practise each section before moving on to the next one.

Skip the topics you do not need at that moment, such as Apple Pay, Apple Fitness Plus, menstrual cycle tracking, braille, or specific health features. Return to the troubleshooting sections when something does not work as expected. Use the exercises at the end to check that you can already handle the watch in real-life situations.

This course does not assume that every person will use every feature. Its purpose is for each person to understand what the device can offer and decide which features are useful for them.

One person may use the Apple Watch mainly for calls, notifications, and timers.

  • Another may use it mostly for walking, recording workouts, and checking activity.
  • Another may be more interested in health, sleep, and heart rate.
  • Another may need vibrations, haptic alerts, and safety features.

And another may simply buy it because they want to find their iPhone every time they leave it in some ridiculous place around the house, something the human species has been doing with impressive consistency since mobile phones first existed. The important thing is that the watch adapts to the person, not that the person becomes a slave to every feature on the watch.

Important warnings before starting

Health warning: the health features of the Apple Watch do not replace a healthcare professional. The watch can record data, show trends, and issue certain alerts, but it should not be interpreted as a definitive medical diagnosis.

Model warning: some features depend on the model. An Apple Watch SE is not the same as an Apple Watch Series or an Apple Watch Ultra. Some features require specific sensors that are not present in all models.

Country or region warning: some features depend on the country or region. Several health features, Siri, maps, keyboard options, Apple Wallet, emergency calling, cellular connectivity, and other services may vary depending on territory, mobile carrier, local regulations, and Apple’s official availability.

Language and option names warning: the paths and option names in this course have been adapted for an English-language iPhone and Apple Watch. Some labels may vary slightly depending on the country, region, iOS or watchOS version, selected language, and device settings. If an option does not appear with exactly the same name, look for an equivalent label within the same section.

Warning about sensitive features: when features such as Emergency SOS, Fall Detection, erasing the watch, unpairing the Apple Watch, or Medical ID are explained, they will be treated with particular care. These are useful options, but they should not be handled as casually as changing the colour of a watch face.

General objective of the course

By the end of this course, the person should be able to:

  • Physically identify the Apple Watch.
  • Place it correctly on the wrist.
  • Charge it and turn it on.
  • Activate VoiceOver.
  • Pair the watch with the iPhone.
  • Configure basic accessibility settings.
  • Move around the watch face, menus, and apps.
  • Use the Digital Crown and the side button.
  • Manage notifications.
  • Answer calls and messages.
  • Use Siri.
  • Set timers, alarms, and reminders.
  • Find the iPhone from the watch.
  • Understand the main physical activity features.
  • Start, pause, and end workouts.
  • Check basic health data.
  • Configure sleep and review related information.
  • Understand which health features depend on the model or country.
  • Configure personal safety features.
  • Use sounds, vibrations, and haptic feedback.
  • Solve common problems.
  • Decide which features are genuinely useful and which ones can be ignored without guilt.

Module 1. What the Apple Watch really is and what it can offer a blind person

The Apple Watch is a smartwatch designed to work together with the iPhone. Although some models with cellular connectivity can do more things without the iPhone nearby, the Apple Watch still depends largely on the iPhone ecosystem for setup, data syncing, app installation, notification management, and checking information more comfortably.

For a blind person, the Apple Watch can be useful because it provides quick access to information from the wrist through VoiceOver, sounds, vibrations, and haptic feedback. The key word here is quick.

The Apple Watch is not designed to replace the iPhone for long tasks. It is not the best device for writing long texts, reviewing large documents, browsing complex web pages, or managing lengthy settings. For that, the iPhone, iPad, Mac, or even a computer with a screen reader will still be much more comfortable.

But it can be very practical for short actions.

  • Checking the time.
  • Knowing who is calling.
  • Answering a call.
  • Reading a notification.
  • Dictating a short reply.
  • Setting a timer.
  • Setting an alarm.
  • Asking Siri for something.
  • Starting a workout.
  • Checking your heart rate.
  • Checking your activity progress.
  • Recording sleep.
  • Receiving a health alert.
  • Finding your iPhone.
  • Using Apple Pay.
  • Receiving a discreet vibration on your wrist.
  • Carrying personal safety features with you.

That is the natural territory of the Apple Watch: small, frequent, quick actions.

What it can offer in daily life

The Apple Watch can reduce the need to take out the iPhone constantly. This may sound like a small thing, but in practice it can be very convenient. If a notification arrives, you can check it from your wrist. If a call comes in, you can know who is calling. If you are cooking, you can set a timer. If you go out for a walk, you can start a workout. If you cannot find your iPhone, you can make it play a sound from the watch. If you have an alarm or reminder, you can receive it through vibration.

For many blind people, that combination of VoiceOver and vibration can be useful. The information does not depend on looking at a screen. The watch can speak, it can vibrate, and it can work as a small personal notification centre.

What it can offer for physical activity

The Apple Watch makes a lot of sense as a physical activity device. It can record daily movement, workouts, steps, distance, exercise minutes, active calories, and heart rate during activity. It can also help build habits, because it shows goals, trends, and progress.

This does not mean that everyone has to become obsessed with closing rings. Life already has enough obligations without a digital circle judging you from your wrist. But used sensibly, the watch can help you move more, measure what you do more accurately, and have a reference point for activity.

For a blind person, it can be especially useful for walks, indoor workouts, stationary bike sessions, strength exercises, guided routines, or daily activity. The important thing will be to learn how to start, pause, resume, and end workouts with VoiceOver, as well as knowing which data is worth checking and which data is not necessary at every moment.

What it can offer for health

The Apple Watch can also provide health-related information. Depending on the model and country, it may offer features such as heart rate, high or low heart rate alerts, irregular rhythm notifications, ECG, sleep tracking, sleep apnoea notifications, atrial fibrillation history, blood oxygen, or hypertension notifications. Here we need to be very careful.

The Apple Watch does not turn anyone into a doctor, nor does it turn your wrist into a portable hospital. It can record data and issue alerts, but any symptom, concerning result, or relevant alert should be discussed with healthcare professionals.

The availability of health features in watchOS varies by country or region. This affects features such as ECG, blood oxygen, hypertension notifications, irregular rhythm notifications, atrial fibrillation history, and sleep apnoea notifications.

For that reason, in this course we will not simply say “the Apple Watch does ECG” or “the Apple Watch detects sleep apnoea” as if it were the same on all models and in all places. We will explain when a feature may be available, what it means, what its limitations are, and how to check it.

What it can offer for safety

The Apple Watch can also be useful for personal safety. Features such as Emergency SOS, Fall Detection, emergency contacts, Medical ID, and location can be important for some people. These are not features to touch without understanding them, but it is useful to know they exist.

Fall Detection can show an alert, tap your wrist, sound an alarm, and allow the watch to call emergency services if it interprets that there has been a hard fall. It must also be made clear that the Apple Watch cannot detect every fall.

For a blind person who lives alone, goes out walking, exercises, or simply wants an additional layer of safety, these features may be of considerable interest. But they must be configured properly and understood properly.

What you should not expect from the Apple Watch

  • You should not expect the Apple Watch to replace the iPhone.
  • You should not expect every app to be equally comfortable on a small screen.
  • You should not expect every health feature to be available on your model.
  • You should not expect all data to be perfect.
  • You should not expect the watch to understand dictation correctly every time.
  • You should not expect VoiceOver on such a small screen to be as comfortable as on the iPhone.
  • You should not expect the battery to last several days if you use it heavily.
  • You should not expect a safety feature to detect absolutely every situation.

This does not make the watch less valuable. It simply puts it in its proper place. The Apple Watch can be very useful if it is understood for what it is: a companion to the iPhone, a tool for alerts, health, activity, safety, and quick actions.

Why it is useful to learn it methodically

The Apple Watch has one particular feature: it is used on a very small screen, with few physical controls and many functions divided between the watch itself and the Apple Watch app on the iPhone.

That can be confusing at first.

  • Sometimes the setting is changed on the watch.
  • Sometimes it is changed on the iPhone.
  • Sometimes it can be changed on both.
  • Sometimes a feature appears in Health.
  • Sometimes it appears in the Watch app.
  • Sometimes it depends on Privacy.
  • Sometimes it depends on Accessibility.

And sometimes Apple decides that an option should be placed exactly where no reasonable person would expect it, because apparently menus need adventure too. That is why this course will move step by step.

We will not begin with advanced health, workouts, watch faces, or Apple Pay. First, the person needs to know what they have in their hand, how to put it on, how to activate VoiceOver, how to pair it, and how to move around the watch. From there, everything else will be easier.

Exercise for module 1

Before continuing, it is useful to answer these questions mentally:

  • What do you mainly want to use the Apple Watch for?
  • What interests you most: notifications, calls, exercise, health, sleep, safety, Siri, payments, or finding the iPhone?
  • Which things would you rather do on the iPhone instead of on the watch?
  • Which features would you like to learn first?
  • Which features do not interest you and can be left for later?

You do not need to have all the answers. But it is useful to start by understanding that the Apple Watch is not used in the same way by everyone. The goal of this course is for each person to decide how they want to use it, not to activate features just for the sake of activating them.

Module 2. What you need before you start

Before taking the Apple Watch out of the box or trying to pair it with the iPhone, it is useful to check a few things. This is not the most exciting part of the course, but it can prevent quite a few problems. Many difficulties with the Apple Watch do not begin on the watch itself, but with incomplete preparation: an iPhone that has not been updated, low battery, Bluetooth turned off, an unstable connection, an account that is not configured properly, or a lack of technological patience, that essential ingredient which, for some mysterious reason, is never included in the box.

The Apple Watch is designed to work together with the iPhone. Although some models allow their own cellular connection, the initial setup is done from the iPhone. So before touching the watch, you need to make sure the iPhone is ready. The first thing you need is a compatible iPhone.

Not every iPhone works with every Apple Watch model. Compatibility depends on the watch model and the version of watchOS it uses. For that reason, before buying or setting up an Apple Watch, it is worth checking that the iPhone you are going to use can be paired with that watch.

This is especially important if the Apple Watch is new and the iPhone is already several years old, or if the watch is second-hand and you do not know exactly which version of watchOS is installed on it.

For this course, we will start from a simple idea: the Apple Watch will be set up with a compatible, updated iPhone that is working correctly with VoiceOver. You also need the iPhone to be updated.

There is no need to become obsessed with installing a new version on the very day it appears, because we all know that freshly released updates sometimes arrive with more excitement than strictly necessary. But to set up an Apple Watch, it is advisable to have the iPhone running a recent and compatible version.

If the iPhone has an old version of iOS, it may not allow the watch to be paired, it may ask you to update before continuing, or some features may not appear.

Before starting, check this on the iPhone:

  1. Settings.
  2. General.
  3. Software Update.

If there is a pending update and it is required in order to pair the Apple Watch, it is better to sort that out before continuing. You also need enough battery.

The iPhone should have a comfortable amount of charge before starting the setup process. Ideally, it should have plenty of battery, or it should be connected to the charger. The pairing process can take a while, especially if the watch needs to be updated.

The Apple Watch must also have enough battery. If it is new, it may come with some charge, but not always. If it does not turn on or appears not to respond, the first thing to do is place it on its charger and wait.

Do not rush at this point. If the watch has been stored for a long time or has just come out of the box, it may need a few minutes of charging before showing clear signs of life. Modern technology has these little sensitivities: it arrives in beautiful boxes, but sometimes needs half an hour plugged in before it can be bothered to exist. You need Bluetooth enabled on the iPhone. The Apple Watch communicates with the iPhone using Bluetooth and Wi-Fi. For the initial setup, Bluetooth must be enabled.

You can check this on the iPhone by going to:

  • Settings.
  • Bluetooth.
  • Bluetooth on.
  • You can also check it from Control Centre, but for a clearer check with VoiceOver, it is usually better to go into Settings.
  • You need Wi-Fi enabled and an internet connection.

During setup, data may be downloaded, services may be activated, the account may be verified, updates may be installed, or information may be synced. So it is best to have the iPhone connected to a stable Wi-Fi network.

If you are in a place with a poor connection, the setup may get stuck, take a long time, or fail. And then it looks as if the watch is to blame, when in fact the drama began with the router, that little box that sits there blinking as if it understood anything about life.

Before starting, check:

  • Settings.
  • Wi-Fi.
  • Wi-Fi on.
  • Connected to a known network.
  • You need an Apple Account configured.

The Apple Watch works with the Apple Account you use on the iPhone. That account allows data to be synced, iCloud to be used, Find My to be activated, apps to be downloaded, some safety features to be used, and Apple services to be managed. If the iPhone is already working normally, the account is usually configured. Even so, it is worth checking.

On the iPhone, go to:

  • Settings.
  • Your name, usually located at the top.
  • From there, you can check that the account is signed in.

If the iPhone asks you to sign in, verify the account, or accept new terms and conditions, it is better to resolve that before starting with the Apple Watch. You need the Apple Watch app on the iPhone. The iPhone includes the Apple Watch app. This app will be essential throughout the course.

It is used to pair the watch, configure many settings, review notifications, manage watch faces, install apps, adjust accessibility, and modify numerous options. The app may appear as Watch or Apple Watch, depending on version and configuration.

Before starting, locate that app on the iPhone. You do not need to open it yet if you are setting up the watch from scratch, but it is useful to know where it is.

You can search for it with Spotlight:

  • From the iPhone Home Screen, perform the gesture used to open Search.
  • Type or dictate Watch.
  • Open the app when it appears.
  • If the app does not appear, check whether it has been removed and download it again from the App Store.
  • You need to be familiar with VoiceOver on the iPhone.

This course is intended for blind people who use VoiceOver. For that reason, before setting up the Apple Watch, it is important that the person can use VoiceOver on the iPhone at least at a basic level.

You do not need to be an expert user, but it is useful to know how to:

  • Move around the screen with swipes.
  • Activate an item with a double tap.
  • Use the Back button when it appears.
  • Explore the screen with your finger.
  • Write or dictate text.
  • Read warning messages.
  • Enter Settings.
  • Open the Watch app.

If someone does not yet know the basics of VoiceOver on iPhone, they can still configure the Apple Watch with help, but it will be harder to do it independently. The Apple Watch is not the best place to learn VoiceOver from scratch. The screen is small, the controls are more limited, and some processes depend on the iPhone. You also need a quiet environment.

The first Apple Watch setup should not be done in the middle of a conversation, with noise, in a hurry, or while someone is standing next to you saying, “That only takes a moment.” That sentence should be banned by technological law.

It is advisable to prepare:

  • The iPhone.
  • The Apple Watch.
  • The watch charger.
  • A nearby power socket.
  • A good Wi-Fi connection.
  • Enough time.
  • A place where you can hear VoiceOver clearly.

If you use headphones, you can keep them nearby, but during the initial setup it may be simpler to use the speaker on the iPhone and the speaker on the watch, so you do not confuse where each message is coming from. It is also useful to have the iPhone charger nearby.

If the process takes longer because the watch needs to be updated, the iPhone may use battery. It is better to have it charging or ready to charge. You need to decide whether the watch is for you or for someone else.

During setup, the iPhone may offer options such as setting up the Apple Watch for yourself or for a family member. In this course, we will mainly work with the most common case: a person setting up their own Apple Watch with their own iPhone.

Setting it up for a family member may make sense in some cases, but it will not be the main route followed in this course. If that option appears, the usual choice will be to set it up for yourself. You need to know whether the Apple Watch is new or used. This point is important. If the Apple Watch is new, it should start the setup process without being linked to any previous account.

If the Apple Watch is used, gifted, bought second-hand, or inherited, it may still be linked to another person’s Apple Account. In that case, Activation Lock may appear. If that happens, restarting or erasing the watch will not be enough. The previous owner will need to remove it from their account.

It is useful to know this before buying a second-hand Apple Watch. If the watch is locked to the previous owner’s account, it can become a very elegant piece of useless technology, which is quite an expensive category of object to keep in a drawer. You need to know whether the model is GPS or GPS plus Cellular.

There are two types of Apple Watch:

  1. GPS models.
  2. GPS plus Cellular models.

GPS models depend more on the iPhone for calls, messages, and connection when you are away from a known Wi-Fi network. GPS plus Cellular models can use a compatible mobile line, provided that a supported carrier in your country or region allows it and the corresponding service is configured. This can offer more independence from the iPhone in some situations.

Not everyone needs Cellular. For many people, a GPS model is enough if they usually carry the iPhone with them. But for someone who goes out walking, exercises, wants to make calls from the watch without carrying the iPhone, or wants more safety outside the home, it may be worth considering a Cellular model. This course will explain the differences where appropriate, but the general setup will be valid for both types of watch. You need to know that some features depend on the model. Not all Apple Watch models have the same sensors.

Some health features may be available only on certain models. For example, ECG, blood oxygen, wrist temperature, advanced alerts, or certain health features are not present on all watches. For that reason, this course will not assume that everyone has every feature. When a feature depends on the model, that will be indicated. This is especially important in the health sections. You need to know that some features depend on the country.

In addition to the model, some features depend on the country or region. Some health features, calling services, Apple Pay, cellular connectivity, maps, Siri, or certain services may vary.

This means that two people with the same Apple Watch may not have exactly the same options if they live in different countries or use different carriers.

The course will explain the main features, but always with this idea in mind: if an option does not appear, it may be because of the model, the country, the system version, or previous configuration. You need to decide whether to install all apps or only some. During the initial setup, the iPhone may offer to install on the Apple Watch the available versions of apps you already have on the iPhone.

When starting out, the most practical approach is usually not to fill the watch with unnecessary apps. The more apps there are, the more items VoiceOver will have to move through, and the more noise may appear in the initial experience. For a person who is just beginning, a simple and well-configured watch is better than a wrist turned into a market stall of icons. Specific apps can always be installed later. You need to understand that many settings are managed from the iPhone. This is key.

The Apple Watch is used on the wrist, but many of its settings are managed more comfortably from the iPhone. In this course, it will always be indicated where each action is performed. Some actions will be done on the Apple Watch. Some actions will be done on the iPhone. And some actions can be done on both.

This distinction will prevent confusion. When an instruction begins with “on the iPhone”, do not look for it on the watch. When it says “on the Apple Watch”, do not lose hope inside the Watch app on the iPhone. It sounds obvious, but in practical courses, the obvious is often exactly what saves the afternoon.

Check before starting

Before moving on to the next module, review this list:

  • You have a compatible iPhone.
  • The iPhone works correctly with VoiceOver.
  • The iPhone has enough battery or is charging.
  • The Apple Watch is charged or connected to its charger.
  • Bluetooth is enabled on the iPhone.
  • Wi-Fi is enabled and connected on the iPhone.
  • The Apple Account is signed in on the iPhone.
  • The Watch app has been located.
  • You are in a place where you can hear VoiceOver clearly.
  • You have the Apple Watch charger nearby.
  • You know whether the watch is new or used.
  • You know whether the watch is GPS or GPS plus Cellular, if that information matters to you.
  • You are not in a hurry to complete the setup.

Practical advice

If the Apple Watch is new, do not try to move forward by touching options at random. First prepare the iPhone, charge the watch if necessary, and make sure VoiceOver is working correctly on the iPhone.

If the watch is used, first check that it is not linked to someone else’s account. If Activation Lock appears, it is not a VoiceOver or configuration problem: it is a security protection and requires action from the previous owner.

Exercise for module 2

Before continuing, carry out this practical check:

  • Open Settings on the iPhone.
  • Check that Wi-Fi is enabled.
  • Check that Bluetooth is enabled.
  • Check that your Apple Account appears at the top of Settings.
  • Locate the Watch app on the iPhone.
  • Place the Apple Watch near the iPhone.
  • Connect the Apple Watch charger and leave the watch charging if you do not know how much battery it has.
  • Once all this is ready, it will make sense to move on to the next module.

Module 3. Choosing a model without getting lost

Before buying an Apple Watch, it is worth being clear about one idea: not everyone needs the most expensive model. The best Apple Watch is not always the most complete one, but the one that fits what a person wants to do, the iPhone they already have, their budget, and the features they are actually going to use.

At the time this course was reviewed, the main current models were Apple Watch Series 11, Apple Watch SE 3, and Apple Watch Ultra 3. This information should be checked again before publishing or re-editing the material, because Apple may update models, remove others, or change product names.

This does not mean that a person necessarily has to buy the latest model. It may also make sense to buy an earlier model if it is in good condition, compatible with the iPhone, receives updates, and has the features that are needed. But in a course like this, it is useful to explain the main Apple Watch families first, because that makes it easier to understand what is gained and what is lost.

The three main Apple Watch families

In simple terms, we can speak of three main lines:

  • Apple Watch SE.
  • Apple Watch Series.
  • Apple Watch Ultra.
  • Each one is aimed at a different type of user.

Apple Watch SE

The Apple Watch SE is usually the entry-level option. It is designed for people who want the basic Apple Watch features without paying for all the sensors and materials of the higher models.

It may be enough for many blind people who want to:

  • Receive notifications.
  • Answer calls.
  • Reply to messages.
  • Use Siri.
  • Check the time.
  • Use timers and alarms.
  • Find the iPhone.
  • Record activity.
  • Start workouts.
  • Have Fall Detection and safety features, depending on model and configuration.
  • Use Apple Pay, if available.
  • In other words, for general daily use, the Apple Watch SE can cover quite a lot.

The important part is this: the SE does not usually include all the advanced health features of the Series or Ultra models. So if a person is buying the watch mainly for specific health features, they should first check whether that model includes them.

For someone who wants to get started, receive notifications, walk, record activity, use Siri, locate the iPhone, and have an accessible watch with VoiceOver, it may be a reasonable option. For someone who wants every available advanced health feature, it may fall short.

Apple Watch Series

The Apple Watch Series is the main line. It usually sits between the SE and the Ultra. It is the model that normally offers the most complete combination for most users: good screen size, better sensors than the SE, more advanced health features, fast charging on compatible models, good performance, and a design that is less bulky than the Ultra.

It may be the most balanced option for someone who wants:

  • Full daily use.
  • Broader health features.
  • Workouts.
  • Good performance.
  • A more advanced screen.
  • Faster charging, if the model supports it.
  • More sensors than the SE.

For a blind person, a larger screen may not seem visually important, but it can affect the layout of elements, touch use with VoiceOver, and general comfort. Obviously, it is not that you need to buy a large screen in order to see better if you do not see. But on a larger screen there may be more space to explore with your finger and locate touch elements with a little less pressure.

The Series line is usually the most advisable option for someone who wants a complete Apple Watch without going all the way to the size, price, and more sports-focused or extreme approach of the Ultra.

Apple Watch Ultra

The Apple Watch Ultra is designed for more demanding use: longer battery life, a more robust case, a large screen, better resistance, and features aimed at sport, adventure, outdoor use, and advanced training.

It may make sense for people who:

  • Do a lot of outdoor exercise.
  • Need more battery life.
  • Want a more resistant watch.
  • Do long activities.
  • Want a large screen.
  • Want more complete sports features.
  • Need a configurable Action button, depending on the model.
  • Value a more robust build.

For a blind person, the Ultra may be interesting not so much because of its appearance, but because of battery life, resistance, physical size, ease of locating controls, and use during physical activity. But it is also larger, more expensive, and may be excessive if all you want is to check notifications, set timers, and go for an occasional walk.

It is worth saying this clearly: if a person is not going to take advantage of the extra battery life, the sports focus, the resistance, or the size of the Ultra, they probably do not need to pay for it. Buying the most expensive model just to use it as a wrist alarm clock is a very elegant way of funding unnecessary titanium.

GPS or GPS plus Cellular

This is one of the most important decisions.

Apple Watch GPS

An Apple Watch GPS connects to the iPhone using Bluetooth and can also use known Wi-Fi networks. For many features, it depends on the iPhone being nearby or on having Wi-Fi available. It can work perfectly well if you normally carry your iPhone with you.

With a GPS model, you can:

  • Receive notifications when the watch is connected to the iPhone.
  • Answer calls if the iPhone is nearby.
  • Reply to messages if the iPhone is nearby or there is a compatible connection.
  • Record activity and workouts.
  • Use timers, alarms, and many apps.
  • Use Apple Pay, if configured.
  • Find the iPhone.
  • Check health and activity.
  • For many people, this will be enough.

Apple Watch GPS plus Cellular

An Apple Watch GPS plus Cellular can connect to a compatible mobile network through an associated line, provided that a supported carrier in your country or region allows it and the service is configured. This allows some features to be used even when the iPhone is not nearby.

It may be interesting if:

  • You go out walking without the iPhone.
  • You exercise without carrying the iPhone.
  • You want to be able to make calls from the watch in certain situations.
  • You want more independence.
  • You are concerned about safety when going out alone.
  • You want to receive messages or alerts even when you do not have the iPhone with you.
  • But several things must be kept in mind.

First, it is not enough to buy the Cellular model. You also need your mobile carrier to support activating the service on the Apple Watch. Second, it may have an additional cost. Third, using a mobile connection consumes more battery. Fourth, not all features will work in the same way in all countries or with all carriers. So Cellular can be very useful for some people, but it is not essential for everyone.

For a blind person who goes out walking alone, exercises, sometimes leaves the iPhone behind, or wants an additional layer of safety, it may be an option to consider. For someone who always carries the iPhone, the GPS model will probably be enough.

Watch size

Apple Watch models are usually offered in different case sizes. The choice depends on wrist size, comfort, budget, battery life, and personal preference.

For a blind person, size can affect several things:

  • Comfort when wearing it.
  • Ease of locating the Digital Crown and the side button.
  • Space for exploring the screen with VoiceOver.
  • Weight on the wrist.
  • Battery life on some models.
  • Touch reading of screen elements.
  • There is no universal answer.

A larger watch may be more comfortable for exploring the screen with your finger, but it may also feel heavier or more uncomfortable on smaller wrists. A smaller watch may be more discreet and comfortable, but the screen is more limited.

Ideally, if possible, it is best to try the size physically before buying. If that is not possible, it is worth checking the measurements carefully and thinking about real use: sleeping with it, exercising, wearing it all day, using it with long sleeves, charging it often, and operating the buttons.

Straps

The strap may seem like a minor detail, but it is not. An uncomfortable strap can make you use the watch less. A poorly adjusted strap can affect sensor readings. A strap that is difficult to put on can become a daily problem for a blind person or someone with mobility difficulties.

When choosing a strap, it is worth considering:

  • That it is easy to put on and take off.
  • That it allows a firm adjustment.
  • That it does not stay too loose.
  • That it does not tighten excessively.
  • That it is comfortable for sleeping, if sleep tracking will be used.
  • That it handles sweat well, if exercise will be done.
  • That it is easy to clean.

For health and exercise tracking, the watch must be correctly positioned on the wrist. If it moves too much, if it is too loose, or if the sensors do not maintain good contact with the skin, some readings may be less accurate.

Health features: what to check before buying

This point is essential. Many people buy an Apple Watch for health reasons. So before choosing a model, it is worth checking what features it really has.

Among the features that may be of interest are:

  • Heart rate.
  • High or low heart rate alerts.
  • Irregular rhythm notifications.
  • ECG.
  • Blood oxygen.
  • Wrist temperature.
  • Sleep tracking.
  • Sleep apnoea notifications.
  • Atrial fibrillation history.
  • Hypertension notifications.
  • Estimates related to the menstrual cycle, if relevant.

Not all models have everything. In addition, some features depend on the country or region. Certain watchOS features may not be available in all countries or languages.

For that reason, if a person wants the Apple Watch mainly for a specific health feature, they should check three things before buying:

  • That the model has the necessary sensor.
  • That the feature is available in their country.
  • That their iPhone and watchOS version are compatible.

Practical example: it is not advisable to buy a watch thinking about ECG, blood oxygen, sleep apnoea, or hypertension without first checking whether that feature is available on that model and in that region.

The Apple Watch can be very useful for health, but not all features are present on all watches. That sentence should really be printed on the box in large letters, alongside another one saying: “No, it will not organise your life by itself.”

Exercise features: what to consider

If the main goal is exercise, it is worth considering:

  • Battery life.
  • Comfort of the strap.
  • Water resistance, if swimming will be involved.
  • Size and weight.
  • Ease of starting workouts with VoiceOver.
  • GPS accuracy during outdoor workouts.
  • Use with headphones.
  • Possibility of using Cellular if you want to go out without the iPhone.
  • Fast charging if you train often.
  • Type of exercises you want to record.

For walking, daily activity, occasional gym use, and simple workouts, the most expensive model is not necessarily needed. For long workouts, outings without the iPhone, hiking, demanding activities, or very intensive use, a model with more battery life and better sports features may make more sense.

Safety features

The Apple Watch can offer important safety features, such as Emergency SOS, Fall Detection, Crash Detection on compatible models, emergency calls, emergency contacts, and Medical ID.

These features may be especially interesting for:

  • People who live alone.
  • Older people.
  • People who go out walking alone.
  • People who exercise outdoors.
  • People with mobility problems or a risk of falling.
  • People who want a quick way to request help.
  • But here too, compatibility, model, country, and configuration must be checked.

These features should also be explained responsibly. They do not replace caution, they do not guarantee detection of every situation, and they should not be activated without understanding how they work.

Battery life and charging

Battery is another important point. The Apple Watch is not a traditional watch that you put on and forget for weeks. It is a smart device and, as such, it needs to be charged frequently. Some models offer longer battery life than others, and some support fast charging. Battery life and charging vary depending on model, use, settings, connection, battery condition, and other factors.

In practice, it is worth thinking about real use:

  • If you are going to use it during the day and also for sleeping, you need to plan when to charge it.
  • If you train a lot, you will use more battery.
  • If you use Cellular, you will use more battery.
  • If you receive many notifications, that will also consume more battery.
  • If you use sleep tracking, you cannot charge it all night, because it will be on your wrist recording sleep.

For someone who wants to use sleep and activity features, fast charging can be quite useful. It allows the watch to be charged at specific times of the day, for example while showering, having breakfast, or resting.

Materials and resistance

Models may vary in materials, glass, dust resistance, water resistance, and robustness.

For most users, this will not be the most important factor. But it may be relevant if:

  • You do intensive sport.
  • You work in environments where the watch may be knocked.
  • You go hiking.
  • You swim.
  • You want a more resistant device.
  • You wear the watch all day in many different situations.

A blind person should also consider that the watch may receive knocks more easily when moving through narrow spaces, doorways, furniture, or public transport. It is not a daily tragedy, but resistance may be worth considering.

Buying new, refurbished, or second-hand

Buying new offers more peace of mind: warranty, battery in good condition, no Activation Lock, and clear compatibility. Buying refurbished can be interesting if it comes from a reliable source and includes a warranty. Buying second-hand can save money, but it requires more caution.

Before buying a used Apple Watch, you should check:

  • That it is not locked to someone else’s Apple Account.
  • That it can be paired with your iPhone.
  • That the battery is in good condition.
  • That there is no damage to the screen, crown, side button, or sensors.
  • That it includes a compatible charger.
  • That it is not too old to receive necessary updates.

The most delicate point is Activation Lock. If the watch is still linked to the previous owner’s account, you will not be able to use it normally. It is not a problem that can be solved with goodwill, restarts, or prayers to Saint Bluetooth. The previous owner must remove it properly from their account.

Which model may suit each type of use

For basic use

If you want the Apple Watch for notifications, calls, messages, timers, alarms, Siri, finding the iPhone, daily activity, and simple workouts, a recent Apple Watch SE may be enough.

For balanced use

If you want a more complete experience, better health features, a good screen, good performance, and more room for future use, a recent Apple Watch Series is usually the most balanced option.

For health

If you are buying the watch mainly for health, do not choose only by price. Check exactly which features the specific model includes: ECG, blood oxygen, temperature, sleep, apnoea, hypertension, irregular rhythm, and any other available features. The priority here is not “which watch looks nicer”, but which sensors and features it includes.

For exercise

If you do walks, gym sessions, moderate workouts, or daily activity, an SE or a Series may be enough. If you do long workouts, outdoor activities, routes, demanding activities, or need more battery life, it may make sense to look at an Ultra.

For safety outside the home

If you want to be able to call or communicate without carrying the iPhone, consider a GPS plus Cellular model, provided that a supported carrier in your country or region allows it. If you always carry the iPhone with you, a GPS model may be enough.

For older people or people at risk of falls

It is worth considering Fall Detection, emergency calls, emergency contacts, ease of use, battery, size, and simple configuration. There is no need to fill the watch with apps. In these cases, it is usually better to have a clean configuration, with few complications and the important features properly set up.

For people who are deafblind or have hearing loss

Here it is especially important to consider:

  • Vibrations.
  • Haptic feedback.
  • Wrist alerts.
  • Ease of configuration from the iPhone.
  • Possibility of using additional support.
  • Battery life.
  • A simple watch face.

The watch may be useful as a tactile alert device, but the experience will depend greatly on each person. If spoken output cannot be used, it will be necessary to study more carefully what can be done through vibration, iPhone support, braille where appropriate, and simplified configuration.

Common mistakes when choosing an Apple Watch

  • Buying the cheapest model without checking health features.
  • Buying the most expensive model thinking that this automatically makes it more accessible.
  • Buying a Cellular model without checking whether a supported carrier in your country or region allows it.
  • Buying a used watch without checking Activation Lock.
  • Choosing an uncomfortable strap.
  • Not checking compatibility with the iPhone.
  • Thinking that all models have ECG.
  • Thinking that all models have blood oxygen.
  • Thinking that all features work in all countries.
  • Thinking that the battery will last like the battery of a traditional watch.
  • Buying for appearance rather than real use.

This last mistake is very human: buying something shiny and then discovering that what you actually needed was battery life, sensors, and a strap that does not torture your wrist. Civilization advances through these small failures with receipts attached.

Practical recommendation

If this is your first Apple Watch and you are not sure how much you are going to use it, avoid buying impulsively.

First think about your main priority:

  • Daily use.
  • Health.
  • Exercise.
  • Safety.
  • Independence without the iPhone.
  • Sleep.
  • Notifications.
  • Then look at which model covers that priority.
  • If your priority is daily use, you may not need the most expensive model.
  • If your priority is health, check specific features.
  • If your priority is intensive exercise, look at battery life and resistance.
  • If your priority is going out without the iPhone, look at Cellular and carrier support.
  • If your priority is sleeping with it, think about battery and charging.
  • If your priority is accessibility, remember that VoiceOver is available on Apple Watch, but comfort may vary depending on size, configuration, and user experience.

Exercise for module 3

Before deciding on a model, answer these questions:

  • Will I always carry the iPhone with me, or do I want to be able to go out without it?
  • Am I mainly interested in health, exercise, notifications, or safety?
  • Do I need advanced features such as ECG, blood oxygen, sleep apnoea, or hypertension?
  • Am I going to use it for sleep?
  • Am I going to do long workouts?
  • Do I need a lot of battery life?
  • Do I prefer a light watch or a larger, more resistant one?
  • Does my carrier support Apple Watch Cellular?
  • Am I buying new, refurbished, or used?
  • Have I checked that the watch is compatible with my iPhone?

If, after answering these questions, you are still undecided between two models, it is usually better to choose the one that best covers your real needs, not the one that has more features on the technical specification sheet.

Summary of module 3

The Apple Watch SE may be enough for daily use, notifications, calls, messages, basic activity, and simple workouts. The Apple Watch Series is usually the most balanced option for someone who wants a complete watch, with more health features and more room for use.

The Apple Watch Ultra makes sense for someone who needs more battery life, resistance, a large screen, and features aimed at sport or more demanding use. GPS may be enough if you always carry the iPhone. GPS plus Cellular may be interesting if you want more independence, to exercise without the iPhone, or to have more safety outside the home. Health features depend on the model and country. The strap matters more than it seems. Buying used requires checking Activation Lock and compatibility. You should not buy on impulse, but according to real use.

Module 4. Physically identifying the Apple Watch

In this module, we will work as if the Apple Watch is already out of the box and in your hand. We are not going to configure it yet, pair it yet, or enter any menus. First, you need to identify the device physically. This is more important than it may seem, because the Apple Watch has few elements, but each one has a specific function. If from the beginning you know where the screen is, where the back is, where the Digital Crown is, where the side button is, and how the strap is attached, everything else will be easier.

A sighted person can look at the watch and orient themselves at a glance. A blind person needs to build that orientation through touch. It is not more difficult, but it does need to be explained properly. And since Apple does not usually include a voice inside the box saying “what you are touching now is the crown”, we will have to do it here. Another minor oversight of civilization.

What you have in front of you

When you take the Apple Watch out of the box, you will usually find the watch, a strap, and the charging cable. The exact contents may vary depending on the model, store, country, or version purchased, but those are the basic elements.

The body of the watch is a small rectangular piece with rounded corners. It has a front side, which is the screen, and a back side, where the sensors are located and which rests against the wrist.

It also has two main physical controls on one side:

  • The Digital Crown.
  • The side button.
  • The Digital Crown is the small wheel or crown.
  • The side button is the elongated button located near that crown.
  • The watch also has slots at the top and bottom for inserting or removing the strap.

First contact with the body of the watch

Hold the Apple Watch carefully between your fingers. You will notice that one side is smooth. That is the screen. The screen is the front of the watch. It is the area you touch to interact with VoiceOver, open items, explore the watch face, read notifications, or move around apps.

The other side has a more raised or circular area in the centre. That is the back of the watch. The sensors are located there. That side must be in contact with your skin when you put on the Apple Watch.

This distinction is essential:

  1. Screen facing outward.
  2. Sensors against the skin.

If you are ever unsure, look for the smoother side: that will be the screen. Look for the side with the raised or more defined central area: that will be the back.

The screen

The screen covers almost the entire front of the Apple Watch. It is smooth, with no physical buttons inside it. With VoiceOver, you will be able to touch the screen to hear which item is under your finger. You will also be able to swipe left or right to move through items, and double tap to activate. At this point, you do not need to practise the gestures yet. The only thing that matters is identifying which side is the screen. When the watch is on your wrist, the screen should face outward so that you can touch it with your other hand.

The back and the sensors

The back of the Apple Watch is the area that rests against the wrist. In the centre, you will notice an area that feels different, usually more rounded or defined. That is where the sensors are located. The watch uses them for certain measurements, such as heart rate and other health features, depending on the model.

This part must be in contact with the skin. If the watch is too loose, if it moves too much, or if the back does not touch the wrist properly, some readings may be less reliable.

There is no need to tighten the watch as if it were a medieval torture device. It should be firm, but comfortable. It needs to stay in place without dancing around on your wrist.

The Digital Crown

The Digital Crown is one of the most important parts of the Apple Watch. It is a small wheel or crown located on one side of the watch. It can be pressed and it can also be turned. With your finger, look on one side of the watch for a rounded piece that sticks out slightly. That is the Digital Crown.

The Digital Crown is used for several things, depending on the context:

  • Returning to the watch face.
  • Opening the app list or app view.
  • Scrolling through screens or lists.
  • Controlling certain settings.
  • Activating accessibility features with a triple-click, if configured.
  • We will use it many times throughout the course, so it is worth locating it properly from the beginning.

To identify it, remember:

  • It is round.
  • It sticks out.
  • It can be turned.
  • It can be pressed.
  • Do not confuse it with the side button. The Digital Crown feels like a wheel. The side button does not turn.

The side button

Very close to the Digital Crown, you will find another physical control. This is the side button. It usually does not stick out as much as the crown and has a more elongated or flat shape. It can be pressed, but it does not turn.

The side button is used for different functions depending on the model and system version. It may provide access to quick options, system features, Apple Pay with a double press, Emergency SOS if held down, and other behaviours depending on configuration. For now, we are not going to use it. The only thing that matters is knowing where it is.

The main difference is this:

  • The Digital Crown is the wheel.
  • The side button is the elongated button.
  • The Digital Crown can be turned.
  • The side button cannot be turned.

This difference seems simple, but it is fundamental. If someone confuses both controls, they may open a feature they did not intend to open, activate an unexpected option, or begin that small festival of panic that starts with “I think I touched something.”

Watch orientation

The Apple Watch can be worn on the left wrist or on the right wrist. In addition, the orientation of the Digital Crown can be configured so that it is on one side or the other. This means there is not one single mandatory position for everyone. Even so, when starting out, it is useful to choose a simple orientation. If you are right-handed, many people prefer to wear the watch on the left wrist and operate it with the right hand. If you are left-handed, it may be more comfortable to wear it on the right wrist and operate it with the left hand. But this depends on each person. The important thing is that you can touch the screen and locate the Digital Crown and side button comfortably.

When the watch is on your wrist, you should be able to do these three things:

  • Touch the screen with the other hand.
  • Locate the Digital Crown.
  • Locate the side button.
  • If an orientation feels uncomfortable, it can be changed later from settings.

Strap slots

At the top and bottom of the body of the watch, there are two areas where the strap is inserted. Depending on the strap model, it slides into slots until it locks into place. You can usually feel when it is properly inserted. To remove a strap, there is usually a small release button on the back of the watch, near each slot. When pressed, the strap can slide out. Do not force the strap.

If it does not go in smoothly, you may be inserting it the wrong way round or it may not be aligned. Forcing small parts is a fairly popular human tradition, but it rarely improves technology.

The strap

The strap may come in two pieces or use a different system depending on the type. There are sport bands, straps with buckles, loop bands, braided bands, metal bands, and other designs. They are not all attached in the same way, but they all have the same purpose: to hold the watch on the wrist securely and comfortably.

When identifying the strap, pay attention to three things:

  • Which part attaches to the watch.
  • What closing system it uses.
  • How it allows you to adjust the pressure on the wrist.

If the strap has two pieces, one will usually be the part with the fastening system and the other the part with holes, magnets, hook-and-loop fastening, buckle, or equivalent system.

Not all straps are equally comfortable for a blind person. Some are easier to adjust by touch than others. A visually attractive strap can be quite uncomfortable if, every time you put it on, it feels as if you are solving a puzzle designed by someone with far too much faith in their fingers.

The charger

The Apple Watch charger is usually a cable with a circular magnetic base at one end. That circular base is the part where the back of the watch is placed for charging. The magnet helps the watch settle into the correct position.

To identify the charger:

  • Find the circular end.
  • That disc will be the charging area.
  • The back of the Apple Watch should rest on that disc.
  • When you bring it close correctly, you will feel the magnet attract the watch.
  • There is no need to plug it in yet if we are not going to charge the watch, but it is useful to recognise it.
  • If the watch does not turn on or does not respond, later we will place it on the charger and wait.

Speaker and microphone

The Apple Watch also has a speaker and microphone. These are not always easy to identify by touch, because they are usually integrated into the body of the watch through small openings or slots. The speaker allows you to hear sounds, calls, Siri, and VoiceOver, depending on configuration. The microphone allows you to dictate messages, speak to Siri, answer calls, and use voice features.

There is no need to locate these openings precisely in order to start. It is enough to know that they exist and that it is not advisable to keep them covered all the time with your hand, clothing, or accessories.

What you should not do when handling it for the first time

  • Do not press buttons without knowing what you are touching.
  • Do not try to remove the strap by force.
  • Do not place sharp objects on the sensors.
  • Do not wet the watch before knowing which model you have and what resistance it offers.
  • Do not charge it with questionable adapters.
  • Do not pair it in a hurry if you do not know whether it is new or used.
  • Do not activate emergency features just to test them.

This last point is important. Emergency SOS and similar features will be explained later, but they are not practised as if they were a game. There is no need to call emergency services just to check that the button exists. Technology already gives us enough chances to embarrass ourselves without involving public services.

How to hold the watch in order to orient yourself

A practical way to orient yourself is this:

  • Place the watch in the palm of one hand.
  • Find the smooth side: that is the screen.
  • Turn it over and find the back with the sensors.
  • Locate the Digital Crown on one side.
  • Very close to the Digital Crown, locate the side button.
  • Find the slots at the top and bottom where the strap goes in.
  • Repeat this recognition several times until you can find each part without thinking too much.

This exercise is worth doing. If you physically recognise the watch well, it will be easier to follow the instructions later. The difference between using it in your hand and using it on your wrist When the watch is in your hand, you can turn it, touch it, and explore it more freely. When it is on your wrist, the orientation changes. The screen faces outward, the back touches the skin, and the side controls are on one side.

That is why it is advisable to do two recognition exercises:

  • First, with the watch in your hand.
  • Then, with the watch on your wrist.

When it is on your wrist, practise locating:

  • The screen.
  • The Digital Crown.
  • The side button.
  • The edge of the watch.
  • The strap fastening.
  • You do not need to turn it on for this.

What should be clear at the end of this module

At the end of this module, you should know:

  • Which part is the screen.
  • Which part is the back.
  • Where the sensors are.
  • Where the Digital Crown is.
  • Where the side button is.
  • Where the strap is attached.
  • How to identify the charger.
  • Which part of the watch touches the skin.
  • Which part faces outward.
  • Why orientation is important.
  • This is the physical foundation of the Apple Watch.

Practical advice

Before configuring the watch, spend a few minutes identifying it by touch. Do not rush to turn it on. If you know what you are touching from the beginning, it will be much easier to follow the course afterwards.

A person who cannot see needs to create a mental map of the device. That map is built with the fingers, not with an image. And the clearer that map is, the less you will depend on someone saying “press there”, a phrase about as useful as telling a cat to file a tax return.

Exercise for module 4

With the Apple Watch turned off, or without interacting with the screen, do this practice:

  • Hold the watch in your hand.
  • Locate the screen.
  • Turn it over and locate the back.
  • Touch the sensor area.
  • Find the Digital Crown.
  • Press the Digital Crown gently once, just to feel the movement, without holding it down.
  • Locate the side button.
  • Press the side button gently once, without holding it down.
  • Locate the strap slots.
  • Find the charger and identify the circular magnetic base.
  • Place the watch on a table and locate all the elements again.

Then, if the strap is already attached, put the watch on your wrist without tightening it too much and locate again:

  • Screen.
  • Digital Crown.
  • Side button.
  • Strap fastening.
  • When you can find all of this without too much hesitation, you will be ready to move on to the next module.

Summary of module 4

  • The Apple Watch has a smooth screen on the front.
  • The back contains the sensors and must touch the skin.
  • The Digital Crown is the wheel that can be turned and pressed.
  • The side button is near the Digital Crown and does not turn.
  • The strap is inserted into slots at the top and bottom of the watch.
  • The charger has a circular magnetic base.
  • The orientation of the watch can be adapted to each person’s wrist and preference.

Before configuring anything, it is useful to physically recognise the device.

Back to table of contents

Module 5. Attaching the strap and adjusting the watch on your wrist

Once you have physically identified the Apple Watch, the next step is to attach the strap and adjust the watch on your wrist. This step seems simple, but it is more important than it appears. The Apple Watch is not worn only to check the time. It can also record activity, heart rate, sleep, workouts, health alerts, and vibrations. For all of this to work properly, the watch must be correctly positioned. It is not about tightening it too much or wearing it too loosely. It is about finding a middle point: firm, comfortable, and stable.

Before attaching the strap

Before putting the Apple Watch on your wrist, it is useful to check three things:

  • That the strap is properly attached to the watch.
  • That you know where the Digital Crown is.
  • That you know which part of the watch must touch the skin.

Remember:

  • The screen must face outward.
  • The back, where the sensors are located, must be in contact with the skin.
  • The Digital Crown and side button must be in a comfortable position so that you can locate them.

How the strap attaches to the Apple Watch

The Apple Watch has two slots, one at the top and one at the bottom of the body of the watch. The strap is inserted by sliding it through those slots. Usually, when it is properly attached, you can feel that it has clicked into place and no longer slides freely. If the strap does not go in properly, do not force it.

Remove it carefully, check the orientation, and try again. Apple Watch straps are designed to slide in smoothly. If you need to use too much force, something is probably not aligned correctly.

On some straps, one piece corresponds to the top part and the other to the bottom part. On others, the system may be different. The important thing is that, once attached, the strap does not come out when you pull it gently.

Checking the strap

Before putting on the watch, do this check:

  • Hold the body of the Apple Watch with one hand.
  • With the other hand, gently pull one part of the strap.
  • Then gently pull the other part.
  • The strap should not come out.
  • If it moves or slides, remove it and attach it again.

Do not do this test with excessive force. The idea is to check that it is attached, not to rip it off as if you were opening a stuck door.

Putting the watch on your wrist

To put on the Apple Watch, first identify the back of the watch. That is the part that must touch the skin. Then place the watch on the top of the wrist, slightly above the wrist bone. It should not sit directly on the wrist bone, because it may move more, feel uncomfortable, or make some measurements harder. Ideally, it should sit slightly higher up, where it can rest better against the skin. The watch should feel stable. If the watch moves around too much when you move your wrist, it is too loose. If it leaves a strong mark, feels uncomfortable, or restricts circulation, it is too tight. It should be firm, but comfortable.

Correct adjustment

A correct adjustment allows the watch to stay in place during normal use.

To check this:

  • Put on the watch.
  • Move your wrist gently.
  • Turn your arm slightly.
  • Raise and lower your hand.
  • Touch the screen with your other hand.
  • Locate the Digital Crown.
  • Locate the side button.
  • If the watch moves too much, tighten the strap slightly.
  • If it feels uncomfortable, loosen it a little.
  • The key is for the sensors to maintain contact with the skin without the watch becoming uncomfortable.

Why adjustment matters

The adjustment of the Apple Watch affects several things:

  • Comfort throughout the day.
  • Sensor readings.
  • Workout recording.
  • Heart rate measurement.
  • Sleep tracking.
  • Receiving vibrations.
  • Ease of using VoiceOver.
  • If the watch is too loose, it may move and lose contact with the skin.
  • If it is too tight, it may become uncomfortable and you will end up taking it off.

A poorly positioned watch cannot be used properly. And if it is used for health or exercise, positioning becomes even more important.

Left wrist or right wrist

The Apple Watch can be worn on the left wrist or the right wrist. There is no single correct option. Many right-handed people prefer to wear it on the left wrist and operate it with the right hand. Many left-handed people prefer to wear it on the right wrist and operate it with the left hand. But this is not compulsory. The best wrist will be the one where the watch feels comfortable and where you can use it more safely.

The important thing is that you can:

  • Touch the screen with the other hand.
  • Locate the Digital Crown.
  • Locate the side button.
  • Feel the vibrations properly.
  • Wear it without discomfort.

If you are not sure which wrist to choose, start with the wrist opposite your dominant hand. If you are right-handed, try the left wrist. If you are left-handed, try the right wrist. You can change later.

Orientation of the Digital Crown

The Digital Crown can be oriented to one side or the other, depending on how the watch is configured. For example, if you wear the Apple Watch on your left wrist, you can have the Digital Crown on the right or on the left. If you wear it on your right wrist, you can also adapt the orientation. This is configured later from Apple Watch settings or from the Watch app on the iPhone. At the beginning, the most practical option is to place the watch so that the Digital Crown is easy to locate and press.

Try this:

  • Put on the watch.
  • With your other hand, find the Digital Crown.
  • Check whether you can reach it naturally.
  • Press it gently.
  • Turn it a little.
  • Find the side button.
  • If everything feels comfortable, that orientation may work for you.

If you have to twist your hand too much or you find it difficult to locate the controls, it may be worth changing the orientation later.

Wearing the watch for sleep

If you are going to use the Apple Watch to track sleep, you will also need to wear it at night. In that case, comfort matters even more. For sleeping, the watch should be firm, but not annoying. If it is too tight, it may be uncomfortable. If it is too loose, it may move during the night and record less accurately. You will also need to organise charging, because if you are wearing it at night, it will not be charging while you sleep.

Many people charge the watch before going to bed, when they get up, while showering, or at some point during the day. The routine will depend on the battery of the model and how you use it.

Wearing the watch for exercise

During exercise, the adjustment should be slightly firmer than during normal use, especially if you are going to walk quickly, run, do gym exercises, or move your arms a lot. If the watch moves too much during a workout, measurements may be less stable.

Before starting a workout, check:

  • That the watch does not move around on your wrist.
  • That the back is touching the skin properly.
  • That the strap is not uncomfortable.
  • That you can use the Digital Crown and side button.
  • That you can feel the vibrations properly.
  • After exercise, you can loosen the strap a little if needed.

Feeling the vibrations

The Apple Watch uses vibrations for alerts, notifications, alarms, timers, directions, and other warnings. For a blind person, these vibrations can be very useful. For a deafblind person or someone with hearing loss, they may be even more important. That is why it is useful to check that the watch is positioned in a way that allows you to feel the vibrations properly. If the watch is too loose, vibrations may be less noticeable. If it is too tight, it may be uncomfortable. When we configure sounds and vibrations later, it will be important to review this point again.

More practical straps

Not all straps are equally comfortable. To begin with, the most practical straps are usually those that allow good adjustment and can be put on easily by touch.

A good strap for a blind person should be:

  • Easy to put on.
  • Easy to take off.
  • Easy to adjust.
  • Comfortable for several hours.
  • Stable during exercise.
  • Suitable for sleeping if sleep tracking will be used.
  • Resistant to sweat if workouts will be done.
  • Easy to clean.

Some straps are very attractive, but not very practical. Others draw less attention and work better. On a device worn for many hours on the wrist, comfort should matter more than appearance.

Removing the watch

To remove the Apple Watch, first locate the strap fastening.

  • Loosen or open the strap carefully.
  • Remove the watch from the wrist without pulling abruptly.
  • Place it on a safe surface or on its charger.

This may seem obvious, but it is worth saying. The Apple Watch is small, smooth, and expensive enough for gravity to take a professional interest in it. Removing it carefully prevents drops, knocks, and unnecessary scares.

Taking care of the skin

Because the Apple Watch is worn directly against the skin, it is useful to pay attention to comfort and cleanliness. If you wear it all day, sweat, dust, soap, or moisture may build up on the watch or strap.

It is advisable to:

  • Clean the strap when needed.
  • Dry the watch after exercise or contact with water.
  • Avoid wearing it too tightly all day.
  • Let the skin breathe if irritation appears.
  • Use suitable straps if you have sensitive skin.

If the skin becomes red, irritated, or painful, remove the watch and review the adjustment, cleanliness, and strap material. If the irritation continues, seek medical advice.

The Apple Watch is useful, but it does not need to become a permanent bracelet of suffering. The wrist also deserves a minimum level of civilisation.

If the watch does not read correctly

If the Apple Watch does not record heart rate or activity properly, one possible cause may be poor placement.

Before assuming that the watch is faulty, check:

  • Whether the watch is too loose.
  • Whether the back is touching the skin.
  • Whether the strap moves during activity.
  • Whether the sensors are clean.
  • Whether the watch is placed too low on the wrist bone.
  • Whether the strap is too tight and uncomfortable.
  • Sometimes a small adjustment is enough to improve readings.
  • If the problem continues, it may depend on the model, sensor condition, skin contact, movement, type of exercise, or other factors.

Practical advice

Once the strap is attached and the watch is on your wrist, spend a few minutes locating the main physical elements again.

Do not assume that the orientation will feel the same on the wrist as it did in your hand. Practise with the watch on:

  • Locate the screen.
  • Locate the Digital Crown.
  • Locate the side button.
  • Touch the edges.
  • Check whether the strap feels secure.
  • Move your wrist and check that the watch does not slide around.
  • This will help you use it more confidently later.

Exercise for module 5

Do this practice before continuing:

  • Attach the strap to the Apple Watch.
  • Gently check that both parts of the strap are secure.
  • Put the watch on your wrist.
  • Adjust the strap so that it is firm but comfortable.
  • Move your wrist and check whether the watch stays in place.
  • Locate the screen.
  • Locate the Digital Crown.
  • Locate the side button.
  • Check whether you can feel the watch clearly on your wrist.
  • Try the watch on the other wrist if you are not sure which one is more comfortable.
  • Remove the watch carefully.
  • Put it on again.
  • Repeat the process until you can do it without difficulty.

Summary of module 5

  • The Apple Watch must be worn with the screen facing outward and the sensors against the skin.
  • The strap should be properly attached before putting the watch on.
  • The watch should sit slightly above the wrist bone.

It should be firm, but comfortable. If it is too loose, sensor readings and vibrations may be affected.

If it is too tight, it may be uncomfortable or irritate the skin.

  • The watch can be worn on the left or right wrist.
  • The orientation of the Digital Crown can be changed later.
  • The strap is important for comfort, exercise, sleep, and accessibility.

Before configuring the watch, it is useful to practise putting it on and removing it safely.

Back to table of contents

Module 6. Charging and turning on the Apple Watch

Before starting setup, it is useful to make sure that the Apple Watch has enough battery. A new Apple Watch may come with some charge, but not always. If it has been stored for a long time, it may be completely discharged. If it is second-hand, refurbished, or inherited, it may also have a low battery. For that reason, before pairing it with the iPhone, the most advisable thing is to connect it to the charger.

Identifying the charger

The Apple Watch charger usually has a circular magnetic base at one end. That circular base is the part that comes into contact with the back of the watch. The other end of the cable connects to a power adapter, a compatible USB port, or another suitable charger, depending on the cable included.

To identify the charger:

  • Find the circular end.
  • Touch the charging surface.
  • Check that the cable is properly connected to a power source.
  • Place the Apple Watch nearby.
  • The back of the watch, where the sensors are located, must rest on the circular base of the charger.

Placing the watch on the charger

To charge the Apple Watch:

  • Place the charger on a stable surface.
  • Hold the Apple Watch with the screen facing upward.
  • Find the back of the watch.
  • Bring the back close to the circular base of the charger.
  • Let the magnet pull it into place.
  • When the watch is positioned correctly, it usually aligns itself magnetically.
  • If it does not stay attached or moves away, lift it and place it again.
  • There is no need to press.
  • There is no need to force it into place.
  • The magnet helps position it correctly.

Checking whether it is charging

  • If the watch has some battery, it may make a sound, vibrate, or show charging information.
  • If VoiceOver were already active, it might speak, but on a new watch it will usually not be configured yet.
  • If the Apple Watch is completely discharged, it may take a few minutes before it shows clear signs of charging.

In that case, leave it on the charger and wait. Do not remove it every few seconds to check whether it is already responding. That habit does not make it charge faster; it only adds unnecessary drama to the table.

How long to leave it charging

To start setup, the Apple Watch does not need to be charged to one hundred per cent, but it does need to have enough battery. If you do not know how much battery it has, leave it charging for a while before starting. If the watch does not turn on, leave it connected to the charger for longer.

If after a considerable time it still shows no sign of life, you will need to check the cable, the adapter, the power socket, and the charger itself. It may also happen that a deeply discharged watch takes a little while to react.

Using a suitable charger
