It is advisable to use a compatible charger in good condition. Not all adapters or charging bases work in the same way. If the watch does not charge, first try another power socket or another compatible adapter before assuming that the watch is faulty. Avoid damaged chargers, cables that are excessively bent, poor-quality adapters, or unreliable charging bases.

An expensive watch connected to a suspicious charger is a combination that humanity still considers acceptable for reasons nobody has managed to justify properly.

Turning on the Apple Watch

To turn on the Apple Watch, locate the side button.

Remember:

  • The Digital Crown is the wheel.
  • The side button is near the Digital Crown, but it does not turn.

To turn on the watch:

  • Press and hold the side button.
  • Wait a few seconds.
  • Release it when the watch begins to turn on.
  • If the watch has battery, it should begin to start up.
  • If nothing happens, place it back on the charger and wait.
  • Do not confuse the side button with the Digital Crown. To turn on the Apple Watch, you use the side button.

What may happen when you turn it on

When turning on the Apple Watch for the first time, several things may happen:

  • It may show the Apple logo.
  • It may ask you to bring it close to the iPhone.
  • It may enter the setup process.
  • It may indicate that it needs charging.
  • It may not respond if it is discharged.
  • It may already be configured if it is used.
  • If it is a new watch, it will usually take you toward the initial setup.
  • If it is a used watch, it may be locked, linked to another account, or waiting to be erased.

If the watch was already configured

If the Apple Watch is not new and, when turned on, it shows a watch face, asks for a passcode, or seems to be configured, it means it has already been used.

In that case, do not start touching options without knowing what is going on.

  • It may be linked to another account.
  • It may have Activation Lock.
  • It may need to be unpaired from the previous iPhone.
  • It may contain another person’s data.

If the watch was yours and you are simply going to set it up again, we will see later how to unpair it, erase it, or change iPhone. If the watch belonged to someone else, it must be completely removed from their account before you can use it without problems.

If the watch does not turn on

If the Apple Watch does not turn on:

  • Check that it is properly placed on the charger.
  • Check that the charger is connected.
  • Try another power socket.
  • Try another compatible adapter.
  • Wait a few minutes.
  • Make sure you are pressing the side button, not the Digital Crown.
  • If it still does not respond, it may need more charging time or technical inspection.
  • It is not advisable to keep pressing random buttons.

It is also not advisable to hold down several controls without knowing what you are doing. Some combinations can restart or force processes that we do not need at this point.

When to charge it before pairing

It is advisable for the Apple Watch to have enough charge before starting pairing. During the process, it may need to update. An update can take time and requires battery. If the watch has too little charge, the process may stop or ask you to connect it to the charger. The most practical approach is to pair it while it is near the charger and with the iPhone also charged or connected.

Preparing the iPhone as well

Before continuing, the iPhone must also be ready.

Check:

  • That it has enough battery.
  • That Wi-Fi is enabled.
  • That Bluetooth is enabled.
  • That VoiceOver is working correctly.
  • That the Watch app is available.
  • That you are near the Apple Watch.
  • The Apple Watch and iPhone must be close to each other during setup.

Do not start the process with the watch in one room and the iPhone in another. It is sometimes difficult enough for two Apple devices to understand each other when they are together, let alone arranging a long-distance relationship for them. What to do if a message appears asking you to bring the iPhone closer If, when you turn on the Apple Watch, it displays an instruction to bring it close to the iPhone, place it near the phone. The iPhone may automatically show a prompt to set up the Apple Watch. If it does not appear, you can open the Watch app manually. We will see this in detail in the pairing module. For now, the important thing is that the watch is turned on, charged, and near the iPhone.

Do not start sensitive configurations yet

At this point, we are not going to configure health, Apple Pay, workouts, sleep, notifications, or emergency features yet.

First, we need:

  • Watch charged.
  • Watch turned on.
  • VoiceOver activated.
  • Pairing with the iPhone.
  • Basic settings completed.
  • After that, we will configure the rest in an orderly way.

Common mistakes when charging or turning on

Placing the watch the wrong way round on the charger.

Not resting the back properly on the circular base.

  • Using an incompatible charger.
  • Thinking the watch is faulty when it is only discharged.
  • Pressing the Digital Crown instead of the side button.
  • Removing it from the charger too soon.
  • Trying to configure it with very little battery.
  • Having the iPhone too far away.
  • Not checking Wi-Fi and Bluetooth.
  • Trying to use a second-hand watch that is locked.

Practical advice

Before pairing the Apple Watch, leave it charging for a while. While it charges, prepare the iPhone. Check Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, battery, and VoiceOver. Locate the Watch app. Make sure you know where the side button and Digital Crown are. When the watch has enough battery, you will be able to begin the process with fewer interruptions.

Exercise for module 6

  • Find the Apple Watch charger.
  • Identify the circular magnetic base.
  • Connect the charger to a power source.
  • Take the Apple Watch.
  • Locate the back of the watch.
  • Place that part on the circular base of the charger.
  • Check that the magnet holds it.
  • Leave it charging.
  • Then locate the side button.
  • Press and hold the side button until the watch tries to turn on.
  • If it does not turn on, place it back on the charger and wait.
  • Place the iPhone near the Apple Watch.
  • Check that the iPhone has Wi-Fi and Bluetooth enabled.
  • When the watch is turned on or charging correctly, you will have completed this module.

Summary of module 6

The Apple Watch is charged by resting the back on the circular magnetic base of the charger. If it is deeply discharged, it may take a few minutes to respond. To turn it on, press and hold the side button. The side button is not the Digital Crown. Before pairing it, it is advisable to have enough battery. The iPhone must also be charged, with Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, and VoiceOver working. If the watch is used, it may already be configured or locked to another account. It is not advisable to move forward by touching options without knowing what state the watch is in.

Back to table of contents

Module 7. Activating VoiceOver

The Apple Watch can be used with VoiceOver, Apple’s screen reader. VoiceOver allows the watch to speak the elements on the screen and lets you interact with them using gestures.

This is one of the most important modules in the course. Without VoiceOver, a blind person will not be able to use the Apple Watch independently. For that reason, it is useful to know the different ways to activate it.

VoiceOver can be activated in several ways:

  • During the initial setup of the Apple Watch.
  • From the Apple Watch itself.
  • From the Watch app on the iPhone.
  • Using Siri, if available and responding correctly.

Later, an accessibility shortcut can also be configured to turn VoiceOver on or off with a triple-click of the Digital Crown. The Digital Crown is the physical wheel on the watch. The side button is the elongated button located near that wheel. It is useful to understand this difference clearly before starting.

Activating VoiceOver during the initial setup

When the Apple Watch is new or has just been erased, it starts a setup process. At that moment, VoiceOver can be activated directly from the watch.

To do this:

  • Locate the Digital Crown.
  • Press the Digital Crown three times quickly.
  • Wait a few seconds.
  • If VoiceOver activates, the watch will start speaking.
  • The triple-click must be done on the Digital Crown, not on the side button.

If nothing happens, there may be several reasons:

  • The watch has not started correctly yet.
  • It does not have enough battery.
  • The side button was pressed instead of the Digital Crown.
  • The presses were not quick enough.
  • The watch is in a different state than expected.
  • If that happens, it is not a disaster. There are other ways to activate VoiceOver.

Activating VoiceOver from the Apple Watch

If the watch already allows you to enter Settings, you can activate VoiceOver from the Apple Watch itself.

The general path is:

  1. Settings.
  2. Accessibility.
  3. VoiceOver.
  4. Turn on VoiceOver.

With VoiceOver turned off, this path will not be independent for a blind person unless they receive sighted help or use another method. For that reason, in practice, for a first setup it is usually more useful to activate it with a triple-click of the Digital Crown or from the iPhone. Even so, it is important to know the path because it will be useful later for reviewing or changing settings.

Activating VoiceOver from the iPhone

This is usually a very practical method when the Apple Watch is already paired with the iPhone.

From the iPhone:

  • Open the Watch app.
  • Go to the My Watch tab.
  • Go to Accessibility.
  • Go to VoiceOver.
  • Turn on VoiceOver.

This option is especially useful if, for some reason, VoiceOver has been turned off on the watch and you cannot use it directly. It will also be useful for adjusting speech rate, voice, volume, and other settings, if they are available from the iPhone.

It is worth remembering that many Apple Watch settings are managed better from the Watch app on the iPhone. The watch is on the wrist, but much of the control lives on the iPhone. Modern technology: two devices to do what a wheel and a battery used to do, but with more possibilities, to be fair.

Activating VoiceOver with Siri

VoiceOver can also be activated using Siri, if Siri is available and responds correctly.

You can try saying:

  • Hey Siri, turn on VoiceOver.
  • Or, if Siri is invoked with a button or the Digital Crown, ask it to turn on VoiceOver.

This method can be convenient, but it is not always the most reliable during the initial setup. It depends on Siri being available, on the watch having a connection, and on the system being at a point where it can follow the command. Siri can help, but it should not be the only method you know.

Turning off VoiceOver

At certain moments, it may be necessary to turn off VoiceOver, for example if a sighted person is going to help you with a specific configuration.

It can be turned off from:

  • Apple Watch Settings.
  • The Watch app on the iPhone.
  • Siri.
  • The accessibility shortcut, if configured.

The Siri command would be:

  • Hey Siri, turn off VoiceOver.
  • If doing it from the iPhone:
  • Open the Watch app.
  • Go to My Watch.
  • Go to Accessibility.
  • Go to VoiceOver.
  • Turn off VoiceOver.
  • In this course, we will assume that VoiceOver should be turned on so that the blind person can follow the steps.

Configuring the accessibility shortcut

Later, we will dedicate a specific section to accessibility shortcuts, but it is useful to introduce the idea here. The Apple Watch can be configured so that a triple-click of the Digital Crown turns an accessibility feature, such as VoiceOver, on or off. This is useful because it allows you to quickly recover VoiceOver if it has been turned off, or temporarily turn it off if needed. But it must be configured correctly. If the triple-click is not configured for VoiceOver, it will not be useful for turning it on or off once the initial setup process has ended. For that reason, when we reach the recommended settings, one of the steps will be to review the accessibility shortcut.

First contact with VoiceOver on the Apple Watch

When VoiceOver is turned on, the watch speaks the elements that are touched or selected. Basic use is based on gestures similar to those on the iPhone, although adapted to a much smaller screen.

At first, the most important things to learn are these:

  • Touch an item to hear it.
  • Swipe right with one finger to move to the next item.
  • Swipe left with one finger to move to the previous item.
  • Double tap with one finger to activate the selected item.
  • Move your finger around the screen to explore.
  • Use the Digital Crown when scrolling or moving through lists is needed.

The Apple Watch screen is small. This means that exploring with your finger may require a little more precision than on the iPhone. Do not rush. On the watch, a badly performed gesture can open something else, go back, or leave you on a different screen. It is not serious, but at first it can be disorienting.

VoiceOver volume

If VoiceOver speaks too quietly, the volume will need to be checked.

The volume may depend on several factors:

  1. Watch volume.
  2. Silent mode.
  3. Audio output.
  4. VoiceOver settings.
  5. A noisy environment.

During the initial setup, if it is difficult to hear the watch, it is useful to bring it a little closer, find a quieter place, or configure the volume later from the Watch app on the iPhone.

Do not confuse silent mode with VoiceOver being muted. The Apple Watch may have sounds limited or silenced, but VoiceOver may still speak depending on configuration. Even so, if nothing is heard, several settings will need to be reviewed.

Speech rate

VoiceOver may speak too quickly or too slowly. For someone starting with the Apple Watch, it is advisable to use a moderate speech rate. Even if VoiceOver is used very quickly on the iPhone, it may be better to lower the speed at first on the watch. The screen is smaller, texts are usually shorter, and gestures require more precision. A voice that is too fast can make details easier to miss. The speed can be adjusted later.

VoiceOver voice

The Apple Watch can use system voices, depending on language and configuration. The available voice may depend on the language, region, and iPhone settings.

In a practical course, the important thing will not be choosing the perfect voice, but making sure that:

  • It is easy to understand.
  • It has adequate volume.
  • It does not speak too fast.
  • It allows you to follow menus without effort.
  • If you want to change it later, this will be done from the corresponding accessibility settings.

If VoiceOver does not activate

If you try to activate VoiceOver and it does not turn on, check:

  • That the Apple Watch has battery.
  • That it is turned on.
  • That you pressed the Digital Crown, not the side button.
  • That the triple-click was quick.
  • That the watch is in the setup process or already paired.
  • That you can activate it from the Watch app on the iPhone, if it is already paired.
  • That Siri is available, if you are going to try using voice.
  • If the watch is new and does not speak, first try the triple-click on the Digital Crown.
  • If it is already paired with the iPhone, try activating it from the Watch app.
  • If the watch is locked, used, or in another state, that problem may need to be solved first.

If VoiceOver speaks, but you do not know where you are

This can happen. The screen is small, and sometimes you enter an option unintentionally.

In that case:

  • Do not keep touching at random.
  • Listen to what VoiceOver says.
  • Swipe left or right to identify the elements.
  • Look for a Back, Cancel, or Close button if one appears.
  • Press the Digital Crown once to try to return to a main screen or the watch face, depending on the context.
  • If you are in the middle of the initial setup, listen to the options before activating anything.

The Digital Crown can be a way to regain orientation, but its behaviour depends on where you are. It is not advisable to press it repeatedly without knowing what is happening.

Common mistakes when activating VoiceOver

Pressing the side button instead of the Digital Crown.

  • Triple-clicking too slowly.
  • Thinking VoiceOver does not work when the watch is discharged.
  • Trying to configure the watch without preparing the iPhone.
  • Not hearing properly because the environment is noisy.
  • Touching the screen without waiting for VoiceOver to finish speaking.
  • Activating an option without listening to it completely.
  • Not knowing that VoiceOver can also be activated from the iPhone.
  • Not configuring the accessibility shortcut later.

Practical advice

The first time you activate VoiceOver on the Apple Watch, do not try to do too many things at once.

  • Turn it on.
  • Listen.
  • Touch the screen.
  • Swipe right and left.
  • Double tap on a simple item only when you know what it is.

The goal of this module is not to master the watch. It is to make the Apple Watch speak and begin to understand how it responds.

Exercise for module 7

  • Locate the Digital Crown.
  • Remember that it is the wheel that can be turned and pressed.
  • With the Apple Watch turned on, press the Digital Crown three times quickly.
  • Wait to hear whether VoiceOver activates.
  • If VoiceOver speaks, touch the screen gently.
  • Listen to what it says.
  • Swipe right with one finger.
  • Listen to the next item.
  • Swipe left with one finger.
  • Listen to the previous item.
  • Double tap only if you are on an option that you understand and want to activate.

If VoiceOver does not activate and the watch is already paired with the iPhone, open the Watch app on the iPhone and look for the VoiceOver option under Accessibility.

Summary of module 7

VoiceOver is the screen reader on the Apple Watch. It can be activated during the initial setup with a triple-click of the Digital Crown. It can also be activated from the watch Settings, from the Watch app on the iPhone, or with Siri. The Digital Crown is the physical wheel on the watch. The side button is not the Digital Crown. With VoiceOver, you touch to hear, swipe to move, and double tap to activate. The Apple Watch screen is small and requires precision. It is useful to configure the accessibility shortcut later. If VoiceOver does not speak, you need to check battery, power, volume, activation method, and pairing with the iPhone.

Back to table of contents

Module 8. First VoiceOver gestures on the Apple Watch

Once VoiceOver has been activated, it is useful to learn the basic gestures before moving on with setup and daily use. The Apple Watch is controlled through a combination of touch screen, Digital Crown, and side button. With VoiceOver turned on, the screen is not used in the same way as when VoiceOver is off. With VoiceOver, you first select or hear an item, and then you activate it with a double tap. This is very similar to the iPhone, but with one important difference: the Apple Watch screen is much smaller. That is why you need to get used to shorter gestures, more controlled movements, and more precise touch exploration.

Touching to hear

The most basic gesture is touching the screen with one finger. When you touch a point on the screen, VoiceOver says which item is in that area. This is used for exploration. For example, if you are on a screen with buttons, you can move your finger around the screen and VoiceOver will announce the items it finds. This gesture does not activate the item. It only selects it or reads it.

It is important to remember this:

  1. Touching does not activate.
  2. Touching is for listening.
  3. Double tap activates.

Exploring with your finger

You can move one finger around the screen to discover what is there. This method is useful when you want to get an idea of the layout of the screen.

On the Apple Watch, because the screen is small, this may be a little more delicate than on the iPhone. If you move your finger too quickly, you may pass over items without hearing them properly. The best approach is to move slowly and listen.

This is especially useful on:

  1. The watch face.
  2. Notifications.
  3. App screens.
  4. Settings.
  5. Lists.
  6. Buttons.

At first, exploration may feel a little awkward. That is normal. The watch screen is small, and your finger covers a larger part of it than on the iPhone. Human fingers were not designed by the same department that designs tiny screens, clearly.

Swiping right

Swiping right with one finger moves VoiceOver to the next item. This gesture is very important. It allows you to move through screen elements in order. For example, if you are on the watch face, swiping right may move through the available complications or elements. If you are in a settings screen, swiping right will move through the options. If you are in a list, swiping right will move to the next item. This gesture is useful when you do not want to explore by touch or when you want to move through everything in order.

Swiping left

Swiping left with one finger moves VoiceOver to the previous item. It is the opposite of swiping right. It is useful when you have gone past an item and want to return to it.

For example:

  • You swipe right and hear an option.
  • You swipe right again and realise that the previous option was the one you needed.
  • You swipe left to go back.
  • On the Apple Watch, swiping left and right will be used constantly.

The basic pair is:

  1. Swipe right to move forward.
  2. Swipe left to move back.

Double tap

The double tap activates the selected item.

It is the equivalent of pressing, opening, confirming, or choosing.

  • If VoiceOver says “Continue, button”, a double tap activates Continue.
  • If VoiceOver says “Back, button”, a double tap activates Back.
  • If VoiceOver says “Start, button”, a double tap activates Start.

The double tap is done with one finger, tapping twice quickly on the screen. You can do it anywhere on the screen, as long as the correct item is selected. This is important. With VoiceOver, selection is what matters.

Example:

  • You swipe until you hear “Continue, button”.
  • You double tap with one finger.
  • The Continue button is activated.

If you double tap without knowing what is selected, you may activate something you did not intend to activate. That is why it is useful to listen first.

Two-finger gesture to pause or resume speech

In many VoiceOver contexts, tapping with two fingers can pause or resume speech. On the Apple Watch, some gestures may depend on the context and the size of the screen, so it is best to use them carefully. To begin with, it is not essential to master this gesture.

The important gestures at the beginning are:

  1. Touch.
  2. Swipe right.
  3. Swipe left.
  4. Double tap.
  5. Digital Crown.

Basic use of the Digital Crown with VoiceOver

The Digital Crown can be used to scroll through lists or move through content. When you are in a long list, turning the Digital Crown can help you move up or down.

The exact behaviour will depend on the screen you are on.

  • In some situations, turning the Digital Crown scrolls the list.
  • In others, it changes values.
  • In others, it may move through options.

That is why, at first, it is better to turn it little by little and listen to what happens. Do not turn it quickly without knowing where you are. The watch may change item or scroll further than you expect.

Pressing the Digital Crown

Pressing the Digital Crown can be used to return to the watch face, open the app view, or leave certain contexts, depending on where you are. In many cases, it will be a way to regain orientation. But it should not be used as a universal gesture for everything. If you are on a screen and do not know what to do, listen first. Then look for Back, Close, or Cancel, if one appears. If you need to leave or return to a main screen, you can try pressing the Digital Crown once.

Pressing and holding the Digital Crown

Pressing and holding the Digital Crown can invoke Siri, depending on configuration. Do not do this if you do not want to speak to Siri.

The difference is important:

  • Pressing once is not the same as holding down.
  • Pressing three times is not the same as holding down.
  • The Digital Crown has several functions, and for that reason it is useful to use it precisely.

Side button

The side button also has important functions, but in this module we will not use it much. Depending on configuration and model, it can be used for system options, Apple Pay with a double press, or Emergency SOS if held down. Because some of its functions can be sensitive, it is better not to experiment with it at random. It will be explained in detail later.

Small and controlled gestures

The Apple Watch screen requires more precision. On the iPhone, a swipe can be wider. On the watch, gestures should be smaller and more controlled.

Recommendations:

  • Do not hit the screen.
  • Do not make gestures that are too long.
  • Do not swipe with too much force.
  • Do not cover the entire screen with several fingers.
  • Do not rush the double tap.
  • Wait for VoiceOver to speak before acting.
  • At first, speed is less important than control.

It is better to go slowly and know what you are doing than to move quickly and end up in a menu that appears to have been designed by a squirrel with a keyboard.

Back, Cancel, and Close

On many screens, you will find buttons such as Back, Cancel, Close, or Done. These buttons are important because they allow you to leave a screen without making unwanted changes. With VoiceOver, you can find them by swiping left or right, or by exploring the screen with your finger.

If you are in a screen and do not want to continue:

  • Look for Back.
  • Look for Cancel.
  • Look for Close.
  • Look for Done if the action has already been completed.
  • Not every screen has the same button. The label depends on the app, system version, and context.
  • When in doubt, listen carefully before activating.

Using lists

Many Apple Watch screens are lists. In a list, you can move by swiping right or left, or by turning the Digital Crown to scroll. If the list is long, not all items may be visible or accessible immediately. Turning the Digital Crown may bring more options into view. When VoiceOver cannot find more items, try scrolling the list with the Digital Crown.

Switches

  • Many settings appear as switches.
  • A switch can be on or off.
  • VoiceOver usually announces the state.

For example:

  • VoiceOver, on.
  • VoiceOver, off.

To change the state of a switch:

  • Select the switch.
  • Double tap.
  • Listen to whether it changes to on or off.
  • This will be important in accessibility, notifications, sound, health, and other settings.

Lists

Many Apple Watch screens are lists. In a list, you can move by swiping right or left, or by turning the Digital Crown to scroll. If the list is long, not all items may be visible or accessible immediately. Turning the Digital Crown may bring more options into view. When VoiceOver cannot find more items, try scrolling the list with the Digital Crown.

Text fields and dictation

Writing text on the Apple Watch can be less comfortable than on the iPhone. To reply to messages or enter information, you will often use dictation, quick replies, or option selection. When a text field appears, VoiceOver will announce it. Later, we will explain the methods for replying to messages and using dictation.

At this point, the only thing that matters is knowing that the Apple Watch is not the ideal device for writing long texts. For that, the iPhone is still better.

Listen before acting

This rule applies throughout the course:

  1. Listen first.
  2. Activate afterwards.

On the Apple Watch, because of its size, it is easy to touch something unintentionally. VoiceOver helps avoid this precisely: first it selects and announces, then the item is activated with a double tap. If this sequence is respected, many errors are avoided.

Common gesture mistakes

Touching while thinking that this activates the item.

Double tapping without knowing what is selected.

  • Swiping too hard.
  • Moving the finger too quickly around the screen.
  • Confusing the Digital Crown and the side button.
  • Holding down a button unintentionally.
  • Pressing the Digital Crown repeatedly out of nerves.
  • Not waiting for VoiceOver to finish speaking.
  • Not using the Watch app on the iPhone when a setting becomes complicated.

Practical advice

During the first few days, use the Apple Watch slowly. Do not try to handle it at the same speed as the iPhone. The watch requires its own learning process. It is smaller, has less space, and combines a touch screen with physical controls. Once the basic gestures are mastered, everything will feel more natural.

Exercise for module 8

With VoiceOver turned on, do this practice:

  • Touch the screen with one finger.
  • Listen to what VoiceOver says.
  • Swipe one finger to the right.
  • Listen to the next item.
  • Swipe one finger to the left.
  • Listen to the previous item.
  • Move your finger slowly around the screen.
  • Check how VoiceOver announces items.
  • Find a simple button or item.
  • Do not activate it yet.
  • Listen to its full name.
  • Double tap only if you are sure you want to activate it.
  • Turn the Digital Crown gently.
  • Listen to whether something changes or whether the screen scrolls.
  • Press the Digital Crown once and observe what happens.
  • Repeat these gestures until they become familiar.

Summary of module 8

With VoiceOver, touching is used to listen. Double tap is used to activate. Swiping right moves to the next item. Swiping left moves to the previous item. Moving your finger around the screen allows you to explore. The Digital Crown can be used to scroll, return to the watch face, or open apps, depending on the context. The Apple Watch screen requires smaller and more controlled gestures than the iPhone. You should not activate anything without listening first. If you get lost, stop, listen, and look for a way back. The iPhone will be an important help for configuring many watch options.

Back to table of contents

Module 9. Pairing the Apple Watch with the iPhone

Once the Apple Watch is charged, turned on, and has VoiceOver activated or ready to be activated, it is time to pair it with the iPhone. Pairing means linking the Apple Watch with an iPhone so that both devices can work together. The watch will use the iPhone to configure itself, sync data, receive settings, install apps, manage notifications, and access many features. This step is required before you can start using the Apple Watch normally.

Before pairing

Before starting the process, check the following:

  • The iPhone is near the Apple Watch.
  • Bluetooth is enabled on the iPhone.
  • Wi-Fi is enabled on the iPhone.
  • The iPhone has enough battery.
  • The Apple Watch has enough battery or is on the charger.
  • VoiceOver is working correctly on the iPhone.
  • The Watch app is available on the iPhone.
  • The Apple Watch is turned on.

If the watch is new or has been erased, it should show a start screen or a screen asking you to bring it close to the iPhone. If the watch is used and already configured, it may ask for a passcode, show a watch face, or be locked to another account. In that case, you should not continue as if it were new. The state of the watch must be resolved first.

Bringing the Apple Watch close to the iPhone

Place the Apple Watch near the iPhone. If the iPhone detects the watch, a prompt to set up the Apple Watch may appear automatically. With VoiceOver on the iPhone, listen to the prompt. There will usually be a Continue button.

If that prompt appears:

  • Swipe until you hear the Continue button.
  • Double tap.
  • If no automatic prompt appears, that is not a problem. The process can also be started manually from the Watch app.

Starting pairing from the Watch app

On the iPhone:

  • Open the Watch app.
  • Find the My Watch tab, if you are not already there.
  • If no watch is paired, the app should offer to start setup.
  • Look for an option such as Start Pairing, Pair Apple Watch, Add Watch, or similar.
  • Activate that option with a double tap.

The exact wording may vary depending on the version of iOS and watchOS. The important thing is to find the option that lets you add or pair an Apple Watch.

Setting up for yourself or for a family member

During the process, the iPhone may ask whether you want to set up the Apple Watch for yourself or for a family member. In this course, we will follow the most common case:

Set Up for Myself. The option to set up for a family member may be useful in some cases, for example for someone who does not have their own iPhone or needs a managed setup. But it will not be the main route in this course.

To continue:

  • Find the Set Up for Myself option.
  • Double tap.

The pairing animation

The Apple Watch may show a special animation on the screen. The iPhone usually asks you to place that animation inside the camera viewfinder in order to pair both devices. For a sighted person, this can be simple. For a blind person, it may be less practical.

There are several possibilities:

  • You may be able to do it by following VoiceOver prompts and moving the iPhone over the watch.
  • Someone with sight may help you place the watch inside the viewfinder.
  • You may prefer to use manual pairing.

Manual pairing is a very important option for blind users, because it avoids relying on visually framing the animation.

Using manual pairing

If you do not want to, or cannot, use the camera to scan the Apple Watch animation, look on the iPhone for an option such as Pair Manually, Pair Apple Watch Manually, or similar. When you activate it, the process will change. The iPhone will ask you to select the Apple Watch or enter a code that appears on the watch. With VoiceOver activated on the Apple Watch, the watch should allow you to hear the necessary information.

The process may vary slightly, but the general idea is this:

  • On the iPhone, choose manual pairing.
  • On the Apple Watch, listen for or locate the watch name or code.
  • On the iPhone, select that Apple Watch or enter the requested code.
  • Confirm to continue.
  • This method may be more accessible than using the camera.

If the watch is not speaking yet, it may be necessary to activate VoiceOver with a triple-click of the Digital Crown before trying manual pairing.

If the manual option does not appear

If you cannot find the manual pairing option:

  • Swipe through the whole iPhone screen with VoiceOver.
  • Explore the bottom of the screen.
  • Look for buttons such as Pair Manually, Set Up Manually, or I Can’t Use the Camera.
  • If you still cannot find it, go back and enter the process again.
  • Do not press options at random. At this step, it is worth listening carefully to each button.

Choosing whether to set up as new or restore a backup

After pairing the Apple Watch, the iPhone may offer two paths:

  • Set Up as New Apple Watch.
  • Restore from Backup.

If this is your first Apple Watch, the usual choice will be:

  • Set Up as New Apple Watch.
  • If you already had a previous Apple Watch and want to recover settings, apps, and data, you can choose to restore a backup.

For a person starting from scratch, setting up as new is usually clearer. It avoids bringing over old settings that you may not know or need.

Accepting terms and conditions

During the process, terms and legal notices will appear. You will need to read or listen to what is necessary and accept in order to continue.

With VoiceOver on the iPhone:

  • Swipe to the Agree button.
  • Double tap.
  • A confirmation may appear.
  • If it does, confirm again.

Signing in or confirming the Apple Account

The process may ask you to confirm the Apple Account on the iPhone.

  • If the account is already signed in, you may only need to wait.
  • If it asks for the password, you will need to enter it.
  • If it asks for verification, follow the instructions on the iPhone.

This step is important for features such as iCloud, Find My, some apps, health data, and Activation Lock.

Apple Watch passcode

During setup, the iPhone may ask you to create a passcode for the Apple Watch. It is advisable to use a passcode. The passcode protects the watch and allows features such as Apple Pay to be used, if configured. You can choose a simple passcode or a longer one, depending on the available options. For a blind person, the important thing is that it should be a code that can be entered safely on the small screen. Do not use a code you will forget. Do not use one so simple that it protects almost nothing.

Once created, the watch will lock when it is removed from the wrist or when the system requires it. When you put it on, you will need to unlock it. Some settings allow the Apple Watch to be unlocked from the iPhone when both devices are nearby.

Configuring services and initial settings

During setup, several options may appear.

These may include:

  • Location Services.
  • Siri.
  • Analytics data.
  • Text size.
  • Passcode.
  • Activity.
  • Health.
  • Apple Pay.
  • App installation.
  • Automatic updates.
  • Not all of them need to be configured in depth at this point.

For a first setup, the recommendation is to move forward with the essentials and leave the more delicate settings for later, when you already know how to move around better.

For example:

  • You can configure the passcode.
  • You can enable Location Services if you want to use features such as outdoor workouts, maps, or Find My.
  • You can leave Apple Pay for later if you prefer to configure it more carefully.
  • You can install only the necessary apps and avoid filling the watch from the very beginning.

Activity and health

The process may ask for information related to activity and health, such as age, height, weight, mobility, goals, or preferences. These data help the Apple Watch calculate activity, workouts, and metrics. It is worth entering them carefully, because they may influence the results. If you do not have an exact piece of information at that moment, you can review it later from the Health app or from the corresponding settings.

Apple Pay

During setup, the iPhone may offer to add cards to Apple Pay. If you already use Apple Pay and want to configure it, you can do so. But if this is your first Apple Watch and you are still learning, it may be more practical to skip this step and configure it later. Apple Pay requires a passcode on the watch and may depend on your bank, card, and country. There is nothing wrong with leaving it for later.

Installing apps

The iPhone may offer to automatically install on the Apple Watch the compatible apps that you already have on the iPhone. To begin with, it may be better not to install everything. A watch full of apps from the first day can make navigation with VoiceOver more complicated. If an option appears to choose later or install manually, that may be a good decision. Later, you can install the apps that are actually useful.

Syncing

Once the initial options have been chosen, the Apple Watch will begin syncing. This process can take some time.

During syncing, the watch and the iPhone must remain close to each other.

  • Do not move the iPhone away.
  • Do not turn off the watch.
  • Do not close the process without a reason.

If the watch needs to update, the process may take longer. While it is syncing, you can leave both devices still and connected to power if necessary. When it finishes, the Apple Watch should be ready to start.

If a watchOS update appears

During setup, the iPhone may indicate that the Apple Watch needs to be updated.

In that case:

  • Make sure the Apple Watch is on the charger.
  • Make sure the iPhone has battery or is charging.
  • Keep both devices close together.
  • Use a stable Wi-Fi connection.
  • Accept the update if it is required to continue.
  • Do not interrupt the process.

Updates can take quite a while. This is one of those situations where the watch, despite being a watch, seems to have a rather flexible relationship with time.

If pairing fails

If the process fails, check:

  • That the Apple Watch is charged.
  • That the iPhone has Wi-Fi.
  • That the iPhone has Bluetooth.
  • That both devices are close together.
  • That the watch is not linked to another account.
  • That the iPhone is compatible.
  • That there is no pending update on the iPhone.
  • That the connection has not been interrupted.
  • You can close the Watch app and open it again.
  • You can restart the iPhone if necessary.
  • You can restart the Apple Watch if you know how to do it and it is not in the middle of an update.
  • Do not erase the watch or force restart it unnecessarily.

If Activation Lock appears

If the Apple Watch asks for someone else’s Apple Account, it is protected by Activation Lock. This happens when the watch is still associated with its previous owner’s account. In that case, erasing it is not enough. Restarting it is not enough. Trying to pair it again is not enough. The previous owner must remove it from their account. If you bought the watch used and cannot contact that person, you will have a significant problem. That is why it is essential to check this point before buying a second-hand Apple Watch.

First start after pairing

When pairing is complete, the Apple Watch should be ready to use.

  • A watch face may appear.
  • VoiceOver should be able to read items on the screen if it is activated.
  • From this moment on, the watch is associated with the iPhone.

Now you will be able to review settings, configure accessibility, adjust notifications, choose a watch face, configure health, workouts, and other features. But it is not advisable to do everything at once. The next step will be to review the first recommended settings.

Common mistakes during pairing

  • Trying to pair with low battery.
  • Having Bluetooth turned off.
  • Having unstable Wi-Fi.
  • Moving the iPhone away from the watch.
  • Not using manual pairing when the camera is difficult to use.
  • Buying a used watch with Activation Lock.
  • Installing all apps from the very beginning.
  • Setting up Apple Pay without yet understanding basic operation.
  • Not activating VoiceOver before needing it.
  • Accepting options without listening to what they say.
  • Interrupting an update.

Practical advice

For a first setup, it is advisable to choose the simplest path:

  • Set up for yourself.
  • Use manual pairing if the camera is not practical.
  • Set up as new if this is your first watch.
  • Create a passcode.
  • Skip Apple Pay if you prefer to do it later.
  • Do not automatically install all apps if you want a cleaner experience.
  • Leave health, workouts, notifications, and safety for later modules.
  • The goal of this module is not to make the watch perfect. It is to pair it correctly with the iPhone.

Exercise for module 9

Place the Apple Watch near the iPhone. Check that Wi-Fi and Bluetooth are enabled on the iPhone.

Open the Watch app if the automatic prompt does not appear.

  • Start Apple Watch setup.
  • Choose to set it up for yourself.
  • If you can use the camera, follow the indicated process.
  • If you cannot use the camera, look for the manual pairing option.
  • Set up the watch as new if this is your first Apple Watch.
  • Accept the necessary terms.
  • Create a passcode for the Apple Watch.
  • Decide whether you want to configure Apple Pay now or skip it.
  • Decide whether you want to install apps automatically or do it later.
  • Keep the watch and iPhone close together during syncing.
  • Wait for the process to finish.
  • When the watch is paired, check that VoiceOver speaks on the Apple Watch.

Summary of module 9

  • The Apple Watch must be paired with a compatible iPhone.
  • The iPhone needs Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, battery, and the Watch app.
  • The process may start automatically when the watch is brought close to the iPhone, or manually from the Watch app.

For a blind person, manual pairing may be more practical than using the camera. The usual choice will be Set Up for Myself. If this is the first watch, setting up as new is usually the clearest option. It is advisable to create a passcode. Apple Pay can be configured during the process or left for later. It is not necessary to install all apps from the first day. If Activation Lock appears, the watch is still associated with another account. When finished, the Apple Watch is paired with the iPhone and ready for the first settings.

Back to table of contents

Module 10. First recommended settings

After pairing the Apple Watch with the iPhone, it is useful to review some settings before starting to use it seriously. The goal is not to configure everything. That will come little by little. The goal now is to make the watch comfortable, accessible, and safe for a blind person who will use it with VoiceOver.

Many settings can be reviewed from the Apple Watch itself, but at the beginning it is usually more comfortable to do this from the iPhone, using the Watch app. The iPhone screen is larger, VoiceOver feels more familiar, and there is less risk of getting lost. In this module, we will work mainly from the iPhone.

Opening the Watch app

On the iPhone:

  • Open the Watch app.
  • Go to the My Watch tab.
  • Most options for the paired Apple Watch are managed from this tab.
  • From here, we will review the first recommended settings.

Checking VoiceOver

The first setting to review is VoiceOver.

On the iPhone:

  • Open the Watch app.
  • Go to My Watch.
  • Go to Accessibility.
  • Go to VoiceOver.
  • Check that VoiceOver is turned on.
  • If it is not, turn it on.
  • Within VoiceOver, several options may appear, depending on version and configuration.

Pay special attention to:

  • Speech rate.
  • Voice.
  • Volume.
  • Hints or verbosity, if available.
  • Screen Curtain, if available.
  • Feedback or related sounds, if available.

At first, it is advisable to use a moderate speech rate. Even if you listen to VoiceOver very quickly on the iPhone, on the Apple Watch it may be better to start a little more slowly. The screen is smaller and gestures require more precision.

Adjusting speech rate

Within the VoiceOver settings, look for the speech rate option. If it is too fast, lower it. If it is too slow, increase it a little. It does not need to be perfect right now. It only needs to be clear enough for you to understand what the watch is saying. Later, when you have more practice, you can increase it.

Checking volume

Volume is important. If VoiceOver is too quiet, the watch may be difficult to use. From the Watch app or from the watch settings, you can review the sound volume, depending on the available options. It is also useful to keep Silent Mode in mind. Silent Mode can affect watch sounds, although vibrations may still work. During the first few days, while you are learning, it may be useful to keep the volume at a level that lets you hear VoiceOver clearly. Later, you can adjust sounds and vibrations according to your preferences.

Configuring the accessibility shortcut

This setting is highly recommended. The accessibility shortcut allows you to turn an accessibility feature on or off by triple-clicking the Digital Crown.

To configure it:

  • Open the Watch app on the iPhone.
  • Go to My Watch.
  • Go to Accessibility.
  • Look for Accessibility Shortcut.
  • Select VoiceOver.
  • From that moment on, a triple-click of the Digital Crown should allow you to turn VoiceOver on or off.
  • This setting can help you out of trouble if VoiceOver is turned off or if you need to turn it on quickly.
  • It is worth testing it carefully.

Do not use it without thinking, because if VoiceOver is on and you triple-click, it may turn off. If that happens, triple-click again to turn it back on.

Checking watch orientation

It is important for the Apple Watch to know which wrist you wear it on and which side the Digital Crown is on. This affects screen orientation and the behaviour of some controls.

From the iPhone:

  • Open the Watch app.
  • Go to My Watch.
  • Go to General.
  • Look for Watch Orientation.
  • Select left wrist or right wrist.
  • Select the position of the Digital Crown.
  • The configuration must match the way you actually wear the watch.
  • If you wear the watch on your left wrist, indicate that.
  • If you wear it on your right wrist, indicate that.
  • Then choose whether the Digital Crown is on the left or on the right.
  • If this orientation is configured incorrectly, the watch may feel uncomfortable or confusing.

Checking the passcode

The passcode protects the Apple Watch.

From the Watch app:

  • Go to My Watch.
  • Go to Passcode.
  • Check that the passcode is enabled.
  • Options such as Unlock with iPhone may appear here.

The Unlock with iPhone option can be convenient. It allows the Apple Watch to unlock when you unlock the iPhone, as long as the watch is on your wrist and nearby. It is also useful to know that if you take the watch off, it will normally lock. This behaviour is important for security, especially if you use Apple Pay or personal data.

Checking sounds and vibrations

Vibrations are very important on the Apple Watch.

From the Watch app:

  • Go to My Watch.
  • Look for Sounds and Haptics.
  • Review alert volume.
  • Review Silent Mode.
  • Review haptic feedback.
  • If an option such as Prominent Haptic or Prominent Alerts appears, it may be useful to turn it on.
  • A stronger vibration can help you notice notifications, alarms, and timers more clearly.

For people who are deafblind or have hearing loss, this section will be especially important and will be discussed in more detail later. For now, leave vibrations at a level you can clearly feel.

Checking notifications

At the beginning, it is advisable not to receive too many notifications on the Apple Watch. If everything vibrates, everything makes sounds, and everything interrupts, the watch becomes a wristband of anxiety. Very modern, yes, but not very useful.

From the Watch app:

  • Go to My Watch.
  • Go to Notifications.
  • Review which apps can send alerts to the watch.
  • You can leave the important ones enabled and turn off the ones you do not need on your wrist.

To begin with, these are often useful:

  • Phone.
  • Messages.
  • Calendar.
  • Reminders.
  • Alarms or timers.
  • Activity.
  • Health.
  • Find My.
  • Communication apps that you actually use.
  • There is no need to enable everything.
  • You can adjust this later.

Checking Siri

Siri can be very useful on the Apple Watch. It allows you to start calls, create timers, set alarms, send messages, start workouts, and make quick queries.

From the Watch app:

  • Go to My Watch.
  • Look for Siri.
  • Review the available activation methods.
  • Options may appear such as Raise to Speak, Listen for “Siri” or “Hey Siri”, or Press Digital Crown.
  • The exact options may vary.
  • If you use Siri often, it is useful to keep at least one comfortable activation method enabled.
  • If you do not want accidental activations, review the options carefully.

Checking display and brightness

Although this course is intended for blind people, some display settings can influence the behaviour of the watch.

From the Watch app:

  • Go to My Watch.
  • Look for Display and Brightness.
  • Here you may find options such as brightness, text size, bold text, wake duration, or Wake on Wrist Raise.
  • For a totally blind person, brightness may not be a priority. But if there is some remaining vision, it may matter.

Wake on Wrist Raise can be useful for many people, but it can also activate the screen at unwanted moments. It can be adjusted according to preference.

Checking privacy and location

Some features need location:

  • Maps.
  • Weather.
  • Outdoor workouts.
  • Find My.
  • Emergency.
  • Safety features.
  • Location is mainly managed from the iPhone.

On the iPhone:

  • Go to Settings.
  • Privacy and Security.
  • Location Services.
  • Check that it is turned on if you want to use features that need it.

There is no need to review every app now, but it is useful to know that location affects several Apple Watch features.

Checking Find My

Find My allows you to locate devices and can help you find the iPhone or the Apple Watch. It is advisable to have Find My enabled in your Apple Account. This helps if you lose the device and also plays a role in Activation Lock. On the iPhone, this is reviewed in the Apple Account settings and in the Find My app. Later, there will be a specific module about finding the iPhone and other location features.

Configuring a simple watch face

After pairing, the Apple Watch will have a watch face. The watch face is the main screen of the watch. To begin with, it is advisable to use a simple watch face. There is no need to choose the most eye-catching one or the one with the most complications. A practical watch face for a blind person should allow useful information to be checked without being full of elements.

Useful complications may include:

  • Battery.
  • Activity.
  • Heart rate.
  • Weather.
  • Calendar.
  • Timer.
  • Workout.
  • Reminders.
  • At first, less is better.
  • An overloaded watch face forces you to move through too many elements with VoiceOver.
  • Later, we will explain how to change and customise watch faces.

Checking app installation

If many apps were installed during setup, that is not a problem, but it may be worth reviewing.

From the Watch app:

  • Go to My Watch.
  • Move down to the list of installed apps.
  • Review which apps are on the Apple Watch.
  • There is no need to remove anything now, but it is useful to know that they can be managed.
  • To begin with, the ideal approach is to keep the watch simple.

Checking activity

If you are going to use the Apple Watch to move, walk, or work out, it is useful to review activity settings. During the initial setup, it may have asked you for some data. If it did not, that information can be completed later. There will be several modules later dedicated to physical activity, workouts, and health. For now, it is enough to know that these data exist and should be configured accurately.

Checking health

The Apple Watch can record health data, but much of the management is done from the Health app on the iPhone. It is not necessary to configure everything now. Later, we will cover heart rate, sleep, ECG, blood oxygen, irregular rhythm, sleep apnoea, hypertension, medication, and other areas.

At this moment, the only important thing is to know that health data should be configured carefully and that some features depend on the model and country.

Checking emergency and contacts

The Apple Watch can use Medical ID and emergency contacts. You do not need to configure everything now if you do not have the information ready, but it is useful to know that it is important.

Later, we will explain:

  • Medical ID.
  • Emergency contacts.
  • Emergency SOS.
  • Fall Detection.
  • Important alerts.
  • These settings can be very useful, but they must be configured with a clear understanding of what they do.
  • They should not be activated or tested lightly.

Recommended order for initial settings

To avoid confusion, the recommended order is this:

  • VoiceOver.
  • Speech rate.
  • Volume.
  • Accessibility shortcut.
  • Watch orientation.
  • Passcode.
  • Sounds and haptics.
  • Basic notifications.
  • Siri.
  • Simple watch face.
  • Installed apps.
  • Find My.
  • After that, later modules will configure health, exercise, safety, and other features.

Common mistakes after pairing

  • Leaving VoiceOver too fast.
  • Not configuring the accessibility shortcut.
  • Having the wrist orientation configured incorrectly.
  • Turning on too many notifications.
  • Installing too many apps.
  • Not reviewing vibrations.
  • Not configuring a passcode.
  • Starting with Apple Pay, advanced health, or workouts before mastering the basics.
  • Not distinguishing between watch settings and iPhone settings.

Practical advice

After pairing the Apple Watch, do not try to configure the whole thing in one session.

First, make the watch accessible and comfortable.

  • Then learn how to move around.
  • After that, configure notifications.
  • Later, move on to health, exercise, and safety.

An Apple Watch configured gradually and sensibly will be more useful than one packed with features turned on without any real plan.

Exercise for module 10

Open the Watch app on the iPhone.

  • Go to My Watch.
  • Go to Accessibility.
  • Check that VoiceOver is turned on.
  • Adjust the speech rate if necessary.
  • Configure the accessibility shortcut for VoiceOver.
  • Return to My Watch.
  • Go to General.
  • Review watch orientation.
  • Return to My Watch.
  • Go to Passcode.
  • Check that the passcode is enabled.
  • Return to My Watch.
  • Go to Sounds and Haptics.
  • Check that vibrations can be clearly felt.
  • Return to My Watch.
  • Go to Notifications.
  • Turn off the notifications you do not want to receive on your wrist.
  • Review Siri if you intend to use it.
  • Check that you have a simple watch face.

Summary of module 10

After pairing the Apple Watch, it is useful to review the first settings.

The most important thing is to check VoiceOver.

  • Speech rate should be comfortable.
  • The accessibility shortcut for VoiceOver is highly recommended.
  • Watch orientation must match the wrist and the real position of the Digital Crown.
  • The passcode protects the watch.
  • Vibrations must be easy to feel.
  • Notifications should be configured with moderation.
  • Siri can be very useful on the Apple Watch.
  • A simple watch face makes learning easier.
  • It is not necessary to configure every feature on the first day.

Back to table of contents

Module 11. The watch face

The watch face is the main screen of the Apple Watch. It is usually the first thing that appears when the watch is unlocked and ready to use. On a traditional watch, the face shows the time. On the Apple Watch, the watch face can show the time and also additional information such as activity, battery, calendar, weather, heart rate, workouts, reminders, alarms, timers, and many other functions. For a blind person who uses VoiceOver, the watch face is not looked at: it is listened to and explored.

That is why, when choosing a watch face, what matters is not so much whether it is visually attractive, but whether it is clear, simple, and useful with VoiceOver.

What a watch face is

The watch face is the main screen of the Apple Watch. From it, you can check the time, move through some quick information, and access certain features through complications. When you press the Digital Crown from many screens, you can usually return to the watch face. The watch face will therefore be a reference point. If you get lost, returning to the watch face can help you regain orientation. Not all watch faces are the same. Some are very simple and show little information. Others are full of data, colours, indicators, graphics, and complications. For someone starting with VoiceOver, it is advisable to use a simple watch face.

What complications are

Complications are small shortcuts or pieces of information placed on the watch face. The name may sound strange, and it is also rather ironic, because sometimes they really do complicate the watch face. But in watchmaking, that word is used to refer to additional information shown on a watch.

On the Apple Watch, a complication can show or open things such as:

  • Battery.
  • Activity.
  • Calendar.
  • Weather.
  • Timer.
  • Alarm.
  • Workout.
  • Heart rate.
  • Reminders.
  • Music.
  • Moon phase.
  • Stocks.
  • Maps.
  • Breathing or mindfulness.
  • Find My.
  • Many more, depending on installed apps.

With VoiceOver, as you move around the watch face, the watch will read the available elements. If there are many complications, you will have to move through more items. That is why, when starting out, fewer complications usually means more clarity.

Which complications may be useful

For a blind person starting with Apple Watch, these complications may be useful:

  • Battery.
  • Activity.
  • Weather.
  • Calendar.
  • Timer.
  • Workout.
  • Heart rate.
  • Reminders.
  • Find Devices or Find iPhone, if available as a shortcut.
  • There is no need to include them all.

A watch face with too many complications can become a long list that has to be explored every time. The ideal approach is to choose the ones that are actually checked every day.

A useful watch face could include:

  1. Time.
  2. Battery.
  3. Activity.
  4. Weather.
  5. Workout.
  6. Timer.
  7. Calendar.

Another person might prefer:

  • Time.
  • Heart rate.
  • Sleep.
  • Reminders.
  • Activity.
  • There is no perfect watch face for everyone.
  • A good watch face is the one that lets you quickly reach what you use.

How to explore the watch face with VoiceOver

With VoiceOver turned on, you can explore the watch face in two ways. First method: touching the screen. Place one finger on the screen. Move it gently. VoiceOver will announce the elements it finds. Second method: swiping. Swipe one finger to the right to move to the next item. Swipe one finger to the left to move to the previous item. This method is usually more orderly. If you want to know everything that is on your watch face, swipe right several times until you have moved through all the elements.

Listening to the time

To check the time with VoiceOver, you can touch the watch face or move through its elements until VoiceOver announces the time. Depending on the watch face, the time may or may not appear as the first element. If you want to check the time quickly, it is useful to use a watch face where the time is easy to find with VoiceOver.

You can also ask Siri:

  • What time is it?
  • Or simply raise your wrist and touch the screen if the watch is active.

Some people prefer to configure hourly vibrations, alerts, or discreet ways to check the time. That will be covered later in the modules on sounds, vibrations, and haptic feedback.

Changing watch face

The Apple Watch allows you to have several watch faces and switch between them.

There are two main ways to do this:

  • From the Apple Watch itself.
  • From the Watch app on the iPhone.
  • For someone starting out, it is usually more comfortable to manage watch faces from the iPhone.
  • It can also be done from the watch, but the small screen may be less comfortable at first.

Changing watch face from the Apple Watch

On the current watch face, with VoiceOver turned on, you can access options to change or edit the watch face. The gesture and behaviour may vary depending on the version of watchOS, but normally you can touch and hold the watch face to enter watch face selection or editing. With VoiceOver, if this gesture does not feel comfortable, it is better to do it from the iPhone. There is no point getting stuck trying to edit a watch face on the tiny screen if it can be done more clearly from the iPhone.

Changing watch face from the iPhone

From the iPhone:

  • Open the Watch app.
  • Go to Face Gallery.
  • Explore the available watch faces.
  • Choose a watch face.
  • Configure the complications.
  • Add it to the Apple Watch.
  • After that, from My Watch, you can review the watch faces you have installed.

This method is usually more comfortable with VoiceOver, because the iPhone screen makes it easier to move through the options.

What type of watch face to choose at first

To begin with, it is useful to choose a simple and functional watch face.

It should meet three conditions:

  • VoiceOver should read the information clearly.
  • It should not have too many elements.
  • It should allow useful complications to be placed.

There is no point choosing a very visual watch face with animations or complex designs if it does not offer anything practical with VoiceOver. It is also not advisable to start with a watch face full of complications. The recommended approach is to begin with a clear watch face, try it for a few days, and then adjust it.

Overloaded watch faces

Some watch faces allow many pieces of information to be shown at the same time. This may seem attractive, but with VoiceOver it can become heavy. Each complication is another item that VoiceOver may read. If the watch face has too many elements, checking something quickly may require more swipes.

A crowded watch face can be useful for a sighted person, because they can glance at several pieces of data at once. For a blind person, that visual advantage does not exist in the same way. With VoiceOver, information is received sequentially: one item after another. That is why it is worth choosing carefully.

Simple watch faces

A simple watch face makes learning easier.

At the beginning, a good configuration could include:

  • Time.
  • Battery.
  • Activity.
  • Weather.
  • Calendar or reminders.
  • Workout or timer.
  • That is already enough to get started.
  • Later, you can add heart rate, sleep, alarms, music, or other functions according to your real use.

Health complications

If you are interested in health, you can consider complications such as:

  • Heart rate.
  • Sleep.
  • Medications, if available.
  • Activity.
  • Blood oxygen, if the model and country allow it.
  • ECG, if the model and country allow it.
  • Mindfulness.

There is no need to have all of them on the watch face. Some features are better checked from the Health app on the iPhone.

Exercise complications

If you are going to use the watch for workouts, it can be useful to have quick access to:

  • Workout.
  • Activity.
  • Heart rate.
  • Timer.
  • Stopwatch.
  • Weather.
  • This allows you to start workouts and review activity with fewer steps.

Daily use complications

For everyday use, these may be useful:

  • Calendar.
  • Reminders.
  • Timer.
  • Alarm.
  • Battery.
  • Weather.
  • Messages.
  • Phone.
  • Find iPhone or Find Devices, if available.
  • The key is to choose what you actually use.

Customising a watch face

Customising a watch face means changing elements such as:

  • Colour.
  • Style.
  • Numerals.
  • Complications.
  • Layout.
  • Visible data.
  • Not all watch faces allow the same customisations.
  • Some offer only a few options.
  • Others allow many things to be changed.

For a blind person, colour will not usually be the most important thing, unless they have some remaining vision. The most important thing will be the information VoiceOver can read and the shortcuts that are useful.

Editing complications

When you edit a watch face, you can choose which complication appears in each position. For example, a watch face may have one complication at the top, another at the bottom, another on the left, and another on the right. With VoiceOver, the iPhone is usually more comfortable for editing these positions. From the Watch app, you can select a watch face and review each available area. In each area, you choose which complication you want to place. Then you save or add the watch face.

Testing a watch face

After configuring a watch face, it is useful to test it on the watch.

With the Apple Watch on your wrist:

  • Return to the watch face.
  • Swipe right to move through the elements.
  • Listen to what VoiceOver says.
  • Check whether the time is easy to locate.
  • Check whether the complications are understandable.
  • Activate a simple complication, such as Timer or Workout, only if you know what you are opening.
  • Return to the watch face with the Digital Crown.
  • If the watch face feels confusing, change to a simpler one.

There is no need to insist on a watch face just because it is popular, attractive, or recommended by someone. If it is not comfortable with VoiceOver, it does not work for your use.

Having several watch faces

You can have several watch faces configured.

For example:

  • A simple watch face for daily use.
  • A watch face with Workout and Activity for exercise.
  • A more health-focused watch face.
  • A minimal watch face for sleep.
  • This can be useful, but it is not advisable to start with too many.
  • At the beginning, one or two well-configured watch faces are enough.
  • Later, when you master the watch, you can create several depending on context.

Watch face for sleep

If you are going to use the Apple Watch for sleep, you may want a simple watch face, with few elements and no unnecessary complications. At night, you do not need twenty shortcuts on your wrist. Time, alarm, sleep, or battery may be enough. In addition, Rest and Sleep modes may change the behaviour of the watch. This will be covered in the health and sleep section.

Watch face for exercise

For exercise, it may be useful to have a watch face with quick access to Workout, Activity, and heart rate. It may also be useful to have Timer or Stopwatch. The idea is that, before starting a walk or workout, you can start what you need with only a few gestures.

Watch face for daily use

For daily use, the most practical things are usually:

  • Time.
  • Battery.
  • Calendar.
  • Weather.
  • Reminders.
  • Timer.
  • Activity.
  • It depends on each person.
  • If you receive many calls, Phone may be useful.
  • If you use Messages a lot, you can add it.
  • If you use music or podcasts from the watch, that may also make sense.

Common mistakes with watch faces

Choosing a watch face that is too crowded.

  • Adding complications that are not used.
  • Constantly changing watch face without learning any of them properly.
  • Not checking how VoiceOver reads it.
  • Choosing by appearance rather than usefulness.
  • Not having battery visible if the watch is used a lot.
  • Not adding Workout if you exercise frequently.
  • Not checking whether complications open useful or confusing apps.
  • Forgetting that some complications depend on installed apps.

Practical advice

To begin with, configure one main watch face with only a few complications. Use that watch face for several days. Then modify only what you miss. Do not start with five watch faces and twenty complications. That looks like organisation, but it is often just disorder with attractive names.

Exercise for module 11

On the Apple Watch, return to the watch face by pressing the Digital Crown if necessary.

With VoiceOver turned on, touch the screen.

  • Listen to which item it announces.
  • Swipe right several times.
  • Listen to all the elements on the watch face.
  • Check whether the time is easy to find.
  • Check which complications appear.
  • Open the Watch app on the iPhone.
  • Go to Face Gallery.
  • Choose a simple watch face.
  • Configure only a few complications.
  • Add it to the Apple Watch.
  • Return to the watch.
  • Move through the new watch face with VoiceOver.
  • Decide whether it feels clear or whether you need to simplify it.

Summary of module 11

The watch face is the main screen of the Apple Watch. With VoiceOver, the watch face is listened to and explored. Complications show information or quick shortcuts. It is not advisable to fill the watch face with unnecessary complications. At the beginning, a simple watch face is better. The Watch app on the iPhone is usually more comfortable for choosing and editing watch faces. You can have several watch faces for different uses. A useful watch face should allow you to quickly check what you need. Visual appearance matters less than clarity with VoiceOver.

Back to table of contents

Module 12. Digital Crown, side button, and main gestures

The Apple Watch combines three ways of interaction:

  1. The touch screen.
  2. The Digital Crown.
  3. The side button.

For a blind person using VoiceOver, it is essential to understand what each of these elements does and when to use each one. The screen is used to explore, select, and activate items. The Digital Crown is used to return to the watch face, open the app view, scroll, change values, or activate shortcuts.

The side button gives access to certain system functions and may also be used for Apple Pay or Emergency SOS, depending on how it is pressed and configured.

The problem is not that there are many buttons. There are very few. The problem is that each one can do several things depending on whether it is pressed once, twice, three times, held down, or used inside a specific screen. A whole universe of gestures hiding in a watch, because apparently a simple button was not enough for civilisation.

The touch screen

The screen is the main surface for using the Apple Watch. With VoiceOver turned on, touching the screen allows you to hear what is under your finger. Swiping right or left moves between items. Double tapping activates the selected item. These gestures have already been introduced, but they are the foundation of using the watch.

The most important gestures are:

  • Touch to hear.
  • Swipe right to move to the next item.
  • Swipe left to move to the previous item.
  • Double tap to activate.
  • Move your finger around the screen to explore.
  • On the Apple Watch, these gestures must be smaller and more controlled than on the iPhone.

The Digital Crown

The Digital Crown is the round wheel on the side of the Apple Watch.

  • It can be pressed.
  • It can be turned.
  • It can be pressed quickly several times.
  • It can be held down.

This makes it one of the most important controls on the watch.

Pressing the Digital Crown once

Pressing the Digital Crown once usually takes you to the watch face or to the app view, depending on where you are. If you are inside an app, pressing the Digital Crown may return you to the watch face or to the app view. If you are on the watch face, pressing the Digital Crown may open the app view.

The exact behaviour may vary depending on watchOS version and the screen you are on, but the Digital Crown is generally a way to return to a main area. For a beginner, this is very useful. If you are lost, pressing the Digital Crown once can help you return to a more familiar place.

But it should not be pressed repeatedly out of panic. Pressing it again may open the app view or move you somewhere else. It is better to press once, listen to VoiceOver, and understand where you are.

Pressing the Digital Crown twice

Depending on the version of watchOS and configuration, pressing the Digital Crown twice may switch between recently used apps or perform another system action.

  • This behaviour can change with updates.
  • For a beginner, it is not necessary to use this gesture at first.
  • It is better to master the single press before using double presses.

Triple-clicking the Digital Crown

Triple-clicking the Digital Crown can activate the accessibility shortcut, if it has been configured. For this course, the recommended configuration is to set the accessibility shortcut to VoiceOver. That way, a triple-click of the Digital Crown can turn VoiceOver on or off. This can be very useful. But it can also be confusing if you do it unintentionally. If VoiceOver suddenly stops speaking after pressing the Digital Crown three times, you may have turned it off. In that case, triple-click the Digital Crown again to turn it back on. The triple-click must be quick. If the three presses are too slow, the watch may interpret them as separate actions.

Holding down the Digital Crown

Holding down the Digital Crown can activate Siri, depending on configuration. This is useful if you want to ask Siri to do something.

For example:

  • Set a timer for ten minutes.
  • Call a contact.
  • Start an outdoor walk.
  • Send a message.
  • What time is it?
  • But if you hold down the Digital Crown by mistake, Siri may open when you did not intend it.

If Siri appears and you do not want to use it, look for a way to cancel or press the Digital Crown again, depending on the context.

Turning the Digital Crown

Turning the Digital Crown is useful for scrolling through lists or moving through content. For example, in Settings or in a long list, turning the Digital Crown may move the list up or down. This can be more comfortable than swiping many times. When using VoiceOver, turning the Digital Crown can help move through items, scroll the screen, or change values, depending on the context. It is important to turn it gently. If you turn it too much, you may move quickly through a list and lose your place.

The Digital Crown during workouts

During workouts, the Digital Crown may be used together with other controls to pause, resume, or navigate workout screens, depending on the watchOS version and settings. This will be explained in the workout modules. For now, it is enough to know that the Digital Crown remains important during exercise.

The side button

The side button is the elongated physical button located near the Digital Crown.

  1. It does not turn.
  2. It can be pressed.
  3. It can be double-pressed.
  4. It can be held down.

Depending on configuration and watchOS version, it can open system options, display recent apps or Control Centre, activate Apple Pay, or start Emergency SOS if held down. Because some of these actions are sensitive, it is important not to press the side button randomly.

Pressing the side button once

Depending on the version of watchOS, pressing the side button once may open Control Centre, the Dock, recent apps, or another system area. Apple has changed some behaviours over time, so it is useful to listen carefully to what appears after pressing it.

For a beginner, the best approach is:

  • Press once.
  • Wait.
  • Listen to what VoiceOver says.
  • Do not continue pressing without knowing where you are.
  • If you end up somewhere unfamiliar, press the Digital Crown once to return to a main screen.

Double-pressing the side button

Double-pressing the side button is commonly used for Apple Pay, if Apple Pay is configured. This can be very useful when paying with the Apple Watch. But it should not be used casually during learning. If Apple Pay is not configured, it may do nothing or show a related message. If Apple Pay is configured, double-pressing the side button may prepare the card for payment. This will be explained in the Apple Pay and Wallet module.

Holding down the side button

Holding down the side button can show power or emergency options, and in some configurations it may start Emergency SOS.

  • This is sensitive.
  • Do not hold down the side button just to experiment.
  • Emergency SOS can contact emergency services, depending on configuration and region.

That is useful when needed, but it should not be triggered accidentally. This will be explained carefully in the safety module.

Difference between Digital Crown and side button

This difference must be clear:

  • The Digital Crown is round, sticks out, and turns.
  • The side button is elongated and does not turn.
  • The Digital Crown is used frequently for navigation.

The side button is used for system functions, Apple Pay, Control Centre or recent apps, and emergency options, depending on configuration. If you confuse them, the watch may do something you did not expect. That is why it is useful to practise locating both by touch.

Main gesture: touch and listen

With VoiceOver, the first rule is to touch and listen. Do not double tap until you know what is selected.

This applies to every part of the watch.
