  • If you touch the screen, VoiceOver announces the selected item.
  • If you swipe right or left, VoiceOver moves to another item.
  • If you double tap, the selected item is activated.

This structure avoids many mistakes.

Main gesture: swipe right and left

Swiping right moves to the next item. Swiping left moves to the previous item.

This is useful in:

  • Watch face.
  • Settings.
  • Notifications.
  • Apps.
  • Lists.
  • Messages.
  • Workout screens.
  • Menus.
  • On the Apple Watch, these gestures must be short and clear.
  • A long, exaggerated swipe is not necessary.

Main gesture: double tap

Double tap activates the selected item. Use it only when you have heard the item and know what it does.

For example:

  • If VoiceOver says “Timer, button”, double tap opens Timer.
  • If VoiceOver says “Back, button”, double tap goes back.
  • If VoiceOver says “Start, button”, double tap starts.
  • Double tap is one of the gestures you will use most.

Main gesture: explore by touch

Exploring by touch means moving your finger across the screen and listening to what VoiceOver finds. This is useful to understand the layout of a screen. It may be less orderly than swiping, but it can be faster when you know roughly where an element is. On the Apple Watch, because the screen is small, this method requires patience.

Main gesture: scroll

Some screens contain more information than what is visible at once.

To scroll, you may be able to:

  • Turn the Digital Crown.
  • Use VoiceOver gestures.
  • Move through items until the screen scrolls automatically.
  • The Digital Crown is often the easiest way to scroll on the Apple Watch.
  • If you cannot find an option, it may be further down the screen.
  • Try turning the Digital Crown gently.

Main gesture: go back

Many screens have a Back button. With VoiceOver, find it by swiping or exploring the screen. When VoiceOver says “Back, button”, double tap. If you cannot find Back, try pressing the Digital Crown once to return to a main area. Do not assume that pressing the side button is the way to go back. It usually is not.

Main gesture: close or cancel

Some screens show buttons such as:

  • Close.
  • Cancel.
  • Done.
  • Dismiss.
  • These buttons allow you to leave a screen or confirm a setting.
  • VoiceOver will read the label.
  • When in doubt, listen carefully.
  • Cancel usually exits without applying a change.
  • Done usually confirms or finishes.
  • Close usually closes a panel or view.

Using the Apple Watch with one hand

Most blind users will operate the Apple Watch using the hand opposite the wrist where the watch is worn.

For example:

  • Watch on left wrist, right hand controls the screen and buttons.
  • Watch on right wrist, left hand controls the screen and buttons.
  • The important thing is to choose the arrangement that gives you more control.
  • There is no universal rule.
  • Some people may prefer a specific orientation because it makes the Digital Crown easier to locate.
  • Others may prioritise comfort while walking, exercising, or sleeping.

Practising the physical controls

It is worth practising the physical controls without entering complicated areas.

Practise:

  • Finding the Digital Crown.
  • Pressing it once.
  • Turning it gently.
  • Finding the side button.
  • Pressing it once.
  • Distinguishing it from the Digital Crown.
  • Do not hold down the side button during this practice.
  • Do not double-press it if Apple Pay is configured.

The goal is to recognise the buttons, not to summon every feature Apple placed behind them, because apparently one small watch needed the emotional range of an aircraft cockpit.

What to do if you get lost

If you do not know where you are:

  • Stop touching.
  • Listen to VoiceOver.
  • Swipe left or right to identify the screen.
  • Look for Back, Close, Cancel, or Done.
  • Press the Digital Crown once if you need to return to a main area.
  • If nothing makes sense, go to the iPhone and check the Watch app if the setting can be managed there.
  • Do not keep pressing buttons out of frustration.
  • That usually makes things worse.

Common mistakes

Confusing the Digital Crown with the side button. Pressing the side button when trying to go back. Holding down the side button and opening emergency options unintentionally. Triple-clicking the Digital Crown without knowing that it controls the accessibility shortcut. Turning the Digital Crown too quickly. Double tapping without listening first. Trying to do everything from the watch instead of using the iPhone when it is easier.

Practical advice

The Digital Crown should become your main physical reference point. If you can locate it easily, you can orient yourself better. Once you know where the Digital Crown is, the side button is nearby. That gives you a tactile map of the side of the watch. Practise this several times during the first days.

Exercise for module 12

Put the Apple Watch on your wrist.

  • Locate the screen.
  • Locate the Digital Crown.
  • Turn the Digital Crown gently.
  • Press the Digital Crown once.
  • Listen to what happens.
  • Locate the side button.
  • Press it once.
  • Listen to what appears.
  • Press the Digital Crown once to return to a main screen if necessary.
  • Swipe right with one finger.
  • Swipe left with one finger.
  • Select a harmless item and double tap only if you know what it does.
  • Look for a Back, Close, or Done button in a simple screen.
  • Return to the watch face.
  • Repeat until the Digital Crown and side button are clearly differentiated.

Summary of module 12

The Apple Watch is controlled with the touch screen, Digital Crown, and side button. With VoiceOver, touching is used to hear and double tapping is used to activate. The Digital Crown is the round wheel that can be pressed and turned. Pressing the Digital Crown once usually helps return to a main area or open the app view. Triple-clicking the Digital Crown can activate the accessibility shortcut if configured. Holding down the Digital Crown can invoke Siri. The side button is elongated and does not turn. Double-pressing the side button can activate Apple Pay if configured. Holding down the side button may open emergency or power options. The Digital Crown and side button should not be confused. If you get lost, stop, listen, look for Back or Close, and use the Digital Crown carefully.

Back to table of contents

Module 13. Control Centre and quick settings

Control Centre on the Apple Watch brings together several quick settings that can be very useful in daily use. From there, you can check the battery, turn certain modes on or off, make the iPhone play a sound, control connections, activate Water Lock, use the flashlight, and access other features depending on the model, the version of watchOS, and the watch configuration.

For a blind person, Control Centre can become a very practical area, because it allows frequent actions to be handled without going into long menus.

What Control Centre is

Control Centre is a quick-access panel. It is not an app as such. It is a system screen where buttons and controls appear for common features.

It may include options such as:

  • Battery.
  • Silent Mode.
  • Do Not Disturb or Focus.
  • Find iPhone.
  • Wi-Fi.
  • Mobile data, if the model has Cellular.
  • Airplane Mode.
  • Water Lock.
  • Flashlight.
  • AirPlay or audio output.
  • Lock.
  • Other controls, depending on configuration.
  • The exact content may vary. Not all watches show the same buttons.

How to open Control Centre

In recent versions of watchOS, Control Centre can be opened by pressing the side button once from the watch face or from many screens. The side button is the elongated button located near the Digital Crown.

To open it:

  • Go to the watch face.
  • Locate the side button.
  • Press the side button once.
  • Wait for VoiceOver to announce the screen.
  • Explore by swiping right or left.

If, in your version of watchOS, the side button opens a different screen, listen to what VoiceOver says and check how your watch behaves. Apple has changed the way some controls are accessed in different versions, so it is worth checking on the device itself. Do not hold down the side button. A short press is not the same as holding it down. Holding it down may show power options, Medical ID, or emergency options, depending on configuration.

How to move around Control Centre

Once Control Centre is open, use VoiceOver as you would on other screens:

  • Swipe right to move forward.
  • Swipe left to move back.
  • Touch an item to hear it.
  • Double tap to activate the selected control.
  • Turn the Digital Crown if you need to move through more controls.
  • Some buttons turn a feature on or off.
  • Others open a screen with more information.
  • For example, the battery button may show the percentage and related options.
  • The Find iPhone button can make the phone play a sound.
  • The Focus button can open the available modes.
  • The Water Lock button can activate water lock.

Checking the battery

One of the most practical uses of Control Centre is checking the battery.

To do this:

  • Open Control Centre.
  • Swipe until you hear the battery percentage.
  • VoiceOver should announce the available charge.
  • In some cases, activating the battery button may open a screen with additional information.

It is useful to check the battery before leaving home, before working out, and before going to sleep if you are going to use sleep tracking. If the watch has low battery, some features may be limited.

Silent Mode

Silent Mode allows you to silence Apple Watch sounds. When it is enabled, the watch can still alert you with vibrations, depending on configuration.

This is useful in meetings, classes, public transport, medical appointments, theatres, or any place where you do not want the watch to make sounds.

To use it:

  • Open Control Centre.
  • Find the Silent Mode button.
  • VoiceOver will indicate whether it is on or off.
  • Double tap to change its state.

For a blind person, it is important to remember that Silent Mode does not necessarily mean that all alerts are lost. Vibrations may continue to work. Later, the difference between sounds, vibrations, and haptic feedback will be explained in detail.

Do Not Disturb and Focus modes

Focus modes allow interruptions to be reduced.

They may include options such as:

  • Do Not Disturb.
  • Personal.
  • Work.
  • Sleep.
  • Other custom modes.
  • From Control Centre, you can turn these modes on or review them.

To do this:

  • Open Control Centre.
  • Find Focus or Do Not Disturb.
  • Activate the mode you need.
  • When a Focus mode is enabled, some notifications may stop arriving or may arrive in a more limited way.

This can be very useful, but it can also create the classic situation of “nothing is alerting me”, when in reality the watch is simply obeying too well. If you are not receiving notifications, one of the first things to check will be whether a Focus mode is enabled.

Find iPhone

This is one of the most useful Apple Watch features. It allows you to make the iPhone play a sound from the watch when you cannot find it.

To use it:

  • Open Control Centre.
  • Find the button to make the iPhone play a sound.
  • VoiceOver may announce it as Ping iPhone, Find iPhone, play sound on iPhone, or a similar expression.
  • Double tap.
  • The iPhone will play a sound to help you find it.

This feature is especially practical at home, when the iPhone is under a cushion, inside a jacket, on a table nobody remembers using, or in any other absurd hiding place the phone has chosen with the usual human collaboration. If the iPhone does not play a sound, check that it is nearby, turned on, and connected to the watch.

Airplane Mode

Airplane Mode disables wireless connections. On the Apple Watch, it can affect Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, mobile data, and other communications, depending on configuration. It should not be enabled without a reason, because it may interrupt important features.

To check it:

  • Open Control Centre.
  • Find Airplane Mode.
  • VoiceOver will indicate whether it is on or off.
  • If it is on and you do not want to use it, double tap to turn it off.

If you notice that the watch is not receiving notifications, is not communicating well with the iPhone, or seems disconnected, check that Airplane Mode is not enabled.

Wi-Fi

The Apple Watch can connect to known Wi-Fi networks. A Wi-Fi-related button may appear in Control Centre. In normal use, the watch communicates mainly with the iPhone by Bluetooth when it is nearby. If the iPhone is not nearby, it can use a known Wi-Fi network for some features. It is not usually necessary to touch this setting constantly.

If something does not work, it can be reviewed, but for daily use the usual thing is to leave it configured and not keep going in and out of Wi-Fi every five minutes, as if the watch needed a connectivity therapy session.

Mobile data on Cellular models

If the Apple Watch is GPS plus Cellular, a mobile data button may appear. This button allows you to review or control the watch’s mobile connection. If the service is configured with your carrier, the watch can use mobile data when the iPhone is not nearby. Keep in mind that mobile data uses more battery. It can also depend on coverage, carrier, and plan. If your Apple Watch is not Cellular, this control will not appear.

Water Lock

Water Lock locks the screen to prevent accidental touches when the watch is wet or used in water. It is useful when swimming, showering if appropriate according to use and model, or when the screen may come into contact with water.

To activate it:

  • Open Control Centre.
  • Find Water Lock.
  • Double tap.
  • When Water Lock is enabled, the screen is locked against accidental touches.

To turn it off, you usually need to hold down or turn the Digital Crown, depending on the system version. The watch may make sounds to eject water from the speaker. Not all users will need this feature daily, but it is useful to know about it. If Water Lock is turned on by mistake, listen to VoiceOver instructions and use the Digital Crown to unlock it as the watch indicates.

Flashlight

The Apple Watch includes a flashlight feature.

For a totally blind person, it may seem of little use, but it can help in certain situations:

  • So another person can see you.
  • To illuminate something for another person.
  • For emergency situations.
  • To walk in dark spaces when accompanied.
  • To signal your presence.

From Control Centre:

  • Find Flashlight.
  • Double tap.
  • The Apple Watch screen will light up.
  • There may be different flashlight modes, depending on version.
  • To turn it off, look for the corresponding option or press the Digital Crown, depending on how the watch behaves.

Lock

On some models and configurations, a control to lock the watch may appear. The Apple Watch normally locks when you take it off your wrist. If you lock it manually, you will need to enter the passcode to use it again. It is not usually necessary to lock it constantly if it is already properly protected.

AirPlay or audio output

Control Centre may include options for selecting audio output. This can be useful if you listen to music, podcasts, calls, or content from the watch. It may allow you to choose Bluetooth headphones or other compatible devices. For people who use headphones with VoiceOver, it is useful to understand that audio output can affect where the sound is heard. If VoiceOver does not seem to be coming through the speaker, the audio may be going to headphones or another device.

Editing Control Centre

Some versions of watchOS allow the buttons in Control Centre to be reorganised or edited. If this option is available, it can be useful to place the controls you use most near the top.

For a blind person, it may be useful to have these controls accessible near the beginning:

  • Battery.
  • Find iPhone.
  • Silent Mode.
  • Focus.
  • Water Lock, if used.
  • Flashlight, if you want it close at hand.
  • There is no point filling Control Centre with shortcuts you do not use.
  • The goal is for important controls to be easy to find.

Which controls to learn first

To begin with, the most useful controls are:

  • Battery.
  • Silent Mode.
  • Find iPhone.
  • Focus or Do Not Disturb.
  • Airplane Mode.
  • Wi-Fi.
  • Water Lock.
  • Flashlight.
  • With that, you already cover a large part of daily use.
  • Other buttons can be explored later.

Using Control Centre carefully

Control Centre allows settings to be changed quickly.

That is convenient, but it can also cause confusion.

  • If you turn on Airplane Mode by mistake, you may lose connection.
  • If you turn on a Focus mode, notifications may stop arriving.
  • If you turn on Water Lock, the screen may become locked.
  • If you turn off Wi-Fi or mobile data, some features may stop working.

For that reason, before double tapping a button, listen carefully to what it is and whether it is on or off.

Common mistakes

Holding down the side button instead of pressing it once.

Not knowing how to leave Control Centre.

  • Turning on Airplane Mode by mistake.
  • Turning on Focus and then thinking notifications are failing.
  • Turning on Water Lock and not knowing how to unlock it.

Not checking the battery before leaving home. Not knowing how to use Find iPhone. Confusing Silent Mode with Do Not Disturb. Thinking Silent Mode removes all vibrations. Not listening to whether a button is on or off before touching it.

Practical advice

During the first few days, open Control Centre several times just to recognise it.

  • Do not activate buttons at random.
  • Move through the controls with VoiceOver.
  • Listen to their names.
  • Identify which ones are useful to you.

Practise three things especially:

  • Checking battery.
  • Turning Silent Mode on and off.
  • Making the iPhone play a sound.
  • These three features are used often and should be mastered early.

Exercise for module 13

  • Return to the Apple Watch face.
  • Press the side button once.
  • Wait for Control Centre to open.
  • Swipe right to move through the controls.
  • Find the battery percentage.
  • Listen to how much battery remains.
  • Find the Silent Mode button.
  • Listen to whether it is on or off.
  • Do not change it yet if you do not want to.
  • Find the button to make the iPhone play a sound.
  • Double tap if you want to test it.
  • Listen to whether the iPhone plays a sound.
  • Find Airplane Mode.
  • Check that it is off.
  • Find Focus or Do Not Disturb.
  • Check whether any mode is enabled.
  • Press the Digital Crown to return to the watch face.
  • Repeat the practice until you can open and close Control Centre without getting lost.

Summary of module 13

Control Centre brings together quick Apple Watch settings. In recent versions, it can be opened by pressing the side button once. From there, you can check battery, Silent Mode, Focus, Airplane Mode, Wi-Fi, mobile data, Water Lock, Flashlight, and Find iPhone. The content may vary depending on model and watchOS version. With VoiceOver, you move through it with swipes and activate items with a double tap. Find iPhone is one of the most practical features.

Silent Mode and Focus are not the same.

  • Airplane Mode can cut connections.
  • Water Lock locks the screen to prevent accidental touches.
  • It is useful to listen carefully to each control before activating it.

Back to table of contents

Module 14. Notifications

Notifications are one of the most commonly used features of the Apple Watch. The watch can alert you on your wrist when you receive a call, a message, an email, a reminder, a calendar appointment, an alarm, a health alert, an activity notification, or a notification from an app.

For a blind person, this can be very convenient. You do not need to take out the iPhone every time something arrives. The watch vibrates, VoiceOver can read the notification, and in some cases you can reply directly from your wrist. But notifications can also become annoying if they are not configured properly. An Apple Watch that vibrates for everything is not a help. It is a small interruption machine tied to your arm.

What notifications are

A notification is an alert sent by the system or by an app.

It can inform you about many things:

  • An incoming call.
  • A message.
  • An appointment.
  • A reminder.
  • An alarm.
  • A timer.
  • An email.
  • A health alert.
  • An activity achievement.
  • An app update.
  • A smart home alert.
  • A WhatsApp, Telegram, or other app message, if configured.
  • On the Apple Watch, notifications usually arrive through vibration, sound, or both, depending on settings.

When notifications arrive on the Apple Watch

Notification behaviour depends on several factors. In general, if the iPhone is locked and the Apple Watch is on your wrist, unlocked, and connected, many notifications can arrive on the watch. If you are using the iPhone, some notifications may appear on the iPhone instead of on the watch. This is normal. The system tries to avoid showing the same alert on both devices unnecessarily. That means that, sometimes, a notification you expected on the watch may appear only on the iPhone because the iPhone was active.

The Apple Watch must be on your wrist

For notifications to work properly, the Apple Watch usually needs to be on your wrist and unlocked. If you take it off, it may lock. If it is locked, notifications may not behave in the same way. This is related to wrist detection and security. If notifications are not arriving, one of the first things to check is whether the watch is properly placed on the wrist and unlocked.

Connection with the iPhone

The Apple Watch must be connected to the iPhone, to Wi-Fi, or to a mobile network if it is a Cellular model and the service is configured.

  • If the watch loses connection, some notifications may not arrive.
  • If you are at home and the iPhone is nearby, the watch normally connects to the iPhone by Bluetooth.
  • If the iPhone is not nearby, the watch may use a known Wi-Fi network.
  • If the watch is Cellular, it may use mobile data when available.
  • If none of these connections is available, notifications may be limited.

How to read a notification with VoiceOver

When a notification arrives, the Apple Watch may vibrate, sound, or both.

To read it:

  • Raise your wrist or touch the screen, depending on how your watch is configured.
  • Listen to what VoiceOver says.
  • Swipe right or left to move through the notification content.
  • If there are actions available, VoiceOver will announce them.
  • You may find options such as Reply, Dismiss, Open, Clear, or other buttons depending on the app.
  • If the notification is short, VoiceOver may read it directly.
  • If it is longer, you may need to move through it with gestures or open it.

Opening a notification

To open a notification:

  • Move to the notification with VoiceOver.
  • Double tap.
  • The corresponding app or notification detail may open.
  • From there, you may be able to read more information or perform actions.
  • Not all notifications behave the same way.
  • A message notification may allow you to reply.
  • A calendar notification may allow you to view the event.
  • A health notification may show important information.

A promotional notification may simply waste your time, because apparently even the wrist is now commercial real estate.

Replying from a notification

Some notifications allow a reply directly from the Apple Watch. This is common with messages and some communication apps.

The available methods may include:

  • Dictation.
  • Quick replies.
  • Emoji.
  • Keyboard, if available in your language and model.
  • Scribble, in some languages and regions.
  • Siri.
  • For a blind person, dictation and quick replies are usually the most practical options.
  • Before sending, it is important to listen to the dictated text if the system allows it.

Dictation works well in many cases, but not always. Background noise, similar names, accents, and long messages can cause errors. For important or delicate messages, it may be better to use the iPhone.

Dismissing a notification

If you do not want to respond or open a notification, you can dismiss it.

Look for a button such as:

  1. Dismiss.
  2. Close.
  3. Clear.
  4. Clear All.
  5. The exact label may vary.

With VoiceOver:

  • Swipe until you find the relevant button.
  • Double tap.
  • Do not dismiss notifications too quickly if they are important, especially health, safety, medication, or calendar alerts.

Notification Centre

Notifications can also be reviewed later from Notification Centre. On the Apple Watch, Notification Centre is accessed differently depending on the watchOS version and the screen you are on.

In many versions, it can be opened from the watch face by swiping down from the top of the screen. With VoiceOver, the gesture may require practice. If this is difficult, it may be easier to review some notifications from the iPhone. The important thing is to know that notifications do not always disappear immediately. Some can be reviewed later. However, if you clear them, they may no longer be available on the watch.

Configuring notifications from the iPhone

The main notification settings are reviewed from the Watch app on the iPhone.

On the iPhone:

  • Open the Watch app.
  • Go to My Watch.
  • Go to Notifications.
  • From there, you can review how notifications behave on the Apple Watch.
  • You may find system apps and apps installed on the iPhone.

For some apps, you may be able to choose between mirroring the iPhone settings or customising the notification behaviour for the Apple Watch.

Mirroring iPhone alerts

Some apps allow the Apple Watch to mirror the iPhone notification settings. This means that if notifications are enabled on the iPhone for that app, they will also be allowed on the Apple Watch according to the available configuration. This can be useful, but it can also create too many alerts. If everything that arrives on the iPhone also arrives on the watch, the watch may vibrate constantly. That is why it is useful to review app by app.

Customising notifications

Some Apple apps allow custom settings on the Apple Watch. For example, you may be able to decide whether the watch should show alerts, send them to Notification Centre, or turn them off. The exact options may vary depending on app and system version.

The general recommendation is:

  • Enable important notifications.
  • Limit useful but non-urgent notifications.
  • Disable unnecessary notifications.
  • Not every app deserves a place on your wrist.

Recommended notifications at the beginning

At the beginning, it is advisable to keep only the notifications that are truly useful.

For example:

  • Phone.
  • Messages.
  • Calendar.
  • Reminders.
  • Timers.
  • Alarms.
  • Health, if configured.
  • Activity, if used.
  • Medication, if used.
  • Find My, if used.
  • Important communication apps.

It may be better to disable or limit:

  • Games.
  • Shopping apps.
  • Constant promotions.
  • Social media apps that are not urgent.
  • News apps with too many alerts.
  • Apps that send repeated or low-value notifications.

The goal is for the Apple Watch to alert you when something matters, not every time an app decides it has discovered the meaning of existence.

Activity notifications

The Apple Watch can send activity-related notifications.

These may include:

  • Stand reminders.
  • Goal progress.
  • Daily achievements.
  • Weekly summaries.
  • Workout reminders.
  • Motivational alerts.
  • For some people, these notifications are useful.
  • For others, they may become annoying.
  • If you are starting to move more or want reminders, you may keep some enabled.
  • If they become too frequent, review them from the Watch app.

On the iPhone:

  • Open the Watch app.
  • Go to My Watch.
  • Go to Activity.
  • Review the available notifications.
  • The goal is to receive helpful reminders, not to be scolded by a circle.

Health notifications

Health notifications must be treated carefully.

Depending on the model, country, and configuration, the Apple Watch may alert you about:

  • High heart rate.
  • Low heart rate.
  • Irregular rhythm.
  • Cardio fitness.
  • Noise.
  • Medication.
  • Sleep.
  • Cycle tracking.
  • Fall Detection.
  • Other available health-related features.
  • These notifications can be important.
  • Do not disable them without understanding what they do.
  • But do not activate them blindly either.

A health notification should be configured based on your needs, your model, your country, and, where appropriate, guidance from healthcare professionals.

Notifications and privacy

Some notifications may contain personal information.

For example:

  • Messages.
  • Medical appointments.
  • Medication reminders.
  • Bank notifications.
  • Private reminders.
  • Health alerts.
  • If VoiceOver reads them aloud, other people nearby may hear them.
  • In public places, it may be advisable to use headphones or adjust notification privacy settings.

Apple Watch can be discreet through vibration, but VoiceOver speech is not discreet if it comes through the speaker in a quiet waiting room. Technology, always one step away from announcing your private life to strangers.

Silent Mode and notifications

Silent Mode prevents many watch sounds, but vibrations may still work. This is useful if you want the watch to alert you discreetly.

Silent Mode is not the same as Do Not Disturb or Focus.

  • Silent Mode controls sound.
  • Focus modes can filter or block notifications.
  • This distinction is important.
  • If the watch is in Silent Mode, you may still receive haptic alerts.
  • If a Focus mode is active, some notifications may not arrive at all.

Focus modes and notifications

Focus modes can affect notifications.

They may include:

  • Do Not Disturb.
  • Sleep.
  • Work.
  • Personal.
  • Exercise.
  • Driving, depending on country and configuration.
  • Custom modes.
  • If a Focus mode is active, some notifications may be silenced or blocked.
  • If you are not receiving alerts, check Control Centre and review whether a Focus mode is enabled.
  • Focus can be very useful, but if configured badly, it may hide important alerts.
  • For example, if Sleep Focus is active, the watch may behave differently at night.
  • If Do Not Disturb is active, many notifications may not interrupt you.
  • If a custom Focus is active, it may allow only certain people or apps.

Notifications from messaging apps

Apps such as Messages usually work well with Apple Watch. Other messaging apps may offer more limited behaviour.

Depending on the app, you may be able to:

  • Read the message.
  • Reply from the notification.
  • Open the app.
  • Send a quick reply.
  • Use dictation.
  • Dismiss the notification.
  • Some apps may not have a full Apple Watch app but may still show notifications.
  • Others may allow replies only from the notification.
  • The experience depends on each app.
  • That is why it is useful to test the apps you actually use.

Mail notifications

Mail notifications can be useful, but they can also become overwhelming. If you receive many emails, having every email vibrate on your wrist may not be practical. You can review whether you want mail notifications on the watch or only on the iPhone. If you use email for important matters, you may allow selected notifications. If most emails are not urgent, it may be better to keep them away from the watch. A wrist is not an inbox, even if some apps seem determined to pretend otherwise.

Calendar and reminder notifications

Calendar and reminder notifications are usually useful. They can alert you about appointments, tasks, medication routines if configured through reminders, calls, meetings, or pending actions. For a blind person, receiving a vibration on the wrist before an appointment can be very practical. It is advisable to review that calendar and reminder notifications are enabled if you depend on them.

Alarm and timer notifications

Alarms and timers are very useful on the Apple Watch. When an alarm or timer goes off, the watch can vibrate and sound. This is especially useful when cooking, exercising, resting, or doing any task where you do not want to depend only on the iPhone. If vibrations are not strong enough, review Sounds and Haptics. If the alarm does not sound as expected, review Silent Mode, Focus, volume, and haptic settings.

What to do if notifications do not arrive

If notifications are not arriving on the Apple Watch, check:

  • The watch is on your wrist.
  • The watch is unlocked.
  • The watch is connected to the iPhone.
  • The iPhone is not actively showing that same notification.
  • Airplane Mode is not on.
  • No Focus mode is blocking notifications.
  • The app has notifications enabled on the iPhone.
  • The app is allowed in the Watch app.
  • The battery is not depleted.
  • The watch is not in Sleep mode blocking alerts.

Also remember that, if you are using the iPhone, some notifications may appear on the iPhone instead of on the Apple Watch.

Too many notifications arrive

If the watch vibrates too much:

  • Open the Watch app on the iPhone.
  • Go to My Watch.
  • Go to Notifications.
  • Disable unnecessary apps.
  • Review social networks.
  • Review news apps.
  • Review mail.
  • Review messaging groups.
  • Review Activity.
  • Review Focus modes.

A watch that vibrates every three minutes stops being a help and becomes an administrative insect tied to your wrist.

The watch does not vibrate

If the Apple Watch does not vibrate:

  • Review haptic feedback.
  • Review prominent haptics.
  • Review Silent Mode.
  • Review Focus.
  • Review notifications.
  • Check that the watch is properly adjusted.
  • Test with a timer.
  • Check that the strap is not too loose.
  • Vibration depends a lot on contact with the skin.

Alarms or timers do not sound

If an alarm or timer does not alert you:

  • Check volume.
  • Check haptic feedback.
  • Check Silent Mode.
  • Check whether you were wearing the watch.
  • Check battery.
  • Check that the alarm was enabled.
  • Check whether it was a one-time or repeated alarm.
  • Check whether Sleep mode changed the behaviour.
  • If you depend on an important alarm, test it beforehand.

Do not use an Apple Watch alarm for the first time on the day of an essential appointment. That is placing too much trust in a battery and too little in the history of human failure.

Notifications and people who are deafblind or have hearing loss

For people who are deafblind or have hearing loss, notifications must be configured with special care. It is not enough for the watch to vibrate. The person needs to know what that vibration means and what action to take.

It is useful to review:

  • Haptic intensity.
  • Prominent haptics.
  • Alarms.
  • Timers.
  • Medication.
  • Important contacts.
  • Emergency alerts.
  • Allowed notifications.
  • Focus modes.

For some people, the Apple Watch can be a useful tactile alert device. But if too many alerts arrive, or if they are not easy to interpret, it can become confusing.

Common mistakes with notifications

  • Turning on all notifications.
  • Not reviewing app by app.
  • Confusing Silent Mode with Do Not Disturb.
  • Forgetting that Focus modes can block alerts.
  • Not checking haptic feedback.
  • Not protecting privacy.
  • Expecting every notification to arrive on both iPhone and Apple Watch.
  • Not understanding that if the iPhone is active, some alerts may go there.
  • Leaving noisy apps enabled.
  • Disabling important health alerts without understanding them.

Practical advice

The best Apple Watch notification setup is usually not the one with the most alerts, but the one with the most useful alerts.

  • Start with the essentials.
  • Use the watch for what deserves your wrist.
  • Leave the rest on the iPhone.
  • If after a few days you miss something, enable it.
  • If something annoys you, disable it.
  • The Apple Watch should inform you, not train you to hate your own arm.

Exercise for module 14

On the iPhone, open the Watch app.

  • Go to My Watch.
  • Go to Notifications.
  • Review the apps that have notifications enabled.
  • Keep enabled only the ones you need on your wrist.
  • Check Phone.
  • Check Messages.
  • Check Calendar.
  • Check Reminders.
  • Check Timers and alarms if available.
  • Check Health if you use health alerts.
  • Disable at least one app that does not need to interrupt you on the watch.
  • On the Apple Watch, ask someone to send you a test message or create a test reminder.
  • When the notification arrives, listen to it with VoiceOver.
  • Swipe through its available actions.
  • If it allows a reply, try a short reply.
  • If you do not want to reply, look for Dismiss or Close.
  • Check whether the vibration is easy to feel.

Summary of module 14

Notifications are a central feature of the Apple Watch. They allow you to receive alerts on your wrist without taking out the iPhone. They can alert you through sound, vibration, or both. With VoiceOver, notifications can be read, explored, and in some cases answered. Not all apps allow the same actions. The main configuration is reviewed from the Watch app on the iPhone. It is advisable to enable only useful notifications. Silent Mode is not the same as Do Not Disturb. Focus modes can block or filter notifications. Health notifications should be configured carefully. If alerts do not arrive, check connection, lock status, Focus modes, permissions, and settings.

Back to table of contents

Module 15. Apps on the Apple Watch

The Apple Watch can run its own apps and also watch versions of some apps installed on the iPhone. This allows you to use quick functions from your wrist: timers, workouts, messages, calls, music, calendar, reminders, health, weather, maps, finding devices, and many others. But one idea should be clear from the beginning: not every app that exists for the Apple Watch deserves to be on the watch.

An app may be useful on the iPhone and uncomfortable on the Apple Watch. The screen is small, space is limited, and with VoiceOver each element is explored sequentially. That is why, on the watch, it is better to have a small number of apps, well chosen and easy to find.

What Apple Watch apps are

Apple Watch apps are applications adapted for the watch.

  • Some come installed with the system.
  • Others appear because you have the corresponding app on the iPhone.
  • Others can be installed from the App Store.
  • Some apps work quite independently.
  • Others depend on the iPhone.
  • Others serve only as a quick companion to a main app that lives on the iPhone.

For example, you can use the Apple Watch to start a workout, check a reminder, reply to a message, or control music. But it would not make much sense to try to do long tasks on the watch when they are better done on the iPhone.

Apps included on the Apple Watch

Depending on the model, watchOS version, and configuration, the Apple Watch may include apps such as:

  • Activity.
  • Workout.
  • Heart Rate.
  • Sleep.
  • Messages.
  • Phone.
  • Mail.
  • Calendar.
  • Reminders.
  • Timers.
  • Alarms.
  • Stopwatch.
  • Weather.
  • Maps.
  • Music.
  • Podcasts.
  • Wallet.
  • Find Devices.
  • Find People.
  • Settings.
  • App Store.
  • Noise.
  • Mindfulness.
  • Medications.
  • Health or health-related features, depending on version.
  • Not everyone will use all these apps.
  • The idea is to learn the important ones first and leave the rest for later.

Opening the app view

From the Apple Watch face, press the Digital Crown once. The Digital Crown is the physical wheel on the watch. When you press it from the watch face, the app view opens. With VoiceOver turned on, the watch will announce the selected item or the screen you are on. From there, you can move through the apps.

Grid View and List View

The Apple Watch can show apps in two main ways:

  • Grid View.
  • List View.
  • Grid View shows the icons arranged in a kind of panel.
  • List View shows the apps arranged in a list.
  • For a blind person using VoiceOver, List View is usually more comfortable.

The reason is simple: a list is explored in order. You swipe right or left, hear the name of each app, and activate the one you want. The grid may be more visual, but with VoiceOver it can be less clear, especially for someone starting out.

Changing to List View

You can change the app view from the Apple Watch or from the iPhone, depending on the system version.

From the Apple Watch:

  • Open Settings.
  • Look for App View or a similar option.
  • Choose List.

From the iPhone:

  • Open the Watch app.
  • Go to My Watch.
  • Look for App View or a similar option, if available.
  • Choose List.
  • The paths may vary depending on the version, but the goal is to show apps in list format.
  • If they are already in a list, there is no need to change anything.

Moving through the app list

Once you are in List View:

  • Press the Digital Crown from the watch face.
  • Listen to the name of the selected app.
  • Swipe right to move forward.
  • Swipe left to move back.
  • Turn the Digital Crown to scroll through the list if there are many apps.
  • When you hear the app you want to open, double tap.
  • To go back or exit, use the Digital Crown or look for a Back button, depending on the context.

Opening an app

To open an app:

  • Enter the app view.
  • Move to the app with VoiceOver.
  • Listen to the app name.
  • Double tap.
  • The app will open.

Once inside, use the usual VoiceOver gestures:

  • Swipe right.
  • Swipe left.
  • Touch to explore.
  • Double tap to activate.
  • Turn the Digital Crown if the app has lists or more content.
  • Each app behaves differently. Some are very simple. Others have more screens and options.

Leaving an app

To leave an app, you can usually press the Digital Crown. Depending on where you are, this may return you to the watch face or the app view. If the app has a Back or Close button, you can also use it. At the beginning, the Digital Crown will be your main way to return to a familiar place. Do not press it repeatedly without listening, because you may move between the watch face and the app view without understanding where you are.

Installing apps on the Apple Watch

Apps can be installed on the Apple Watch from the iPhone or from the App Store on the watch, depending on the app and system version. For most users, especially at the beginning, it is more comfortable to manage apps from the iPhone.

From the iPhone:

  • Open the Watch app.
  • Go to My Watch.
  • Move through the list of apps.
  • There you may find apps installed on the Apple Watch and apps available to install.
  • If an app has a watch version, it may appear in this section.
  • You can choose whether to install it on the Apple Watch.
  • Not every iPhone app has an Apple Watch version.
  • This is important. Having an app on the iPhone does not mean it will also exist on the watch.

Removing apps from the Apple Watch

If you have too many apps on the Apple Watch, you can remove the ones you do not use. This does not necessarily remove the app from the iPhone. In many cases, it only removes the Apple Watch version.

From the iPhone:

  • Open the Watch app.
  • Go to My Watch.
  • Find the app you want to review.
  • Enter its settings.
  • Turn off the option to show or install it on the Apple Watch, if available.
  • The exact wording may vary.
  • The idea is to keep only the apps that are useful on the wrist.
  • This can make the app list shorter and easier to use with VoiceOver.

Apps that are useful at the beginning

For a person starting with the Apple Watch, some apps are more useful than others.

A reasonable first group could be:

  • Phone.
  • Messages.
  • Timers.
  • Alarms.
  • Calendar.
  • Reminders.
  • Activity.
  • Workout.
  • Heart Rate.
  • Weather.
  • Find Devices.
  • Settings.
  • This does not mean that these are the only useful apps. It simply means that they cover many everyday situations.

Activity and health apps

The Apple Watch has several apps related to activity and health.

The most important ones may include:

  • Activity.
  • Workout.
  • Heart Rate.
  • Sleep.
  • Medications.
  • Mindfulness.
  • Noise.
  • ECG, if available on the model and in the country.
  • Blood Oxygen, if available on the model and in the country.
  • Other health-related features, depending on model, country, and watchOS version.
  • These apps will be explained later in the health and exercise modules.
  • For now, it is enough to know that they exist and that not all of them will appear on every Apple Watch.

Workout apps

For physical activity, the most important app is Workout.

From it, you can start activities such as:

  • Outdoor walk.
  • Indoor walk.
  • Outdoor run.
  • Indoor run.
  • Cycling.
  • Pool swim, if appropriate for the model and use.
  • Strength training.
  • Other available workouts.

Depending on your activity, other apps may also be useful, such as:

  • Activity, to review daily progress.
  • Heart Rate, to check your pulse.
  • Weather, before going out.
  • Maps, if you follow outdoor routes.
  • The Workout app will be one of the most important apps in the course.

Communication apps

The main communication apps are:

  • Phone.
  • Messages.
  • Mail.
  • Compatible messaging apps, depending on what you have installed.
  • With them, you can receive calls, reply to messages, or check alerts.
  • Not all of them allow the same actions from the watch.
  • Some only show notifications.
  • Others allow replies.
  • Others have their own app on the Apple Watch.

Daily use apps

Other apps may also be useful:

  • Calendar.
  • Reminders.
  • Weather.
  • Wallet.
  • Music.
  • Podcasts.
  • Maps.
  • Find Devices.
  • Home, if you use smart home devices.
  • Their usefulness depends on personal use.
  • There is no need to fill the watch with apps just because they exist.
  • The right question is not “what can I install?”, but “what do I need on my wrist?”

Apps that may not be comfortable

Some apps are not especially comfortable on the Apple Watch.

This may happen because:

  • They have too many elements.
  • They depend heavily on visual information.
  • They are not well adapted to VoiceOver.
  • They require too much writing.
  • They are slow.
  • They show little useful information.
  • They repeat something you already do better on the iPhone.
  • If an app is not comfortable, there is no obligation to use it on the watch.

The Apple Watch should be used for quick actions. If an app requires too many steps, it may be better to use the iPhone.

Organising apps

If you use List View, the order may be alphabetical or may depend on the system configuration. If you use Grid View, icons can be rearranged, but for VoiceOver this is usually less useful.

The most practical way to “organise” the watch for a blind person is not always to move apps around, but to remove or avoid installing the ones that are not used. A shorter list is easier to explore.

Complications as quick access to apps

Some apps can be placed as complications on the watch face. This allows you to open them without entering the app list.

For example, you can have a complication for:

  • Workout.
  • Timer.
  • Activity.
  • Heart Rate.
  • Calendar.
  • Weather.
  • Reminders.
  • This can be faster than looking for the app in the list.
  • But it is not advisable to fill the watch face with shortcuts. Choose only the most important ones.

Using Siri to open apps

You can also ask Siri to open an app.

For example:

  • Open Workout.
  • Open Timers.
  • Open Heart Rate.
  • Open Reminders.
  • This can be very convenient if Siri understands the command correctly.
  • To invoke Siri, use the method you have configured: voice, Digital Crown, or another available option.
  • Siri does not replace learning navigation, but it can save many steps.

What to do if an app does not appear

If an app does not appear on the Apple Watch:

  • Check whether it has an Apple Watch version.
  • Open the Watch app on the iPhone.
  • Review the list of available apps.
  • Check whether it is installed.
  • Check whether there are restrictions or pending updates.
  • Check whether the Apple Watch is updated.
  • Not every iPhone app has an Apple Watch version.
  • And even if an app has notifications on the watch, that does not necessarily mean it has a full Apple Watch app.

What to do if an app is not accessible

If an app does not work well with VoiceOver:

  • First try moving through it with swipes.
  • Explore with your finger.
  • Check whether it offers better options from the iPhone.
  • Check whether there are updates.
  • Consider whether you really need that app on the watch.
  • If it is not usable, it is not worth insisting too much.
  • On the Apple Watch, a poorly adapted app can be especially uncomfortable because of the size of the screen.

Common app mistakes

Installing too many apps from the first day. Using Grid View when it is more confusing. Not knowing that an app can be managed from the iPhone. Not removing apps that are not used. Thinking that every iPhone app has an Apple Watch version. Thinking that every notification means there is an app installed. Looking on the watch for something that is better configured on the iPhone. Putting too many complications on the watch face. Not using Siri to open frequent apps.

Practical advice

To begin with, keep the Apple Watch with only a few apps and learn the basic ones well.

A good first selection could be:

  • Phone.
  • Messages.
  • Timers.
  • Alarms.
  • Calendar.
  • Reminders.
  • Activity.
  • Workout.
  • Heart Rate.
  • Weather.
  • Find Devices.
  • Settings.
  • When you have mastered these apps, add others.
  • The watch should be practical, not a display case for icons.

Exercise for module 15

  • Return to the Apple Watch face.
  • Press the Digital Crown to open the app view.
  • Check whether you are in List View or Grid View.
  • If you are in Grid View and it feels confusing, change to List View from Settings or from the Watch app on the iPhone.
  • Move through the app list with swipes.
  • Find the Timers app.
  • Open it.
  • Press the Digital Crown to leave.
  • Return to the app list.
  • Find the Workout app.
  • There is no need to start any workout yet.
  • Press the Digital Crown to return.
  • Open the Watch app on the iPhone.
  • Review the apps installed on the Apple Watch.
  • Find an app you do not need.
  • Consider whether it should be removed from the watch.

Summary of module 15

The Apple Watch can use its own apps and companion apps from the iPhone. Not every iPhone app has an Apple Watch version. List View is usually more comfortable with VoiceOver than Grid View. Apps are opened from the app view, by pressing the Digital Crown from the watch face. Many apps are better managed from the Watch app on the iPhone. It is not advisable to install too many apps at the beginning. Complications can serve as quick shortcuts to important apps. Siri can open apps and save steps. A short app list makes the Apple Watch easier to use with VoiceOver.

Back to table of contents

Module 16. Calls

The Apple Watch can be used to receive and make phone calls from your wrist. This is one of the most practical features of the watch. It allows you to answer without taking out the iPhone, check who is calling, and have a quick conversation using the watch speaker and microphone or connected headphones.

For a blind person, it can be very convenient to feel the vibration on the wrist, hear who is calling with VoiceOver, and decide whether to answer, decline, or ignore the call.

When the Apple Watch can receive calls

The Apple Watch can receive calls in different situations. If you have an Apple Watch GPS, you will usually need the iPhone to be nearby or to have a connection that allows communication.

If you have an Apple Watch GPS plus Cellular with an active mobile plan, you can receive and make calls in more situations, even when the iPhone is not with you, provided there is coverage and the service is correctly configured.

In both cases, behaviour may depend on:

  • Apple Watch model.
  • Type of connection.
  • Mobile carrier.
  • Coverage.
  • iPhone settings.
  • Call settings.
  • Bluetooth and Wi-Fi status.

If the watch does not receive calls, do not automatically assume that something is wrong with it. First check connection, iPhone, carrier, Focus, Airplane Mode, and settings.

Receiving a call

When a call comes in, the Apple Watch may vibrate, ring, or both. VoiceOver may announce information about the call, such as the contact name or number, depending on whether it is saved in Contacts and on privacy settings. Options to answer or decline will appear on the screen.

With VoiceOver:

  • Touch the screen to listen.
  • Swipe right or left to move through the options.
  • Find Answer if you want to accept the call.
  • Double tap.
  • Find Decline if you do not want to answer.
  • Double tap.
  • Do not answer without listening to who is calling.
  • The wrist is practical, but it should not become an open door for every unknown number eager to sell something.

Answering a call

To answer:

  • Wait for VoiceOver to announce the call.
  • Find the Answer button.
  • Double tap.
  • The call will be answered from the Apple Watch.

You will be able to speak using the watch microphone and listen through the speaker, unless you have headphones connected or the audio is routed to another device. The Apple Watch speaker may be enough in a quiet place, but outdoors or in noisy environments it may be uncomfortable.

Using headphones

If you have Bluetooth headphones connected, the call may be heard through them. This can be better for privacy and clarity. It also prevents other people from hearing the conversation. For many blind people, using headphones with the Apple Watch can be practical, especially outdoors, on public transport, or in noisy places.

Declining a call

To decline a call:

  • Find the Decline button.
  • Double tap.
  • The call will end or be sent to voicemail, depending on your carrier and configuration.
  • You can also simply not answer.
  • If you use Focus modes or Silent Mode, you can reduce interruptions at specific times.

Silencing an incoming call

If a call comes in and you do not want to answer or decline immediately, you can silence the alert. Depending on configuration, it may be enough to cover the watch with your hand or use an on-screen option. This gesture may vary depending on settings, so it is worth testing it with a non-important call. It is not a good idea to practise with an urgent call, for fairly obvious reasons that someone would still probably need to read in a manual.

Making a call from the Apple Watch

There are several ways to make calls from the watch:

  • Using Siri.
  • From the Phone app.
  • From Contacts.
  • From a complication or recent contact, if configured.
  • From a notification or message.
  • The quickest way is usually Siri.

Calling with Siri

You can ask Siri:

  • Call Anna.
  • Call John mobile.
  • Call home.
  • Call emergency services, only if it is truly necessary.
  • To use Siri, use the method you have configured.

This may be:

  • Saying Siri or Hey Siri, if enabled.
  • Holding down the Digital Crown.
  • Raising your wrist and speaking, if that option is enabled.
  • Siri can be very useful, but you need to speak clearly and check that it has understood the correct contact.
  • If you have several contacts with similar names, Siri may ask for confirmation.

Calling from the Phone app

You can also make a call from the Phone app on the Apple Watch.

To do this:

  • Press the Digital Crown from the watch face.
  • Find Phone.
  • Double tap.

Inside Phone, options may appear such as:

  • Favourites.
  • Recents.
  • Contacts.
  • Keypad.
  • Voicemail, if available.
  • Choose the option you want.
  • With VoiceOver, Recents or Favourites may be more comfortable than searching through a long contact list.

Favourites

Favourites can be very useful on the Apple Watch. If you have frequent contacts, you can mark them as favourites from the iPhone so that they are easier to find. This avoids having to move through a huge contact list on the small screen. For someone who uses calls from the watch often, configuring favourites is a good idea.

Recents

  • The Recents option shows recent calls.
  • It can be useful for quickly returning a call.
  • Open Phone.
  • Find Recents.
  • Choose the contact or number.
  • Double tap to call.

Contacts

The contact list allows you to search or move through saved people. On the Apple Watch, it may be less comfortable if you have many contacts. For frequent calls, it is better to use Siri, Favourites, or Recents.

Keypad

The keypad allows you to dial a number manually. With VoiceOver on a small screen, this may be less comfortable. Use it only if you need to call a number you have not saved. For regular calls, save the contact on the iPhone.

Changing call audio

During a call, there may be options to change the audio output.

For example:

  • Apple Watch.
  • iPhone.
  • Headphones.
  • Speaker.
  • The options depend on the connected devices.
  • If a call is heard from an unexpected place, check the audio output.
  • Sometimes the sound may be going to Bluetooth headphones, to the iPhone, or to the watch itself.

Raising or lowering the volume during a call

During a call, you can adjust the volume. Depending on the context, the Digital Crown may be used to raise or lower the volume. Turn it slowly and listen to whether the volume changes. There may also be on-screen controls. Do not raise the volume to maximum unless necessary, especially if you are using headphones.

Ending a call

To end a call:

  • Find the End, Hang Up, or similar button.
  • Double tap.
  • The call will end.

Make sure you have ended the call before continuing to talk about it, because human history is full of awkward endings caused by badly pressed buttons.

Calls with a GPS model

If your Apple Watch is GPS only, it will usually depend on the iPhone for making and receiving calls outside the home or away from Wi-Fi. If the iPhone is nearby, there should be no problem. If you go out without the iPhone, the watch may be limited.

Even so, it can still record activity, workouts, and other features that do not require an active call, but it will not have the same independence as a Cellular model.

Calls with a Cellular model

If your Apple Watch is GPS plus Cellular and you have the service activated with your carrier, you can make and receive calls without carrying the iPhone, provided there is coverage.

This can be useful for:

  • Going out walking without the iPhone.
  • Exercising.
  • Going shopping.
  • Moving around the house or outdoors with more freedom.
  • Having a safety communication option.

But remember:

  • It requires configuration with the carrier.
  • It may have an additional cost.
  • It uses more battery.
  • It depends on coverage.
  • Not all carriers support it.

Emergency calls

The Apple Watch may allow emergency calls under certain conditions. This topic will be covered in the personal safety section, because it needs to be explained very carefully. For now, it is enough to know that you should not practise a real emergency call. Emergency features are configured and understood, but they are not tested by calling emergency services without a reason.

Privacy during calls

Talking from the Apple Watch uses the watch speaker if you do not have headphones. That means nearby people may hear the conversation. If the conversation is private, use headphones or transfer the call to the iPhone. The watch is convenient for quick calls, but it is not always suitable for long or sensitive conversations.

When it is useful to use the Apple Watch for calls

The Apple Watch is useful for:

  • Answering quickly.
  • Knowing who is calling.
  • Speaking briefly.
  • Answering while cooking.
  • Answering if you cannot find the iPhone.
  • Taking a call during a walk.
  • Calling with Siri.
  • Receiving calls during exercise.

When it is better to use the iPhone

The iPhone may be better for:

  • Long conversations.
  • Noisy places.
  • Private calls without headphones.
  • Important administrative calls.
  • Calls where you need to check documents or data.
  • Situations where the watch battery is low.
  • The Apple Watch does not always have to replace the iPhone. It should give you a quick option when it is useful.

Common problems with calls

  • The call does not arrive on the watch.
  • The sound is not clear.
  • The other person cannot hear you.
  • The audio comes through headphones.
  • The audio comes through the iPhone.
  • Siri calls the wrong contact.
  • The watch has no connection.
  • Airplane Mode is enabled.
  • A Focus mode is filtering calls.
  • The Apple Watch is locked.
  • The watch is not on your wrist.
  • The GPS model is far from the iPhone.
  • The Cellular model does not have service activated.

What to check if calls do not arrive

Check:

  • That the Apple Watch is on your wrist.
  • That it is unlocked.
  • That the iPhone is nearby, if it is a GPS model.
  • That Bluetooth is enabled.
  • That Wi-Fi works.
  • That Airplane Mode is not enabled.
  • That no Focus mode is blocking calls.
  • That Phone notifications are allowed.
  • That the Apple Watch is paired correctly.
  • That the carrier supports the service if you use Cellular.

What to check if you cannot hear well

Check:

  • Call volume.
  • Audio output.
  • Connected headphones.
  • Silent Mode.
  • Background noise.
  • Watch position.
  • Coverage.
  • If you are outdoors, it may be better to use headphones.

What to check if the other person cannot hear you well

Check:

  • That you are not covering the microphone.
  • That there is not too much noise.
  • That the watch is relatively close to your mouth.
  • That you are not using a strap, case, or accessory that covers areas of the watch.
  • That the connection is stable.

There is no need to speak to the watch as if it were a megaphone, but it is also not advisable to keep it buried under your sleeve.

Common mistakes with calls

Answering without listening to who is calling.

  • Confusing Decline with Answer.
  • Not knowing how to hang up.
  • Speaking through the speaker in a public place unintentionally.
  • Thinking a GPS model works like a Cellular model.
  • Going out without the iPhone believing that the GPS watch will be able to call.
  • Not configuring favourites.
  • Asking Siri to call someone with an ambiguous name.
  • Not checking audio output.
  • Not checking Focus modes.

Practical advice

Configure some favourite contacts on the iPhone. That will make it easier to call from the Apple Watch.

It is also useful to practise with a trusted person:

  • Receive a call.
  • Answer from the watch.
  • Raise or lower the volume.
  • Hang up.
  • Make a call with Siri.
  • Make a call from Recents.
  • This will give you confidence before using it in a real situation.

Exercise for module 16

  • Put on the Apple Watch.
  • Check that it is unlocked.
  • Ask a trusted person to call you.
  • When the call arrives, listen to what VoiceOver announces.
  • Find the Answer button.
  • Double tap.
  • Speak for a few seconds from the watch.
  • Find the button to end the call.
  • Double tap.

Then, from the Apple Watch:

  • Open the Phone app.
  • Go to Recents.
  • Find the call you have just received.
  • Double tap to return it, if you want to practise.
  • Hang up correctly.

Then try with Siri:

  • Invoke Siri.
  • Ask it to call a known contact.
  • Confirm that it calls the correct person.
  • End the call.

Summary of module 16

The Apple Watch allows you to receive and make calls. With a GPS model, it will usually depend on a nearby iPhone. With a GPS plus Cellular model, it can work more independently if a supported carrier in your country or region allows it. Incoming calls can alert you with vibration, sound, and VoiceOver. With VoiceOver, you can answer, decline, or end a call. Siri is a quick way to call. The Phone app allows you to use favourites, recents, contacts, and the keypad. For a blind person, favourites and Siri are usually comfortable methods. Calls from the watch are useful for quick conversations. For long or private calls, it may be better to use the iPhone or headphones. If calls do not work, check connection, Focus, lock status, carrier, and model type.

Back to table of contents

Module 17. Messages

The Apple Watch can be used to receive and reply to messages from your wrist. This is one of its most practical everyday features. If a message arrives, you can read who sent it, listen to the content with VoiceOver, and reply briefly without taking out the iPhone.

But it is important to be clear from the beginning: the Apple Watch is useful for short messages, quick replies, and urgent responses. It is not the best device for long conversations, delicate explanations, or writing paragraphs. For that, the iPhone is still much more comfortable.

Messaging on the Apple Watch

The Apple Watch can show messages from Apple’s Messages app and notifications from other messaging apps, depending on compatibility.

Apple’s Messages app usually has better integration with the watch.

  • Other apps may behave differently.
  • Some apps allow replies from the notification.
  • Others only allow you to read the alert.
  • Others have more integration.

For that reason, in this module we will focus first on Apple’s Messages app, and then we will discuss the general behaviour of other apps.

Receiving a message

When a message arrives, the Apple Watch may alert you with vibration, sound, or both, depending on configuration. VoiceOver may announce the notification.

To read it:

  • Touch the Apple Watch screen.
  • Listen to what VoiceOver says.
  • Swipe right to move through the content.
  • Listen to the sender’s name.
  • Listen to the message.
  • Look for the available options.
  • An option to reply may appear.
  • An option to close, dismiss, or open the message may also appear.

Reading messages from the notification

When the message arrives as a notification, you can read it directly from that alert.

With VoiceOver:

  • Touch the notification.
  • Swipe to move through its elements.
  • Listen to the content.
  • Look for Reply if you want to answer.
  • If the message is short, you will usually be able to read it from the notification.
  • If it is longer, you may need to open it.

Opening the Messages app

You can also open the Messages app from the app list.

To do this:

  • Return to the watch face.
  • Press the Digital Crown.
  • Find Messages.
  • Double tap.
  • Inside Messages, you will find recent conversations.

With VoiceOver:

  • Swipe right or left to move through conversations.
  • Listen to the contact or group name.
  • Double tap to open a conversation.
  • Swipe to read messages and options.

On the small screen of the watch, a long conversation can be uncomfortable. The Apple Watch is useful for checking and replying to something brief, not for reviewing an entire novel written in chopped-up messages.

Replying to a message

To reply from a notification or from the Messages app:

  1. Find the Reply button.
  2. Double tap.

The Apple Watch may offer several ways to reply:

  • Dictation.
  • Quick replies.
  • Emoji.
  • Audio.
  • Keyboard, if available.
  • Other methods depending on language, model, and version.
  • For a blind person, the most practical methods are usually dictation and quick replies.

Replying with dictation

Dictation allows you to speak and have your voice converted into text.

To reply with dictation:

  • Open the Reply option.
  • Find Dictation or the microphone button, depending on how it appears.
  • Double tap.
  • Speak clearly.
  • When you finish, stop dictation if necessary.
  • Review the recognised text if VoiceOver allows it.
  • Find Send.
  • Double tap.
  • It is very important to review the text before sending it, especially if the message is important.

Dictation can make mistakes. Sometimes only small ones. Sometimes it decides to create experimental literature. That is why listening before sending can prevent more than one problem.

Tips for dictating

  • Speak clearly.
  • Avoid too much background noise.
  • Use short sentences.
  • Do not dictate very long messages from the watch.
  • Review before sending.
  • If the text is wrong, cancel or delete it and dictate again.
  • If the message is delicate, use the iPhone.

Quick replies

Quick replies are predefined responses that can be sent with very few gestures.

They may include phrases such as:

  • Yes.
  • No.
  • Okay.
  • I’ll call you later.
  • I’m on my way.
  • Thanks.
  • I’ll look at it later.
  • The exact replies may vary depending on language, system version, and configuration.
  • Quick replies are very useful on the Apple Watch because they avoid dictation.

To use a quick reply:

  • Open the message.
  • Choose Reply.
  • Look for the list of suggested or quick replies.
  • Choose the one you want.
  • Double tap to send.
  • These replies are especially useful when you only need to confirm, acknowledge, or send a short answer.

Customising quick replies

On the iPhone, you may be able to customise the default replies used by Messages on the Apple Watch.

To review this:

  • Open the Watch app on the iPhone.
  • Go to My Watch.
  • Go to Messages.
  • Look for Default Replies or a similar option.
  • There, if available, you can add or edit replies.

For a blind person, it can be useful to have practical phrases such as:

  • I’ll call you in a moment.
  • I’m on my way.
  • I can’t reply right now.
  • Received, thank you.
  • Please send me an audio message.
  • I’ll check it later.
  • This saves time and reduces dictation errors.

Replying with emoji

The Apple Watch may offer emoji as a reply option. This can be useful for informal messages, but it is not always the best option for practical communication. With VoiceOver, emoji should be read before sending to avoid sending something unintended.

A misplaced emoji can be harmless, but it can also make a message look strange. Humanity has already created enough confusion with tiny faces; there is no need for the watch to add more.

Replying with audio

In some contexts, the Apple Watch may allow you to send an audio message.

This can be useful when dictation does not work well or when speaking is faster than writing.

  • But keep privacy in mind.
  • If you record audio in a public place, other people may hear what you say.
  • Also, the recipient must be able to listen to the audio comfortably.

Using the keyboard

Some Apple Watch models, languages, or regions may offer a keyboard. With VoiceOver, typing on the Apple Watch keyboard may not be the most comfortable method. For short corrections or very brief texts, it may be useful. For longer messages, the iPhone is usually better. If the keyboard is not available in your language or model, that is normal. Availability varies.

Using Siri to send messages

Siri can be one of the fastest ways to send a message from the Apple Watch.

You can say something like:

  • Send a message to Anna.
  • Tell John I’m on my way.
  • Send a message to Maria saying I’ll call you later.
  • Siri may ask you to confirm the contact or the message.
  • Before sending, listen carefully.
  • If Siri has misunderstood the contact or the text, cancel.
  • This is especially important when you have contacts with similar names.
  • A message sent to the wrong person is one of those small technological disasters that nobody needs.

Reading previous messages

From the Messages app, you can open recent conversations and read previous messages.

With VoiceOver:

  • Open Messages.
  • Choose a conversation.
  • Swipe through the available messages and controls.
  • If the conversation is long, the watch may not be the most comfortable place to review it.
  • For long conversations, search, attachments, links, or important details, use the iPhone.

Messages from groups

Group messages can also arrive on the Apple Watch. They may be useful, but they can also generate many notifications. Before replying, make sure you know whether you are replying to one person or to a group. With VoiceOver, listen carefully to the conversation name and sender. If you are not sure, it is better to open the conversation on the iPhone. Replying to the wrong group is a very efficient way of creating unnecessary social archaeology.

Attachments, links, and images

Messages may include links, images, audio, locations, or other attachments. On the Apple Watch, these elements may be limited or less comfortable to handle. VoiceOver may announce that there is an attachment, image, link, or other content. For some items, you may be able to open or interact with them. For others, the iPhone will be better. If the content is important, use the iPhone to review it in more detail.

Privacy when reading messages

Messages can contain private information. If VoiceOver reads them aloud from the watch speaker, people nearby may hear them. This matters in public places, at work, in medical waiting rooms, on public transport, or around other people.

To protect privacy:

  • Use headphones when necessary.
  • Lower the volume if appropriate.
  • Read sensitive messages on the iPhone.
  • Avoid opening private messages aloud in public.
  • Remember that a vibration on the wrist is discreet, but VoiceOver through the speaker is not.

Managing message notifications

If messages do not arrive on the Apple Watch, check notification settings.

On the iPhone:

  • Open the Watch app.
  • Go to My Watch.
  • Go to Notifications.
  • Look for Messages.
  • Review whether notifications are allowed.
  • You should also check the iPhone’s own notification settings.

On the iPhone:

  • Open Settings.
  • Go to Notifications.
  • Go to Messages.
  • Check that notifications are enabled.
  • Also check Focus modes.
  • If a Focus mode is active, some messages may be silenced or filtered.

Messages and Focus modes

Focus modes can affect messages.

For example:

  • Do Not Disturb may silence messages.
  • Sleep Focus may limit alerts.
  • Work or Personal Focus may allow only certain contacts.
  • If a message does not arrive, check whether a Focus mode is active.
  • This can be reviewed from Control Centre on the Apple Watch or from the iPhone.

Messages from other apps

Other messaging apps may behave differently from Apple’s Messages app.

For example, an app may allow you to:

  • Read the notification.
  • Reply from the notification.
  • Open a limited watch app.
  • Dismiss the alert.
  • Or it may only notify you and nothing else.
  • The behaviour depends on whether that app supports Apple Watch properly.
  • Do not assume that all messaging apps work the same.
  • Some applications do not offer the same features as Apple’s Messages app.

Using the Apple Watch for urgent messages

The Apple Watch is very useful for brief and urgent messages.

For example:

  • I’m arriving.
  • Call me when you can.
  • I can’t reply right now.
  • Received.
  • I’m on my way.
  • I’ll look at it later.
  • For long replies, use the iPhone.

The wrist is not a writing desk. Although some people try, because there is always someone willing to dictate three paragraphs to a watch in the middle of a windy street.

Common mistakes with messages

  • Sending without reviewing dictation.
  • Replying to the wrong group.
  • Reading private messages aloud in public.
  • Thinking all apps allow replies in the same way.
  • Dictating messages that are too long.
  • Not configuring quick replies.
  • Not checking whether the notification comes from the iPhone or the watch.
  • Not checking Focus modes.
  • Believing that if an app appears in notifications, it also has a full Apple Watch app.

Practical advice

To use messages comfortably, configure useful quick replies.

  • Practise dictation with simple messages.
  • Use Siri to start short messages.
  • Do not use the watch for long conversations.
  • If the message is important, private, or long, move to the iPhone.

Exercise for module 17

Ask a trusted person to send you a message.

When it arrives on the Apple Watch, listen to the notification.

  1. Swipe through the content.
  2. Look for Reply.
  3. Choose dictation.

Dictate a short phrase, for example: Received, thank you.

Listen to the recognised text before sending it.

  1. Send the message.
  2. Then try a quick reply.
  3. Ask for another message.
  4. Look for Reply.
  5. Choose a predefined reply.
  6. Send it.

Then try with Siri:

  • Invoke Siri.
  • Ask it to send a message to a known contact.
  • Dictate a short sentence.
  • Confirm only if the contact and text are correct.

Summary of module 17

The Apple Watch allows you to receive and reply to messages. Apple’s Messages app usually offers better integration. Other apps may allow reading or replying from notifications, depending on compatibility. With VoiceOver, you can read the sender, content, and options. The most practical replies are usually dictation and quick replies. It is advisable to review dictated text before sending it. For long or delicate messages, it is better to use the iPhone. Notifications must be enabled on the iPhone and allowed on the Apple Watch. Not all messaging apps work the same way on the watch. Privacy matters if VoiceOver reads aloud.

Back to table of contents

Module 18. Siri on the Apple Watch

Siri can be a very useful tool on the Apple Watch. The watch has a small screen, and some actions can require several steps with VoiceOver. Siri allows you to perform many of those actions by voice, more quickly.

With Siri, you can request calls, messages, timers, alarms, reminders, workouts, weather information, simple queries, playback control, smart home actions, and other compatible tasks. For a blind person, Siri can save time. It does not replace learning how to use the watch, but it can avoid many trips through menus.

What Siri can do on the Apple Watch

Siri can help you with actions such as:

  • Calling a contact.
  • Sending a message.
  • Creating a timer.
  • Creating an alarm.
  • Creating a reminder.
  • Starting a workout.
  • Checking the weather.
  • Checking the time.
  • Opening an app.
  • Controlling music or podcasts.
  • Searching for brief information.
  • Checking calendar events.
  • Turning some features on or off, depending on availability.
  • Controlling Home accessories, if they are configured.

The usefulness of Siri depends on whether it understands the command correctly, the connection, the configured language, and the available permissions.

Ways to activate Siri

On the Apple Watch, there may be several ways to activate Siri.

Depending on configuration and model, these options may be available:

  • Saying Siri or Hey Siri.
  • Holding down the Digital Crown.
  • Raising your wrist and speaking.
  • Tapping a Siri-related complication or shortcut, if configured.
  • Not everyone uses the same method.

For a blind person, holding down the Digital Crown can be a clear and controlled method, because it does not depend as much on the watch correctly detecting the activation phrase.
