Activating Siri with the Digital Crown

To use Siri with the Digital Crown:

  • Locate the Digital Crown.
  • Hold down the Digital Crown.
  • Wait for the Siri signal.
  • Say your request.
  • Release or wait for the response, depending on behaviour.

Example:

  • Hold down the Digital Crown.
  • Say: set a timer for ten minutes.
  • Siri should confirm the timer.

This method is practical because it is started physically. You do not have to depend on the watch listening for the activation phrase.

Activating Siri with your voice

If you have the option to listen for Siri or Hey Siri enabled, you can say the activation phrase and then the command.

Example:

  • Siri, call Anna.
  • Or:
  • Hey Siri, set an alarm for seven o’clock.

This can be convenient, but it can also fail if there is noise, if the watch does not detect your voice properly, or if the setting is not enabled.

Activating Siri by raising your wrist

Some Apple Watch models allow you to raise your wrist and speak without saying the activation phrase, if the option is enabled. This can be quick, but it is not always reliable for everyone. It may depend on how you raise your wrist, the orientation, background noise, and configuration. If it works well, it can be very convenient. If it often fails, it is better to use the Digital Crown.

Configuring Siri from the iPhone

To review Siri:

  • Open the Watch app on the iPhone.
  • Go to My Watch.
  • Look for Siri.
  • Review the available options.
  • You can turn invocation methods on or off.
  • You can also review language, voice, and behaviour, depending on the available options.
  • It is advisable to leave at least one method enabled that feels comfortable and reliable.

Using Siri for calls

Siri can call contacts.

Examples:

  • Call Anna.
  • Call John mobile.
  • Call home.
  • Call Mum.
  • If you have several contacts with similar names, Siri may ask you to choose.
  • Listen carefully before confirming.
  • If Siri understands the name incorrectly, cancel.
  • For frequent contacts, it is useful to have clear names in your address book.

Using Siri for messages

Siri can send messages.

Example:

  • Send a message to Anna.
  • Siri will ask what you want to say.
  • Dictate the message.
  • Listen to the confirmation.
  • Send only if the text and contact are correct.

You can also say the full command:

  • Send a message to Anna saying I’ll be there in ten minutes.
  • Then listen to the confirmation.
  • Do not send important messages without reviewing them.

Siri can confuse words, names, and punctuation. Artificial intelligence and dictation have improved a lot, but they still retain an admirable ability to embarrass anyone.

Using Siri for timers

This is one of the most useful features.

Examples:

  • Set a timer for five minutes.
  • Set a timer for twenty minutes.
  • Set a ten-minute pasta timer.
  • Set a timer for one hour.
  • The Apple Watch is especially convenient for timers because you wear it and can feel the vibration on your wrist.
  • This is useful for cooking, medication, breaks, exercises, or any timed task.

Using Siri for alarms

You can also create alarms.

Examples:

  • Set an alarm for seven in the morning.
  • Wake me up at eight.
  • Set an alarm for tomorrow at six thirty.
  • Siri will confirm the alarm.
  • It is useful to check whether the alarm has been created correctly, especially if it is important.

Using Siri for reminders

Siri can create reminders.

Examples:

  • Remind me to call Martha at five.
  • Remind me to take my medication at nine.
  • Remind me to buy bread when I leave home.
  • Remind me to check my email tomorrow.
  • Reminders can sync with the iPhone.

This feature can be very useful, because the Apple Watch allows you to create the reminder at the moment it occurs to you.

Using Siri for workouts

Siri can start workouts.

Examples:

  • Start an outdoor walk workout.
  • Start an indoor walk workout.
  • Start a strength training workout.
  • Start a cycling workout.
  • This avoids having to find the Workout app and move through the list.
  • It is especially useful if you already know which workout you want to do.

When the workout starts, you will need to learn how to pause it, resume it, and end it. That will be covered in the exercise section.

Using Siri to open apps

Siri can open apps.

Examples:

  • Open Workout.
  • Open Timers.
  • Open Heart Rate.
  • Open Reminders.
  • Open Weather.
  • This can save steps.
  • If you do not remember where an app is in the list, asking Siri to open it may be faster.

Using Siri to check information

You can ask for brief information.

Examples:

  • What’s the weather like?
  • Is it going to rain today?
  • What time is it?
  • What’s on my calendar?
  • What’s my next appointment?
  • How long until my alarm?
  • How much battery does my Apple Watch have, if supported?
  • The answer may depend on connection, permissions, and available services.

Using Siri to control playback

If you listen to music, podcasts, or compatible audio, Siri can help.

Examples:

  • Play music.
  • Pause.
  • Next song.
  • Turn up the volume.
  • Play my playlist.
  • Open Podcasts.
  • The behaviour depends on the apps and services you use.

Using Siri for Home

If you have smart home accessories configured in the Home app, Siri can control them from the Apple Watch.

Examples:

  • Turn on the living room light.
  • Turn off the fan.
  • Raise the blind.
  • Set the temperature to twenty-two degrees.
  • This can be very useful for a blind person, provided the home is well configured and accessory names are clear.

Siri and privacy

When you use Siri, you are speaking out loud. In public places, other people may hear your request. If you are going to send messages, make calls, check personal data, or control private items, keep this in mind. It is also advisable to review Siri and privacy settings from the iPhone if you have doubts about what is shared and how it is managed.

Siri without connection

Some Siri features may work better or worse depending on the connection. If the Apple Watch is far from the iPhone, has no Wi-Fi, or has no Cellular connection, Siri may be limited. On Cellular models with an active plan, Siri can work more independently, provided there is coverage. If Siri does not respond, check connection, Airplane Mode, Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, and the status of the iPhone.

When Siri misunderstands

If Siri misunderstands a command:

  • Cancel.
  • Repeat with a simpler phrase.
  • Use the exact name of the contact or app.
  • Avoid long sentences.
  • Divide the action into steps.

For example, instead of saying:

Send a message to Anna saying that I’ll be late because I’m still waiting for transport and that she shouldn’t worry.

It may be more reliable to say:

  • Send a message to Anna.
  • When Siri asks for the text, dictate a short sentence:
  • I’ll be late. Don’t worry.
  • The clearer the command, the less chance there is of disaster.

Setting clear names in Contacts

Siri works better if contacts have clear names. Avoid having several contacts with very similar names and no surnames or labels. If you have two people called Anna, Siri may ask you to choose. You can improve this by adding surnames, labels, or relationships in Contacts.

For example:

  • Anna Pérez.
  • Anna physiotherapist.
  • John brother.
  • Home.
  • Doctor.
  • Pharmacy.
  • This makes calls and messages easier.

Siri does not replace VoiceOver

Siri helps, but it should not be the only way to use the watch.

There are several reasons:

  • Siri can fail.
  • There may be no connection.
  • It can misunderstand.
  • It may not work well in noisy environments.
  • It may not be discreet.
  • Some actions require navigating the screen.
  • That is why the goal is to combine Siri with VoiceOver.
  • Siri for quick actions.
  • VoiceOver for control, review, and configuration.

Common mistakes with Siri

  • Not reviewing before sending a message.
  • Using commands that are too long.
  • Having contacts with confusing names.
  • Speaking with too much background noise.
  • Thinking Siri can do everything.
  • Having no connection.
  • Not knowing which activation method is configured.
  • Activating Siri accidentally.
  • Dictating private information in public.
  • Trusting Siri with delicate actions without confirming.

Practical advice

Use Siri for simple and repetitive actions.

Start with:

  • Timers.
  • Alarms.
  • Calls.
  • Short messages.
  • Reminders.
  • Opening apps.
  • Starting workouts.
  • When you see what works well in your case, you can expand its use.
  • Do not start by using Siri for complex tasks or long messages.

Exercise for module 18

Put on the Apple Watch. Activate Siri using the method you have configured.

Try a simple command:

  • Set a timer for two minutes.
  • Wait for confirmation.
  • Cancel the timer or let it finish.

Then try:

  • What’s the weather like?
  • Then try:
  • Open Workout.
  • Do not start any workout yet if you do not want to.
  • Return to the watch face.

Then try a call with a trusted person:

  • Call a known contact.
  • Check that Siri understands the name correctly.
  • Cancel if you are not sure.

Finally, try a reminder:

  • Remind me to drink water in one hour.
  • Then check in Reminders whether it was created correctly.

Summary of module 18

Siri can save many steps on the Apple Watch. It can be activated by voice, with the Digital Crown, or by raising your wrist, depending on configuration. It is useful for calls, messages, timers, alarms, reminders, workouts, queries, and opening apps.

For a blind person, Siri is especially useful for quick actions.

  • Messages must be reviewed before sending.
  • Short commands usually work better.
  • Siri depends on configuration, connection, language, and permissions.
  • It does not replace VoiceOver.
  • The ideal approach is to combine Siri for quick actions and VoiceOver for reviewing and controlling.

Back to table of contents

Module 19. Timers, alarms, and reminders

The Apple Watch is especially useful for managing quick alerts.

Timers, alarms, and reminders are simple features, but they are very practical. In many cases, these three features alone justify wearing the watch on your wrist.

  • They do not require looking at the screen.
  • They can alert you with vibration.
  • They can be created with Siri.
  • They can be checked with VoiceOver.

And they are always close at hand. For a blind person, this can be very convenient in everyday tasks: cooking, taking medication, leaving at a specific time, managing breaks, organising routines, remembering calls, not forgetting appointments, or timing exercise.

Difference between a timer, an alarm, and a reminder

Although they are sometimes confused, they are not the same. A timer counts down a period of time.

For example:

  • Five minutes for tea.
  • Ten minutes for pasta.
  • Thirty minutes of rest.
  • One hour before taking something out of the oven.
  • An alarm alerts you at a specific time.

For example:

  • At seven in the morning.
  • At half past twelve.
  • At nine at night.
  • A reminder helps you remember a task.

For example:

  • Call someone.
  • Take medication.
  • Buy something.
  • Send a message.
  • Review a document.
  • Leave home.
  • Each feature has its place.
  • Timer: countdown.
  • Alarm: specific time.
  • Reminder: pending task.

Timers

The timer is one of the most convenient Apple Watch features. Because the watch is on your wrist, the alert reaches you directly through vibration, sound, or both. This is very useful if you are cooking, walking around the house, listening to audio, exercising, or away from the iPhone.

Creating a timer with Siri

The quickest way to create a timer is Siri.

You can say:

  • Set a timer for five minutes.
  • Set a timer for ten minutes.
  • Set a timer for half an hour.
  • Set a fifteen-minute food timer.
  • Siri should confirm that the timer has started.

If the timer is important, listen to the confirmation. It is not enough to say the command and assume that it has been created. Siri sometimes understands strange things, because even artificial intelligence apparently needs to contribute its share of domestic confusion.

Creating a timer from the Timers app

You can also create timers from the app.

To do this:

  • Press the Digital Crown from the watch face.
  • Find Timers.
  • Double tap.
  • Move through the options with VoiceOver.
  • A list of preset timers may appear.
  • Choose one if it matches what you need.
  • If there is a custom timer option, activate it.
  • Adjust hours, minutes, or seconds as needed.
  • Start the timer.
  • The exact controls may vary depending on the version, but the general idea is to choose a duration and start.

Preset timers

The Timers app may show common durations.

For example:

  • One minute.
  • Three minutes.
  • Five minutes.
  • Ten minutes.
  • Fifteen minutes.
  • Thirty minutes.
  • One hour.
  • These shortcuts are practical because they avoid setting the time manually.

With VoiceOver:

  • Swipe to the duration you want.
  • Double tap.
  • The timer will start.

Custom timer

If you need a specific time that does not appear in the list, use the custom option.

For example:

  1. Seven minutes.
  2. Twenty-five minutes.
  3. One hour and ten minutes.

With VoiceOver, adjusting values may require moving through hours, minutes, and seconds. It may be quicker to ask Siri. For less common times, Siri is usually the most convenient method.

Checking an active timer

If you have a timer running, you can check it.

You can do this in several ways:

  • By asking Siri.
  • By opening the Timers app.
  • From a complication on the watch face, if you have configured one.

Example with Siri:

  • How much time is left on the timer?
  • You can also open Timers and listen to the remaining time.

Pausing or cancelling a timer

During an active timer, you can pause or cancel it.

From the Timers app:

  • Open Timers.
  • Find the active timer.
  • Look for Pause, Cancel, or Stop, depending on what appears.
  • Double tap.

With Siri, you can also say:

  • Cancel the timer.
  • Pause the timer.
  • If you have several timers, Siri may ask for clarification or act on the most obvious active timer.

When a timer ends

When the time ends, the Apple Watch may vibrate, make a sound, or both. With VoiceOver, you can listen to the alert and look for the button to stop it.

To stop it:

  • Touch the screen.
  • Listen to the options.
  • Look for Stop, Close, or a similar option.
  • Double tap.
  • If there is an option to repeat, it may also appear.

Multiple timers

Depending on the watchOS version, the Apple Watch may allow several timers at the same time. This can be useful for cooking or managing several tasks.

For example:

  • One timer for rice.
  • Another for the oven.
  • Another for resting.
  • If you use several timers, it is useful to name them with Siri whenever possible.

For example:

  • Set a ten-minute timer for pasta.
  • Set a thirty-minute timer for the oven.
  • That will make them easier to distinguish.

Alarms

Alarms are used to alert you at a specific time. They can be used to wake up, take medication, leave home, call someone, or manage any daily routine.

Creating an alarm with Siri

The quickest way is Siri.

Examples:

  • Set an alarm for seven.
  • Set an alarm for tomorrow at eight thirty.
  • Wake me up at six forty-five.
  • Set an alarm every day at nine.
  • Siri should confirm the alarm.
  • Listen to the confirmation to make sure it understood the time correctly.

Creating an alarm from the Alarms app

You can also use the Alarms app.

To do this:

  • Press the Digital Crown.
  • Find Alarms.
  • Double tap.
  • Look for Add Alarm, if it appears.
  • Set the time.
  • Confirm.
  • The controls may vary, but you will usually need to select hours and minutes.

With VoiceOver on the watch, it may be more comfortable to create alarms with Siri, especially if the time is simple.

Turning alarms on or off

In the Alarms app, you can find alarms you have already created. Each one may have a switch to turn it on or off.

With VoiceOver:

  • Open Alarms.
  • Swipe to the alarm.
  • Listen to the time and state.
  • If you want to change the state, double tap the corresponding switch.
  • Do not delete an alarm if you only want to turn it off temporarily.

Repeated alarms

Some alarms can repeat.

For example:

  • Every day.
  • Monday to Friday.
  • Weekends only.
  • Specific days.
  • This is useful for regular routines.
  • If you need a repeated alarm, it may be easier to configure it from the iPhone or with Siri, depending on the case.

Stopping an alarm

When an alarm goes off, the Apple Watch may vibrate and make a sound.

With VoiceOver:

  • Touch the screen.
  • Listen to the options.
  • Look for Stop.
  • Double tap.
  • A Snooze option may also appear.
  • If you choose Snooze, the alarm will sound again after a few minutes.
  • If you really want to end it, look for Stop.

Alarms and Sleep mode

If you use sleep tracking, alarms can be integrated with sleep schedules. This will be covered in the sleep module. For now, it is enough to know that regular alarms and sleep schedules can coexist, but they are not exactly the same thing.

Reminders

  • Reminders help you not forget tasks.
  • They can be linked to a time, a date, a location, or a list.
  • The Apple Watch can alert you on your wrist when a reminder is due.
  • You can also create reminders quickly with Siri.

Creating a reminder with Siri

Examples:

  • Remind me to call Peter at five.
  • Remind me to take my medication at nine.
  • Remind me to buy bread tomorrow.
  • Remind me to check my email when I get home.
  • Remind me to drink water in an hour.
  • Siri will create the reminder and should confirm it.
  • Listen to the confirmation, especially if the reminder includes a time or location.

Creating reminders from the app

You can also open the Reminders app on the Apple Watch. From there, you can check lists and pending tasks. To create reminders manually on the watch, some options may be available, but in many cases it will be more comfortable to use Siri or the iPhone. The Apple Watch is very good for capturing a quick idea. For organising long lists, the iPhone is still more comfortable.

Receiving a reminder

When a reminder is due, the watch may vibrate, make a sound, or both. VoiceOver can read the alert.

You may find options such as:

  • Mark as Completed.
  • Snooze.
  • Close.
  • Open.
  • If you have already done the task, mark it as completed.
  • If you cannot do it at that moment, you can snooze it if that option appears.

Marking a reminder as completed

When the alert appears:

  • Touch the screen.
  • Swipe to Completed or Mark as Completed.
  • Double tap.
  • You can also open the Reminders app, find the task, and mark it.

Reminder lists

Reminders can be organised into lists.

For example:

  • Home.
  • Work.
  • Shopping.
  • Health.
  • Calls.
  • Channel.
  • Personal.
  • On the Apple Watch, reviewing very long lists can be uncomfortable. For full management, use the iPhone.
  • For marking tasks, receiving alerts, or creating quick reminders, the watch works very well.

Medication reminders

Medication can be managed from the Health app on the iPhone, if you use that feature. The Apple Watch can alert you when it is time to take medication and allow you to log that it has been taken. This will be explained in more detail in the module on medication and health reminders. This is a special case, because it is not just any reminder. It has health importance and must be configured carefully.

Practical use in the kitchen

Apple Watch timers are very useful in the kitchen.

Examples:

  • Set a ten-minute timer for pasta.
  • Set a twenty-minute timer for vegetables.
  • Set a forty-minute timer for the oven.
  • Set a five-minute timer for resting.
  • If the watch allows multiple named timers, it becomes even more convenient.

For a blind person, receiving the alert on the wrist can avoid having to rely on hearing the iPhone from another room.

Practical use in health

Alarms and reminders can help with health routines.

Examples:

  • Taking medication.
  • Drinking water.
  • Measuring glucose with another device, if applicable.
  • Doing prescribed exercises.
  • Going to bed at a certain time.
  • Getting up.
  • Walking for a few minutes.
  • You should not rely only on the watch for critical matters, but it can be a very useful support.

Practical use in exercise

Timers and reminders can also help with training.

Examples:

  • Rest between sets.
  • Stretching time.
  • Intervals.
  • Walks.
  • Reminders to stand and move.
  • In the exercise modules, we will see how this combines with the Workout app.

Practical use in daily organisation

The Apple Watch is useful for small tasks.

Examples:

  • Remind me to call my sister this afternoon.
  • Remind me to take out the rubbish at eight.
  • Remind me to send the document tomorrow.
  • Remind me to check the washing machine in an hour.
  • Remind me to leave at six.
  • These actions are quick and work very well with Siri.

Configuring which alerts you receive

For timers, alarms, and reminders to be useful, you need to notice them properly.

Review:

  • Sounds.
  • Vibrations.
  • Silent Mode.
  • Focus.
  • Notifications.
  • If you do not notice alerts, review haptic feedback.
  • If you are in Sleep mode or Do Not Disturb, some alerts may behave differently.

Privacy and discretion

Timers and alarms are usually discreet. Reminders may contain personal information. If VoiceOver reads a reminder aloud, other people may hear it. If you have private reminders, use headphones or configure how notifications are shown.

Common mistakes

Creating a timer and not listening to the confirmation.

  • Confusing an alarm with a timer.
  • Creating an alarm for the wrong time.
  • Not checking whether an alarm repeats.
  • Snoozing an alarm when you meant to stop it.
  • Dictating a reminder and not checking whether Siri understood correctly.
  • Having too many reminders and then ignoring them.
  • Not feeling vibrations because the watch is too loose.
  • Having a Focus mode filtering alerts.
  • Using the watch to manage long lists when the iPhone would be better.

Practical advice

Use Siri to create quick timers, alarms, and reminders. Use the iPhone to organise long lists or review complex settings. Configure clear haptic feedback so you notice alerts properly. Start with a few alarms and reminders. If you create too many, they will stop being useful and become noise.

Exercise for module 19

Activate Siri on the Apple Watch.

Say:

  • Set a timer for two minutes.
  • Listen to the confirmation.
  • Wait for it to finish.
  • When it alerts you, find Stop and double tap.

Then create a test alarm:

  • Set an alarm for five minutes from now.
  • Listen to the confirmation.
  • When it goes off, stop the alarm.

Then create a reminder:

  • Remind me to check the Apple Watch in ten minutes.
  • Listen to the confirmation.
  • When the alert arrives, mark it as completed if the option appears.
  • Then open the Reminders app on the Apple Watch.
  • Check whether you can locate the reminder you created or completed.

Summary of module 19

A timer counts down a period of time. An alarm alerts you at a specific time. A reminder alerts you about a task. Siri is a quick way to create timers, alarms, and reminders. The Apple Watch is very useful because it alerts you on the wrist. It is worth always checking Siri’s confirmation. Haptic feedback is important for noticing alerts. For long lists, the iPhone is usually more comfortable. For cooking, health, exercise, and daily organisation, these features are especially practical.

Module 20. Finding the iPhone and other location features

One of the most practical Apple Watch features is being able to find the iPhone when you do not know where you left it. This situation is more common than anyone would like to admit. The iPhone may be on a table, under a cushion, in a pocket, next to the charger, in another room, or in that mysterious place where things end up when you had them in your hand thirty seconds ago. The Apple Watch can help you locate it by making the iPhone play a sound.

In addition, the watch can also take part in other location features, such as Find Devices, Find People, sharing location, or receiving directions, depending on configuration, model, and available services.

Finding the iPhone from Control Centre

The quickest way to find the iPhone is from Control Centre on the Apple Watch.

To do this:

  • Return to the watch face.
  • Press the side button once to open Control Centre.
  • Swipe with VoiceOver until you find the button to find or make the iPhone play a sound.
  • Double tap.
  • The iPhone will play a sound.
  • Listen to where the sound is coming from.
  • Move closer until you find it.

The exact name of the button may vary. VoiceOver may announce something like find iPhone, locate iPhone, ping iPhone, or play sound on iPhone.

When it works best

This feature works best when:

  • The iPhone is nearby.
  • The Apple Watch is connected to the iPhone.
  • The iPhone is turned on.
  • Bluetooth or the connection between both devices is working correctly.
  • If the iPhone is in the same house, it is usually very useful.
  • If the iPhone is far away, turned off, out of battery, or without a connection, it may not play a sound.

What to do if the iPhone does not play a sound

If you try to make it play a sound and nothing happens, check:

  • The Apple Watch is connected.
  • The iPhone has battery.
  • The iPhone is not too far away.
  • It is not turned off.
  • Airplane Mode is not affecting the connection.
  • The Apple Watch is not disconnected.
  • If the iPhone is not nearby, you may need to use the Find My app from another device or from iCloud, where appropriate.

Using the Find Devices app

The Apple Watch may include an app called Find Devices or similar. This app allows you to locate devices associated with your Apple Account, provided that Find My is enabled and the device can communicate its location.

It can be used to locate:

  • iPhone.
  • iPad.
  • Mac.
  • AirPods.
  • Apple Watch.
  • Other compatible devices.

To use it:

  • Press the Digital Crown.
  • Find Find Devices.
  • Double tap.
  • Move through the list with VoiceOver.
  • Choose the device you want to locate.
  • Listen to the available options.
  • Information such as location, distance, status, or the option to play a sound may appear, depending on the device.

Playing a sound on a device

If the device allows it, you can choose to play a sound. This is useful for locating it nearby.

With VoiceOver:

  • Find the device.
  • Double tap.
  • Find Play Sound.
  • Double tap.
  • Listen for the sound emitted by the device.
  • This feature can help with AirPods, iPhone, or other compatible devices.

Find People

The Apple Watch may also have an app for finding people, if you share location with relatives or contacts. This can allow you to know where a person is if they are sharing their location with you.

To use it:

  • Press the Digital Crown.
  • Find Find People.
  • Double tap.
  • Move through the list of people.
  • Choose a person.
  • Listen to the available information.
  • Shared location depends on permissions, connection, and the other person’s settings.

This feature may be useful for relatives, companions, older people, couples, or groups who want to share location voluntarily. It should not be used as a surveillance system. Location sharing must be agreed and configured by the people involved.

Sharing your location

Within the Apple ecosystem, you can share your location with other people. This can be done from the iPhone and, depending on version, it may also be partially checked or managed from the Apple Watch.

It can be useful if:

  • You go out for a walk.
  • You are going to an appointment.
  • You are travelling.
  • You need a trusted person to know where you are.
  • You are accompanying someone.
  • You are in a personal safety situation.
  • The main configuration is usually more comfortable from the iPhone, in the Find My app.
  • The Apple Watch can then be used to check or use that information.

Finding items

If you use AirTag or other accessories compatible with Find My, you can locate them from Apple devices. The Apple Watch may allow access to some related features, depending on version and configuration.

This can be used to find:

  • Keys.
  • Backpack.
  • Bag.
  • Wallet.
  • Other objects with an AirTag or compatible accessory.

For a blind person, an AirTag can be useful when combined with sound and location from the Find My app. The experience will depend on the environment, the object, and the device used. In many cases, the iPhone may offer more options than the Apple Watch for finding items precisely.

Using Maps from the Apple Watch

The Apple Watch can use Maps for directions. It can show or announce route information, turns, distance, and alerts, depending on configuration. It can also use vibrations to indicate certain actions during navigation, depending on the route and mode of travel.

To open Maps:

  • Press the Digital Crown.
  • Find Maps.
  • Double tap.
  • From there, you can search for destinations, review routes, or continue navigation started from the iPhone.

For a blind person, it may be more comfortable to start the route from the iPhone and use the Apple Watch as a companion for alerts on the wrist.

Navigation with vibrations

One of the interesting possibilities of the Apple Watch is receiving haptic alerts during a route. This can help you notice directions without depending only on audio. The behaviour may vary depending on the type of route, the app being used, and the configuration. It should not replace orientation and mobility skills by itself, nor other accessible navigation tools. The Apple Watch can complement navigation, but it should not be the only reference for moving safely.

Finding places with Siri

Siri can also help search for locations.

Examples:

  • Where is the nearest pharmacy?
  • Take me home.
  • How do I get to the station?
  • Open Maps.
  • Find a nearby café.
  • These features depend on connection, location, and available data.
  • For important routes, it is advisable to review the information on the iPhone before starting.

Location and privacy

Location features are useful, but they involve privacy. The Apple Watch and iPhone can use your location for maps, workouts, finding devices, emergencies, weather, automations, and other services. It is worth reviewing which apps have permission to use location.

From the iPhone:

  • Settings.
  • Privacy and Security.
  • Location Services.
  • There, you can review permissions.
  • There is no need to turn everything off. If location is disabled, some useful features will stop working.
  • The important thing is to understand what is being shared and with whom.

Find My and Activation Lock

Find My is also related to device security. When Find My is enabled, it helps locate lost devices and takes part in protection mechanisms such as Activation Lock. This is important if you lose the Apple Watch or if you buy a used one. If the Apple Watch is still associated with someone else’s account, it may remain locked and you will not be able to use it normally. That is why we insisted earlier on checking second-hand watches carefully.

Using the Apple Watch to find the iPhone at home

This is one of the most common uses.

Typical situations:

  • The iPhone is in Silent Mode.
  • You do not remember where you left it.
  • It is in another room.
  • It is in a backpack.
  • It is on the sofa.
  • It is under papers.
  • It is in the bathroom, because apparently phones also go on little excursions.

In these cases:

  • Open Control Centre.
  • Find the button to make the iPhone play a sound.
  • Double tap.
  • Follow the sound.
  • It is a simple feature, but a very useful one.

Using the iPhone to find the Apple Watch

The opposite can also happen: you cannot find the Apple Watch. From the iPhone, you can use the Find My app to locate it or make it play a sound, provided that Find My is enabled and the watch can communicate. This is useful if you left it charging, on a table, in a backpack, or among clothes. If the watch has no battery, location may be limited.

Location during exercise

The Apple Watch can use location for outdoor workouts.

For example:

  • Outdoor walking.
  • Running.
  • Cycling.
  • Routes.
  • Distance.
  • Route map.
  • This will depend on model, connection, and permissions.
  • If you exercise outdoors, it is useful to have location properly configured.
  • This will be explained in more detail in the exercise section.

Location in emergencies

Location can also be important in emergency features. If an emergency call is made or safety features are used, location may be relevant. This topic will be covered in the personal safety section. It is useful to keep it in mind, but not configure it blindly without understanding it.

Common mistakes

Not knowing how to open Control Centre.

Not finding the button to make the iPhone play a sound.

  • Having the iPhone too far away.
  • Having Bluetooth disabled.
  • Having Airplane Mode enabled.

Thinking the watch will locate a turned-off iPhone without conditions. Turning off location and then expecting Maps or Find My to work. Buying a used Apple Watch locked to the previous owner’s account. Sharing location without reviewing with whom. Relying only on the watch for outdoor orientation.

Practical advice

Learn as soon as possible how to make the iPhone play a sound from the Apple Watch. It is one of the simplest and most useful features. Then review the Find My app on the iPhone and make sure your devices are correctly associated with your Apple Account. If you use AirPods, AirTag, or other Apple devices, also try locating them from the Find My app.

Exercise for module 20

Place the iPhone in a nearby room.

  • Put on the Apple Watch.
  • Return to the watch face.
  • Press the side button once to open Control Centre.
  • Swipe until you find the button to find or make the iPhone play a sound.
  • Double tap.
  • Listen for the sound of the iPhone.
  • Go to where it is.
  • Then open the Apple Watch app list.
  • Find Find Devices.
  • Open it.
  • Move through the available devices.
  • Choose the iPhone if it appears.
  • Check whether there is an option to play a sound.
  • Do not change settings you do not understand.
  • Then, on the iPhone, open the Find My app.
  • Check that the Apple Watch appears.

Summary of module 20

The Apple Watch can make the iPhone play a sound from Control Centre. This feature is very useful when you cannot find the phone nearby. The Find Devices app allows you to locate devices associated with your Apple Account. Find People allows you to check voluntarily shared locations. Location is useful for maps, exercise, safety, and finding devices. Some features depend on connection, battery, permissions, and configuration. Privacy should be reviewed from the iPhone. The Apple Watch can complement orientation, but it should not replace specific mobility tools.

Module 21. Apple Pay and Wallet

Apple Pay and Wallet may vary depending on country or region, bank, card issuer, type of card, shop, and device configuration. If Apple Pay does not appear, or if a card cannot be added, that does not necessarily mean that VoiceOver is failing.

The Apple Watch can be used to pay in shops, use compatible cards, show passes, tickets, boarding passes, or loyalty cards, as long as they have been added to Wallet and are compatible.

This feature can be very convenient because it allows you to pay from your wrist without taking out the iPhone, without looking for the physical card, and without depending on seeing the payment terminal screen. For a blind person, this can be useful as long as it is configured correctly and the procedure is well understood.

However, Apple Pay is not available with every bank, every card, every country, or every shop. So before relying on this feature, it is worth checking that your card and bank are compatible.

What Wallet is

Wallet is Apple’s app for storing cards and passes.

It can include:

  • Bank cards compatible with Apple Pay.
  • Transport cards, where available.
  • Boarding passes.
  • Tickets.
  • Passes.
  • Loyalty cards.
  • Digital keys, if compatible.
  • Other documents or items supported by Apple and by each service.
  • On the Apple Watch, Wallet allows you to use some of these items directly from your wrist.

What Apple Pay is

Apple Pay is Apple’s payment system. It allows you to pay by bringing the iPhone or Apple Watch close to a compatible payment terminal. On the Apple Watch, Apple Pay is usually activated by double-pressing the side button. The side button is the elongated button located near the Digital Crown. It must not be confused with the Digital Crown.

To use Apple Pay on the Apple Watch, you need:

  • A compatible Apple Watch.
  • A paired iPhone.
  • A compatible bank card.
  • A compatible bank or issuer.
  • A passcode enabled on the Apple Watch.
  • Wallet configured.
  • The watch unlocked and worn on your wrist.

Why the passcode is required

To use Apple Pay on the Apple Watch, the watch must have a passcode. This is a security measure. When you put on the Apple Watch, you unlock it with the passcode. While it remains on your wrist, it stays unlocked. If you take it off, the watch locks and the passcode will need to be entered again. This prevents another person from simply taking the watch and paying with it. So if you want to use Apple Pay, do not disable the passcode.

Adding a card to the Apple Watch

The most convenient way to add a card to the Apple Watch is usually from the iPhone.

On the iPhone:

  • Open the Watch app.
  • Go to My Watch.
  • Find Wallet and Apple Pay.
  • Enter that option.
  • Choose to add a card.
  • Follow the steps shown by the iPhone.
  • It may ask you to verify the card with the bank.
  • Verification may be done by SMS, banking app, phone call, email, or the method determined by the issuer.
  • The exact process depends on the bank.
  • If you already have cards in Apple Pay on the iPhone, an option may appear to add them to the Apple Watch as well.

Adding a card from Wallet

It can also be done from the Wallet app on the iPhone, but for the Apple Watch it is usually clearer to do it from the Watch app. The important thing is that the card must be added to the watch, not only to the iPhone. Having a card on the iPhone does not automatically mean it is ready on the Apple Watch. You need to check it.

Checking cards on the Apple Watch

To review the cards that have been added:

  • Double-press the side button.
  • VoiceOver should announce Wallet or the available card, if Apple Pay is configured.
  • You can also open Wallet from the app list.

With VoiceOver:

  • Move through the cards.
  • Listen to which one is selected.
  • If you have several cards, you need to know which one will be used for payment.
  • It is advisable to have a clear default card.

Default card

If you have several cards in Wallet, one of them can be set as the default. That will be the one used first when Apple Pay is activated, unless you choose another one. From the iPhone, you can review or change the default card in Wallet and Apple Pay settings. For a blind person, having the default card configured correctly helps avoid mistakes at the moment of payment.

Paying with the Apple Watch

To pay with the Apple Watch:

  • Check that you are wearing the watch and that it is unlocked.
  • In the shop, when the terminal is ready for payment, double-press the side button on the Apple Watch.
  • Wait for Wallet to appear.
  • VoiceOver may announce the card.
  • Bring the Apple Watch close to the payment terminal.
  • Keep the watch close until you feel the confirmation.
  • There may be a vibration, sound, or on-screen confirmation.
  • Then move the watch away.
  • You do not need to open the Wallet app manually if you use the double-press of the side button.
  • The double-press must be done on the side button, not on the Digital Crown.

Where to place the watch

The Apple Watch should be brought close to the payment terminal, usually with the watch screen area facing the terminal. There is no need to hit the terminal or press the watch hard against it. Bring it close and keep it there for a few seconds. If the payment does not go through the first time, move your wrist slightly and bring it close again.

Some terminals have the contact area at the top, others on the side, others near the screen. If you do not know where it is, you can ask the cashier to indicate where to place the watch.

Privacy when paying

When you pay with Apple Watch, you do not need to hand over your physical card. This can be convenient and secure. Even so, it is useful to listen to which card is selected if you have several.

It is also useful to pay attention to the amount shown on the payment terminal. If you cannot see it, you can ask for the amount to be confirmed before bringing the watch close.

A simple sentence can help:

  • Could you confirm the amount before I pay, please?
  • It is a simple phrase, but it avoids mistakes.

What to do if you have several cards

If you have several cards and want to choose a specific one:

  • Double-press the side button.
  • When Wallet appears, move through the cards with VoiceOver or with the available gestures.
  • Select the card you want.
  • Bring the watch close to the terminal.
  • In fast payment situations, this may be less convenient.
  • That is why it is advisable to set as default the card you usually use.

What to do if Apple Pay does not work

If Apple Pay does not work, check:

  • The watch is unlocked.
  • The watch is on your wrist.
  • A passcode is configured.
  • The card has been added to the Apple Watch.
  • The card is still active.
  • The bank has not blocked the card.
  • The shop accepts contactless payments.
  • The terminal is ready.
  • You have double-pressed the side button.
  • You have placed the watch correctly near the terminal.
  • You are not using a card that still requires pending verification.
  • If the problem continues, review Wallet and Apple Pay on the iPhone.

Limits and confirmations

Some payments may ask for additional confirmation depending on amount, bank, country, or terminal. In some cases, you may need to enter the card PIN on the shop’s payment terminal. This does not depend on the Apple Watch, but on the bank, the shop, and payment regulations. If the terminal asks for a PIN, you will need to enter it on the shop terminal.

For a blind person, entering a PIN on touch terminals or poorly accessible terminals can be a problem. In those cases, it is useful to ask for assistance carefully, always protecting the privacy of the code. If the terminal has a physical keypad with tactile markings, it will be easier.

Using Wallet for cards, passes, and tickets

In addition to payments, Wallet can contain other items.

For example:

  • Boarding passes.
  • Event tickets.
  • Travel tickets.
  • Passes.
  • Loyalty cards.
  • Transport cards, where available.

To use them from the Apple Watch:

  • Open Wallet.
  • Find the corresponding pass.
  • Double tap or select it.
  • Bring the watch close to the reader if required.
  • The behaviour depends on the type of pass.
  • Some show a code.
  • Others use contactless communication.
  • Others only show information.

Using transport cards

In some places, Wallet allows transport cards to be used on the Apple Watch. This depends on the country, city, transport system, and compatible card. If available, it may allow access to transport by bringing the watch close to the reader. In some cases, there is an Express Mode that allows a transport card to be used without opening Wallet each time. This feature must be configured carefully, because it is not available everywhere. For a blind person, it can be very useful if it works well in their city. But it should not be taken for granted.

Wallet and VoiceOver

Wallet is compatible with VoiceOver, but use may vary depending on the type of card or pass.

With VoiceOver, you can hear:

  1. Card name.
  2. Type of pass.
  3. Available information.
  4. More options buttons.
  5. Card status.

If a pass has visual codes, the person scanning it may need to use their reader or terminal. In that case, you only need to show the pass on the screen or bring the watch close, depending on what is required.

Security if you lose the Apple Watch

If you lose the Apple Watch, you can use the Find My app from the iPhone or another device to try to locate it or mark it as lost. Because the watch has a passcode and Apple Pay requires it to be unlocked on your wrist, there are security measures.

Even so, if you lose the watch, it is advisable to act quickly:

  • Use Find My.
  • Mark the device as lost if appropriate.
  • Contact your bank if you have doubts.
  • Review your cards in Wallet.
  • Do not wait several days if cards are configured.

Removing a card from the Apple Watch

You can remove a card from the Watch app on the iPhone.

On the iPhone:

  • Open the Watch app.
  • Go to My Watch.
  • Go to Wallet and Apple Pay.
  • Select the card.
  • Look for the option to remove or delete the card.
  • Confirm.
  • It may also be managed from Wallet or from account settings, depending on the case.
  • Do not remove a card if you only want to change the default card.

Apple Pay and battery

Apple Pay requires the watch to have battery and work correctly. If the Apple Watch is turned off or has no battery, you will not be able to pay with it. If you depend on the watch for payments, check the battery before leaving home. Carrying an alternative physical card may be advisable, especially at the beginning. Technology is very convenient until the battery decides to remind you that you still live in the real world.

When it is useful to use Apple Pay on the watch

It can be very useful:

  • In shops.
  • In cafés.
  • On compatible transport systems.
  • For quick purchases.
  • When you do not want to take out the iPhone.
  • When your hands are busy.
  • When you want to avoid handling cash.

When it may be better to use another method

It may be better to use another method:

  • If you do not know the amount.
  • If the terminal is not accessible and asks for a PIN.
  • If the watch has low battery.
  • If you are not sure which card is selected.
  • If the shop does not accept contactless payment.
  • If there are connection or verification problems.
  • If it is an important purchase and you prefer to review everything from the iPhone.

Common mistakes

Thinking that having a card on the iPhone means having it on the watch.

Double-pressing the Digital Crown instead of the side button.

  • Not having a passcode enabled.
  • Not wearing the watch unlocked.
  • Not knowing which card is selected.

Placing the watch incorrectly near the terminal.

  • Not confirming the amount before paying.
  • Depending only on the watch without carrying an alternative.
  • Not checking whether the bank is compatible.
  • Not knowing how to remove a card if you lose the watch.

Practical advice

If you are going to use Apple Pay on the Apple Watch, practise first without pressure. Add a card. Check that it appears in Wallet.

Double-press the side button at home to hear how Wallet opens, without bringing it close to any terminal.

  • Learn to recognise the default card.
  • Then make a first small purchase in a quiet shop.
  • Ask them to confirm the amount before paying.
  • Once you know how the watch responds, using it will feel much more natural.

Exercise for module 21

Open the Watch app on the iPhone.

  • Go to My Watch.
  • Find Wallet and Apple Pay.
  • Check whether there is a card added to the Apple Watch.
  • If there is not and you want to use Apple Pay, start the process to add a card.
  • Follow the bank verification steps.
  • When the card has been added, put on the Apple Watch.
  • Unlock it if necessary.
  • Double-press the side button.
  • Listen to what VoiceOver announces.
  • Check which card appears.
  • Do not bring the watch close to any terminal during this practice.
  • Close Wallet or return to the watch face.
  • Then review which card is set as default from the iPhone.

Summary of module 21

Wallet allows you to use cards, passes, and other compatible items. Apple Pay allows you to pay with the Apple Watch in compatible shops. To use Apple Pay, you need a passcode enabled on the watch. The card must be added to the Apple Watch, not only to the iPhone. To pay, double-press the side button. The side button is not the Digital Crown. It is useful to confirm the amount before paying. If you have several cards, review which one is the default. Apple Pay depends on the bank, card, country, and shop. If you lose the watch, use Find My and review your cards. It is advisable to carry an alternative payment method, especially at the beginning.

Module 22. What the Apple Watch records when you move

The Apple Watch is not only useful for receiving notifications, answering calls, or checking the time. One of its main functions is recording physical activity.

The watch can measure daily movement, exercise minutes, stand time, steps, approximate distance, workouts, heart rate during activity, and other related data, depending on model and configuration.

This part of the course is important because many people buy an Apple Watch precisely to move more, monitor their activity better, or have a daily reference for health and exercise. For a blind person, this information can be useful if it is presented clearly with VoiceOver and if each item of data is properly understood. The idea is not to become obsessed with numbers. The idea is to use the watch as support.

Activity is not the same as workout

Before starting, it is useful to distinguish between two concepts:

  1. Daily activity.
  2. Workout.

Daily activity is everything you do throughout the day: moving around at home, walking, standing up, getting from one place to another, climbing stairs, running errands, cleaning, cooking, or any movement the watch can record.

A workout is a specific session that you start or that the watch detects, such as outdoor walking, running, cycling, strength training, swimming, or specific exercises.

  • Activity is recorded throughout the day.
  • A workout is started to measure a specific activity in more detail.
  • Both things are related, but they are not the same.

The Activity rings

The Apple Watch organises daily activity into three main rings:

  • Move.
  • Exercise.
  • Stand.
  • These rings are a simple way to show daily progress.
  • The Move ring records active calories.
  • The Exercise ring records minutes of activity with a certain level of intensity.
  • The Stand ring records the hours in which you have stood up and moved a little.
  • The rings can be motivating for some people.
  • For others, they may be irrelevant, uncomfortable, or even annoying.

There is no need to turn three coloured rings into a moral judgment about your existence. They are data, not a court sentence.

Move ring

The Move ring measures active calories. Active calories are the calories the watch estimates you burn through movement and activity, beyond resting energy. This is an estimate.

It is calculated using several factors, such as:

  • Movement.
  • Heart rate.
  • Age.
  • Weight.
  • Height.
  • Registered sex.
  • Type of activity.
  • Personal settings.
  • Apple Watch model.
  • Sensor data.
  • This means the number is not an exact laboratory measurement.

It is a useful reference for comparing activity between days or weeks, but it should not be treated as an absolute truth. If your personal data are not configured correctly in the Health app on the iPhone, the estimate may be less useful.

Exercise ring

The Exercise ring measures minutes of activity that the watch interprets as having a certain level of intensity. Not every movement counts as exercise. A gentle walk around the house may count partly or may not count in the same way as a brisk walk. If you start a workout, the Apple Watch can record that session more accurately. This is important. If you want the watch to measure a walk, a training session, or a specific activity properly, it is best to start the corresponding workout. The watch may detect some activities automatically, but it is better not to rely only on that.

Stand ring

The Stand ring is designed to encourage you to move during different hours of the day. It does not simply mean standing still. The Apple Watch usually looks for a certain amount of movement during an hour in order to count that hour as achieved. If, near the end of an hour, the watch detects that you have not moved enough, it may send you a reminder to stand or move. This can be useful for people who spend many hours sitting. But it may not suit every person.

For example, a person with reduced mobility, certain disabilities, fatigue, pain, or a specific health condition may need to adjust this feature or not give it too much importance. The Apple Watch should adapt to the person, not the other way around.

Steps

The Apple Watch can count steps. This information can be useful to know approximately how much you have walked during the day. However, step counting may vary depending on movement, how the watch is worn, whether you also carry the iPhone, the type of activity, and other factors. It is a useful estimate, but it should not be treated as a perfect measurement.

For many people, steps are an easy reference:

  • Today I walked more.
  • Today I walked less.
  • This week I moved more.
  • This month I have been more sedentary.
  • That kind of comparison is usually more useful than obsessing over the exact number.

Distance

The Apple Watch can estimate distance. For outdoor activity, it may use GPS, either from the watch itself or from the iPhone, depending on model and situation. Indoors, it may use estimates based on movement, calibration, and other data. Distance may be more accurate in some situations than in others. Walking outdoors with a good signal usually provides better data than moving indoors.

Heart rate

The Apple Watch can measure heart rate. During the day, it can record values at rest, while walking, or during activity. During workouts, heart rate can be especially useful for understanding intensity. For a person who exercises, it can help indicate whether they are walking gently, moderately, or more intensely. But it is important to remember something: the Apple Watch does not replace a medical evaluation. If alerts, unusual data, or symptoms appear, healthcare professionals should be consulted.

Active calories

Active calories are an estimate. The watch calculates this using information such as movement, heart rate, age, weight, height, registered sex, activity, and other factors. It should not be understood as an exact absolute figure. It is useful as a reference for comparing days, seeing trends, and adjusting goals. If personal data are configured incorrectly, estimates may be less useful. For that reason, it is advisable to review age, weight, height, and other data in the Health app on the iPhone.

Exercise minutes

Exercise minutes help show how long you have been doing activity with a certain intensity. If you start workouts, the watch can record those minutes more accurately. If you do not start workouts, the Apple Watch may detect part of the activity, but not always with the same level of detail. For people who want to monitor their walks or sessions properly, it is advisable to start the corresponding workout.

Stand time

Stand time does not simply mean standing without moving. The watch looks for a certain amount of movement during an hour in order to count it as achieved. It may alert you near the end of an hour if you have not met that goal. If this feature does not interest you or does not suit your physical situation, it can be adjusted.

Workouts

When you start a workout, the Apple Watch records the activity in more detail.

It can measure:

  • Time.
  • Distance.
  • Pace.
  • Heart rate.
  • Active calories.
  • Total calories.
  • Route, where appropriate.
  • Elevation, where appropriate.
  • Other data depending on the workout type.

Exercising without starting the Workout app may record part of the activity, but starting the workout helps provide more complete data.

Automatic workout detection

The Apple Watch can detect that you have started certain workouts and suggest recording them. For example, it may detect that you are walking or running. If a notification appears, you can accept recording the workout. It may also remind you to end a workout if it detects that you have stopped. This feature can be useful, but it is not advisable to depend only on it. If you are going to work out, the best approach is to start the workout manually or with Siri.

Trends

Over time, the Apple Watch and iPhone can show activity trends. Trends help show whether your activity is increasing, decreasing, or staying the same.

This can be more useful than looking at an isolated number.

  • One bad day means very little.
  • A trend over several weeks can say more.
  • That is why it is useful not to judge everything by a single day.

The body is not a spreadsheet, even if technology sometimes behaves as if life should fit neatly into cells and graphs.

Personal data matter

For activity data to be more useful, personal information must be properly configured.

This may include:

  • Age.
  • Height.
  • Weight.
  • Registered sex.
  • Wheelchair use, if applicable.
  • Health information relevant to activity.
  • Some of these data are configured in the Health app on the iPhone.
  • If the data are wrong, calculations for calories, activity, and other metrics may be less useful.
  • It is advisable to review them from time to time, especially weight if it changes significantly.

Wheelchair use

The Apple Watch includes options related to wheelchair use. When wheelchair use is configured, some activity measurements and goals can change. For example, Stand goals may be adapted to rolling or movement goals. This is important because the same movement pattern does not apply to all bodies.

If the person uses a wheelchair, it is advisable to configure that information correctly in the Health app so the watch offers more appropriate activity data.

Movement and disability

Not everyone moves in the same way.

A blind person may walk, train, run, or do sport.

  • Another person may have additional mobility difficulties.
  • Another may have fatigue, balance issues, chronic pain, or other conditions.
  • Another may be a wheelchair user.

That is why activity goals should be realistic and adapted to each person. The Apple Watch can encourage movement, but it should not become pressure. If a goal is too high, it can discourage. If a goal is too low, it may not help. The goal should be useful, not decorative.

How VoiceOver reads activity data

With VoiceOver, activity data can be checked from the watch or from the iPhone. On the Apple Watch, you can open apps such as Activity, Workout, or Heart Rate. On the iPhone, you can review more detailed data in the Fitness app and Health app. For many people, the watch is useful for quick checks. The iPhone is better for reviewing data in more detail.

This distinction is important:

  • Apple Watch for quick information.
  • iPhone for detailed review.

Data that may be better checked on the iPhone

Some information is easier to review on the iPhone.

For example:

  • Daily activity history.
  • Weekly trends.
  • Health graphs.
  • Sleep details.
  • Heart rate history.
  • Workout summaries.
  • Routes.
  • Monthly progress.
  • Data comparisons.
  • The iPhone screen and the Health and Fitness apps make detailed exploration easier with VoiceOver.
  • The Apple Watch is useful, but it is not the best place for long data analysis.

When the data may be wrong or incomplete

Some data may be inaccurate or incomplete.

Possible reasons include:

  • The watch is too loose.
  • The sensors are dirty.
  • The activity type was not started.
  • The movement was irregular.
  • The GPS signal was poor.
  • The iPhone was not nearby, depending on the model.
  • Personal data are outdated.
  • The battery ran out.
  • The watch was not worn properly.
  • A feature is not available on that model.
  • This does not mean the Apple Watch is useless.
  • It simply means that activity data should be interpreted as guidance.

How to improve activity records

To improve records:

  • Wear the watch properly adjusted.
  • Keep sensors clean.
  • Update personal data in Health.
  • Start workouts when you exercise.
  • Choose the correct workout type.
  • Check that location is enabled for outdoor activities.
  • Keep the watch charged.
  • Use a strap that holds the watch firmly.
  • Review settings if data seem strange.
  • These simple steps can improve the usefulness of the data.

What not to do with activity data

  • Do not obsess over one day.
  • Do not compare yourself constantly with other people.
  • Do not treat calories as an exact figure.
  • Do not ignore symptoms because the watch shows normal data.
  • Do not panic over one unusual reading.
  • Do not start an exercise routine without medical advice if your health situation requires it.
  • Do not let the watch decide your self-worth.

An Apple Watch can measure movement. It cannot measure common sense, although judging by some behaviour, that feature would have a market.

Practical use for a blind person

For a blind person, activity data can be useful to:

  • Know whether they are moving more or less.
  • Record walks.
  • Track exercise routines.
  • Receive vibration alerts.
  • Check heart rate during activity.
  • Review daily goals.
  • Monitor trends.
  • Use Siri to start workouts.
  • Receive reminders to move.
  • The key is to configure the watch so that the information is easy to access and the alerts are not excessive.

Common mistakes

Thinking that activity and workout are the same.

  • Not starting workouts.
  • Interpreting active calories as exact.
  • Having personal data configured incorrectly.
  • Wearing the watch too loose.
  • Ignoring model limitations.
  • Obsessing over rings.
  • Not reviewing data on the iPhone.
  • Disabling useful alerts without understanding them.
  • Activating too many notifications.

Practical advice

Use the Apple Watch as an activity guide, not as a judge.

  • Start with simple goals.
  • Learn to start a workout.
  • Review daily activity without obsessing.
  • Use weekly trends to understand progress.
  • If a health-related figure concerns you, consult healthcare professionals.

Exercise for module 22

Put on the Apple Watch properly adjusted.

  • Open the Activity app.
  • Listen to what VoiceOver announces.
  • Move through the Move, Exercise, and Stand rings.
  • Check whether steps or distance appear.
  • Open the Heart Rate app.
  • Listen to the available data.
  • Open the Fitness app on the iPhone.
  • Review the activity summary.
  • Compare what is easier to check on the watch and what is easier on the iPhone.
  • If you go for a walk, start an Outdoor Walk workout and check the data afterwards.

Summary of module 22

The Apple Watch records daily activity and workouts. Activity and workout are not the same.

The main rings are Move, Exercise, and Stand.

  • Move measures active calories.
  • Exercise measures minutes of activity with a certain intensity.
  • Stand encourages movement during different hours of the day.
  • The watch can also record steps, distance, and heart rate.
  • Starting a workout provides more complete data.
  • Personal data influence calculations.
  • The watch must be properly adjusted on the wrist.
  • The data are guidance, not punishment.

Module 23. The Activity or Fitness app

The Apple Watch and iPhone work together to show information about movement, exercise, and daily habits. On the Apple Watch, the main app for checking these data is usually called Activity. On the iPhone, the app where this information is reviewed in more detail is usually called Fitness.

The general idea is simple:

  • The Apple Watch records what you do during the day.
  • The iPhone allows you to review that information with more space, more detail, and more comfort.

For a blind person using VoiceOver, it is useful to learn both parts. The watch is useful for quick checks. The iPhone is better for reviewing details.

What the Activity app on Apple Watch is

The Activity app on the Apple Watch allows you to check your daily progress.

It shows the three main rings:

  • Move.
  • Exercise.
  • Stand.
  • It may also show steps, distance, weekly activity, awards, trends, or summaries, depending on the system version.
  • On the watch screen, information is shown in a compact way.
  • With VoiceOver, you can move through the information with swipes and listen to each piece of data.

Opening the Activity app

To open Activity on the Apple Watch:

  • Return to the watch face.
  • Press the Digital Crown to open the app list.
  • Find Activity.
  • Double tap.
  • When it opens, VoiceOver will read the first available item.
  • From there, move through the screen with swipes.
  • If there is more information further down, use the Digital Crown to scroll.

Listening to the rings with VoiceOver

Although the rings are visual, VoiceOver can read the information.

When you move through the Activity app, VoiceOver can announce data such as:

  • Move progress.
  • Exercise minutes.
  • Stand hours.
  • Steps.
  • Distance.
  • Trends or summaries, if available.
  • The exact wording may vary depending on the version and configuration.
  • The important thing is not to see the rings, but to understand what each one represents.

Move

The Move section shows active calories. It tells you how much movement the watch estimates you have done in relation to your daily goal. This figure is an estimate. It depends on movement, heart rate, personal data, and other factors. It is useful for following a trend, but it should not be treated as a perfect number.

Exercise

The Exercise section shows minutes of activity that the watch considers intense enough. The usual goal is thirty minutes a day, although this may be adjusted depending on the person and configuration. If you do a workout and start it from the Workout app, those minutes are usually recorded more clearly.

Stand

The Stand section shows how many hours of the day you have stood up and moved a little. For wheelchair users, this may be adapted to a different movement metric, depending on configuration. This point is important, because not all bodies move in the same way. If the person uses a wheelchair, mobility settings must be configured correctly in the Health app on the iPhone.

Steps and distance

The Activity app may also show steps and distance. These data can help you understand how much you have moved during the day. Again, they are useful references, not perfect measurements. A blind person may find steps and distance especially useful when going for walks, moving around the city, or comparing activity between days.

Weekly summary

The Activity app may show a weekly summary. This summary helps you see how the week has gone and adjust goals. It may show averages, progress, and recommendations. With VoiceOver, it is useful to move through it slowly. A weekly summary is more useful than looking only at one day. One day can be unusual for a thousand reasons. A week gives a clearer idea.

Awards and achievements

The Apple Watch can give awards or achievements for meeting goals, closing rings, keeping streaks, or completing challenges.

  • These awards can motivate some people.
  • Others will not care about them at all, and that is also fine.
  • Motivation should adapt to each person.
  • If awards help, use them.
  • If they are annoying, ignore them.

The important thing is to move better, not to collect digital medals as if the watch were a school with too many stickers.

Activity notifications

The Apple Watch can send activity-related notifications.

For example:

  • Stand reminders.
  • Daily progress.
  • Goal completed.
  • Activity summary.
  • Challenges.
  • Achievements.
  • Suggestions.
  • These notifications can be adjusted from the Watch app on the iPhone.
  • If they help you, keep them.
  • If they interrupt too much, reduce or turn off some of them.

To review these options:

  • Open the Watch app on the iPhone.
  • Go to My Watch.
  • Find Activity.
  • Review the available notifications.

Fitness app on the iPhone

The Fitness app on the iPhone allows you to review activity in more detail. From the iPhone, VoiceOver usually offers a more comfortable experience because there is more space and navigation is more precise.

The Fitness app may show:

  • Daily summary.
  • Rings.
  • Workouts.
  • Trends.
  • Awards.
  • History.
  • Activity sharing.
  • Fitness Plus, if available and used.
  • For reviewing data in detail, the iPhone will almost always be better than the watch.

Opening Fitness on the iPhone

On the iPhone:

  • Open the Fitness app.
  • Explore the screen with VoiceOver.
  • Find the activity summary.
  • Review Move, Exercise, and Stand.
  • Find workouts, if there are any.
  • Find trends or history, if available.
  • If you are using Fitness for the first time, introductory screens or permissions may appear.
  • Listen carefully to each option before accepting or configuring anything.

Difference between Activity and Fitness

The Activity app on the Apple Watch is for quickly checking progress. The Fitness app on the iPhone is for reviewing more information, history, and details.

The watch answers the question:

  • How am I doing today?
  • The iPhone is better for questions such as:
  • How was my week?
  • What workouts did I do?
  • How am I progressing?
  • What trends do I have?
  • What awards or records appear?
  • What data can I review in more detail?

In other words: the watch alerts you and accompanies you; the iPhone lets you analyse. Because apparently even walking now needs charts, trends, and a small statistical committee in your pocket.

Sharing activity

The Fitness app may allow you to share activity with other people. This can be used for motivation with friends, relatives, or groups. You can see the progress of other people and they can see part of yours, depending on configuration. This feature can be useful if used with trusted people. It is not advisable to share activity just for the sake of sharing. Information about movement and exercise is also personal. Not everything that can be shared needs an audience. Astonishing, but true.

Activity and privacy

Physical activity is personal information. Before sharing data, challenges, or progress with other people, it is worth thinking about whether you really want to do it. The watch can motivate you without turning your daily movement into social content.

No obsessing over the data

The Apple Watch can motivate, but it can also create obsession if used badly.

  • Closing rings can be useful.
  • Seeing trends can help.
  • Receiving alerts can encourage you.
  • But no watch should become a constant source of guilt.
  • There are days with less activity.
  • There is illness.
  • There is tiredness.
  • There is work.
  • There is necessary rest.
  • There are personal situations.
  • The goal is to use the data for guidance, not punishment.

Which data to look at first

At the beginning, it is enough to pay attention to only a few data points:

  • Daily movement.
  • Exercise minutes.
  • Stand hours or equivalent metric.
  • Steps.
  • Completed workouts.
  • Heart rate during exercise.
  • There is no need to review everything from the first day.
  • Later, you can explore trends, heart rate zones, sleep, advanced health, and other sections.

Where to check activity

You can check activity from:

  • The Apple Watch, in the Activity app.
  • The iPhone, in the Fitness app.
  • The iPhone, in the Health app for certain data.
  • On the watch, the check is quick.
  • On the iPhone, the information is usually broader and more comfortable to review with VoiceOver.
  • For detailed analysis, the iPhone will be better.
  • For a quick check, the Apple Watch will be enough.

Personal data

Activity estimates depend on personal data.

For example:

  • Age.
  • Height.
  • Weight.
  • Registered sex.
  • Wheelchair use, if applicable.
  • Other relevant data.
  • If these data are wrong, some estimates may be less useful.
  • They do not need to be updated every week, but they should not be completely outdated.

Common mistakes

Never opening the Fitness app on the iPhone. Looking only at the watch and not reviewing trends.

Thinking the rings are an absolute obligation.

  • Not adjusting goals.
  • Adjusting goals too often.
  • Ignoring wheelchair use or reduced mobility in the configuration.
  • Obsessing over awards.
  • Not reviewing personal data.
  • Sharing activity without thinking about privacy.
  • Confusing daily activity with workouts.

Practical advice

During the first week, use Activity and Fitness only to observe. Do not worry too much about closing all the rings. See what the watch records on a normal day. Then adjust goals if needed.

The Apple Watch is more useful when it adapts to your real life, not when it tries to turn you overnight into a different person with new trainers and too much motivation.

Exercise for module 23

On the Apple Watch:

  • Open Activity.
  • Move through the data with VoiceOver.
  • Listen to Move, Exercise, and Stand.
  • Look for steps and distance if they appear.
  • Check whether there is a weekly summary.

Then, on the iPhone:

  • Open Fitness.
  • Find the daily summary.
  • Listen to the main data.
  • Find workouts, if any exist.
  • Explore whether trends or awards appear.
  • Compare which information is more comfortable on the watch and which is better on the iPhone.
  • For one week, review Activity once a day and Fitness two or three times.
  • Do not change goals until you have a clear idea of your real data.

Summary of module 23

  • The Activity app on Apple Watch shows daily progress.
  • The Fitness app on iPhone allows you to review data in more detail.
  • The main rings are Move, Exercise, and Stand.

VoiceOver allows you to listen to the data even if you cannot see the rings. The watch is useful for quick checks. The iPhone is better for reviewing history, trends, and details.

Activity notifications can motivate or annoy, depending on the person.

  • Goals should be realistic.
  • Personal data influence estimates.
  • Physical activity should be used as guidance, not as constant pressure.
