Module 24. Setting activity goals

Activity goals are the daily targets that the Apple Watch uses to measure your progress. These goals help you know whether you have moved, whether you have exercised, and whether you have avoided spending too many hours without activity. They can be motivating, as long as they are well adjusted. A well-chosen goal can encourage you to move a little more. A poorly chosen goal can frustrate you, bore you, or make you ignore the watch completely. That is why activity goals should be configured sensibly.

Which goals can be adjusted

Depending on the version of watchOS, the Apple Watch may allow you to adjust one or more goals.

The main ones are:

  • Move.
  • Exercise.
  • Stand.
  • The Move goal is usually the one most commonly changed.
  • The Exercise goal and the Stand goal may also be available for adjustment, depending on version and configuration.
  • If an option does not appear on your watch, it may depend on the system version.

Move goal

The Move goal is based on active calories. These are not the total calories your body uses during the day. They are the calories associated with movement and activity. This goal is represented by the Move ring. If you complete it, the ring closes. There is no perfect number for everyone.

It depends on:

  • Age.
  • Weight.
  • Height.
  • Daily activity.
  • Fitness level.
  • Mobility.
  • Routine.
  • Health.
  • Personal goals.
  • If the goal is too high, it may be difficult to complete.
  • If it is too low, it may not encourage you to improve.

Exercise goal

The Exercise goal is based on minutes of activity at a certain intensity. The usual value may be set to a specific daily amount.

This goal is represented by the Exercise ring.

  • Not every movement counts as exercise.
  • The watch tries to detect when activity reaches a certain level of intensity.
  • Starting workouts helps record these minutes more accurately.

Stand goal

The Stand goal aims to encourage you to get up and move during several hours of the day. It is not about standing still without moving. The watch needs to detect some movement during an hour for that hour to count. This goal may not suit every person in the same way. For people with reduced mobility or wheelchair users, the configuration must be adapted correctly so that the watch uses appropriate metrics.

When to change goals

It is useful to change goals when:

  • They are too easy for many days.
  • They are too difficult to reach.
  • Your routine changes.
  • You start exercising.
  • You have reduced activity because of health, injury, or recovery.
  • You want to create a gradual habit.
  • You need a more realistic target.
  • It is not advisable to change goals out of frustration after a bad day.
  • Nor is it advisable to raise them too much just because one day went especially well.
  • Goals should be based on trends, not impulses.

How to know whether a goal is well chosen

A good goal should be:

  • Achievable.
  • Slightly motivating.
  • Realistic.
  • Adapted to your situation.
  • Sustainable for several days.
  • Flexible when life changes.
  • If you complete it effortlessly every day, it may be too low.
  • If you never complete it, it may be too high.
  • If you complete it some days and not others, it may be reasonable.
  • Not every day has to be the same.

Physical activity is not a production line. Although some watches seem determined to turn life into shifts measured by rings.

Adjusting goals from the Apple Watch

To adjust goals from the watch:

  • Open the Activity app.
  • Move through the screen until you find options related to changing goals.
  • Activate Change Goals, if it appears.
  • Adjust the Move goal.
  • Continue.
  • Adjust Exercise, if the system allows it.
  • Continue.
  • Adjust Stand, if the system allows it.
  • Confirm.
  • With VoiceOver, use swipes to move through the controls.
  • The Digital Crown may be used to change values in some contexts.
  • Listen carefully to each amount before confirming.

Adjusting the Move goal

When you are on the Move goal:

  • VoiceOver should announce the current value.
  • Find the controls to increase or decrease it.
  • Change the value gradually.
  • Do not make extreme changes.
  • Confirm when the value makes sense.
  • If you do not know what to set, use the current goal for a few days and observe.

Adjusting the Exercise goal

If the watch allows you to adjust Exercise:

  • Listen to the number of minutes.
  • Increase or decrease it according to your situation.
  • Confirm.
  • For many people, starting with a moderate target is more useful than trying to do too much from the first day.

Adjusting the Stand goal

If the watch allows you to adjust Stand:

  • Listen to the number of hours.
  • Adjust it if appropriate.
  • Confirm.
  • This goal should be adapted to each person’s routine and mobility.
  • If it does not fit your situation well, also review health and mobility data on the iPhone.

Using the Digital Crown to change values

In some settings, turning the Digital Crown can increase or decrease values. Do it slowly. Then listen to the selected value. Do not confirm until you are sure. If you go too far, turn it in the opposite direction or use the corresponding control to decrease the value.

Adjusting goals from the iPhone

Some options may be reviewed from the iPhone, in Fitness or Health, depending on version. The iPhone may be more comfortable for reviewing data, but daily goals are usually adjusted from Activity on the Apple Watch. If you cannot find an option on the iPhone, check the watch. If you cannot find it on the watch, it may depend on the version.

Starting with gentle goals

If you are starting out, it is better to choose gentle goals.

Examples:

  • Walk a little more.
  • Complete some exercise minutes.
  • Reduce long periods without moving.
  • Create a routine.
  • The goal is not to impress the watch.
  • The goal is to build a habit.
  • A small goal completed consistently can be more useful than a huge goal abandoned after a week.

Increasing goals gradually

When a goal is completed easily for several days or weeks, you can increase it.

  • Do it gradually.
  • There is no need to double it.
  • You can increase it slightly and observe.

For example:

  • Raise the Move goal a little.
  • Add a few exercise minutes.
  • Increase the Stand goal by one hour if it makes sense.
  • Then observe for a week.

Lowering goals when needed

Lowering a goal is not failure.

It may be necessary if:

  • You have been ill.
  • You are recovering.
  • Your routine has changed.
  • You have less mobility temporarily.
  • The previous goal was not realistic.
  • It was creating unnecessary pressure.
  • The Apple Watch should adapt to your real life.
  • There is no point maintaining an impossible goal just so a number appears more dignified.

Rest days

  • Rest also matters.
  • The Apple Watch can encourage you to maintain streaks, but the body needs rest.
  • If you train, lighter days or recovery days are part of the process.
  • Not every day should have the same intensity.
  • For some people, closing rings every day can be motivating.
  • For others, it can lead to doing activity when it is not advisable.
  • Health comes before the digital medal.

Walking goals

If your main activity is walking, you can use the Apple Watch to:

  • Monitor daily movement.
  • Record walks as workouts.
  • Review distance.
  • Review time.
  • Review heart rate.
  • Observe trends.
  • For walking, it can be useful to start an Outdoor Walk or Indoor Walk workout, depending on the situation.
  • This helps the watch record the session better.

Goals for older people

For older people, goals should be reasonable. Consistency may matter more than intensity.

The most relevant areas are usually:

  • Gentle movement.
  • Avoiding too many hours without moving.
  • Walks.
  • Safe routines.
  • Important alerts.
  • Fall Detection, if appropriate.
  • Excessive goals should not be configured without good reason.

Goals for people with reduced mobility

If there is reduced mobility, goals must be adapted. Health data and wheelchair settings should be reviewed if applicable. The watch can be useful, but the targets must make sense for the person. One person’s activity should not be compared with another’s without considering their physical situation.

Goals for active people

If you already exercise frequently, you can use more demanding goals.

But it is advisable to review:

  • Recovery.
  • Sleep.
  • Heart rate.
  • Trends.
  • Workouts.
  • Injuries or overload.
  • Increasing goals can be motivating, but it should not replace sensible physical planning.

Progress notifications

The Apple Watch can send notifications related to goals.

  • It may tell you that you are close to completing them.
  • It may encourage you to move.
  • It may congratulate you when you close them.
  • It may suggest challenges.

If these notifications help, leave them on. If they are annoying, adjust Activity notifications.

Motivation without pressure

Goals are useful when they motivate. They stop being useful when they create guilt, anxiety, or an absurd relationship with the watch. The Apple Watch should be a tool. It should not decide your daily value. You are not a better person because you closed a ring. You are not a disaster because one day you did not close it. This seems obvious, but quantified technology has a talent for turning obvious things into vibrating statistics.

Common mistakes

Setting goals too high from the beginning.

  • Never changing goals.
  • Changing goals every day.
  • Obsessing over closing rings.
  • Not starting workouts and then being surprised by the data.
  • Ignoring rest days.
  • Not adapting goals to health or mobility.
  • Not reviewing personal data.
  • Comparing yourself with other people.
  • Treating active calories as exact data.

Practical advice

Use the first week as observation. Do not try to adjust everything on the first day. See what the watch records in your normal life. Then choose a goal that you can complete most days, but that encourages you to move a little more. Review every few weeks. Not every few hours.

Exercise for module 24

For one week, review your daily activity without changing goals.

At the end of the week, open Activity on the Apple Watch.

  • Find the option to change goals.
  • Listen to the current Move goal.
  • Think about whether it was easy, difficult, or reasonable.
  • If it was too easy, raise it a little.
  • If it was impossible, lower it.
  • If it was reasonable, leave it as it is.
  • If the watch allows you to adjust Exercise and Stand, review those values too.
  • Then use the new goals for another week before changing them again.

Summary of module 24

Activity goals help measure movement, exercise, and stand time.

  • The Move goal is based on active calories.
  • The Exercise goal is based on minutes of activity at a certain intensity.
  • The Stand goal aims to avoid too many hours without movement.
  • Goals should be realistic and sustainable.
  • It is not advisable to raise them too quickly.
  • Lowering them may be necessary and reasonable.
  • Personal data influence calculations.
  • Activity should serve as support, not pressure.
  • The Apple Watch should adapt to the person, not the other way round.

Back to table of contents

Module 25. Workouts: starting, pausing, and ending

The Workout app is one of the most important parts of the Apple Watch. It is used to record a specific physical activity: walking, running, cycling, swimming, strength training, using an elliptical machine, functional training, and many other options.

When you start a workout, the Apple Watch pays closer attention to that activity. It records duration, calories, heart rate, distance, pace, and other data, depending on the type of workout selected.

This is different from normal daily activity. The watch can record movement even if you do not start a workout, but if you want to measure a specific session properly, it is advisable to open Workout and start it.

For a blind person, learning how to start, pause, resume, and end a workout with VoiceOver is essential. It is not enough to start. You also need to know how to stop it correctly. Otherwise, the watch may keep recording activity after you have finished, and then absurd data appears. Technology measures, yes, but it does not guess that you sat down for coffee after walking.

What the Workout app is

The Workout app allows you to choose a type of exercise and record a session.

It may include activities such as:

  • Outdoor Walk.
  • Indoor Walk.
  • Outdoor Run.
  • Indoor Run.
  • Outdoor Cycle.
  • Indoor Cycle.
  • Elliptical.
  • Rower.
  • Stair Stepper.
  • Pool Swim.
  • Open Water Swim.
  • Traditional Strength Training.
  • Functional Strength Training.
  • Yoga.
  • Pilates.
  • Dance.
  • Hiking.
  • Other.
  • The list may vary depending on watchOS version, model, and configuration.
  • You do not need to know all workouts from the beginning.
  • At first, it is enough to learn the ones you are actually going to use.

Difference between activity and workout

Daily activity is recorded automatically throughout the day. A workout is a specific session that you choose to start.

For example:

  • If you move around the house, the watch may count part of that movement as daily activity.
  • If you go out for a thirty-minute walk and start Outdoor Walk, the watch records that session as a workout.
  • The workout gives you more organised data.

It may show:

  • Duration.
  • Distance.
  • Pace.
  • Heart rate.
  • Active calories.
  • Total calories.
  • Route, if applicable.
  • Other metrics depending on the type of workout.

Opening the Workout app

To open Workout from the Apple Watch:

  • Return to the watch face.
  • Press the Digital Crown.
  • Find Workout.
  • Double tap.
  • The list of available workouts will open.
  • With VoiceOver, move through the list by swiping right or left.
  • If there are many workouts, you can turn the Digital Crown to scroll.

Opening Workout with Siri

You can also use Siri.

Examples:

  • Start an outdoor walk workout.
  • Start an indoor walk workout.
  • Start a traditional strength training workout.
  • Start a cycling workout.
  • This can be faster than opening the app and searching the list.
  • However, you need to make sure Siri has understood the correct workout.
  • If the command is misunderstood, cancel and try again.

Choosing the correct workout type

Choosing the correct workout helps the Apple Watch record better data.

Examples:

  • If you are walking outdoors, choose Outdoor Walk.
  • If you are walking on a treadmill or indoors, choose Indoor Walk.
  • If you are cycling outdoors, choose Outdoor Cycle.
  • If you are using a stationary bike, choose Indoor Cycle.
  • If you are doing strength exercises with weights, choose Traditional Strength Training.
  • If you are doing general bodyweight or mixed exercises, Functional Strength Training may be more suitable.
  • If you are unsure, choose the closest workout.
  • If nothing fits, you can use Other.

Outdoor Walk

Outdoor Walk is one of the most useful workouts. It is used when you walk outside. The watch can record time, distance, pace, heart rate, calories, and route if location is available. For many blind people, this will be one of the most common workouts.

Before starting:

  • Check that the watch is properly adjusted.
  • Check that battery is sufficient.
  • Check that location is enabled if you want route and distance data.
  • Make sure you can move safely.

Indoor Walk

Indoor Walk is used when walking indoors.

For example:

  • Walking at home.
  • Walking in a corridor.
  • Walking on a treadmill.
  • Walking in a gym.
  • In indoor workouts, distance is estimated differently.
  • It may be less precise than outdoors with GPS.

Outdoor Run and Indoor Run

These work in a similar way to walking, but are designed for running. They may measure pace, distance, heart rate, and other data. If you do not run, there is no need to use them.

Outdoor Cycle and Indoor Cycle

Outdoor Cycle is for cycling outside. Indoor Cycle is for stationary bikes. The distinction matters because outdoor cycling can use GPS and route information, while indoor cycling uses other estimates.

Strength training

The Apple Watch can record strength training.

There may be options such as:

  • Traditional Strength Training.
  • Functional Strength Training.
  • Traditional Strength Training may be used for weights or strength routines.
  • Functional Strength Training may be more suitable for mixed movements, bodyweight exercises, or general conditioning.
  • The watch may not recognise every repetition or exercise in detail.
  • Its main use is recording duration, heart rate, and estimated calories.

Other

The Other workout is useful when your activity does not fit any specific category. It can record time, heart rate, and calories in a general way. It is not always the most precise option, but it can be useful if you do not find a better category.

Starting a workout

To start a workout:

  • Open the Workout app.
  • Find the type of workout you want.
  • Double tap on the workout.
  • In many cases, the workout will start after a countdown.
  • The watch may say or show a countdown such as three, two, one, start.
  • When it starts, the watch begins recording.
  • On some workouts, there may be options before starting, such as goal, time, distance, calories, or open goal.

Open goal workout

An open goal workout means you start without setting a specific time, distance, or calorie target. This is usually the easiest option at first. You simply start, do the activity, and end it when you finish. For beginners, open goal is practical because it avoids extra settings.

Goal-based workout

Some workouts allow you to set a goal.

For example:

  • Time.
  • Distance.
  • Calories.
  • This can be useful when you already know what you want to do.

For example:

  • Walk for thirty minutes.
  • Run five kilometres.
  • Burn a specific number of active calories.
  • At the beginning, open goal is usually easier.
  • Later, goals can be used when the person is more comfortable.

During the workout

During a workout, the Apple Watch can show several metrics.

Depending on the workout type, these may include:

  • Elapsed time.
  • Distance.
  • Current pace.
  • Average pace.
  • Heart rate.
  • Active calories.
  • Total calories.
  • Elevation.
  • Route.
  • Exercise zones, depending on configuration.
  • With VoiceOver, you can listen to the data by moving through the workout screen.
  • Swipe right or left.
  • Touch the screen to explore.
  • Use the Digital Crown if needed.
  • Do not spend too much time manipulating the watch while moving, especially outdoors. Safety comes first.

Pausing a workout

Sometimes you need to pause a workout.

For example:

  • You stop to talk.
  • You wait at a crossing.
  • You enter a shop.
  • You take a break.
  • You need to adjust something.
  • To pause, look for the Pause option on the workout screen.

With VoiceOver:

  • Move through the screen.
  • Find Pause.
  • Double tap.
  • The workout will stop recording actively until you resume it.
  • The exact gesture or location may vary depending on watchOS version.
  • In some cases, there may also be button combinations or automatic pause options.
  • For a beginner, it is better to learn the on-screen Pause control.

Resuming a workout

After pausing, you need to resume if you continue the activity.

To resume:

  • Find Resume.
  • Double tap.
  • The workout will continue recording.
  • This step is important.
  • If you forget to resume, the rest of the activity may not be recorded properly.
  • If you forget to pause during a long stop, the workout may include time that was not really exercise.

Ending a workout

When you finish the activity, you must end the workout. This is one of the most important steps.

To end:

  • Look for End or Finish on the workout screen.
  • Double tap.
  • Confirm if the watch asks.
  • The watch will stop recording and show a summary.
  • Do not simply press the Digital Crown and assume the workout has ended.
  • Leaving the app is not the same as ending the workout.
  • If you do not end it, the watch may continue recording.

Workout summary

When you end a workout, the Apple Watch usually shows a summary.

It may include:

  • Duration.
  • Distance.
  • Calories.
  • Heart rate.
  • Average pace.
  • Route, if available.
  • Other metrics.
  • With VoiceOver, move through the summary slowly.
  • At the end, look for Done, OK, or Close, depending on the version.
  • Double tap to finish.
  • The workout should then be saved.

Reviewing workouts on the iPhone

For reviewing details, the iPhone is usually more comfortable.

Open the Fitness app on the iPhone.

  • Find the workout.
  • Open it.
  • Review duration, distance, heart rate, calories, route, and other data.
  • The watch is useful during the activity.
  • The iPhone is better afterwards.

Automatic workout detection

The Apple Watch can detect some activities and suggest starting a workout. For example, if you have been walking for a while, it may ask whether you want to record an Outdoor Walk.

If that alert appears:

  • Listen to it with VoiceOver.
  • Choose whether to start recording.
  • If you accept, the watch may include some of the activity already done.

This feature can be useful, but it should not replace starting workouts manually when you know you are going to exercise.

Reminder to end workout

The watch can also detect that you may have stopped and suggest ending the workout.

  • This is useful if you forget.
  • But again, do not depend entirely on automatic detection.
  • Learn to end the workout yourself.

Auto-pause

Some workouts may have automatic pause options. For example, running or cycling may pause automatically when you stop, depending on settings. This can be useful, but it can also behave differently depending on the activity. At the beginning, it is better to understand manual pause and resume first.

Battery during workouts

Workouts use more battery than normal use, especially if they use GPS, heart rate, Cellular, or audio. Before starting a long workout, check battery. If the watch battery is low, consider charging it first. If you are going outdoors, especially alone, do not leave with a battery that is almost empty and rely on the watch for safety or communication.

Using workouts safely

When working out with VoiceOver:

  • Do not manipulate the watch while crossing streets.
  • Do not focus on data if you need to pay attention to the environment.
  • Use headphones carefully if you need to hear traffic or surroundings.
  • Check the route and safety before starting.
  • If you walk or run outdoors, prioritise orientation and mobility.
  • The Apple Watch can help record activity, but it does not replace safe movement skills.

Workout with headphones

If you use headphones, you may hear VoiceOver or workout information more clearly. This may be useful outdoors or in noisy places. However, avoid blocking important environmental sounds if you need them for safety. Some people prefer bone conduction headphones or one ear uncovered, depending on their needs and environment.

Workout and Cellular

If you have an Apple Watch GPS plus Cellular with service activated, you may be able to exercise without carrying the iPhone while still having calls, messages, or data connection. This can be useful, but it uses more battery.

If your watch is GPS only, you will usually need the iPhone nearby for connection outside Wi-Fi, although the workout itself may still be recorded.

Workout and location

Outdoor workouts can use location to record distance and route. To make this work properly, location services must be enabled.

If route or distance data are missing, check:

  • Location permissions.
  • Apple Watch connection.
  • GPS signal.
  • Whether the workout type was correct.
  • Whether the iPhone was nearby, depending on model and situation.

Choosing data shown during workouts

The Apple Watch allows some workout views and metrics to be configured. This may include what data appear on the screen during each workout. These settings can often be adjusted from the Watch app on the iPhone. For a blind person, it may be useful to simplify the data shown. Too many metrics can make review with VoiceOver slower.

Useful data may include:

  • Elapsed time.
  • Distance.
  • Heart rate.
  • Pace.
  • Calories.
  • The best set depends on the type of workout.

Using Siri to start workouts

Siri can be very practical.

Examples:

  • Start an outdoor walk.
  • Start an indoor walk.
  • Start a traditional strength training workout.
  • Start a ten-minute outdoor walk.
  • If Siri starts the wrong workout, stop it and start the correct one.
  • Always listen to the confirmation.

What not to do during workouts

  • Do not start a workout and forget about it for hours.
  • Do not choose a random workout type every time.
  • Do not manipulate the watch in unsafe places.
  • Do not obsess over every metric while moving.
  • Do not ignore pain, dizziness, or discomfort because the watch says the workout is going well.
  • Do not rely on the watch as a medical device.

If something feels wrong physically, stop and seek help if needed.

Common mistakes

  • Not starting the workout.
  • Choosing the wrong type.
  • Choosing Indoor Walk when you are outdoors.
  • Choosing Outdoor Cycle when you are on a stationary bike.
  • Not adjusting the watch properly.
  • Not checking battery.
  • Not pausing during a long stop.
  • Forgetting to resume after pausing.
  • Forgetting to end.
  • Not reviewing the summary.
  • Always depending on automatic detection.
  • Checking the watch in places where you should pay attention to your surroundings.

Practical advice

To begin with, practise with a simple workout. The best first workout is usually Outdoor Walk or Indoor Walk, depending on the situation. Do a short test of five or ten minutes. Learn how to start, check, pause, resume, and end.

Do not wait until you are on a long walk to learn how to end a workout. That is the kind of idea that sounds reasonable until you get home with the watch still recording your existence as sport.

Exercise for module 25

Put on the Apple Watch properly adjusted.

  • Return to the watch face.
  • Press the Digital Crown.
  • Find Workout.
  • Double tap.
  • Find Outdoor Walk if you are going outside, or Indoor Walk if you are practising at home.
  • Start an open goal workout.
  • Walk for two or three minutes.
  • During the workout, touch the screen.
  • Listen to the data with VoiceOver.
  • Find the Pause option.
  • Pause the workout.
  • Find Resume.
  • Resume the workout.
  • Walk for one more minute.
  • Find End.
  • Double tap.
  • Confirm if the watch asks.
  • Listen to the summary.
  • Find Done, OK, or Close.
  • Exit the summary.
  • Then open Fitness on the iPhone and check whether the workout appears.

Summary of module 25

The Workout app records specific exercise sessions. Daily activity is not the same as a workout. To record a session better, it is advisable to start the corresponding workout. Workout can be opened from the app list or with Siri. Choosing the correct workout type improves the data. An open goal workout is the easiest option when starting. During the workout, you can check time, distance, heart rate, and other data. It is important to know how to pause, resume, and end. When finished, the watch shows a summary. Workouts use more battery. For reviewing details, the iPhone is usually more comfortable.

Module 26. The most useful workout types

The Workout app on the Apple Watch includes many activities. Some will be very useful for most people. Others will only matter to those who practise specific sports. You do not need to know them all from the first day. The important thing is to choose the right workout type so the watch records the activity in the most appropriate way.

Choosing the wrong one is not usually a catastrophe, but it can produce less useful data. If you are walking outdoors and choose Indoor Walk, distance may not be recorded in the same way. If you are using a stationary bike and choose Outdoor Cycle, the watch may expect movement data that simply does not exist. And so it goes, because even exercise now requires choosing the correct category before sweating.

Outdoor Walk

Outdoor Walk is one of the most important workouts. It should be used when you go walking in the street, in a park, along an avenue, on an outdoor track, or in any open environment.

It can record:

  • Time.
  • Distance.
  • Pace.
  • Heart rate.
  • Calories.
  • Route, if location is available.
  • It is a highly recommended option for starting out.

For a blind person, outdoor walking may be part of daily travel, walks, physical activity, or regular orientation routes.

Before starting this workout, it is worth checking:

  • Battery.
  • Watch fit.
  • Location enabled.
  • Safe environment.
  • Whether you are carrying the iPhone or not.
  • Whether you need headphones.
  • If you go out alone, safety comes first.

Indoor Walk

Indoor Walk should be used when walking inside a closed space.

For example:

  • Treadmill.
  • Corridors.
  • Home.
  • Gym.
  • Shopping centre.
  • Large indoor spaces.
  • This workout does not depend on GPS in the same way. The watch estimates the activity using sensors and movement.
  • If you are walking on a treadmill, this is the correct option.

It can record:

  • Time.
  • Calories.
  • Heart rate.
  • Estimated distance.
  • Distance may be less accurate than outdoors, because there is no real GPS movement.

Outdoor Run

Outdoor Run is used when running outdoors.

It can record:

  • Distance.
  • Pace.
  • Time.
  • Heart rate.
  • Calories.
  • Route.
  • Other data depending on version.
  • For a blind person who runs with a guide, on a track, in controlled spaces, or with support, it can be useful.

Before using it, it is worth being clear about how you are going to check information during the run. It is not always comfortable to touch the watch while running. It may be better to use alerts, headphones, or review the summary at the end.

Indoor Run

Indoor Run is used for a treadmill. The watch estimates distance and pace using sensors. It may not match the treadmill data exactly. If there is a difference, it does not necessarily mean that one of them is broken. They are different systems measuring in different ways.

When reviewing the workout, it is useful to look at:

  • Duration.
  • Heart rate.
  • Calories.
  • Physical feeling.
  • This is often more useful than obsessing over small distance differences.

Outdoor Cycle

Outdoor Cycle is used when cycling outdoors. It can record route, distance, speed, heart rate, and other data. For a blind person, this workout may apply if they use a tandem, adapted bicycle, guide, or safe environments. It may also be useful for cycling with support. Safety, route, accompaniment, and connection must be considered. If you go out without the iPhone and the watch is Cellular, there may be more independence for calls. If the watch is GPS, carrying the iPhone may be advisable.

Indoor Cycle or stationary bike

This workout is used for a stationary bike or indoor cycling sessions. There is no real movement from one place to another, so distance may depend on estimates or data from other equipment if there is integration.

It can record:

  • Time.
  • Heart rate.
  • Calories.
  • Approximate intensity.
  • It is a good option for training at home or in a gym.

Elliptical

The Elliptical workout is used with elliptical machines. It can record time, heart rate, and calories. It is useful for indoor cardiovascular exercise. With VoiceOver, the important thing is to start the workout before beginning and end it when you finish. You should not manipulate the watch too much while using the machine if that affects stability or safety.

Rower

The Rower workout can be used on a rowing machine. It can record time, heart rate, and calories. It can be an intense activity, so the watch should be properly adjusted so the sensors maintain contact with the skin.

Strength Training

Strength Training is used for exercises with weights, machines, resistance bands, or muscle work. It can record duration, heart rate, and calories. It will not always count repetitions specifically, except through certain features or specific apps. For strength work, the watch is more useful as a general record of the session than as a perfect counter of every movement.

It is advisable to pause if you take long breaks, although in strength training, rests are part of the session. It depends on how you want to record it.

Functional Training

Functional Training can be used for varied routines.

For example:

  • Bodyweight exercises.
  • Circuits.
  • Mobility.
  • Mixed routines.
  • Guided exercises.
  • General physical activity.
  • If you do not fit neatly into a more specific category, Functional Training may be a useful option.

Yoga

The Yoga workout can record yoga sessions, guided stretching, or similar practices. It can measure duration, heart rate, and calories. For blind people, it can be useful if they follow accessible classes, audio instructions, or familiar routines.

Pilates

Pilates can be used for mat Pilates, machine-based Pilates, or adapted routines. As with Yoga, the watch records the general session, not necessarily each exercise in detail.

Dance

The Dance workout records physical activity related to dancing. It can be useful for classes, home practice, or rhythmic activity. If movement is varied, the Apple Watch will make an estimate using sensors and heart rate.

Pool Swim

Pool Swim should be used when swimming in a pool. It can record length, time, calories, pace, and other data, depending on model and configuration. Before using this workout, you must check that your model is suitable for swimming and understand Apple’s water resistance recommendations. During swimming, the watch may activate Water Lock to prevent accidental touches. When you finish, you will need to unlock it using the Digital Crown as the system indicates.

For a blind person, it is advisable to practise how to start and end this workout before getting into the water. Improvising with a wet screen, VoiceOver, and a swimming pool is not exactly the brightest plan of the week.

Open Water Swim

This workout is used for swimming in the sea, a lake, or other open-water spaces. It may use GPS to record the route if the model and conditions allow it. This activity requires special safety. For a blind person, it should only be done with support, a controlled environment, and appropriate safety measures.

Hiking

Hiking can be used for walks on trails, in the mountains, or on uneven terrain. It can record time, distance, elevation gain, pace, heart rate, and route, depending on model. It is useful for long outings.

Before using it, check:

  • Battery.
  • Route.
  • Coverage.
  • Whether you are carrying the iPhone.
  • Whether you have Cellular.
  • Emergency contacts.
  • Weather.
  • Support or accompaniment if needed.
  • When hiking, battery and safety matter more than closing rings.

Other

The Other option can be used when you cannot find a suitable category. The watch will record the session in a general way.

It can be used for activities such as:

  • Adapted exercise.
  • Mixed routines.
  • Unclassified movements.
  • Intense household activities.
  • Classes or sessions that do not appear in the list.
  • It should not be the first choice if a more precise category exists.
  • But it is useful when nothing fits.

Adapted workouts

Some people will need to adapt Apple Watch use to their physical situation.

There may be differences due to:

  • Reduced mobility.
  • Wheelchair use.
  • Injuries.
  • Age.
  • Fitness level.
  • Illnesses.
  • Use of a cane or guide dog.
  • Training with a guide.
  • Activity at home.
  • The important thing is to choose the category that is closest to the real activity.
  • If you use a wheelchair, check that the Health settings are correctly adapted.

Choosing a workout according to your goal

If the goal is walking for health:

  1. Outdoor Walk.
  2. Indoor Walk.

If the goal is cardiovascular exercise:

  1. Walking.
  2. Running.
  3. Cycling.
  4. Elliptical.
  5. Rower.

If the goal is strength:

  1. Strength Training.
  2. Functional Training.

If the goal is mobility or flexibility:

  1. Yoga.
  2. Pilates.
  3. Functional Training.

If the goal is recording an activity that does not appear:

  • Other.
  • Most recommended workouts for starting out

For a person starting with Apple Watch, the most useful ones are usually:

  • Outdoor Walk.
  • Indoor Walk.
  • Strength Training.
  • Functional Training.
  • Stationary bike.
  • Elliptical.
  • Yoga or Pilates, if practised.
  • These cover many common situations.

Workouts and VoiceOver

With VoiceOver, the workout should be easy to start and end. That is why, at the beginning, it is a good idea to practise with only a few workout types. You do not need to go through the whole list every time.

You can use Siri:

  • Start an outdoor walk workout.
  • Start a strength training workout.
  • Start a stationary bike workout.
  • If Siri starts the wrong workout, cancel it and start again.

Workout and water mode

During swimming workouts or activities involving water, the Apple Watch may activate Water Lock. This mode locks the screen to prevent accidental touches. When you finish, you will need to turn off Water Lock by following the watch instructions, usually using the Digital Crown. Not all models or straps are suitable for every water use. Before using the watch in water, it is worth knowing the water resistance of your model and Apple’s recommendations.

Working out with the iPhone nearby or without it

If you have an Apple Watch GPS and you go outdoors, it may be advisable to carry the iPhone for some features, especially calls, connection, and certain data. If you have GPS plus Cellular and the mobile plan is active, you can go out without the iPhone with more independence. For physical activity, this can be important. If you go out alone, also think about safety, battery, and the ability to make calls.

Workouts and battery

Workouts use more battery than normal use.

  • They use more battery if they use GPS.
  • They use more battery if you use Cellular.
  • They use more battery if you listen to music or podcasts.
  • They use more battery if the session is long.

Before working out, check the battery. If you are going on a long walk, a route, or an important session, do not start with the watch almost discharged.

Workouts and health

During a workout, the Apple Watch can record heart rate and other data. If you notice symptoms such as chest pain, dizziness, unusual shortness of breath, concerning palpitations, or intense discomfort, stop the activity and seek help. The watch can provide data, but it should not replace your judgement or medical attention.

Common mistakes

  • Not starting the workout.
  • Choosing the wrong type.
  • Choosing Indoor Walk when you are outdoors.
  • Choosing Outdoor Cycle when you are on a stationary bike.
  • Not adjusting the watch properly.
  • Not checking battery.
  • Not pausing when taking a long stop.
  • Forgetting to resume after pausing.
  • Forgetting to end.
  • Not reviewing the summary.
  • Always relying on automatic detection.
  • Checking the watch in places where you should be paying attention to your surroundings.

Practical advice

For starting out, practise with a simple workout. The best first workout is usually Outdoor Walk or Indoor Walk, depending on the situation. Do a short test of five or ten minutes. Learn how to start, check, pause, resume, and end.

Do not wait until you are on a long walk to learn how to end a workout. That is the kind of idea that seems reasonable until you get home with the watch still recording your existence as sport.

Exercise for module 26

Open the Workout app on the Apple Watch.

  • Move through the list with VoiceOver.
  • Listen to the names of the available workouts.
  • Find Outdoor Walk.
  • Find Indoor Walk.
  • Find Strength Training.
  • Find Functional Training.
  • Find Other.
  • Do not start them yet if you do not want to.
  • Choose one simple workout.
  • Start it as an open goal.
  • Do the activity for a few minutes.
  • Pause it.
  • Resume it.
  • End it.
  • Listen to the summary.
  • Then open the Fitness app on the iPhone and review how the workout has been recorded.

Summary of module 26

The Workout app includes many types of exercise. You do not need to know them all from the first day. Outdoor Walk and Indoor Walk are usually the most useful for starting out. Choosing the correct workout type improves the data. Indoor and outdoor activities are not recorded in exactly the same way. Strength Training and Functional Training are useful for many routines. Other is useful when no category fits. Water workouts require checking model, strap, safety, and Water Lock. For outdoor activities, battery, location, connection, and safety matter. With VoiceOver, it is best to practise with a few frequent workouts first.

Module 27. Working out with VoiceOver

Working out with the Apple Watch using VoiceOver requires learning a simple and repeatable workflow. The Workout app allows you to record the session, but during exercise it is not always comfortable to manipulate the watch. If you are walking in the street, running, using a machine, or doing a strength routine, it is not advisable to keep touching the screen all the time.

For that reason, the goal of this module is not to check every piece of data every minute. The goal is to learn how to start the workout properly, receive the information you need, check only what matters, and end the workout correctly. The Apple Watch should accompany the activity, not interrupt it.

Before working out

Before starting any workout, check these points:

  • The Apple Watch is properly positioned.
  • The strap is firm, but comfortable.
  • The back of the watch is touching the skin properly.
  • VoiceOver is turned on.
  • Battery is sufficient.
  • The correct workout type is clear.
  • The environment is safe.
  • You know how to pause and end the workout.

If you are going outside, you have considered whether you need the iPhone, headphones, a cane, a guide dog, a guide person, route information, or any other support. This may seem like many checks, but after a few days it becomes routine.

Starting the workout with Siri

For many people, the quickest method is Siri.

You can say:

  • Start an outdoor walk workout.
  • Start an indoor walk workout.
  • Start a strength training workout.
  • Start a stationary bike workout.
  • Start a functional training workout.
  • After giving the command, listen to the confirmation.
  • Do not start walking or training without checking that the watch has started the correct workout.

Siri can misunderstand a word. It is not personal. It is technology doing what it does best: promising intelligence and then confusing cycling with something else at exactly the wrong moment.

Starting the workout manually

You can also start from the Workout app.

  • Return to the watch face.
  • Press the Digital Crown.
  • Find Workout.
  • Double tap.
  • Find the type of workout.
  • Double tap.
  • Choose Open Goal if it appears.
  • Wait for the countdown.
  • Start the activity.

This method is important because Siri may not be available, may not understand correctly, or may fail because of connection.

Which information is useful during the workout

Not all data are equally useful during activity.

For walking, you may want:

  1. Time.
  2. Distance.
  3. Pace.
  4. Heart rate.
  5. Active calories.

For running:

  • Time.
  • Distance.
  • Pace.
  • Heart rate.
  • Heart rate zones, if available.

For cycling:

  1. Time.
  2. Distance.
  3. Speed.
  4. Heart rate.

For strength training:

  1. Time.
  2. Heart rate.
  3. Calories.

For gentle or mobility workouts:

  • Time.
  • Heart rate.
  • Physical feeling.
  • At the beginning, do not try to check everything.
  • Choose two or three important pieces of data.

Checking data with VoiceOver

During a workout:

  • Raise your wrist or touch the screen.
  • Wait for VoiceOver to speak.
  • Swipe right to move through data.
  • Listen to each metric.
  • If you need to scroll, turn the Digital Crown slowly.
  • Do not make too many gestures while moving.
  • If you are outdoors, stop in a safe place before manipulating the watch.

The information is there to help you, not to distract you from kerbs, crossings, obstacles, traffic, or people walking while staring at their phones as if the world were optional.

Using headphones during the workout

Headphones can be useful for listening to VoiceOver, Siri, music, podcasts, or directions.

Advantages:

  • More privacy.
  • Better listening outdoors.
  • Less dependence on the watch speaker.
  • More comfort for calls.
  • But safety must also be considered.
  • If you are outdoors, it is advisable to keep enough awareness of your surroundings.
  • Do not use a volume that isolates you completely if you need to hear traffic, warnings, people, or sound references.
  • For blind people, hearing can be an important reference for orientation and safety.
  • For that reason, headphones should be used sensibly.

Pausing the workout

During a workout, you may need to pause.

For example:

  • You stop to talk.
  • You cross a difficult area.
  • You need to answer a call.
  • You stop for a long time.
  • You need to rest.

To pause:

  • Touch the workout screen.
  • Explore with VoiceOver.
  • Find Pause.
  • Double tap.
  • Listen for confirmation that the workout has paused.
  • When the workout is paused, it stops recording the activity as active time.
  • This is useful if the stop is long.
  • If it is just a few seconds, it may not be necessary.

Resuming the workout

If you have paused and want to continue:

  • Touch the screen.
  • Find Resume.
  • Double tap.
  • Listen to confirm that the workout has resumed.
  • Then continue the activity.
  • It is easy to forget this step.
  • If you pause and do not resume, the rest of the activity may not be recorded correctly.

Ending the workout

When you finish, you must end the workout. Do not just press the Digital Crown and leave the app. Leaving the screen is not the same as ending the workout.

To end:

  • Touch the workout screen.
  • Explore with VoiceOver.
  • Find End or Finish.
  • Double tap.
  • Confirm if the watch asks.
  • Listen to the summary.
  • Find Done, OK, or Close.
  • Double tap.
  • Now the workout has been saved.
  • This is one of the most important habits to learn.

Consulting the summary

When the workout ends, the Apple Watch shows a summary.

It may include:

  • Total time.
  • Distance.
  • Average pace.
  • Heart rate.
  • Calories.
  • Route, if available.
  • Other metrics depending on the workout.
  • With VoiceOver, move through the summary slowly.
  • You do not need to memorise everything.
  • The full review will be more comfortable later on the iPhone, in the Fitness app.

Reviewing the workout on the iPhone

After finishing, open the Fitness app on the iPhone.

There you can review:

  • Workout type.
  • Duration.
  • Distance.
  • Heart rate.
  • Calories.
  • Route.
  • Pace.
  • Trends.
  • History.
  • The iPhone is more comfortable for detailed review.
  • The Apple Watch is better during the activity.

Using workouts outdoors

When training outdoors with VoiceOver, safety must come first.

Before checking data, make sure you are not:

  • Crossing a street.
  • Near traffic.
  • In a complicated area.
  • On stairs.
  • In a narrow space.
  • In a place with obstacles.
  • Walking with other people around you.
  • If you need to check the watch, stop in a safe place.
  • The watch can wait.
  • A kerb usually does not.

Working out with a cane or guide dog

If you use a cane or guide dog, you may need to adapt how you interact with the watch.

It may be more practical to:

  • Start the workout before leaving.
  • Use Siri.
  • Use headphones at moderate volume.
  • Avoid checking data while moving.
  • Review the summary at the end.
  • Pause only when stopped.
  • The goal is for the watch not to interfere with your mobility technique.

Walking outdoors

For outdoor walking, the recommended workout is usually Outdoor Walk. It can record distance, route, pace, time, and heart rate. You can start it manually or with Siri.

Suggested workflow:

  1. Check battery.
  2. Check watch fit.
  3. Start Outdoor Walk.
  4. Listen for confirmation.
  5. Walk.
  6. Check data only if safe.
  7. End when finished.
  8. Review the summary.

Walking indoors

For walking indoors, use Indoor Walk. This may be used on a treadmill, corridor, home, or indoor space. Distance may be estimated differently from outdoor walking. If you are on a treadmill, the treadmill and watch may not show exactly the same distance. That is normal.

Strength training

For strength training, it is not usually necessary to check the watch constantly.

The most useful data are usually:

  • Time.
  • Heart rate.
  • Estimated calories.
  • You can start Strength Training or Functional Training, depending on the routine.
  • If you rest between sets, you do not always need to pause. Rest can be part of the workout.
  • But if the pause is very long, you may choose to pause.

Stationary bike

For a stationary bike, choose Indoor Cycle. Do not choose Outdoor Cycle unless you are actually cycling outdoors. The watch can record time, heart rate, and calories, but distance may depend on the bike or not be directly comparable.

Using machines at the gym

If you use gym machines, choose the closest workout:

  • Indoor Walk for treadmill walking.
  • Indoor Run for treadmill running.
  • Indoor Cycle for stationary bike.
  • Elliptical for elliptical.
  • Rower for rowing machine.
  • Strength Training for weights.
  • Functional Training for mixed routines.
  • It is useful to start the correct workout before beginning.
  • If you change machines several times, you can use Functional Training or another general workout, depending on the type of session.
  • If you want to record each part precisely, you can start separate workouts, but that requires more handling.
  • For starting out, one general session may be simpler.

Working out at home

At home you can use:

  • Indoor Walk.
  • Functional Training.
  • Strength Training.
  • Yoga.
  • Pilates.
  • Other.
  • The Apple Watch can help measure duration and heart rate.
  • You can also use timers for rests or intervals.

Gentle exercise and older people

For older people or people who are starting out, walking and gentle exercises may be enough.

The important things are:

  • Consistency.
  • Safety.
  • Realistic goals.
  • Clear alerts.
  • Not forcing.
  • Recording what is done helps show progress.
  • But it should not become pressure.

Heart rate during exercise

During a workout, heart rate can help indicate intensity.

  • If it rises much more than usual for you, reduce intensity.
  • If you notice concerning symptoms, stop the activity.
  • If you have medical doubts, consult healthcare professionals.

The Apple Watch can show data, but it does not interpret the full context of your health.

Working out without checking data

You can also train without checking data during the session. You can start the workout, do the activity, and review the summary at the end. This can be safer and less distracting. For many people, it is the best option. Especially outdoors.

Common mistakes

  • Starting the wrong workout.
  • Not listening to Siri’s confirmation.
  • Not checking battery.
  • Wearing the watch too loosely.
  • Checking data in an unsafe place.
  • Pausing and forgetting to resume.
  • Finishing the activity and not ending the workout.
  • Training with headphone volume too high.
  • Depending on automatic detection.
  • Not reviewing the data later in Fitness.

Practical advice

Create a fixed routine for each workout:

  • Before starting, check battery and fit.
  • Start the workout.
  • Listen for confirmation.
  • Work out.
  • Check data only if it is safe.
  • Pause if you make a long stop.
  • Resume if you continue.
  • End when finished.
  • Listen to the summary.
  • Review details on the iPhone.
  • Repeating the same pattern prevents forgotten steps.

Exercise for module 27

  • Choose a simple workout.
  • For example, Outdoor Walk or Indoor Walk.
  • Put on the Apple Watch properly adjusted.
  • Check battery.
  • Start the workout with Siri or from Workout.
  • Listen to the confirmation.
  • Walk for five minutes.
  • During the walk, stop in a safe place.
  • Check time and heart rate with VoiceOver.
  • Pause the workout.
  • Wait a few seconds.
  • Resume.
  • Walk for one more minute.
  • End the workout.
  • Listen to the summary.
  • Then open Fitness on the iPhone and review the completed workout.

Summary of module 27

Working out with VoiceOver requires preparing the watch well and using only a few gestures during activity. Siri can start workouts quickly. The Workout app allows you to choose the type of activity. During the workout, it is best to check only essential data. If you are outdoors, safety is more important than checking metrics. Headphones can help, but they should not isolate you from the environment. It is important to know how to pause, resume, and end. The summary can be reviewed on the watch, but details are more comfortable on the iPhone. The goal is for the Apple Watch to support activity, not interrupt it.

Module 28. Safety during exercise

The Apple Watch can be very useful during exercise, but it should not distract from what matters most: safety. When a blind person trains or walks outdoors, they need to pay attention to the environment, orientation, traffic, crossings, other people, obstacles, and sound or tactile references. The watch can provide information, record activity, and help in certain situations, but it does not replace mobility skills or common sense. This module focuses on how to use the Apple Watch safely during exercise.

Before going out

Before exercising away from home, check:

  • Apple Watch battery.
  • iPhone battery, if you are going to carry it.
  • Strap adjustment.
  • Type of workout you are going to start.
  • Planned route.
  • Weather conditions.
  • Whether you need headphones.
  • Whether a Focus mode is active.
  • Whether emergency contacts are configured.
  • Whether you have identification or Medical ID configured.
  • Whether the watch has enough connection.
  • If you are going out without the iPhone, check even more carefully.

Going out without the iPhone can be convenient, but it is only advisable if you know which features your Apple Watch keeps in those conditions.

Apple Watch GPS and outdoor exercise

If your Apple Watch is GPS, it will normally depend on the iPhone for calls, messages, and connection when it is not connected to Wi-Fi. If you go out walking or training without the iPhone, you will be able to record some activities, but you will lose part of the communication.

For many blind people, carrying the iPhone is still advisable during outdoor outings, especially if they need to make calls, use orientation apps, share location, or receive assistance.

Apple Watch GPS plus Cellular and outdoor exercise

If your Apple Watch is GPS plus Cellular and you have a mobile plan activated, you can have more independence. It may allow calls, messages, and data without carrying the iPhone, depending on coverage and carrier.

This can be useful for:

  • Walking without the iPhone.
  • Running.
  • Going to the gym.
  • Running errands.
  • Having a way to communicate if needed.
  • But Cellular uses more battery and depends on coverage.
  • Before relying on this feature, test it in simple situations.

Do not debut the watch’s independence on a long and unfamiliar route. That kind of experiment belongs more to the genre of recklessness than accessible technology.

Battery

Exercise uses battery.

Battery use increases if you use:

  • GPS.
  • Cellular.
  • Music.
  • Podcasts.
  • Calls.
  • Maps.
  • Active screen.
  • Long workouts.
  • Before going out, check the battery percentage from Control Centre.
  • If you are doing a short session near home, a medium battery level may be enough.
  • If you are going for a long walk or going out without the iPhone, it is better to have the watch well charged.
  • Also check the iPhone battery if you are going to depend on it.

Strap adjustment

During exercise, the watch must sit firmly. If it is loose, it may move and record less accurately. If it is too tight, it may be uncomfortable.

Before starting:

  • Move your wrist.
  • Check whether the watch moves around.
  • Adjust the strap.
  • Check that the sensors touch the skin.
  • This is especially important for heart rate and workouts.

Headphones

Headphones can be useful for listening to VoiceOver, directions, calls, or audio. But outdoors, they must be used with great care. A blind person may need sound references for orientation. If headphones block too much environmental sound, they can increase risk.

Recommendations:

  • Use moderate volume.
  • Avoid isolating yourself completely.
  • If your headphones have ambient or transparency mode, consider using it.
  • At crossings or in complicated areas, pay attention to the environment.
  • Do not check the watch while crossing.
  • Convenience should not defeat safety.

VoiceOver while moving

During a walk or outdoor workout, it is not advisable to manipulate the watch too much.

The safest approach is:

  • Start the workout before beginning.
  • Leave the watch alone during complicated sections.
  • Check data only in safe places.
  • Stop if you need to manipulate the screen.
  • Use Siri only if it does not compromise attention.
  • End the workout when you are stopped.
  • Touching the watch while walking can distract you.
  • If you use a cane, guide dog, or human guide, always prioritise mobility.

Crossings and traffic

  • Do not check the Apple Watch while crossing a street.
  • Do not listen to workout data at a crossing.
  • Do not adjust headphones in the middle of a dangerous area.
  • Do not start or end workouts while crossing a complicated area.

Stop before or after. This may seem obvious, but technology has a special talent for making us do absurd things at delicate moments.

Known and unknown routes

On known routes, the Apple Watch can be a convenient companion. On unknown routes, more planning is needed.

Before going out on a new route:

  • Review the route on the iPhone.
  • Consider whether you need someone with you.
  • Check battery.
  • Check connection.
  • Share location if appropriate.
  • Carry the iPhone if you need orientation.
  • Do not depend only on the watch.
  • The Apple Watch can record and support, but it is not a specialised orientation tool for blind people.

Sharing location

If you are going to exercise outside, it may be useful to share your location with a trusted person. This is configured through the Find My ecosystem.

It can be useful for:

  • Long routes.
  • Going out alone.
  • Hiking.
  • Walks in less familiar areas.
  • Older people.
  • People with health problems.
  • Location sharing should be voluntary and deliberate.

Emergency contacts

It is useful to have emergency contacts configured. These contacts may be used in safety features, Medical ID, or emergency functions, depending on configuration. They should be people who can actually help you or receive an important alert. This will be explained in detail later in the personal safety section. For exercise, especially outdoors, it is advisable to have this information ready.

Medical ID

Medical ID can contain important information:

  • Name.
  • Age.
  • Allergies.
  • Medications.
  • Medical conditions.
  • Emergency contact.
  • Blood type, if desired.
  • Other relevant information.
  • If a person has an emergency, this information can help.
  • It is not compulsory to include everything, but it is worth considering which data would be useful.

Fall Detection

The Apple Watch may offer Fall Detection on compatible models. If it detects a hard fall, it can show an alert, tap the wrist, issue a warning, and allow emergency services to be called. This feature can be useful for older people, people at risk of falling, or those who train outdoors.

But it has limitations.

  • It does not detect every fall.
  • It may activate by mistake during some high-impact activities.
  • It requires proper configuration.
  • It may depend on age, model, and settings.
  • It should not replace caution or accompaniment when needed.

Emergency SOS

The Apple Watch may allow you to call emergency services. This feature is important, but it should only be used in real situations. It should not be tested by calling emergency services. It will be explained in detail later. During exercise, it is useful to know that it exists, especially if you go out alone. But the side button should not be manipulated unnecessarily, because holding it down may open sensitive options.

Noise and environment

The Apple Watch may include environmental noise alerts on compatible models. During exercise, it may warn you if the surroundings have high noise levels. This can be useful in gyms, streets with heavy traffic, events, or noisy areas. For a blind person, environmental sound also has orientation value. If the environment is too noisy, it can make mobility and communication more difficult.

Weather and temperature

Before training outside, check the weather. You can check it from the Apple Watch or with Siri.

It is useful to know:

  • Whether it is going to rain.
  • Temperature.
  • Wind.
  • Extreme heat.
  • Cold.
  • Adverse conditions.
  • For long walks, this matters.

The Apple Watch can record the activity, but it will not protect you from heat, cold, or rain that appears with the cruel punctuality clouds seem to enjoy.

Hydration and breaks

The watch can help you with reminders, but the responsibility is still yours.

During physical activity:

  • Drink water if you need to.
  • Rest if you feel fatigued.
  • Do not ignore signals from your body.
  • Do not push yourself just to close rings.
  • Do not continue if there are concerning symptoms.
  • You can use timers or reminders to drink water or rest.

Symptoms during exercise

If during exercise you notice symptoms such as:

  • Chest pain.
  • Dizziness.
  • Severe shortness of breath.
  • Concerning palpitations.
  • Sudden weakness.
  • Confusion.
  • Severe pain.
  • Loss of balance.
  • Stop the activity.
  • Seek help.
  • Call emergency services if necessary.
  • The Apple Watch can show data, but it should not be used to justify continuing to train when your body is warning you.

Training at home

At home, safety also matters.

Before training:

  • Remove obstacles.
  • Leave enough space.
  • Use suitable footwear if appropriate.
  • Adjust the watch properly.
  • Do not leave the charger or cables where you could trip over them.
  • If you do floor exercises, check that you can get up safely.

The Apple Watch can record the session, but it will not prevent a badly placed chair from being in the way, because that still requires humans to tidy rooms, a task that clearly remains in the experimental stage.

Training at the gym

At the gym:

  • Identify the machine properly.
  • Set the correct workout.
  • Do not manipulate the watch while moving if it is dangerous.
  • Use headphones attentively.
  • Ask for help locating machines if you need it.
  • End the workout when you finish.
  • Clean or protect the watch according to use and sweat.
  • If you use a treadmill, bike, elliptical, or rowing machine, start the workout before the movement begins.

Training in a swimming pool

If you are going to swim:

  • Check that your model is suitable for swimming.
  • Use an appropriate strap.
  • Start the workout before entering the water or at a safe moment.
  • Be clear about how Water Lock works.
  • Be clear about how to end the workout.
  • Do not practise for the first time in a complicated situation.
  • For a blind person, the swimming pool should be a familiar environment or one with appropriate support.

Hiking and long routes

For hiking or long routes, safety requires more preparation.

Check:

  • Apple Watch battery.
  • iPhone battery.
  • Coverage.
  • Route.
  • Water.
  • Weather.
  • Companionship.
  • Emergency contacts.
  • Shared location.
  • Time of departure and return.
  • Way to get back if there is a problem.
  • The Apple Watch can be a companion, especially an Ultra model or models with longer battery life, but it should not be the only resource.

Training while listening to music or podcasts

Listening to audio during exercise can make the activity more pleasant. But for a blind person, audio can also interfere with the environment.

Recommendations:

  • Low or moderate volume.
  • Prefer headphones that allow you to hear your surroundings.
  • Pause audio at crossings.
  • Do not listen to highly absorbing content in complex areas.
  • Use the watch to control playback only when it is safe.

Focus mode during exercise

A Focus mode can reduce distractions during workouts. It can be useful if you do not want social networks, non-urgent messages, or minor alerts. But it is worth allowing important calls or contacts if you train alone. Do not block everything without thinking.

A good exercise Focus mode can allow:

  1. Favourite contacts.
  2. Important calls.
  3. Health alerts.
  4. Essential warnings.
  5. And block everything else.

What to do if you get lost during an outing

If you are using the Apple Watch during an outing and become disoriented:

  • Stop in a safe place.
  • Do not keep walking while manipulating devices.
  • Use the iPhone if you have it with you.
  • Call a trusted person.
  • Use Find My or share location if appropriate.
  • Use Maps if it is useful to you.
  • If there is risk, ask for help.
  • The watch can help, but the iPhone is usually more practical for navigation and full communication.

Common mistakes

  • Going out with low battery.
  • Not carrying the iPhone when the watch needs it.
  • Using headphones too loudly.
  • Checking metrics at a crossing.
  • Not configuring emergency contacts.
  • Not knowing how to end a workout.
  • Relying only on Fall Detection.
  • Not checking the weather.
  • Doing new routes without planning.
  • Pushing yourself just to close rings.
  • Not stopping when symptoms appear.

Practical advice

Before training outside, use a simple mental checklist:

  • Watch charged.
  • Watch properly adjusted.
  • iPhone if needed.
  • Clear route.
  • Safe headphones.
  • Correct workout.
  • Emergency contact configured.
  • End the workout when finished.
  • This prevents many problems.

Exercise for module 28

Before your next walk or exercise session, do this check:

  • Check the Apple Watch battery.
  • Check that the watch is properly adjusted.
  • Decide whether you will carry the iPhone.
  • Check whether you need headphones.
  • Check the weather if you are going outside.
  • Start the appropriate workout.
  • During the activity, do not check the watch in unsafe areas.
  • When finished, end the workout correctly.
  • Then review the workout on the iPhone.
  • Mentally note what worked well and what should be adjusted next time.

Summary of module 28

Safety comes first during exercise. The Apple Watch helps, but it does not replace mobility, orientation, or caution. Before going out, check battery, connection, route, and watch fit. Headphones should be used without isolating you from the environment. The watch should not be manipulated at crossings or in complicated areas. If the watch is GPS, carrying the iPhone may be important. If it is Cellular, there is more independence, but it depends on coverage and battery. Emergency contacts, Medical ID, and Fall Detection can be useful. Emergency calls should not be tested without a real reason. Workout data should never come before health or safety.
