Module 29. Apple Fitness Plus, where available

Apple Fitness Plus is Apple’s guided workout service. It is not essential in order to use the Apple Watch. The watch can record activity, workouts, heart rate, and progress without requiring a Fitness Plus subscription.

Even so, it may be interesting for some people because it offers guided classes for different types of exercise, with trainers, music, and sessions of different durations.

For a blind person, the usefulness of Fitness Plus will depend on several factors: the type of workout, the clarity of the spoken instructions, whether visual movements need to be followed, the person’s physical level, the available language, the device used to play the class, and the accessibility of the complete experience.

What Apple Fitness Plus is

Apple Fitness Plus is a subscription-based workout service. It allows you to follow guided sessions from compatible Apple devices.

It may include workouts such as:

  • Walking.
  • Running.
  • Strength.
  • HIIT.
  • Yoga.
  • Pilates.
  • Core.
  • Dance.
  • Cycling.
  • Rowing.
  • Meditation.
  • Stretching or recovery.
  • Other types depending on availability.

The Apple Watch integrates with the service to record the session and show data such as heart rate, calories, time, and progress. Not everyone will need this service. For many people, the Workout app will be enough.

What Fitness Plus offers

Fitness Plus can offer:

  • Guided workouts.
  • Sessions of different durations.
  • Routines for different levels.
  • Integrated music.
  • Trainers who explain exercises.
  • Integration with Apple Watch.
  • Motivation for people who prefer to follow a class.
  • Variety of disciplines.
  • It can be useful for those who want to train at home, in a gym, or in controlled spaces.
  • It can also help people who do not know what routine to do and prefer to follow a session that has already been prepared.

What limitations it may have for a blind person

Fitness Plus may have limitations if the instructions depend heavily on seeing the trainer. In some workouts, the instructor explains verbally what needs to be done, but may also rely on visual gestures, postures, demonstrations, or references that are not always described in enough detail. For that reason, not all workouts will be equally comfortable for a blind person. It may work better in activities where the verbal instructions are clear and the movement is simple to follow. It may be more difficult in activities with rapid changes, complex positions, or visual corrections.

The fact that a workout has audio does not automatically mean that it is fully accessible. This needs to be said clearly, because we have already learned plenty from interfaces that think speaking a little is the same as being accessible.

When Fitness Plus may make sense

It may make sense if:

  • You want to train at home.
  • Guided classes motivate you.
  • You have a safe space.
  • You can follow verbal instructions.
  • You already know the basic exercises.
  • You want variety.
  • You use Apple Watch regularly.
  • You have an active subscription.
  • You want to record sessions in an integrated way.
  • It may also be useful if you train with someone who can help you understand postures or movements at the beginning.

When it may not be worth it

It may not be worth it if:

  • You only want to walk or do basic exercise.
  • You prefer your own workouts.
  • You do not want to pay for a subscription.
  • The instructions are not clear enough for you.
  • You do not have a safe space to move.
  • You need more adapted explanations.
  • You do not use Apple services for training.
  • The Workout app is enough for you.
  • You do not need to subscribe to Fitness Plus in order to get value from the Apple Watch.
  • The watch already offers many features without that service.

Devices you can use it from

Fitness Plus can be used from compatible Apple devices. The experience may be more comfortable on a larger screen, such as iPhone, iPad, or Apple TV, although the Apple Watch records the data. For a blind person, the iPhone may be more comfortable for navigating classes with VoiceOver. The Apple Watch acts as a workout companion.

Before starting a class

Before starting a Fitness Plus session, it is useful to prepare:

  • Apple Watch charged.
  • iPhone, iPad, or Apple TV ready.
  • Headphones if you need them.
  • Clear space.
  • Comfortable clothing.
  • Water if appropriate.
  • Basic knowledge of the exercise.
  • A workout suited to your level.
  • If you are going to do floor exercises, prepare a mat or safe surface.
  • If you are going to do strength training, place the necessary equipment in an orderly way.

Do not start a class with objects in the way. The Apple Watch records activity, but it does not yet include a feature for apologising to the table after you trip over it.

Choosing a workout

When choosing a class, review:

  • Type of workout.
  • Duration.
  • Level or intensity.
  • Equipment required.
  • Music, if it matters to you.
  • Trainer.
  • Session description.
  • If you are starting out, choose short, low-intensity sessions.
  • Do not begin with a demanding class just because it is short.

Ten minutes can be very long if someone has designed those ten minutes to remind you that you have muscles you had not consulted.

More suitable workouts for starting out

For someone starting out, the following may be more suitable:

  • Guided walks, if available and suited to your environment.
  • Basic strength.
  • Basic core, if the postures are already well understood.
  • Gentle yoga.
  • Basic Pilates.
  • Meditation.
  • Stretching or recovery.

Classes with fast movements, dance, or HIIT may be more difficult if the verbal instructions are not detailed enough. That does not mean they are impossible, but they should be tried cautiously.

Using Fitness Plus with VoiceOver

To navigate Fitness Plus with VoiceOver:

  • Use the iPhone or main device.
  • Explore categories.
  • Read descriptions.
  • Review duration and intensity.
  • Select the class.
  • Start the workout.
  • Check that the Apple Watch is connected.
  • During the class, listen to the instructions.
  • If a class is not easy to understand, stop and choose another one.
  • There is no need to insist on a class that depends too much on visual information.

Tracking from the Apple Watch

During a Fitness Plus session, the Apple Watch can record:

  • Time.
  • Heart rate.
  • Calories.
  • Progress.
  • Activity.
  • When the session ends, the workout can be saved in Fitness.
  • This allows you to review the data later from the iPhone.

The Apple Watch provides recording and tracking, but the main class guidance will come from the Fitness Plus content.

Safety in guided workouts

Safety is especially important in guided workouts.

  • Do not do an exercise if you do not clearly understand the posture.
  • Do not follow fast movements if you do not have enough space.
  • Do not use equipment without knowing where it is placed.
  • Do not do balance exercises without support if you are not sure.
  • Do not force your joints.

Stop if you feel abnormal pain, dizziness, or discomfort. The trainer is not seeing you. They cannot correct you. So if a movement is not clear, it is better to skip it, modify it, or look for an easier class.

Training with support

Some blind people may get more out of Fitness Plus if, at the beginning, they train with someone who can describe or correct postures.

This can be useful in:

  • Yoga.
  • Pilates.
  • Strength.
  • Core.
  • Dance.
  • HIIT.
  • Once the movements have been learned, they may be able to follow more classes independently.
  • But it is advisable to learn the technique properly before repeating exercises.

Fitness Plus and Apple Watch without obsession

Fitness Plus can show data and motivation.

But metrics should not be pursued at any cost.

  • If a class is too intense, lower the pace.
  • If an exercise is not safe, adapt it.
  • If it is not a training day, rest.

The watch should not rule the body. The body leads. The watch records. A simple hierarchy that technology seems to forget rather often.

Fitness Plus compared with the Workout app

The Workout app is used to record an activity you do on your own. Fitness Plus is used to follow a guided class.

Example:

  • If you go out walking on your own, use Workout.
  • If you do a guided Fitness Plus strength class, use Fitness Plus.
  • If you do your own routine at home, you can use Workout with strength, functional, yoga, Pilates, or another suitable type.
  • If you follow a Fitness Plus class, the system can record the session integrated with the Apple Watch.

Alternatives to Fitness Plus

Fitness Plus is not compulsory.

You can also train with:

  • The Workout app.
  • Your own routines.
  • In-person classes.
  • Accessible audio workouts.
  • Videos by professionals who describe clearly.
  • Accessible exercise apps.
  • Guidance from physiotherapists or trainers.
  • Adapted programmes.
  • The important thing is that the workout is safe, understandable, and suitable for the person.

Common mistakes

Thinking Fitness Plus is necessary in order to use the Apple Watch. Subscribing without checking whether the classes are understandable.

Choosing workouts that are too intense at the beginning.

  • Following movements that are not understood.
  • Training in a space with obstacles.
  • Not checking the equipment required.
  • Not wearing the Apple Watch properly adjusted.
  • Not stopping when there is pain or dizziness.
  • Thinking all guided workouts are accessible just because they have audio.
  • Not reviewing the data afterwards in Fitness.

Practical advice

If you want to try Fitness Plus, start with short and simple classes.

  • Choose a category you already know.
  • Listen carefully to the description.
  • Do the first test in a clear space.
  • Do not look for intensity at the beginning.
  • Look for understanding, safety, and continuity.

If a class does not adapt well to a blind person, nothing is wrong. Change it. There is no need to fight with a video as if it were a moral debt.

Exercise for module 29

  • Open Fitness on the iPhone.
  • Look for the Fitness Plus section, if available.
  • Explore the categories with VoiceOver.
  • Choose a short and simple class.
  • Read the description.
  • Check duration, type of exercise, and required equipment.
  • Prepare the space.
  • Put on the Apple Watch properly adjusted.
  • Start the class only if you understand what you are going to do.
  • During the session, stop if an instruction is not clear.
  • When finished, review the workout in Fitness.
  • Consider whether the experience was comfortable, clear, and safe.

Summary of module 29

Apple Fitness Plus is a subscription-based guided workout service. It is not necessary in order to use the Apple Watch. It can be useful for people who want guided classes. Its accessibility depends greatly on the type of workout and the clarity of the instructions. The Apple Watch records data during sessions. When starting out, short, simple, and safe classes are best. Not all workouts will be equally comfortable for a blind person. The Workout app remains enough for many people. Safety and understanding the exercise are more important than completing a class.

Module 30. What the Apple Watch can and cannot do in health

Before looking at specific features, it is useful to remember one general idea: health features depend on the Apple Watch model, the version of watchOS, the country or region and, in some cases, local health authorisations. If an option does not appear on the watch or in the Health app, this may be due to regional availability, model compatibility, or configuration, and not necessarily to a VoiceOver problem. The Apple Watch has become a device closely linked to health.

It can record heart rate, activity, sleep, workouts, and other data. Depending on the model and country, it may also offer features such as ECG, blood oxygen, irregular rhythm notifications, atrial fibrillation history, sleep apnoea notifications, medication, cycle tracking, wrist temperature, or notifications related to hypertension.

  • These features can be very useful.
  • But they must be explained carefully.
  • The Apple Watch does not replace a doctor.
  • It does not replace a medical appointment.
  • It does not replace clinical tests.
  • It does not replace a diagnosis.

It does not replace a blood pressure monitor, a medical electrocardiogram, a professional pulse oximeter, or a health assessment when there are symptoms. The watch can provide data, trends, and alerts. That is already quite a lot. But it should not be turned into something it is not.

What the Apple Watch can be useful for in health

The Apple Watch can help with:

  • Observing trends.
  • Recording activity.
  • Measuring heart rate.
  • Receiving high or low heart rate alerts.
  • Receiving irregular rhythm notifications, if available.
  • Taking an ECG, if the model and country allow it.
  • Recording sleep.
  • Receiving notifications related to sleep apnoea, if available.
  • Recording medication through the Health ecosystem.
  • Checking data in the Health app on the iPhone.
  • Sharing certain data with professionals, if desired.
  • Becoming more aware of daily habits.
  • Detecting changes that may be worth discussing with a professional.
  • That is its main role: to accompany, record, and alert.

What should not be expected from the Apple Watch

  • You should not expect it to diagnose every disease.
  • You should not expect it to detect every heart problem.
  • You should not expect it to measure blood pressure like a conventional blood pressure monitor.
  • You should not expect it to replace a sleep study.
  • You should not expect every measurement to be perfect.
  • You should not expect every feature to be available on every model.
  • You should not expect every feature to be available in every country.
  • You should not expect every alert to be an emergency.
  • You should not expect the absence of alerts to mean the absence of problems.

This last point is very important. If the watch does not alert you, that does not mean everything is perfect. If a person has symptoms, they should seek medical advice. The Apple Watch is not an absolute guarantee.

Features that depend on the model

Not all Apple Watch models have the same sensors. Some features are available only on certain models.

For example, there may be differences in:

  1. ECG.
  2. Blood oxygen.
  3. Wrist temperature.
  4. Sleep apnoea notifications.
  5. Hypertension notifications.
  6. Detection of certain advanced metrics.

For that reason, in the health modules, it will be indicated that you need to check whether the feature is available on the specific model. It is not enough to say “the Apple Watch has this feature”.

The correct question is:

  • Does this model have it, in this country, with this system version and this configuration?
  • Less elegant, yes. But much more accurate.

Features that depend on the country or region

Some health features require approval or availability by country. This may affect features such as ECG, irregular rhythm, blood oxygen, sleep apnoea, hypertension, or others. Two people with similar watches may not have exactly the same options if they live in different countries.

For that reason, if a feature does not appear, it may be due to:

  • Unsupported model.
  • Unsupported country.
  • Unsupported age.
  • Incomplete configuration.
  • Old version of watchOS.
  • Old version of iOS.
  • Missing permissions in Health.
  • You should not automatically assume that the user has done something wrong.

Heart rate

Heart rate is one of the most basic and important features. The Apple Watch can measure beats per minute during the day, at rest, while walking, and during workouts. It can also offer alerts if it detects high or low heart rate under certain conditions. This can help identify changes or situations that deserve attention. But one isolated measurement does not always mean there is a problem.

Many factors can influence it:

  • Exercise.
  • Stress.
  • Coffee.
  • Medication.
  • Fever.
  • Sleep.
  • Anxiety.
  • Dehydration.
  • Physical condition.
  • For that reason, data should be interpreted with caution.

Irregular rhythm

Some Apple Watch models can offer irregular rhythm notifications. These notifications can alert you if the watch detects patterns compatible with certain irregular heart rhythms. This does not mean a definitive diagnosis. If an irregular rhythm alert appears, it is advisable to consult a healthcare professional. This feature should also not be used to rule out problems if there are symptoms.

ECG

On compatible models and in countries where it is available, the Apple Watch can take an ECG from the wrist. This feature can record an electrical signal from the heart and offer a classification. For example, it may indicate whether it detects sinus rhythm or signs compatible with atrial fibrillation, according to its capabilities. But it does not detect every heart problem. It does not replace a complete clinical ECG. It should not be used to decide on your own to stop treatments, ignore symptoms, or avoid a medical appointment. If the ECG gives a concerning result, if there are symptoms, or if there are doubts, seek medical advice.

Blood oxygen

Some models can measure blood oxygen, if the feature is available.

This measurement may be affected by:

  • How the watch is positioned.
  • Movement.
  • Skin temperature.
  • Strap fit.
  • Tattoos.
  • Circulation.
  • Environmental conditions.
  • Regional availability.
  • It should not replace a medical pulse oximeter or a health assessment.

If a person has breathing difficulty, chest pain, bluish lips, confusion, or significant symptoms, they should not start debating with the watch. They should seek help.

Sleep

The Apple Watch can record sleep.

It can help you understand:

  • Duration.
  • Schedules.
  • Routine.
  • Sleep stages, if available.
  • Trends.
  • Consistency.
  • It can also integrate with sleep schedules, alarms, and sleep modes.
  • Sleep tracking can be useful for detecting habits.
  • But it does not replace a sleep study if there is suspicion of an important sleep disorder.

Sleep apnoea

On models and in countries where it is available, the Apple Watch may offer notifications related to sleep apnoea. These notifications may indicate patterns that should be discussed with a professional. They do not replace a medical diagnosis. They do not replace polysomnography or other tests indicated by professionals. If an alert appears, it should be discussed with a healthcare professional.

Hypertension

Some features related to hypertension may be available on specific models and in specific regions. This point requires great clarity. The Apple Watch should not be presented as a traditional blood pressure monitor.

If it offers notifications related to possible hypertension, they should be understood as alerts based on patterns, not as a direct measurement equivalent to an upper-arm blood pressure monitor.

If this type of notification appears, the sensible thing is to follow the system instructions and consult healthcare professionals, using appropriate measurements when necessary.

Medication

The Health ecosystem allows medication to be recorded and reminders to be received. The Apple Watch can help by alerting you on the wrist and allowing you to log doses. This can be useful for people with daily treatments. But it must be configured carefully. A reminder does not guarantee that the medication has been taken. Marking a dose as taken without actually taking it can create confusion. If medication is critical, it is useful to have clear routines and, if necessary, other forms of support.

Cycle tracking and temperature

The Apple Watch can take part in menstrual cycle tracking and, depending on the model, record wrist temperature during the night. These features can help observe trends and estimates. They do not replace medical advice, diagnosis, or contraception. The information must be interpreted within its limits.

Noise

The Apple Watch can alert you about high noise levels, depending on model and configuration. This can help protect hearing. For blind people, the sound environment can also be important for orientation. Noise alerts may be useful in places with traffic, machinery, events, loud music, or gyms.

Health data on the iPhone

Although the Apple Watch records many data points, the Health app on the iPhone is usually the most complete place to review them.

From Health, you can check:

  • Heart rate.
  • Sleep.
  • Activity.
  • Trends.
  • Medication.
  • Respiratory data.
  • Cycle tracking.
  • Hearing.
  • Medical ID.
  • Data sources.
  • Permissions.
  • Information sharing.
  • For detailed analysis, the iPhone is better than the watch.
  • The watch records and alerts.
  • The iPhone is used to review.

Privacy of health data

Health data are sensitive information.

It is useful to review:

  • Which apps have access to Health.
  • Which data are being shared.
  • Who information is being shared with.
  • Which devices record data.
  • Which permissions have been granted.
  • Not every app needs access to everything.
  • An exercise app may need certain data.
  • A random app should not ask for access to information it does not need.
  • Health is not an area where permissions should be accepted without reading.

What to do when a health alert appears

If the Apple Watch shows a health alert:

  • Read the full alert.
  • Do not ignore it without understanding it.
  • Do not automatically panic.
  • Check the Health app if appropriate.
  • If there are significant symptoms, seek medical help.
  • If the alert recommends consultation, do so.
  • If you have doubts, save or share the information with a healthcare professional.
  • The watch can be wrong.
  • But it can also detect something worth reviewing.
  • The appropriate response is neither panic nor automatic dismissal. It is reasonable attention.
  • What to do if you have symptoms and the watch does not alert you
  • If you have concerning symptoms, do not wait for the watch to alert you.
  • Seek help.

Symptoms such as chest pain, breathing difficulty, loss of consciousness, sudden weakness, confusion, intense palpitations, severe dizziness, or unusual pain should be taken seriously. The absence of an alert does not rule out a problem. The Apple Watch is a support tool, not an absolute guardian.

Common mistakes

Thinking every health feature is available on every model.

Thinking they work the same way in every country.

  • Confusing an alert with a diagnosis.
  • Confusing the absence of an alert with the absence of a problem.
  • Using the watch as a substitute for medical care.
  • Not reviewing data in the Health app.
  • Not updating personal data.
  • Wearing the watch too loosely.
  • Not configuring permissions correctly.
  • Ignoring important alerts.
  • Obsessing over isolated figures.

Practical advice

Use health features as guidance. Review trends, not only individual data points. Configure your personal data properly. Wear the watch correctly adjusted. Consult professionals when there are alerts, symptoms, or doubts. Do not turn every number into a concern, but do not ignore relevant information either. The balance is to use the watch as a tool, not as an oracle.

Exercise for module 30

Open the Health app on the iPhone.

  • Review your personal data.
  • Check age, height, and weight.
  • Review which data the Apple Watch is recording.
  • Look for heart rate.
  • Check the available records.
  • Look for sleep if you have already slept with the watch.
  • Review app permissions if you have several apps connected to Health.
  • Then open the Watch app.
  • Go to My Watch.
  • Review the sections related to health, heart, sleep, or privacy that are available.
  • Do not activate sensitive features without understanding them.
  • Only observe which options appear on your model.

Summary of module 30

The Apple Watch can record and show useful health data. It can measure heart rate, activity, sleep, and other metrics depending on the model. Some advanced features depend on the model and country. The watch does not replace healthcare professionals or medical tests.

An alert should be treated with caution and attention.

  • The absence of an alert does not rule out a problem.
  • The Health app on the iPhone is the main place to review data in detail.
  • The privacy of health data must be protected.

Health features should be used as support, not as an absolute diagnosis.

Module 31. Heart rate

Heart rate is one of the most useful and most frequently used health features on the Apple Watch. The watch can measure how many times the heart beats per minute. This value is usually expressed as beats per minute, or BPM.

The Apple Watch can record heart rate during the day, during rest, during walks, during workouts, and during certain situations where the system considers it useful. For many people, this information can help them understand their activity, exercise intensity, stress, recovery, and general trends.

For a blind person, the Apple Watch can make this information accessible through VoiceOver, both on the watch and in the Health app on the iPhone.

What heart rate is

Heart rate is the number of heartbeats per minute.

  • It changes constantly.
  • It can be lower when resting.
  • It can increase when walking.
  • It can rise during exercise.
  • It can change with emotions, stress, fever, medication, caffeine, dehydration, sleep, illness, or physical condition.

That is why one isolated number should not be interpreted without context. A single reading can be useful, but trends are usually more informative.

What the Apple Watch can do

The Apple Watch can:

  • Measure current heart rate.
  • Record heart rate during the day.
  • Record resting heart rate.
  • Record walking heart rate.
  • Record heart rate during workouts.
  • Show heart rate recovery after exercise, depending on available data.
  • Send high heart rate notifications, if configured.
  • Send low heart rate notifications, if configured.
  • Provide data to the Health app on the iPhone.
  • Show heart rate trends over time.
  • The available options may vary depending on Apple Watch model, watchOS version, settings, and country or region.

What the Apple Watch cannot do

The Apple Watch cannot diagnose every heart problem.

  • It cannot replace medical evaluation.
  • It cannot replace professional heart monitoring.
  • It cannot guarantee that everything is fine because it has not sent an alert.
  • It cannot interpret symptoms in their full medical context.
  • It cannot measure heart rate perfectly in every situation.
  • It is a support tool.

If there are concerning symptoms, medical advice should be sought.

Where to check heart rate on the Apple Watch

The Apple Watch usually has a Heart Rate app.

To open it:

  • Press the Digital Crown.
  • Find Heart Rate.
  • Double tap.
  • Wait for the app to open.
  • VoiceOver will read the available information.

You may hear data such as:

  • Current heart rate.
  • Resting heart rate.
  • Walking average.
  • Workout heart rate.
  • Other available measurements.
  • The exact information may vary depending on the watchOS version and available data.

Checking current heart rate

When you open the Heart Rate app, the Apple Watch may try to measure your current heart rate.

To get a better reading:

  • Keep the watch properly adjusted.
  • Keep the arm still.
  • Wait a few seconds.
  • Do not move the watch around.
  • Make sure the back of the watch is touching the skin.
  • If the watch cannot measure correctly, it may show no reading or take longer.
  • If the strap is too loose, the reading may be worse.

Heart rate during workouts

Heart rate during workouts can help you understand intensity. For example, during a walk, it can show whether you are walking gently, moderately, or with more effort. During strength training, it may show how your body responds to the session. During cycling, running, or other exercise, it may help monitor effort.

But it should not be used alone to decide whether an exercise is safe.

  • If you feel unwell, stop.
  • Do not continue just because the watch shows a number that looks acceptable.
  • The body is not a widget. Unfortunately for designers, it remains complicated.

Resting heart rate

Resting heart rate is the heart rate when the body is at rest. This value can vary from person to person.

It may change with:

  • Physical condition.
  • Sleep.
  • Stress.
  • Illness.
  • Medication.
  • Caffeine.
  • Hydration.
  • Age.
  • General health.
  • For many people, resting heart rate trends are more useful than a single value.
  • If there is a significant change that persists or causes concern, it may be worth discussing it with a healthcare professional.

Walking heart rate

The Apple Watch may record walking heart rate. This can help show how the heart behaves during normal walking. It can be useful for observing trends over time. As always, the value must be interpreted with context.

Heart rate recovery

After exercise, the Apple Watch and Health app may show heart rate recovery. This refers to how heart rate decreases after stopping exercise. It can be a useful fitness-related indicator, but it should not be interpreted in isolation as a diagnosis. For detailed review, the iPhone will usually be more comfortable.

High heart rate notifications

The Apple Watch can notify you if it detects a high heart rate while you appear to be inactive. This can be configured from the iPhone or Apple Watch settings, depending on version. A high heart rate alert does not automatically mean there is a serious problem. But it should not be ignored without understanding it. If the alert appears repeatedly, if it is accompanied by symptoms, or if there is concern, it is advisable to consult healthcare professionals.

Low heart rate notifications

The Apple Watch can also notify you if it detects a low heart rate under certain conditions. Some people naturally have a lower heart rate, especially trained people.

But if a low heart rate alert appears with symptoms such as dizziness, fainting, weakness, confusion, or shortness of breath, medical advice should be sought. Again, the watch provides an alert. It does not provide a complete diagnosis.

Configuring heart rate notifications

To review heart rate notifications from the iPhone:

  • Open the Watch app.
  • Go to My Watch.
  • Look for Heart.
  • Review high heart rate notifications.
  • Review low heart rate notifications.
  • Review irregular rhythm notifications, if available.
  • The exact path and options may vary depending on country, region, model, and system version.
  • If the option does not appear, it may be due to compatibility or availability.

Choosing alert thresholds

The Apple Watch may allow you to choose thresholds for high or low heart rate notifications. Do not choose these values randomly. If you are unsure, use the default values or consult a healthcare professional, especially if you have known heart conditions, take medication affecting heart rate, or have symptoms.

This is not the place for adventurous experimentation. Changing health thresholds without understanding them is not a hobby; it is a small invitation to confusion.

Irregular rhythm notifications

Irregular rhythm notifications are related to possible signs of atrial fibrillation or other rhythm irregularities, depending on Apple’s supported feature. This will be covered in more detail in the next module. For now, it is enough to know that irregular rhythm is not the same as simple high or low heart rate. High or low heart rate refers to how fast or slow the heart is beating. Irregular rhythm refers to the pattern of the beats.

Checking heart rate on the iPhone

The Health app on the iPhone is the best place to review heart rate data in detail.

On the iPhone:

  • Open Health.
  • Go to Browse.
  • Look for Heart.
  • Enter Heart Rate.
  • Review the available data.
  • There you may find daily, weekly, monthly, and longer-term views.

VoiceOver can be used to review the data, although graphs may be easier or harder depending on how the app presents them.

You may also find:

  • Resting heart rate.
  • Walking heart rate average.
  • Heart rate variability, if available.
  • Heart rate recovery.
  • High and low heart rate notifications.
  • Irregular rhythm notifications, if available.

Heart rate and personal data

Some interpretations and estimates depend on personal data.

It is useful to keep Health information updated:

  • Age.
  • Height.
  • Weight.
  • Registered sex.
  • Medications if relevant.
  • Health conditions if you choose to record them.

The Apple Watch records data, but the usefulness of some estimates depends on the quality of the information provided.

When readings may be less accurate

Heart rate readings may be less accurate if:

  • The watch is too loose.
  • The watch moves during exercise.
  • The sensors are dirty.
  • The skin is very cold.
  • There is poor contact with the skin.
  • There are tattoos under the sensor area.
  • The activity involves irregular arm movement.
  • The strap does not hold the watch well.
  • The watch is not placed correctly.
  • This does not mean the feature is useless.
  • It means that proper placement matters.

How to improve heart rate readings

To improve readings:

  • Wear the watch slightly above the wrist bone.
  • Adjust the strap firmly, but comfortably.
  • Make sure the back touches the skin.
  • Clean the sensors if needed.
  • Use a suitable strap for exercise.
  • Avoid wearing the watch too loose during workouts.
  • Keep the arm still when taking a specific reading.
  • For exercise, tighten the strap slightly if the watch moves too much.

Heart rate and symptoms

If you have symptoms, symptoms matter. Do not rely only on the watch.

Seek medical help if you have:

  • Chest pain.
  • Difficulty breathing.
  • Fainting.
  • Severe dizziness.
  • Confusion.
  • Strong or unusual palpitations.
  • Sudden weakness.
  • Pain spreading to arm, jaw, back, or neck.
  • A feeling that something is seriously wrong.
  • If symptoms are significant, do not wait for the Apple Watch to decide whether the situation deserves attention.
  • Health does not work by waiting for a notification.

Heart rate and anxiety

Heart rate can increase with anxiety, stress, fear, or tension. Seeing the number on the watch may sometimes make a person more anxious. If checking heart rate repeatedly creates worry, it may be better to reduce constant checking and focus on trends or professional guidance. The Apple Watch can inform, but it should not feed a loop of checking and worrying.

Heart rate during sleep

The Apple Watch may record heart rate during sleep if you wear it at night and sleep tracking is configured. This data can help show resting trends. If you use sleep tracking, make sure the watch is comfortable and charged enough. Detailed sleep and night heart rate data are usually better reviewed from the Health app on the iPhone.

Heart rate and medications

Some medications can affect heart rate. For example, some may lower it, raise it, or affect rhythm. If you take medication and receive alerts, or if you notice unusual changes, it is advisable to discuss it with healthcare professionals. Do not stop or change medication because of Apple Watch data without medical advice.

Sharing heart rate data

The Health app may allow you to share or export certain data. This can be useful for discussing trends with a healthcare professional. If you decide to share data, make sure it is with someone appropriate. Health information is personal. Do not share it casually.

Common mistakes

  • Wearing the watch too loose.
  • Checking heart rate constantly without context.
  • Panicking over a single reading.
  • Ignoring repeated alerts.
  • Believing the watch replaces medical care.
  • Not checking data in Health on the iPhone.
  • Not reviewing notification thresholds.
  • Assuming no alert means no problem.
  • Using the watch during symptoms instead of seeking help.
  • Forgetting that readings may be affected by movement and fit.

Practical advice

Use heart rate as a reference. Look at trends. Check it during workouts if useful. Pay attention to alerts. Consult professionals if alerts repeat or symptoms appear. Do not turn the heart rate app into something you check every five minutes unless there is a specific reason. The watch should help you understand your body, not make you negotiate with your pulse all day.

Exercise for module 31

  • Put on the Apple Watch properly.
  • Make sure the strap is firm but comfortable.
  • Open the Heart Rate app.
  • Keep your arm still.
  • Listen to the current reading with VoiceOver.
  • Then open the Health app on the iPhone.
  • Go to the Heart section.
  • Find Heart Rate.
  • Review the available data.
  • Look for resting heart rate if it appears.
  • Look for walking heart rate average if it appears.
  • Open the Watch app.
  • Go to the Heart section, if available.
  • Review whether high and low heart rate notifications are configured.
  • Do not change thresholds unless you understand what you are doing.

Summary of module 31

The Apple Watch can measure heart rate. Heart rate is expressed in beats per minute.

It changes throughout the day and depends on many factors.

  • The Heart Rate app allows quick checking from the watch.
  • The Health app on the iPhone allows detailed review.
  • The watch can send high or low heart rate notifications, if configured.

Alerts should be taken seriously, but they are not a definitive diagnosis. The absence of alerts does not guarantee absence of problems. Proper watch fit improves readings. If symptoms appear, seek medical help and do not rely only on the watch.

Module 32. Irregular rhythm and atrial fibrillation

Some Apple Watch models can notify you if they detect signs of an irregular heart rhythm. This feature is mainly intended to help identify patterns that may be compatible with atrial fibrillation, often abbreviated as AFib. This is an important health feature, but it must be understood properly. An irregular rhythm notification is not a definitive diagnosis. The Apple Watch does not detect every heart rhythm problem. The absence of a notification does not mean that everything is fine. If there are symptoms, doubts, repeated notifications, or known heart problems, the appropriate thing is to consult healthcare professionals.

What atrial fibrillation is

Atrial fibrillation is a type of irregular heart rhythm. In simple terms, the heart does not beat with its usual regular pattern. Some people may notice symptoms. Others may not notice anything.

Possible symptoms can include:

  • Palpitations.
  • Fast or irregular heartbeat.
  • Fatigue.
  • Shortness of breath.
  • Dizziness.
  • Weakness.
  • Chest discomfort.
  • But not everyone experiences the same thing.
  • Some people may have atrial fibrillation without obvious symptoms.
  • That is why detection tools can be useful, but they should never replace medical evaluation.

What the Apple Watch can do

Depending on model, country, age, configuration, and watchOS version, the Apple Watch may offer:

  • Irregular rhythm notifications.
  • ECG app.
  • AFib History, in some regions and models.
  • Heart rate data.
  • Health records in the Health app.
  • The irregular rhythm feature checks the heart rhythm from time to time when the person appears to be at rest.
  • If it detects a pattern that may suggest atrial fibrillation, it can send a notification.

What the Apple Watch cannot do

The Apple Watch cannot diagnose all cases of atrial fibrillation.

  • It cannot detect every irregular rhythm.
  • It cannot detect heart attacks.
  • It cannot detect strokes.
  • It cannot replace a medical ECG.
  • It cannot replace a cardiologist.
  • It cannot replace professional monitoring.
  • It cannot interpret symptoms in their full context.
  • It can alert you to something that may need attention.

That is useful, but it is not the same as a medical diagnosis.

Availability of irregular rhythm notifications

Irregular rhythm notifications are not available everywhere.

They depend on:

  • Apple Watch model.
  • watchOS version.
  • Country or region.
  • Age requirements.
  • Health configuration.
  • Regulatory availability.
  • If the option does not appear, this may be due to availability or compatibility.
  • It is not necessarily a VoiceOver problem.

Where to configure irregular rhythm notifications

On the iPhone:

  • Open the Health app.
  • Go to Browse.
  • Go to Heart.
  • Look for Irregular Rhythm Notifications.
  • Follow the setup instructions if the feature is available.
  • You may need to confirm information such as age and whether you have been diagnosed with atrial fibrillation.
  • You can also review related settings from the Watch app, depending on the system version.

On the iPhone:

  1. Open the Watch app.
  2. Go to My Watch.
  3. Look for Heart.
  4. Review the available heart notifications.
  5. The exact path may vary.

If the option is unavailable

If you cannot find irregular rhythm notifications, check:

  • Your Apple Watch model.
  • Your iPhone and watchOS versions.
  • Your country or region.
  • Age requirements.
  • Health app setup.
  • Whether the feature has been officially made available in your location.
  • Do not assume that the option has disappeared or that the watch is faulty.

Many Apple health features behave like a bureaucratic border crossing: model, region, version, age, permission, and then maybe the button appears.

When an irregular rhythm notification appears

If the Apple Watch sends an irregular rhythm notification:

  • Read the full notification.
  • Do not ignore it automatically.
  • Do not panic automatically.
  • Check whether you have symptoms.
  • Open the Health app for more information if needed.
  • Consider contacting a healthcare professional.
  • If you have chest pain, severe shortness of breath, fainting, confusion, sudden weakness, or serious symptoms, seek urgent medical help.
  • The notification may be useful information to share with healthcare professionals.
  • It may indicate that further assessment is needed.

Repeated notifications

If you receive repeated irregular rhythm notifications, it is advisable to consult a healthcare professional. Repeated alerts may indicate that something deserves review.

The professional may request tests such as:

  • Clinical ECG.
  • Holter monitor.
  • Blood tests.
  • Medical history review.
  • Medication review.
  • Other studies depending on the case.
  • Do not make treatment decisions based only on the watch.

No notification but symptoms

If you have symptoms but the Apple Watch does not send a notification, do not ignore the symptoms. Seek medical advice.

The Apple Watch does not monitor continuously in the same way as professional equipment.

  • It may not detect every episode.
  • It may not check at the exact moment when the problem happens.
  • It may not be able to classify some rhythms.

Symptoms matter. Do not wait for technology to give permission to take your own body seriously.

Difference between irregular rhythm notifications and ECG

Irregular rhythm notifications are background checks that the watch may perform from time to time. The ECG app is a specific test that you start manually, if available on your model and in your country.

Irregular rhythm notification:

  • Works in the background under certain conditions.
  • Can send an alert if a pattern is detected.
  • Does not require you to start it manually each time.

ECG app:

  • Is opened manually.
  • Requires you to stay still.
  • Requires placing a finger on the Digital Crown.
  • Records a short ECG.
  • Gives a classification, within its limits.
  • These two features are related, but not identical.

AFib History

In some regions and models, Apple Watch may offer AFib History. This feature is intended for people already diagnosed with atrial fibrillation. It can estimate how often the heart shows signs of AFib over time. This is not the same as irregular rhythm notifications for people without a diagnosis. If this feature appears, follow the Health app instructions carefully. If you have not been diagnosed with AFib, do not configure health features by guessing.

What to share with a healthcare professional

If you receive an alert, it may be useful to share:

  • Date and time of the notification.
  • Whether there were symptoms.
  • What you were doing.
  • Heart rate data around that time.
  • ECG recording if you took one and the feature is available.
  • Any repeated alerts.
  • Medication or relevant health conditions.
  • The Health app on the iPhone can help review this information.
  • Do not rely on memory alone if the data are available.

Heart rhythm and exercise

Heart rhythm may behave differently during exercise. Irregular rhythm notifications usually work under specific conditions and may not be active during all workouts. If you feel palpitations, dizziness, chest pain, unusual shortness of breath, or faintness during exercise, stop. Do not continue just because the workout screen still looks normal. The watch records data. It does not carry responsibility for your decisions, which is unfair but accurate.

Heart rhythm and anxiety

Anxiety or stress can make the heart beat faster or make a person notice palpitations more intensely. This does not mean that every palpitation is dangerous. But it also does not mean that every symptom should be dismissed as anxiety. If symptoms are new, intense, repeated, or concerning, consult a professional. The Apple Watch can provide information, but medical context matters.

Heart rhythm and medication

Some medications can affect heart rate or rhythm. If you take medication and receive alerts, or if you notice changes, discuss it with healthcare professionals. Do not stop, start, or change medication because of Apple Watch data without professional guidance.

Privacy

Heart rhythm data are health data. They should be treated as private information. Review which apps can access Health data. Do not share screenshots, reports, or data publicly unless you are sure you want to. Health data may be useful for professionals, but not every app or person needs access to it.

Common mistakes

Thinking an irregular rhythm notification is a definitive diagnosis.

Thinking no notification means no rhythm problem exists.

  • Ignoring repeated notifications.
  • Panicking over one alert without reading the information.
  • Not consulting professionals when symptoms appear.
  • Confusing ECG with irregular rhythm notifications.
  • Trying to activate a feature not available in the country.
  • Assuming the feature fails because VoiceOver cannot find it.
  • Changing medication based on watch data.
  • Checking heart data obsessively without medical reason.

Practical advice

If irregular rhythm notifications are available, configure them carefully from the Health app.

Read Apple’s explanations during setup.

  • If an alert appears, use it as information.
  • If symptoms appear, act based on symptoms, not only on the watch.
  • If alerts repeat, consult healthcare professionals.

If the feature is not available, do not build the course around it as if everyone had it. Availability varies, because apparently even health features need passports.

Exercise for module 32

On the iPhone, open the Health app.

  • Go to Browse.
  • Go to Heart.
  • Look for Irregular Rhythm Notifications.
  • If the option appears, open it and listen to the explanation with VoiceOver.
  • Do not activate it without understanding the conditions.
  • If you decide to activate it, follow the setup steps.
  • Then open the Watch app.
  • Go to My Watch.
  • Look for Heart.
  • Review whether irregular rhythm options appear there too.
  • If the option does not appear, note that it may depend on model, country, age, or system version.

Summary of module 32

Some Apple Watch models can offer irregular rhythm notifications.

These notifications may detect patterns compatible with atrial fibrillation.

  • They are not a definitive diagnosis.
  • They do not detect every heart problem.
  • The absence of a notification does not guarantee that everything is fine.
  • Availability depends on model, country, age, and system version.
  • If a notification appears, it may be useful to consult healthcare professionals.
  • If there are symptoms, seek medical help even if the watch has not alerted you.
  • Irregular rhythm notifications and ECG are related, but they are not the same.
  • Health data should be treated as private information.

Module 33. ECG

Some Apple Watch models allow you to take an ECG from your wrist, provided that the feature is available in your country or region and the setup requirements are met. ECG stands for electrocardiogram.

An electrocardiogram records the electrical activity of the heart. In the case of the Apple Watch, it is a single-lead ECG taken using the watch itself and the Digital Crown.

This feature can be useful for recording information at a specific moment, especially if a person notices palpitations, irregularity, or wants to save a record to discuss with healthcare professionals.

But something must be made very clear from the beginning: the Apple Watch ECG does not replace a full medical electrocardiogram.

  • It can provide information.
  • It can classify some results.
  • It can save a record.
  • It can help you decide to seek advice.

But it does not detect every heart problem.

  • It is not for self-diagnosis.
  • It should not be used to ignore symptoms.
  • It should not replace medical care.

What the Apple Watch ECG needs

To use ECG, you need:

  • A compatible Apple Watch model.
  • A compatible version of watchOS.
  • A compatible iPhone.
  • The Health app configured.
  • The feature available in your country or region.
  • To meet the age and setup requirements.
  • The watch correctly positioned.

If the ECG app does not appear, or if the option to configure it does not appear, this may be due to the model, country, age, system version, or incomplete setup. Not every Apple Watch has ECG.

What the Apple Watch ECG measures

The Apple Watch ECG records an electrical signal from the heart for a few seconds. It is usually taken by placing a finger from the opposite hand on the Digital Crown while the watch is on your wrist. The watch records the signal and then may offer a classification.

Possible results may include terms such as:

  • Sinus rhythm.
  • Atrial fibrillation.
  • High or low heart rate.
  • Inconclusive result.
  • Poor recording.
  • The exact wording may vary depending on language, version, and country.

What sinus rhythm means

If the ECG shows sinus rhythm, it means that during that recording the watch has detected a regular heart rhythm within the range it can analyse. This is usually a normal result. But it does not mean that every possible heart problem has been ruled out. If a person has significant symptoms, they should seek medical advice even if the Apple Watch shows sinus rhythm.

What atrial fibrillation means

If the ECG indicates atrial fibrillation, it means the recording may show signs compatible with that rhythm. This does not replace medical diagnosis.

A healthcare professional should review the situation, especially if the result repeats, if there are symptoms, or if the person has risk factors.

The Apple Watch can give a warning, but it is not a cardiologist strapped to the wrist. That would be uncomfortable, quite expensive, and probably illegal in several countries.

Inconclusive result

An inconclusive result means the Apple Watch could not classify the recording clearly.

This can happen for several reasons:

  • Movement during the recording.
  • Poor contact with the skin.
  • Watch too loose.
  • Finger not correctly placed on the Digital Crown.
  • Heart rate outside the range the feature can analyse.
  • Electrical noise or interference.
  • Other rhythm patterns.
  • A single inconclusive result does not necessarily mean there is a serious problem.
  • But if it happens repeatedly, or if there are symptoms, it should be discussed with healthcare professionals.

Poor recording

If the watch indicates a poor recording, it means the ECG was not captured properly.

Possible causes:

  • The person moved.
  • The watch was not well adjusted.
  • The finger was not properly resting on the Digital Crown.
  • The wrist was not stable.
  • There was poor skin contact.
  • The sensors were dirty.
  • The person pressed instead of resting the finger.
  • In that case, repeat the recording correctly.

How to take an ECG

To take an ECG on the Apple Watch:

  • Put the watch on correctly.
  • Make sure it is firm but comfortable.
  • Sit down.
  • Rest your arm on a table, your lap, or a stable surface.
  • Open the ECG app on the Apple Watch.
  • Place a finger from the opposite hand on the Digital Crown.
  • Do not press the Digital Crown.
  • Keep your finger resting on it.
  • Stay still.
  • Wait until the recording finishes.
  • Listen to the result with VoiceOver.
  • The key point is this: the finger rests on the Digital Crown, it does not press it.
  • This is a very common mistake.
  • If you press the Digital Crown, you may leave the app or interrupt the process.

Where the ECG app is

The ECG app may appear in the Apple Watch app list.

To open it:

  • Press the Digital Crown.
  • Look for ECG.
  • Double tap.
  • If the app does not appear, review the configuration from the Health app on the iPhone.
  • It may also be unavailable because of model, country, age, or system version.

Configuring ECG from the iPhone

The ECG feature is usually configured from the Health app on the iPhone.

On the iPhone:

  • Open Health.
  • Go to Browse.
  • Go to Heart.
  • Look for ECG.
  • Follow the setup instructions if the feature is available.
  • The system may ask for information and show explanations about the feature and its limitations.
  • Listen to all the information with VoiceOver before completing setup.
  • If the option does not appear, check compatibility and availability.

Using VoiceOver during ECG

With VoiceOver, the ECG app can be used by listening to the instructions and the result. During the recording, avoid touching the screen unnecessarily. The most important thing is to stay still and keep the finger resting on the Digital Crown. When the recording ends, VoiceOver should allow you to hear the result. If there are buttons such as Done, Add Symptoms, or similar options, listen carefully before activating them.

Adding symptoms

After taking an ECG, the system may allow you to add symptoms.

For example:

  • Palpitations.
  • Rapid heartbeat.
  • Fatigue.
  • Shortness of breath.
  • Chest discomfort.
  • Dizziness.
  • Other symptoms.
  • This information can help provide context to the recording.
  • Do not add symptoms that are not real.
  • If you had no symptoms, do not invent any.
  • If you had symptoms, record them as accurately as possible.

Where ECG recordings are saved

ECG recordings are saved in the Health app on the iPhone.

To find them:

  • Open Health.
  • Go to Browse.
  • Go to Heart.
  • Look for ECG.
  • Open the records.
  • There you can review date, time, result, and details.
  • The iPhone is the best place to review ECG records in detail.

Sharing an ECG with a healthcare professional

The Health app may allow ECG records to be exported or shared, for example as a PDF, depending on version and region. This can be useful if you need to show the result to a doctor. Before sharing, make sure it is the correct recording. Health data are personal. Do not send them to people who do not need them.

When to take an ECG

It may make sense to take an ECG:

  • If you notice palpitations.
  • If you feel an irregular heartbeat.
  • If the Apple Watch has sent an alert.
  • If a healthcare professional has asked you to keep records, where appropriate.
  • If you want to record a specific moment to discuss later.
  • It is not necessary to take ECGs constantly without a reason.
  • Repeated measurements without purpose can create anxiety.
  • The watch is useful, but it should not become a small factory of worry.

When not to rely only on the ECG

Do not rely only on the Apple Watch ECG if you have serious symptoms.

Seek medical help if you have:

  • Chest pain.
  • Shortness of breath.
  • Fainting.
  • Severe dizziness.
  • Sudden weakness.
  • Confusion.
  • Pain spreading to the arm, jaw, back, or neck.
  • Intense or unusual palpitations.
  • A feeling that something is seriously wrong.
  • A normal Apple Watch ECG does not justify ignoring important symptoms.

Limitations of the Apple Watch ECG

The Apple Watch ECG has limitations.

  • It is a single-lead ECG.
  • It does not replace a full clinical ECG.
  • It does not detect every arrhythmia.
  • It does not detect heart attacks.
  • It does not detect strokes.
  • It does not detect every heart condition.
  • It may produce inconclusive results.
  • It may fail if the recording is poor.
  • It depends on proper use.

This does not make it useless. It simply defines what it can and cannot do.

ECG and irregular rhythm notifications

ECG is not the same as irregular rhythm notifications.

ECG:

  • You start it manually.
  • It records a specific moment.
  • It requires placing a finger on the Digital Crown.
  • It gives a classification of that recording.

Irregular rhythm notifications:

  • Work in the background under certain conditions.
  • Can alert you if the watch detects a possible irregular rhythm pattern.
  • Do not require you to start each recording manually.
  • Both can be related to heart rhythm, but they are different functions.

ECG and atrial fibrillation

The Apple Watch ECG can classify some recordings as showing signs of atrial fibrillation, if the feature is available and the recording meets the required conditions.

If this result appears, especially repeatedly, it should be discussed with a healthcare professional.

  • Do not self-diagnose.
  • Do not start or stop medication because of the watch.
  • Do not assume that one recording explains everything.

The professional will decide whether more tests are needed.

ECG and anxiety

This is an important point. The ECG feature can help, but it can also increase anxiety if used compulsively. Taking recordings constantly after every sensation can turn the watch into a source of worry. If you notice that you are checking ECG obsessively, it may be useful to discuss this with a professional and limit its use. Technology can help, but it can also feed concerns when consulted without judgement.

Common mistakes

Thinking ECG is available on every Apple Watch.

  • Thinking it works in every country.
  • Pressing the Digital Crown instead of resting the finger on it.
  • Moving the wrist during the recording.
  • Interpreting a result as a definitive diagnosis.
  • Ignoring symptoms because the ECG looks normal.
  • Panicking over an isolated result.
  • Not saving important records.
  • Not consulting repeated or concerning results.
  • Using ECG compulsively.

Practical advice

Take a first practice measurement when you are calm. Learn the process before you need it. Check that you know how to open the ECG app, rest your finger on the Digital Crown, wait for the result, and find the record in Health. Do not wait until you are nervous to learn it.

Exercise for module 33

If ECG is available on your Apple Watch, do this practice:

  • Put the watch on properly adjusted.
  • Sit down.
  • Rest your arm.
  • Open the ECG app on the Apple Watch.
  • Place a finger from the opposite hand on the Digital Crown.
  • Do not press.
  • Wait until the recording finishes.
  • Listen to the result.
  • Then open Health on the iPhone.
  • Go to Heart.
  • Go to ECG.
  • Find the record you have just made.
  • Listen to the date, time, and result.
  • Do not interpret the result as a diagnosis. The goal of the exercise is to learn the procedure.

Summary of module 33

Some Apple Watch models allow you to take an ECG. The feature depends on model, country, age, version, and configuration. The Apple Watch ECG does not replace a full medical electrocardiogram. To take it, you rest a finger on the Digital Crown without pressing it. The watch must be properly adjusted and the person must remain still. Records are saved in the Health app on the iPhone. A concerning result should be discussed with a healthcare professional. A normal result does not allow important symptoms to be ignored. The feature should be used as support, not as an absolute diagnosis.

Module 34. Blood oxygen

Some Apple Watch models can measure blood oxygen, provided that the feature is available in the country or region and there are no specific restrictions for that model.

This feature can provide an estimate of the percentage of oxygen in the blood. It may also take background measurements, depending on configuration. It is an interesting feature, but it must be explained with great caution. The Apple Watch does not replace a medical pulse oximeter. It does not replace healthcare assessment. It should not be used to decide whether breathing difficulty is important or not. If a person has concerning symptoms, they should seek help even if the watch shows a value that appears normal.

What blood oxygen is

Blood oxygen is expressed as a percentage. It refers to the estimated level of oxygen carried in the blood. In health contexts, oxygen saturation is often measured with a pulse oximeter, usually placed on a finger. The Apple Watch tries to estimate this from the wrist. That means the result depends greatly on correct placement, stillness, skin contact, sensor quality, and other conditions. It should be understood as guidance, not as a clinical measurement.

What the Apple Watch can do

If the feature is available, the Apple Watch can:

  • Take a blood oxygen measurement manually.
  • Record some measurements in the background.
  • Save values in the Health app on the iPhone.
  • Show trends over time.
  • Provide extra context together with other health data.
  • This can be useful if you are interested in observing general trends.

It may also provide information that can be discussed with healthcare professionals if there are doubts or repeated unusual values.

What the Apple Watch cannot do

The Apple Watch cannot replace a medical pulse oximeter.

  • It cannot diagnose respiratory disease.
  • It cannot decide whether a person needs urgent care.
  • It cannot rule out a health problem if symptoms are present.
  • It cannot guarantee perfect accuracy in every measurement.
  • It cannot be used as the only reference in a serious situation.

This is important because breathing is not a minor issue. If there is shortness of breath, chest pain, bluish lips, confusion, fainting, severe weakness, or a feeling of serious illness, the person should seek medical help. A normal value on the watch does not cancel symptoms.

Availability of blood oxygen

Blood oxygen is not available on every Apple Watch model. It is also not available in the same way in every country or region. In addition, there may be specific restrictions affecting certain models, countries, or versions.

If the Blood Oxygen app does not appear, possible reasons include:

  • The Apple Watch model is not compatible.
  • The feature is not available in the country or region.
  • The system version is not compatible.
  • The Health app has not been configured correctly.
  • There are specific restrictions for that model or market.
  • It is not necessarily a VoiceOver problem.

This point should be explained clearly, because otherwise people waste time looking for a button that does not exist. A classic human pastime, now with health sensors.

Where to find the Blood Oxygen app

If the feature is available, the Apple Watch may include an app called Blood Oxygen.

To open it:

  • Press the Digital Crown.
  • Find Blood Oxygen.
  • Double tap.
  • Follow the instructions shown on the Apple Watch.
  • With VoiceOver, listen carefully to each instruction.
  • If the app does not appear, check compatibility, country or region, and system version.

How to take a measurement

To take a blood oxygen measurement:

  • Put the Apple Watch on properly.
  • Make sure the strap is firm but comfortable.
  • Sit down.
  • Rest your arm on a table or on your lap.
  • Keep the watch facing upward.
  • Open the Blood Oxygen app.
  • Start the measurement.
  • Stay still.
  • Wait until the measurement finishes.
  • Listen to the result with VoiceOver.
  • Stillness is very important.
  • If you move, speak too much, change the position of your wrist, or the watch is loose, the measurement may fail or be less reliable.

Correct watch position

For the measurement to work better:

  • The watch should be slightly above the wrist bone.
  • The back of the watch should touch the skin.
  • The strap should not be loose.
  • The watch should not move.
  • The wrist should be relaxed.
  • The arm should be supported.
  • Do not measure while walking, exercising, moving your arm, or adjusting the strap.

If the measurement fails

A failed measurement does not necessarily mean there is a health problem. It may simply mean the watch could not read properly.

Possible causes include:

  • The watch is too loose.
  • The wrist moved.
  • The arm was not supported.
  • The watch was too low on the wrist.
  • The sensors were not in good contact with the skin.
  • The person was moving.
  • The skin or wrist position made the reading difficult.
  • There were tattoos or other factors in the sensor area.
  • If it fails, adjust the watch, sit still, support the arm, and try again.
  • Do not panic over a failed measurement.

A failed reading is not a diagnosis. Sometimes it is just the watch saying, in its own expensive way, that your wrist did not cooperate.

Background measurements

The Apple Watch may take blood oxygen measurements in the background, if the feature is enabled and available. These measurements may happen during the day or while sleeping, depending on configuration. However, background measurements also depend on conditions. If the watch is poorly positioned, if there is movement, or if the feature is limited by settings, some data may not be recorded.

Checking data on the iPhone

Blood oxygen data are usually reviewed better in the Health app on the iPhone.

On the iPhone:

  • Open Health.
  • Go to Browse.
  • Look for Respiratory or Blood Oxygen, depending on how the app is organised.
  • Open Blood Oxygen.
  • Review the available data.
  • There you may find measurements by day, week, month, or longer periods.
  • The iPhone is more comfortable than the watch for reviewing history and trends with VoiceOver.

Understanding values

Blood oxygen values are shown as percentages. A single value should not be interpreted without context.

Values can vary because of:

  • Measurement conditions.
  • Movement.
  • Watch position.
  • Skin contact.
  • Temperature.
  • Altitude.
  • Health status.
  • Device limitations.
  • Sensor conditions.
  • If a value seems low but there are no symptoms, it may be useful to repeat the measurement correctly.
  • If values are repeatedly low, or if there are symptoms, consult healthcare professionals.
  • Symptoms are more important than the watch value.

When to seek help

Seek medical help if there are symptoms such as:

  • Shortness of breath.
  • Chest pain.
  • Bluish lips or face.
  • Confusion.
  • Fainting.
  • Severe weakness.
  • Difficulty speaking because of breathlessness.
  • Severe dizziness.
  • A feeling that something is seriously wrong.
  • Do not wait for the watch to confirm the problem.
  • Do not use a normal watch reading to dismiss symptoms.
  • Health does not ask permission from a sensor before becoming urgent.

Blood oxygen during sleep

If the feature is available and background measurements are enabled, the Apple Watch may record blood oxygen during sleep. This can provide extra context together with other sleep and respiratory data. However, it still does not replace a sleep study or medical assessment.

If there are symptoms such as loud snoring, observed pauses in breathing, daytime sleepiness, morning headaches, or persistent fatigue, healthcare professionals should be consulted. This will be discussed again in the sleep and sleep apnoea modules.

Blood oxygen and altitude

Blood oxygen may vary at high altitude. If a person is in the mountains or travelling to areas at high elevation, values may change. The Apple Watch may record information, but any concerning symptoms should be taken seriously.

Blood oxygen and exercise

During exercise, breathing and heart rate change. The Apple Watch blood oxygen feature is not mainly intended as a sports performance tool for constant checking during activity. If you feel unwell during exercise, stop. Do not continue because the watch has not shown anything alarming. If you want to review health data after workouts, use the Health and Fitness apps on the iPhone.

Blood oxygen and illness

Respiratory illness, fever, infection, asthma, chronic lung disease, heart problems, and other conditions can affect oxygen levels. If someone has a known condition, the Apple Watch should not replace the tools or instructions given by healthcare professionals. If a doctor has recommended a medical pulse oximeter, use that device according to medical guidance. The Apple Watch can be additional information, not a replacement.

Privacy

  • Blood oxygen is health information.
  • It should be treated as private data.
  • Review which apps have access to Health data.
  • Do not share readings casually.
  • If you share data with someone, do it consciously.

Common mistakes

Thinking every Apple Watch has blood oxygen.

Not checking availability by country or model.

  • Measuring with the watch loose.
  • Moving during the measurement.
  • Interpreting one isolated value as a diagnosis.
  • Ignoring symptoms because the value looks normal.
  • Getting frightened by a failed measurement.
  • Using the watch as a substitute for a medical pulse oximeter.
  • Not reviewing data in Health.
  • Not understanding that there may be specific restrictions.

Practical advice

If your watch has this feature, learn to take a measurement at rest and with good placement. Do not use it as an emergency tool. Do not measure continuously without a reason. Review trends in Health if you are interested. If important symptoms appear, seek healthcare attention. The Apple Watch can provide information, but breathing remains far too important to leave entirely in the hands of a wrist with sensors.

Exercise for module 34

If your Apple Watch has the Blood Oxygen app:

  • Put the watch on properly adjusted.
  • Sit down.
  • Support your arm.
  • Open the Blood Oxygen app.
  • Start a measurement.
  • Remain still until it finishes.
  • Listen to the result.
  • Then open Health on the iPhone.
  • Look for Blood Oxygen.
  • Check whether the measurement appears.
  • Review date, time, and value.
  • Do not draw medical conclusions from a single measurement.

If the app does not appear:

  • Check whether your model is compatible.
  • Check whether the feature is available in your country or region.
  • Check whether the system version is up to date.

Summary of module 34

Some Apple Watch models can measure blood oxygen. The feature depends on model, country, version, and possible restrictions.

It does not replace a medical pulse oximeter.

  • It does not replace healthcare attention.
  • Correct watch placement and stillness are essential.
  • The data are best reviewed in Health on the iPhone.
  • A low value should be interpreted with caution, but symptoms come first.
  • A normal value does not rule out a problem if symptoms are present.
  • The feature should be used as guidance, not as a diagnosis.
