Module 35. Sleep

The Apple Watch can help record sleep and create a more orderly rest routine. To use this feature, you need to sleep with the watch on. During the night, the Apple Watch can record data such as sleep duration, time in bed, sleep stages if available, heart rate, respiratory rate, wrist temperature on compatible models, and other related data.

Sleep tracking can be useful for understanding habits and trends. It can help detect whether you sleep too little, whether your schedule is irregular, or whether your nights change over time. But, as with other health features, the data must be interpreted carefully. The Apple Watch does not replace a medical sleep evaluation. It does not diagnose a sleep disorder by itself.

It should not be used as the only reference if there is persistent tiredness, loud snoring, observed pauses in breathing, daytime sleepiness, or frequent awakenings. For that, healthcare professionals should be consulted.

What the Apple Watch can record during sleep

Depending on model, system version, and configuration, the Apple Watch can record data such as:

  • Time asleep.
  • Time in bed.
  • Sleep stages.
  • Heart rate during the night.
  • Respiratory rate.
  • Wrist temperature, if the model allows it.
  • Blood oxygen, if the model and country allow it.
  • Data related to sleep apnoea, if the feature is available.
  • Sleep schedules.
  • Rest routine.
  • Not all data appear on all models.
  • Not all features are available in all countries.
  • Not every isolated data point should cause concern.
  • The important thing is to observe trends.

What you need to record sleep

To record sleep, you need:

  • To sleep with the Apple Watch on.
  • Enough battery.
  • Sleep configured on the iPhone or Apple Watch.
  • The watch properly adjusted.
  • The corresponding tracking feature enabled.
  • A comfortable strap for sleeping.
  • If the watch has no battery, it will not record the night.
  • If you take it off before sleeping, it will not record either.
  • If it is too loose, some data may be less reliable.

Battery and sleep

Recording sleep requires organising charging. Many people charge the Apple Watch overnight. But if you want to use it while sleeping, you cannot charge it while wearing it. So you need to find another moment.

It could be:

  • Before going to bed.
  • When you get up.
  • While showering.
  • During breakfast.
  • While resting for a while.
  • During part of the day when you do not need it.
  • If your model has fast charging, this may be more convenient.
  • Before going to bed, check the battery. If it is very low, it may not last through the night.

Configuring Sleep from the iPhone

The most comfortable setup is usually done from the iPhone.

On the iPhone:

  • Open the Health app.
  • Find Sleep.
  • Enter the section.
  • Follow the instructions to configure sleep schedules.
  • Set a sleep goal if requested.
  • Configure a schedule for weekdays and weekends if you want.
  • Turn on sleep tracking with Apple Watch if the option appears.
  • You can also review options in the Watch app, in the settings related to Sleep.
  • The exact path may vary depending on version, but the Health app on the iPhone is usually the main centre.

Configuring Sleep from the Apple Watch

You can also review some options from the Apple Watch.

To do this:

  • Press the Digital Crown.
  • Find Sleep.
  • Double tap.
  • Explore the options with VoiceOver.
  • You can check schedules, rest, and other available data.
  • Even so, for configuring everything more comfortably, the iPhone is usually better.

Sleep goal

The sleep goal is the amount of time you want to sleep each night. It does not mean the watch will force you to sleep those hours. It serves as a reference. You can configure a realistic goal.

For example, if you usually sleep five and a half hours, it may not make sense to suddenly set nine hours. It may be better to observe first and adjust routines gradually.

The goal should help you, not become another number to feel guilty about at seven in the morning. Waking up early already comes with enough punishment.

Sleep schedule

You can configure schedules for going to bed and waking up. This helps create a routine.

The schedule may include:

  • Bedtime.
  • Wake-up time.
  • Days of the week.
  • Alarm.
  • Sleep mode.
  • Wind Down period before sleep, if available.
  • You can have a different schedule for weekdays and weekends.
  • Fixed schedules are not compulsory, but they usually help make tracking more orderly.

Sleep mode

Sleep mode reduces distractions during the night. It can silence notifications, simplify the screen, and prevent interruptions. This can be useful if you wear the Apple Watch while sleeping. If Sleep mode is enabled, some notifications will not arrive in the same way. It is worth reviewing which alerts are allowed and which are silenced. If you expect important calls during the night, configure allowed contacts or exceptions properly.

Sleep alarm

You can configure an alarm associated with your sleep schedule. The Apple Watch can wake you with a vibration on your wrist. This can be very useful for a blind person and also for people with hearing loss, if they can feel the vibration clearly. A haptic alarm can be more discreet than a sound alarm.

For it to work well:

  • The watch must be worn.
  • It must have battery.
  • The vibration must be noticeable.
  • The strap must be adjusted.
  • If the watch is loose, the vibration may be less noticeable.

Sleeping with the Apple Watch

Sleeping with the watch takes some getting used to.

  • At first, it may feel strange.
  • The strap must be comfortable.
  • The watch should not be too tight.
  • It should not move too much either.
  • If it bothers you, try another adjustment or a more comfortable strap.
  • A strap that works well during the day may not be the best one for sleeping.

Checking sleep data on the Apple Watch

You can check basic information from the watch.

To do this:

  • Press the Digital Crown.
  • Find Sleep.
  • Double tap.
  • Move through the data with VoiceOver.
  • It may show duration, schedule, and other available data.
  • A quick check on the watch is useful, but the iPhone is better for reviewing details.

Checking sleep data on the iPhone

On the iPhone:

  1. Open Health.
  2. Find Sleep.
  3. Enter the section.
  4. Explore the data with VoiceOver.

You may find information such as:

  • Time asleep.
  • Time in bed.
  • Sleep stages, if available.
  • Averages.
  • Trends.
  • Schedules.
  • Heart rate during sleep.
  • Respiratory rate.
  • Other related data.
  • The iPhone allows you to review progress in more detail.

Sleep stages

On some models and versions, the Health app may show sleep stages.

Stages may include:

  • Awake.
  • REM sleep.
  • Core or light sleep.
  • Deep sleep.
  • The exact names may vary.
  • These stages are estimates.
  • They should not be interpreted as a medical sleep study.
  • They are useful for observing general patterns.
  • If one night shows less deep sleep, that does not automatically mean there is a problem.
  • It is more useful to look at several nights or weeks.

Time asleep and time in bed

Time in bed does not always match time asleep.

  • You may be in bed without sleeping.
  • You may wake up during the night.
  • You may take time to fall asleep.

That is why the Apple Watch tries to distinguish, using its sensors, how much time you actually slept. The difference between time in bed and time asleep can help you understand your routine. But there is no need to obsess over it either. One bad night does not define anything. Several bad nights in a row may deserve attention.

Heart rate during sleep

The Apple Watch can record heart rate during the night. This data can help observe rest and recovery. In many people, heart rate drops during sleep.

Noticeable changes can have many causes:

  • Stress.
  • Alcohol.
  • Fever.
  • Medication.
  • Tiredness.
  • Intense exercise.
  • A bad night.
  • Illness.
  • An isolated data point should not be interpreted without context.

Respiratory rate

The Apple Watch can record respiratory rate during sleep on compatible models and versions. This data can provide additional information about rest. If there are important changes or symptoms, it is worth consulting. It should not be used as a diagnosis by itself.

Wrist temperature

Some models can record wrist temperature during sleep. This data can be used for trends and some health features. It is not the same as taking body temperature with a clinical thermometer. It serves as a reference for relative changes, not as a direct diagnosis of fever.

Blood oxygen during sleep

If the model has blood oxygen available, it may record measurements during sleep. These data may be affected by placement, movement, and availability. They do not replace a medical test. If there is suspicion of breathing problems during sleep, consult a healthcare professional.

Sleep and sleep apnoea

The Apple Watch may offer notifications related to sleep apnoea on compatible models and in compatible regions. This topic will be explained in the next module. For now, it is enough to know that sleep tracking can provide data, but it does not replace a medical sleep test.

Rest routines

The Apple Watch and iPhone can help you create a routine before going to bed.

For example:

  • Reducing notifications.
  • Turning on Sleep mode.
  • Using a bedtime reminder.
  • Setting an alarm.
  • Checking sleep in the morning.
  • This can help maintain more regular schedules.
  • But technology will not sleep for you.

You can have the best schedule configured and still go to bed late by choice, because of noise, because of worries, or because of that human habit of looking at one more thing before sleeping and ending up an hour later wondering why you are still awake.

Notifications during the night

If you use Sleep mode, many notifications may be silenced. This can be positive.

But exceptions must be reviewed.

  • You may want to allow calls from certain contacts.
  • You may want to receive important alerts.
  • You may prefer to block everything except emergencies.

Configure it according to your situation. If you care for someone, expect important calls, or have a delicate family situation, do not block notifications without reviewing them.

Waking up with vibration

One of the advantages of the Apple Watch is waking up with vibration on the wrist. This can be discreet and effective.

To use it well:

  • Configure the sleep alarm.
  • Check that the watch is worn.
  • Check that it vibrates with enough intensity.
  • Make sure it has battery.
  • If you sleep deeply, test it first on a day without an important commitment.

Do not try a new alarm for the first time on the day you have an essential appointment. That is the kind of trust in technology that later becomes an excuse.

Sleep and charging

One possible routine would be:

  • Charge the Apple Watch before going to bed.
  • Sleep with it on.
  • Charge it for a while when you get up.

Another routine:

  • Charge it while having dinner.
  • Use it at night.
  • Charge it while showering.
  • There is no single correct way.
  • The important thing is that it does not reach the night without battery.

What to do if sleep is not recorded properly

If sleep is not recorded correctly, check:

  • The watch was worn.
  • It had battery.
  • It was unlocked.
  • The strap was properly adjusted.
  • Sleep tracking was enabled.
  • The sleep schedule was configured.
  • It did not turn off during the night.
  • The Health app received data.
  • If only part of the night was recorded, it may be due to low battery, movement, fit, or configuration.

What to do if the data seem strange

If the data seem odd:

  • Do not draw conclusions from a single night.
  • Review several nights.
  • Check watch placement.
  • Check battery.
  • Check whether you slept outside the configured schedule.
  • Check whether there were awakenings.
  • Review the data from Health.
  • If there are symptoms or persistent tiredness, consult a professional.

Sleep and mental health

Sleep can be affected by stress, anxiety, changes in routine, worries, pain, medication, or emotional state. The Apple Watch can show data, but it does not explain everything. If you sleep badly over a sustained period, it is worth seeking help or reviewing habits with professionals where appropriate. Do not turn every night-time data point into another reason to worry.

Use in older people

In older people, sleep tracking can help observe routine and rest. It can also be combined with alarms, medication, and safety. But it should not be used for invasive monitoring. Health information must be handled with respect and consent.

Use in people who are deafblind or have hearing loss

The haptic alarm can be especially useful. Night-time vibrations may help wake the person or provide alerts. But it is necessary to check that the person can feel the vibration clearly. It is also advisable to configure the watch with a comfortable strap and stable fit.

Common mistakes

  • Not charging the watch before sleeping.
  • Sleeping with the watch too loose.
  • Not enabling sleep tracking.
  • Confusing time in bed with time asleep.
  • Obsessing over one bad night.
  • Not reviewing data in Health.
  • Not configuring exceptions for important notifications.
  • Trying a haptic alarm for the first time on a critical day without testing it.
  • Thinking the Apple Watch diagnoses sleep disorders.
  • Ignoring persistent tiredness because the data look normal.

Practical advice

Use sleep tracking for several nights before drawing conclusions. Review weekly trends, not just one night.

Test the haptic alarm on a day without risk.

  • Adjust the strap for sleeping.
  • Organise a charging routine.
  • If the data or symptoms are concerning, consult professionals.

Exercise for module 35

  • On the iPhone, open Health.
  • Find Sleep.
  • Configure a sleep schedule if one does not already exist.
  • Turn on sleep tracking with Apple Watch if the option appears.
  • Set an alarm for a test day.
  • Before sleeping, check the Apple Watch battery.
  • Put on the watch with a comfortable fit.
  • Sleep with the watch on.
  • When you wake up, stop the alarm if it sounds or vibrates.
  • Then open Health on the iPhone.
  • Find Sleep.
  • Review the recorded information.
  • Do not draw conclusions from a single night.
  • Repeat for several days.

Summary of module 35

The Apple Watch can record sleep if it is worn during the night. The main configuration is done from the Health app on the iPhone. It can record duration, schedules, stages, heart rate, and other data depending on the model. Sleeping with the watch requires organising charging. The haptic alarm can be very useful. Sleep stages are estimates.

The Apple Watch also needs several nights to show sleep stage data with some consistency. On the first night, complete information may not appear, or no information may appear at all. That is completely normal. The Apple Watch does not replace a medical sleep evaluation. Trends are more useful than one isolated night. If there is persistent tiredness, symptoms, or suspicion of a sleep disorder, consult a professional.

Module 36. Sleep apnoea, where available

Some Apple Watch models can offer notifications related to sleep apnoea, provided that the feature is available in the country or region and the necessary requirements are met.

Sleep apnoea is a disorder in which breathing repeatedly stops or is reduced during sleep. It can cause poor-quality rest, daytime sleepiness, headaches on waking, loud snoring, difficulty concentrating, and other effects.

The Apple Watch can help detect certain patterns that may be related to breathing disturbances during sleep, but it does not replace a medical diagnosis. If a notification related to sleep apnoea appears, it should be treated as a signal to seek advice, not as a definitive diagnosis.

What sleep apnoea is

Sleep apnoea consists of repeated pauses or reductions in breathing while a person is asleep. It may happen without the person being fully aware of it. Sometimes it is detected by another person because they notice loud snoring, pauses in breathing, gasping, or sudden awakenings.

It may also be suspected if there is:

  • Daytime sleepiness.
  • Persistent tiredness.
  • Headache on waking.
  • Unrefreshing sleep.
  • Difficulty concentrating.
  • Frequent awakenings.
  • Dry mouth on waking.
  • Loud snoring.
  • Not everyone with sleep apnoea snores in the same way.
  • Not all snoring means sleep apnoea.
  • That is why professional assessment is needed.

What the Apple Watch can do

On compatible models, the Apple Watch can analyse certain data during the night and notify you if it detects patterns that may be related to sleep apnoea. To do this, it needs the person to sleep with the watch on for several nights. The feature may require a minimum amount of data before it can offer conclusions or notifications. The watch does not listen to snoring like another person lying nearby. It does not replace a sleep study. It does not measure everything that a clinical test measures. Its role is to provide a potentially useful signal.

What it cannot do

The Apple Watch cannot diagnose sleep apnoea by itself.

  • It cannot identify every type of sleep disorder.
  • It does not replace polysomnography or any tests requested by a professional.
  • It should not be used to start or change treatments on your own.
  • It should not make a person ignore symptoms if no alert appears.

If there is a clear suspicion of sleep apnoea, seek advice even if the watch does not send a notification.

Availability of the feature

Sleep apnoea notifications may depend on:

  • Apple Watch model.
  • Country or region.
  • watchOS version.
  • iPhone version.
  • Health app configuration.
  • Age or other requirements.
  • If the feature does not appear, this may be due to compatibility or availability.
  • It does not necessarily mean that the user is doing something wrong.
  • It is also not necessarily a VoiceOver problem.

With Apple health features, the absence of an option is often not a mystery: sometimes the model does not support it, sometimes the country does not have it, sometimes the system needs updating, and sometimes the setting is simply not available. A beautiful little administrative garden, now growing on your wrist.

Where to configure sleep apnoea notifications

If the feature is available, it will usually be configured from the Health app on the iPhone.

On the iPhone:

  • Open Health.
  • Look for Sleep.
  • Review sections related to breathing or sleep apnoea.
  • If sleep apnoea notifications appear, open that section.
  • Listen carefully to the information with VoiceOver.
  • Follow the setup steps only if you understand what the system is asking.
  • The exact path may vary depending on iOS version, watchOS version, country, and model.
  • If the option does not appear, check compatibility and availability.

Several nights of data

This feature cannot usually be judged from one single night. The Apple Watch may need several nights of sleep data in order to analyse possible patterns.

This means:

  • You need to sleep with the watch on.
  • The watch must have enough battery.
  • The watch must fit properly.
  • Sleep tracking must be configured.
  • Data must be recorded for several nights.
  • It is normal for no useful information to appear on the first night.
  • That does not mean the feature is failing.
  • It simply needs data.

How to sleep with the watch for this feature

To improve the quality of the data:

  • Wear the Apple Watch properly adjusted.
  • Make sure it is not too loose.
  • Make sure it is comfortable enough to sleep with.
  • Charge it before going to bed if needed.
  • Keep sleep tracking enabled.
  • Use a strap that does not bother you during the night.
  • Check in the morning that the night was recorded.
  • If the watch moves too much, if the battery runs out, or if you take it off during the night, the data may be incomplete.

Relationship with sleep and blood oxygen

Sleep apnoea can affect sleep quality and night-time breathing. In some cases, it may be related to changes in blood oxygen, respiratory rate, or awakenings. But the Apple Watch does not replace specific medical tests. Watch data can provide context, not a closed diagnosis.

Use in people who sleep alone

This feature may be especially interesting for people who sleep alone. Sometimes sleep apnoea is suspected because another person hears snoring or notices pauses in breathing. Someone who sleeps alone may not have that external observation. In that case, the Apple Watch may provide an additional signal if the feature is available. Even so, if there is persistent tiredness or symptoms, medical advice should still be sought.

Use in older people

In older people, sleep-related notifications can be useful, but they should be handled sensibly. Not every alert means an emergency. Not every bad night means illness. But if there are repeated alerts, sleepiness, falls, tiredness, or concentration problems, it is advisable to consult a professional.

What to do if a notification appears

If the Apple Watch sends a notification related to sleep apnoea:

  • Read the full notification.
  • Do not ignore it.
  • Do not panic automatically.
  • Open the Health app on the iPhone.
  • Review the available information.
  • Save the notification or note the date if needed.
  • Consult a healthcare professional if the alert recommends it or if there are symptoms.
  • The notification should be used as information.
  • It should not be used to self-diagnose or start treatment.

What to do if no notification appears but symptoms exist

If there are symptoms that suggest a possible sleep disorder, do not wait for the Apple Watch.

Consult a healthcare professional if there is:

  • Persistent tiredness.
  • Daytime sleepiness.
  • Loud snoring.
  • Observed pauses in breathing.
  • Gasping during sleep.
  • Morning headaches.
  • Frequent awakenings.
  • Difficulty concentrating.
  • Nocturnal breathing problems.
  • The absence of a watch alert does not rule out sleep apnoea.
  • The watch may not detect every case.
  • The feature may not be active.
  • The feature may not be available.
  • The watch may not have enough data.
  • Symptoms come first.

Treatment and medical decisions

Sleep apnoea may require professional assessment and, in some cases, treatment. Possible approaches may include medical evaluation, sleep studies, changes in habits, specific devices, or other measures decided by professionals. Do not start, stop, or modify treatment based only on Apple Watch data. The watch may help point toward a possible issue. It does not decide the treatment.

Common mistakes

Thinking the Apple Watch diagnoses sleep apnoea.

Thinking that without a notification, sleep apnoea is impossible.

  • Sleeping with the watch poorly adjusted.
  • Not having enough battery.
  • Expecting results from a single night.
  • Ignoring symptoms because the watch does not alert you.
  • Getting frightened without reading the full notification.
  • Not consulting after repeated alerts.
  • Confusing sleep tracking with a medical sleep study.
  • Using watch data to start treatments on your own.

Practical advice

If you have a compatible model, activate the feature only after carefully reading the setup information.

Sleep with the watch for several nights.

  • Review the data in Health.
  • If a notification appears, discuss it with a healthcare professional.
  • If no notification appears but you have clear symptoms, seek advice anyway.

The watch can alert you. It cannot breathe for you or replace a medical test. That is already quite a lot for an object that also tries to count steps, receive calls, and wake you up with vibrations.

Exercise for module 36

On the iPhone, open Health. Look for Sleep. Look for sections related to breathing or sleep apnoea, if they appear. Check whether the feature is available. If sleep apnoea notification setup appears, open it and listen to the information. Do not activate or confirm data without understanding the questions. If you decide to configure it, follow the indicated steps.

For several nights:

  • Sleep with the Apple Watch on.
  • Check that it has enough battery.
  • Review the data in Health in the morning.
  • Observe whether notifications or new information appear.
  • If an alert appears, save it and consult if appropriate.

Summary of module 36

Some Apple Watch models can offer notifications related to sleep apnoea. The feature depends on model, country, version, and configuration. Sleep apnoea requires professional assessment. The Apple Watch does not diagnose sleep apnoea by itself. The feature needs data from several nights. You need to sleep with the watch on and with enough battery. A notification should be treated as a signal to seek advice, not as a definitive diagnosis. The absence of a notification does not rule out sleep apnoea if symptoms exist. Sleep data are best reviewed in the Health app on the iPhone.

Module 37. Hypertension, where available

Some Apple Watch models can offer hypertension notifications, provided that the feature is available in the country or region and the setup requirements are met. This feature should be explained with particular care.

The Apple Watch does not measure blood pressure in the same way as a traditional blood pressure monitor.

  • It does not replace a medical blood pressure cuff.
  • It does not diagnose hypertension by itself.
  • It does not replace medical follow-up.
  • It can analyse certain heart data over time and notify you if it detects patterns that may be related to chronic high blood pressure.

This means that the feature is about patterns over time, not about taking an instant blood pressure reading from the wrist.

What hypertension is

Hypertension means persistently high blood pressure. It can increase the risk of heart disease, stroke, kidney problems, and other health complications. Many people with hypertension do not notice symptoms. That is why measurement with a proper blood pressure monitor and medical review are important. A person may feel fine and still have high blood pressure. A person may also feel unwell for reasons unrelated to blood pressure. The Apple Watch can help with alerts where available, but it cannot replace proper measurement.

What the Apple Watch can do

Where available and on compatible models, the Apple Watch can look for patterns that may suggest possible hypertension. It may analyse data collected by the optical heart sensor over evaluation periods. If the system detects a pattern that may be compatible with hypertension, it can send a notification. The notification is a reason to measure blood pressure properly and discuss the result with a healthcare professional. It is not a final diagnosis.

What the Apple Watch cannot do

The Apple Watch cannot measure systolic and diastolic blood pressure directly from the wrist like a blood pressure cuff.

  • It cannot confirm that a person has hypertension.
  • It cannot rule out hypertension if no notification appears.
  • It cannot replace a medical blood pressure monitor.
  • It cannot replace healthcare professionals.
  • It cannot detect every case.
  • It cannot detect a heart attack.

If there is chest pain, pressure, tightness, severe shortness of breath, fainting, confusion, sudden weakness, or a feeling of serious illness, emergency medical help should be sought. Do not wait for the Apple Watch to decide whether a symptom deserves attention.

Availability

Hypertension notifications depend on model, watchOS version, iPhone model, iOS version, age, country or region, and configuration. If the option does not appear, it may be because the feature is not available for that model or region, because the system is not updated, or because the setup requirements are not met. This is not necessarily a VoiceOver problem.

As usual, health features enjoy making users pass through the small bureaucratic obstacle course of model, region, age, version, and settings before they agree to appear.

General setup path

If the feature is available, setup is usually done from the Health app on the iPhone.

On the iPhone:

  • Open Health.
  • Open your profile or Health Checklist.
  • Look for Hypertension Notifications.
  • Follow the setup instructions.
  • Read the explanations carefully with VoiceOver.
  • Confirm only information that is accurate.

The system may ask whether you meet certain conditions, such as age requirements or whether you have already been diagnosed with hypertension. Do not answer these questions by guessing. If you are unsure, consult healthcare professionals.

What to do if a notification appears

If the Apple Watch sends a hypertension notification:

  • Read the full notification.
  • Do not panic automatically.
  • Do not ignore it either.
  • Open the Health app for more information.
  • Use a proper blood pressure monitor if the system recommends it.
  • Record measurements as indicated.
  • Discuss the notification and measurements with a healthcare professional.
  • The notification is useful because it may encourage proper measurement.
  • It is not useful if it becomes a reason for self-diagnosis or anxiety.

Blood pressure log

The iPhone may prompt you to record blood pressure measurements with a third-party blood pressure cuff. This is important because the Apple Watch itself is not giving a traditional blood pressure reading.

If you record blood pressure manually:

  • Use a reliable blood pressure monitor.
  • Follow the monitor instructions.
  • Sit properly.
  • Rest before measuring.
  • Use the correct cuff size.
  • Record values accurately.
  • Do not invent values.
  • Do not round values carelessly if accuracy matters.
  • If readings are high, repeated, or concerning, consult healthcare professionals.

If no notification appears

No notification does not guarantee that blood pressure is normal.

  • The feature may not be available.
  • It may not have enough data.
  • It may not detect every case.
  • The person may not meet setup requirements.
  • The watch may not be worn consistently.
  • The watch may not have enough battery.
  • The absence of an alert should not replace regular blood pressure checks when they are medically recommended.

Who should be especially careful

People with known hypertension, cardiovascular disease, pregnancy, medication affecting blood pressure, kidney disease, diabetes, or relevant symptoms should follow medical advice. The Apple Watch feature may not be intended for all situations. If the system says the feature is not for people already diagnosed with hypertension or for certain groups, that warning should be respected. Do not try to bypass setup questions just to activate a feature. Health settings are not a game menu.

Privacy

Blood pressure and hypertension information are health data. Review which apps can access Health data. Do not share health screenshots or records casually. Share them with healthcare professionals or trusted people only when appropriate.

Common mistakes

  • Thinking the Apple Watch measures blood pressure directly.
  • Thinking a notification is a diagnosis.
  • Thinking no notification means there is no hypertension.

Trying to activate the feature on an unsupported model.

  • Ignoring age, pregnancy, or diagnosis requirements.
  • Not using a proper blood pressure cuff when asked to measure.
  • Recording inaccurate measurements.
  • Ignoring symptoms because the watch has not alerted.
  • Changing medication without medical advice.

Practical advice

If the feature is available, treat it as a useful alert system. Use it to prompt proper measurement and professional discussion. Do not use it as a substitute for a blood pressure monitor. Do not use it to make treatment decisions by yourself. For people with blood pressure concerns, the most reliable routine remains proper measurement, medical advice, and consistent follow-up.

Exercise for module 37

On the iPhone, open Health. Look for Health Checklist or the Heart section. Check whether Hypertension Notifications appears. If it appears, open it and listen to the explanation with VoiceOver. Do not activate it unless you understand the requirements. If you decide to configure it, follow the setup steps accurately. If the option does not appear, note that this may depend on model, country, version, age, or configuration. Do not keep searching endlessly for an option that may simply not be available.

Summary of module 37

Hypertension notifications may be available on compatible Apple Watch models and in supported countries or regions. The feature looks for patterns that may be related to chronic high blood pressure. The Apple Watch does not measure blood pressure like a medical cuff. A notification is not a diagnosis. No notification does not rule out hypertension. If a notification appears, proper blood pressure measurements and professional advice are recommended. Health data should be treated as private. Symptoms and medical guidance remain more important than the watch.

Module 38. Medication reminders

The Apple Watch and the Health app on the iPhone can help manage medication routines. This can be useful for people who take medication regularly, especially when there are several medicines, different schedules, or long-term treatments. The Apple Watch can show reminders directly on the wrist and allow you to mark medications as taken. But this feature must be understood correctly. The Apple Watch does not verify whether a medication was truly taken. It only records what the user indicates. If someone marks a medication as taken without actually taking it, the system cannot detect that mistake. This is a reminder and logging tool, not a medical supervision system.

What medication reminders can do

Depending on version and configuration, the Health ecosystem can:

  • Create medication lists.
  • Schedule reminders.
  • Send notifications.
  • Allow medications to be marked as taken.
  • Record history.
  • Show missed medications.
  • Display schedules.
  • Allow custom notes or details.
  • Provide interaction warnings in some regions and situations.
  • Synchronise with the Apple Watch.
  • This can help maintain a more organised routine.

Why reminders can be useful

Medication reminders may help:

  • Avoid forgetting doses.
  • Maintain regular schedules.
  • Reduce confusion.
  • Record whether medication was taken.
  • Support older people.
  • Support people with many medications.
  • Support routines linked to meals or sleep.
  • Create consistency.

For a blind person, receiving a discreet vibration and spoken notification on the wrist can be especially practical. It avoids depending only on memory, alarms on other devices, or written notes.

What reminders cannot do

Medication reminders cannot:

  • Confirm that the medication was actually swallowed.
  • Decide whether the medication should be taken.
  • Replace medical instructions.
  • Replace pharmacists or doctors.
  • Automatically detect mistakes.
  • Prevent double doses if the person logs incorrectly.
  • Know whether the medication was taken at the correct quantity.
  • Interpret symptoms.
  • This is important because medication management is a health issue, not just a list on a screen.
  • The watch can help organise, but responsibility still belongs to the person and their healthcare guidance.

Where medication is configured

Medication is usually configured from the Health app on the iPhone.

On the iPhone:

  • Open Health.
  • Go to Browse.
  • Look for Medications.
  • Enter the section.
  • Follow the setup instructions.
  • From there, medications can be added and reminders configured.
  • The Apple Watch then receives the notifications if synchronisation is active.

Adding a medication

When adding a medication, the system may ask for information such as:

  • Medication name.
  • Type.
  • Schedule.
  • Frequency.
  • Time of day.
  • Appearance or colour, depending on the system.
  • Notes.
  • This can help distinguish medications more easily.
  • If several medications sound similar, it is useful to review the names carefully with VoiceOver before confirming them.

Dictation can misunderstand medication names, and that is not a category where creative interpretation is especially welcome.

Schedules and frequency

The Health app may allow schedules such as:

  • Once daily.
  • Several times daily.
  • Specific days.
  • As needed.
  • Weekly.
  • Other patterns depending on the system version.
  • Choose the schedule carefully.
  • Do not configure random times simply to finish the setup quickly.
  • If the medication is important, accuracy matters.

Medication reminders on the Apple Watch

When a reminder appears on the Apple Watch:

  • The watch may vibrate.
  • VoiceOver may read the notification.
  • You can interact with the reminder.

Possible actions may include:

  • Mark as taken.
  • Skip.
  • Review details.
  • Dismiss.
  • The exact wording may vary depending on system version and language.

Marking medication as taken

If you take the medication, you can mark it as taken. This records the time in Health. This may help maintain an organised history. But only mark it if you actually took it. Otherwise, the history becomes unreliable. The Apple Watch trusts the user completely here, which is touching, optimistic, and occasionally disastrous.

Medication history

Medication history can usually be reviewed from the Health app on the iPhone.

There you may see:

  • Taken medications.
  • Missed medications.
  • Schedules.
  • Logs.
  • Frequency.
  • History by day.
  • This may be useful if you are unsure whether you already took a medication.
  • But again, the history only reflects what was recorded.
  • It cannot correct incorrect logging.

Medication interactions

In some regions and versions, the Health app may warn about possible interactions between medications, alcohol, or substances. These warnings can be useful. But they do not replace professional advice. Do not change treatment because of an app warning without consulting healthcare professionals. Use the information as guidance and discuss doubts properly.

Medication and privacy

Medication information is highly sensitive.

Review carefully:

  • Which apps can access Health data.
  • Whether information is shared.
  • Which permissions have been granted.
  • Who can see the data.
  • Health information should not be shared casually.

Medication and Focus modes

Be careful with Focus modes. Some Focus settings may silence notifications. If medication reminders are important, check whether they are allowed during the corresponding Focus mode.

Especially:

  • Sleep.
  • Do Not Disturb.
  • Custom Focus modes.
  • Work modes.
  • If reminders are silenced accidentally, the system may become much less useful.

Medication and travel

If you travel across time zones, review medication schedules carefully. The Health app may adjust times depending on configuration and device time. For important medication schedules, double-check times manually and follow medical advice where necessary.

When to seek help

If there is confusion about medications, doses, schedules, interactions, or symptoms, consult healthcare professionals or pharmacists. Do not rely only on the Apple Watch or the Health app for important medication decisions. The system helps organise information. It does not replace professional care.

Common mistakes

  • Entering the wrong medication name.
  • Not reviewing dictated names.
  • Configuring the wrong schedule.
  • Marking medications as taken when they were not.
  • Ignoring reminders.
  • Silencing notifications accidentally with Focus modes.
  • Not reviewing medication history.
  • Thinking the app replaces professional advice.
  • Ignoring interaction warnings without consulting.
  • Sharing medication information without thinking about privacy.

Practical advice

When starting, configure one medication first and learn the process. Review reminders carefully with VoiceOver. Check that notifications arrive properly on the Apple Watch. Only mark medications as taken when they actually are. Keep schedules realistic and clear. If the medication is important, combine reminders with routines and, if needed, other support systems.

Exercise for module 38

  • On the iPhone, open Health.
  • Go to Browse.
  • Find Medications.
  • Enter the section.
  • If you do not want to use a real medication for practice, create a temporary reminder with a clearly identifiable test name.
  • Configure a simple reminder.
  • Choose a time a few minutes ahead.
  • Wait for the notification to arrive on the Apple Watch.
  • Listen to it with VoiceOver.
  • Review the available actions.
  • Mark it appropriately.
  • Then open Health again on the iPhone and review the history.
  • If you created a temporary test medication, delete it afterwards.

Summary of module 38

The Health app and Apple Watch can manage medication reminders. Reminders can help maintain routines and avoid forgotten doses. Medication setup is mainly done from the Health app on the iPhone. The Apple Watch can show notifications on the wrist. The system records what the user marks, but it cannot verify whether medication was truly taken. Medication data are sensitive information and should be protected. Interaction warnings do not replace professional advice. Focus modes can affect reminders. The feature should be used as organisational support, not as a substitute for healthcare professionals.

Module 39. Menstrual cycle and related tracking

The Apple Watch and iPhone can help record information related to the menstrual cycle. This feature may be useful for people who want to track menstruation, symptoms, fertility, period estimates, fertile windows, wrist temperature on compatible models, and other related data. Not everyone using this course will need this module. Anyone who does not need it can skip it without any problem.

Even so, it is useful to include it because it is part of the health features available in the Apple ecosystem and may be important for some users.

As always with health, we need to be clear: cycle tracking on the Apple Watch and iPhone is used to record, observe, and estimate. It does not replace a gynaecological consultation, it does not diagnose diseases, and it should not be used as the only method of contraception.

What cycle tracking can record

From the Health app on the iPhone, you can record information such as:

  • Menstrual period.
  • Symptoms.
  • Spotting.
  • Flow.
  • Pain.
  • Mood.
  • Ovulation test results, if recorded.
  • Sexual activity, if the person decides to record it.
  • Wrist temperature, if a compatible Apple Watch records it during sleep.
  • Estimates of the next period.
  • Estimates of the fertile window.
  • Other related data, depending on version and configuration.

The Apple Watch can be used to record some data quickly or receive alerts, but detailed setup and review are usually more comfortable from the iPhone.

Where it is configured

The main configuration is done from the Health app on the iPhone.

On the iPhone:

  • Open Health.
  • Look for Cycle Tracking.
  • Enter the section.
  • Follow the setup instructions.
  • Enter the requested information.
  • Review prediction, notification, and privacy options.
  • The exact names may vary depending on the system version.
  • With VoiceOver, it is advisable to move slowly and listen carefully to each screen.

What the Apple Watch can do

The Apple Watch can complement cycle tracking.

Depending on model and configuration, it may allow you to:

  • Record information from the wrist.
  • Receive period alerts.
  • Receive estimates or reminders.
  • Record wrist temperature during sleep, if the model is compatible.
  • Provide data to the Health app.

For some features to be useful, it may be necessary to sleep with the Apple Watch for several nights and have sleep tracking configured correctly.

Wrist temperature

Some Apple Watch models can record wrist temperature during the night. This information may be used by the Health app to improve some estimates related to the menstrual cycle. It is important to understand that wrist temperature is not the same as taking body temperature with a medical thermometer. It is mainly used to observe relative changes over time. It should not be interpreted as a clinical fever measurement.

Period predictions

Cycle Tracking can offer period predictions based on the data entered and on the information recorded by the system. These predictions are estimates. They are not guarantees.

The cycle can vary for many reasons:

  • Stress.
  • Illness.
  • Medication.
  • Hormonal changes.
  • Travel.
  • Sleep changes.
  • Weight changes.
  • Physical activity.
  • Pregnancy.
  • Perimenopause.
  • Other health conditions.
  • For that reason, predictions should be used as guidance, not as certainty.

Fertile window estimates

The Health app may also offer fertile window estimates.

This information may be useful for personal tracking, but it should not be used as the only method of contraception.

  • This point must be stated clearly.
  • Fertility estimates from an app are not enough to prevent pregnancy reliably.
  • Anyone who needs contraception advice should consult healthcare professionals.

The Apple Watch is very clever in many ways, but placing full contraceptive responsibility on a wrist device is asking technology to do far more than it should.

Notifications

Cycle Tracking can send notifications.

These may include:

  • Possible upcoming period.
  • Fertile window estimate.
  • Log reminders.
  • Other alerts depending on configuration.
  • These notifications can be useful, but they are also personal.
  • It is worth reviewing whether you want them to appear on the Apple Watch, on the iPhone, or both.
  • Privacy matters here.

Privacy of cycle data

  • Cycle data are sensitive health information.
  • Before using this feature, review privacy carefully.
  • On the iPhone, in Health, you can check which apps have access to health data.

It is advisable to review:

  • Which apps can read cycle data.
  • Which apps can write cycle data.
  • Whether any third-party app has access.
  • Whether data are being shared.
  • Whether you really need those permissions.
  • This information should not be shared casually.
  • Health data deserve careful handling, and cycle data even more so.

Use with VoiceOver

The Health app on the iPhone is usually the most comfortable place to review and configure this feature.

With VoiceOver:

  • Explore the sections slowly.
  • Review dates.
  • Listen to button labels.
  • Do not record data without confirming which date you are on.
  • Be careful with calendar fields.
  • If the app allows recording from the Apple Watch, use it for quick actions.
  • For a full review, the iPhone will be better.

Recording from the Apple Watch

If the Apple Watch allows cycle data to be recorded:

  • Open the corresponding app.
  • Look for Cycle Tracking.
  • Explore the options with VoiceOver.
  • Select the data you want to record.
  • Confirm the date and type of entry.
  • Save.
  • If the screen is uncomfortable, use the iPhone.
  • There is no need to do everything from the wrist.

When to consult a healthcare professional

It is advisable to consult healthcare professionals if there is:

  • Very heavy bleeding.
  • Bleeding between periods.
  • Intense pain.
  • Newly irregular cycles.
  • Absence of period without explanation.
  • Suspected pregnancy.
  • Symptoms that worsen.
  • Noticeable changes.
  • Fever or significant discomfort.
  • Questions about contraception.
  • Symptoms that affect daily life.
  • The watch can record data, but it should not normalise important problems.

Using records in a consultation

Cycle data can be useful when speaking with a healthcare professional.

They can help explain:

  • Dates.
  • Symptoms.
  • Pain.
  • Changes.
  • Bleeding.
  • Irregularities.
  • Associated notes.
  • This may make it easier to explain what happened without relying only on memory.
  • It does not replace medical assessment, but it can be a useful record.

Common mistakes

  • Thinking predictions are certainties.
  • Using fertility estimates as the only method of contraception.
  • Not reviewing privacy.
  • Allowing unnecessary apps to access data.
  • Recording data on the wrong date.
  • Not consulting when important symptoms appear.
  • Interpreting wrist temperature as clinical fever.
  • Expecting absolute precision with little data.
  • Not taking medication or hormonal changes into account.
  • Forgetting that the cycle can vary for many reasons.

Practical advice

If this feature is useful to you, start by recording the basics:

  • Start and end dates of the period.
  • Main symptoms.
  • Pain, if present.
  • Noticeable changes.
  • Then, if you want, add more data.
  • Do not turn tracking into an exhausting task. A health tool should help, not create another administrative job for the body.

Exercise for module 39

On the iPhone, open Health. Look for Cycle Tracking. Enter the section.

Listen to the configuration options.

  • Review which data can be recorded.
  • Review notifications.
  • Review privacy and permissions.

If you are going to use the feature, record only real and verified data. If your Apple Watch allows you to check or record cycle data, open the corresponding app on the watch and explore its options with VoiceOver. Do not modify sensitive data unless you are sure what you are recording.

Summary of module 39

Cycle tracking is configured mainly from the Health app on the iPhone. It can record periods, symptoms, predictions, and other related data.

Some Apple Watch models can provide wrist temperature during sleep.

  • Predictions are estimates, not certainties.
  • It should not be used as the only method of contraception.
  • Cycle data are sensitive information and must be protected.
  • The Apple Watch can help with alerts and quick records.
  • For important symptoms or noticeable changes, consult healthcare professionals.

Module 40. Checking health data on the iPhone

  • The Apple Watch records a lot of data, but the iPhone is the most comfortable place to review it in detail.
  • The watch is used to measure, alert, and check quick information.
  • The iPhone is used to review history, trends, charts, records, permissions, and complete data.

For a blind person using VoiceOver, the Health app on the iPhone is usually more practical than the small Apple Watch screen. There is more space, more information, and better control for exploring the data. That is why it is important to learn how to check on the iPhone what the Apple Watch records during the day and night.

What the Health app is

The Health app brings together information related to health and activity.

It can receive data from:

  • Apple Watch.
  • iPhone.
  • Compatible apps.
  • External devices.
  • Manually entered data.
  • Connected health services, where available.

Inside Health, you can review data such as:

  • Activity.
  • Heart rate.
  • Sleep.
  • Respiratory rate.
  • Blood oxygen, if available.
  • ECG, if available.
  • Medication.
  • Menstrual cycle.
  • Hearing.
  • Mobility.
  • Body measurements.
  • Blood pressure, if recorded.
  • Medical ID.
  • Trends.
  • App permissions.
  • Not all sections will appear in the same way on every device or in every country.

Opening the Health app

On the iPhone:

  • Find the Health app.
  • Open it.
  • With VoiceOver, explore the main screen.
  • The Summary tab usually shows highlighted data.
  • The Browse tab allows you to search through categories.

Using the Summary tab

The Summary tab can show important data or favourites.

For example:

  • Steps.
  • Heart rate.
  • Sleep.
  • Activity.
  • Trends.
  • Medication.
  • Other data you have marked.
  • With VoiceOver, move through the items.
  • If a data type matters to you, you can mark it as a favourite so that it appears more easily in the summary.
  • This avoids having to search for it every time.

Using the Browse tab

The Browse tab allows you to navigate through health categories.

It may include categories such as:

  • Activity.
  • Heart.
  • Sleep.
  • Respiratory.
  • Medication.
  • Hearing.
  • Mobility.
  • Nutrition.
  • Body Measurements.
  • Symptoms.
  • Cycle Tracking.
  • Other data.
  • If you cannot find a data type in Summary, use Browse.
  • You can also use search inside Health if it is available.

Searching for a specific data type

To search for a specific data type:

  • Open Health.
  • Use Browse or the search field.
  • Type or dictate the data type.

For example:

  1. Heart rate.
  2. Sleep.
  3. Steps.
  4. ECG.
  5. Blood oxygen.
  6. Blood pressure.
  7. Medications.
  8. Then open the corresponding result.

Checking heart rate

To review heart rate:

  1. Open Health.
  2. Search for Heart.
  3. Enter Heart Rate.
  4. Explore the data.

You may find:

  • Current or recent heart rate.
  • Resting heart rate.
  • Walking heart rate.
  • Values during workouts.
  • History.
  • Trends.
  • With VoiceOver, listen to dates, values, and ranges.
  • If any value concerns you, review the context and consult if appropriate.

Checking sleep

To review sleep:

  • Open Health.
  • Search for Sleep.
  • Enter the section.
  • Listen to time asleep.
  • Review schedules.
  • Explore sleep stages if they appear.
  • Check trends.
  • Review related data.
  • Sleep data are more useful when observed over several days or weeks.
  • It is not advisable to draw conclusions from a single night.

Checking workouts

Workouts are normally reviewed in the Fitness app, although some related data also appear in Health.

In Fitness, you can find:

  • Completed workouts.
  • Duration.
  • Distance.
  • Calories.
  • Heart rate.
  • Pace.
  • Route, where applicable.
  • Trends.
  • In Health, you can find data related to activity, heart, and mobility.
  • For workouts, Fitness is usually more comfortable.
  • For general health, Health is more complete.

Checking ECG

If your Apple Watch has ECG:

  • Open Health.
  • Search for Heart.
  • Look for ECG.
  • Enter the records.
  • Listen to date, time, and classification.
  • If you need to share a record with a professional, review the available options.
  • Do not interpret an ECG as a definitive diagnosis by yourself.

Checking blood oxygen

If your Apple Watch records blood oxygen:

  • Open Health.
  • Search for Blood Oxygen.
  • Enter the section.
  • Listen to measurements.
  • Review history.
  • Observe trends if there are enough data.
  • Remember that it is guidance and may depend on placement, movement, and availability.

Checking medication

To review medication:

  • Open Health.
  • Search for Medications.
  • Check the list.
  • Review schedules.
  • Review logged doses.
  • Check whether there are alerts.
  • Correct records if the app allows it and if necessary.
  • Do not mark doses without being sure.
  • If you are unsure whether you took a medication, do not take additional doses without professional guidance.

Checking mobility data

Health may include mobility data.

For example:

  • Walking speed.
  • Step length.
  • Asymmetry.
  • Walking steadiness.
  • Stair ascent.
  • Other data depending on the device.
  • These data may be useful for older people, rehabilitation, or physical monitoring.
  • But they must be interpreted carefully.
  • If there are falls, instability, or significant changes, it is advisable to consult.

Checking Medical ID

Medical ID contains information that may be useful in emergencies.

It may include:

  1. Name.
  2. Age.
  3. Medical conditions.
  4. Allergies.
  5. Medications.
  6. Blood type.
  7. Emergency contacts.
  8. Other important data.

To review it:

  • Open Health.
  • Search for Medical ID.
  • Check that the information is correct.
  • Update what is needed.
  • This information can be important if an emergency occurs.

Trends

  • The Health app can show trends.
  • Trends compare data over time.
  • They can indicate whether something is rising, falling, or changing.

For example:

  • Activity.
  • Heart rate.
  • Sleep.
  • Respiratory rate.
  • Mobility.
  • Trends are more useful than isolated data.
  • One unusual day may mean nothing.
  • A trend over several weeks may deserve attention.

Favourites

In Health, you can mark data types as favourites. This allows them to appear in Summary.

It may be useful to mark:

  • Heart rate.
  • Sleep.
  • Steps.
  • Activity.
  • Medication.
  • Blood pressure, if you record it.
  • Blood oxygen, if you use it.
  • ECG, if you use it.
  • That way, you do not have to navigate through many categories every time.

Data sources

Health receives data from different sources.

For example:

  • Apple Watch.
  • iPhone.
  • Exercise apps.
  • Medical apps.
  • External devices.
  • Manual data.
  • In some sections, you can review data sources and access.
  • This allows you to know which device is writing information.
  • If you see duplicated or strange data, it is worth reviewing sources.

App permissions

Some apps may request access to Health. It is not advisable to accept everything without reviewing it. From Health, you can review which apps have permission to read or write data. An exercise app may need activity and heart rate. A medication app may need medication data. But an app that has nothing to do with health should not request broad access without a clear reason. Health privacy is not managed with “next, next, accept.” That recipe has already created enough problems in digital history.

Sharing health data

The Health app may allow you to share data with trusted people or professionals, depending on availability.

Sharing can be useful for:

  • Family members.
  • Carers.
  • Healthcare professionals.
  • Monitoring an older person.
  • Following a specific situation.
  • But it must be done with consent and with a clear understanding of which data are being shared.
  • Do not share sensitive data without reviewing it.

Exporting or showing data

In some cases, you can show data to a healthcare professional during an appointment. There may also be options to export certain records, such as ECG.

For appointments, it may be useful to bring:

  • Heart rate records.
  • Alerts received.
  • ECG.
  • Sleep data.
  • Blood pressure records.
  • Medication.
  • Noted symptoms.
  • But the data should support the conversation, not replace it.

Adding data manually

Health allows some data to be added manually.

For example:

  • Weight.
  • Blood pressure.
  • Glucose, if recorded.
  • Temperature.
  • Symptoms.
  • Medication.
  • Other data.
  • Adding manual data can be useful, but it must be done accurately.
  • Do not enter invented or approximate data if it may later confuse you.

Reviewing data with VoiceOver

With VoiceOver, it is advisable to:

  • Explore slowly.
  • Listen to date and value.
  • Enter each section.
  • Use favourites.
  • Use search.
  • Do not depend only on visual charts.
  • Look for buttons such as Show More Data, All Data, or History.

In some sections, information may appear in charts. VoiceOver may read values or summaries, but not always as clearly as a table. If a data type is important, look for history or all data options.

Common problems

It may happen that:

  • No data appear.
  • Data appear incomplete.
  • Duplicated data appear.
  • The Apple Watch did not record one night.
  • A workout was not saved.
  • An app does not have permissions.
  • The watch had no battery.
  • The feature is not available.
  • The watch was poorly positioned.
  • Before assuming something is failing, review configuration, permissions, battery, and data sources.

What to do if Apple Watch data are missing

If data from the watch do not appear:

  • Check that the Apple Watch is paired.
  • Check that you are using the same Apple Account.
  • Check that the watch has battery.
  • Check that you were wearing the watch.
  • Review Health permissions.
  • Review data sources.
  • Open the Watch app.
  • Check privacy and health settings.
  • Restart if necessary, but not as the first reflex.

When to review data

There is no need to check Health all day.

It may be useful to check it:

  • In the morning for sleep.
  • After training for activity.
  • Once a week for trends.
  • Before an appointment if you need data.
  • When you receive an alert.
  • If you notice health changes.
  • Checking constantly can create unnecessary worry.
  • The Health app should inform, not become a personal surveillance room open twenty-four hours a day.

Common mistakes

Looking only at the Apple Watch and not reviewing Health.

  • Not using favourites.
  • Not reviewing data sources.
  • Giving apps permissions without reading.
  • Interpreting charts without context.
  • Obsessing over daily data.
  • Not consulting when symptoms appear.
  • Not updating medication or personal data.
  • Not reviewing Medical ID.
  • Not protecting privacy.

Practical advice

Configure the Health app so the Summary shows what you actually use. Do not fill favourites with data you never check.

Start with a few:

  • Activity.
  • Heart rate.
  • Sleep.
  • Medication, if you use it.
  • Blood pressure, if you record it.
  • Then add others according to need.

Exercise for module 40

  • On the iPhone, open Health.
  • Enter Summary.
  • Move through the data that appear.
  • Mark as favourites the sections you want to check often.
  • Enter Browse.
  • Search for Heart.
  • Check heart rate.
  • Return to Browse.
  • Search for Sleep.
  • Check the available data.
  • Search for Medications if you use it.
  • Review Medical ID.
  • Review permissions for apps connected to Health.
  • Then open Fitness and review the latest workout, if there is one.
  • Compare which data you prefer to check in Health and which in Fitness.

Summary of module 40

  • The Apple Watch records many data points, but the iPhone lets you review them better.
  • The Health app brings together information about health, sleep, heart, medication, mobility, and other areas.
  • The Fitness app is more useful for workouts and physical activity.
  • Favourites help you check frequent data.
  • Trends are more useful than isolated data.
  • Permissions and data sources should be reviewed.
  • Medical ID should be up to date.
  • Health data are private and must be protected.
  • Information from the Apple Watch helps, but it does not replace healthcare.

Module 41. Emergency SOS

Emergency SOS is one of the Apple Watch’s personal safety features. Its purpose is to allow you to contact emergency services quickly from the watch in a serious situation. This feature must be understood very clearly.

Emergency SOS is not for testing.

  • It is not for curiosity.
  • It is not for practice calls.
  • It is not for checking whether the button works.
  • It is for real emergencies.

If you activate it and the call connects, emergency services may receive the call. If it was accidental, you must explain that it was a mistake. Hanging up without explanation can create unnecessary confusion for emergency operators, who already have enough to deal with without a watch joining the circus.

What Emergency SOS is

Emergency SOS allows the Apple Watch to contact emergency services.

The exact behaviour may vary depending on:

  • Country or region.
  • Apple Watch model.
  • GPS or Cellular model.
  • Whether the iPhone is nearby.
  • Mobile coverage.
  • Carrier.
  • Settings.
  • watchOS version.
  • Emergency contacts.
  • Medical ID.

In some cases, the Apple Watch can also notify emergency contacts after the emergency call, if they have been configured.

Emergency numbers by country or region

Emergency numbers are not the same everywhere.

  • In some countries, the emergency number is 911.
  • In others, it is 112.
  • In others, there may be different numbers for police, ambulance, fire, or general emergency services.

The Apple Watch may try to contact the appropriate local emergency number, depending on country, network, and configuration. That is why this course will not say that Emergency SOS always calls one specific number. The correct idea is this:

Emergency SOS attempts to contact the emergency services available in the country or region where the device is being used, according to Apple’s system behaviour, local networks, and configuration. If you travel, do not assume that everything will behave exactly as it does in your usual country.

GPS model and Cellular model

Emergency SOS may behave differently depending on the Apple Watch model. If you have an Apple Watch GPS, the watch may need the iPhone nearby in order to make the emergency call, unless it has access to a compatible Wi-Fi calling situation or another available method.

If you have an Apple Watch GPS plus Cellular with an active mobile plan, it may be able to make emergency calls with more independence, provided there is coverage and the service is available. This distinction is important. A GPS watch is not the same as a Cellular watch.

If someone goes out alone without the iPhone and relies on the Apple Watch for emergency communication, they should know whether the watch can actually make calls in those conditions. The wrist is not a magic antenna. Disappointing, yes, but useful to know.

The side button

Emergency SOS is related to the side button. The side button is the elongated button located near the Digital Crown. It is not the Digital Crown.

This difference must be clear:

  • The Digital Crown is the round wheel.
  • The side button is the elongated button.
  • Emergency SOS is related to the side button.
  • Depending on configuration, holding down the side button may show emergency options or start an emergency process.
  • That is why you should not hold down the side button casually.

Opening emergency options

On the Apple Watch, holding down the side button may show options such as:

  • Power Off.
  • Medical ID.
  • Emergency SOS.
  • Other options depending on version and configuration.
  • With VoiceOver, if this screen appears, listen carefully.
  • Do not activate Emergency SOS unless you are in a real emergency.
  • If you opened it by mistake, look for Cancel, Close, or return safely without starting the call.

Automatic call behaviour

Depending on settings, holding down the side button may start a countdown and then call emergency services automatically. This can be useful in a real emergency. But it can also create accidental calls if the user does not know how the feature works. That is why it is important to review Emergency SOS settings before relying on it. Not all users should configure it in the same way. Some people may prefer easier activation. Others may prefer to reduce accidental activation risk.

Reviewing Emergency SOS settings

From the iPhone, you can review settings related to Emergency SOS.

On the iPhone:

  • Open the Watch app.
  • Go to My Watch.
  • Look for Emergency SOS.
  • Review the available options.
  • There may also be related settings on the iPhone itself.
  • The exact names may vary.
  • Listen to each option with VoiceOver before changing it.
  • Some options may allow automatic calls when holding the side button or when Fall Detection is triggered.
  • Do not turn features on or off without understanding them.

Medical ID and emergency contacts

Emergency SOS is more useful when Medical ID and emergency contacts are configured. These are managed mainly from the Health app on the iPhone.

Medical ID can include information such as:

  1. Medical conditions.
  2. Allergies.
  3. Medication.
  4. Blood type.
  5. Emergency contacts.
  6. Other relevant notes.

Emergency contacts are people who may be notified after an emergency call, depending on configuration and availability. These contacts should be chosen carefully. Do not add someone as an emergency contact if you do not want them to receive this type of alert.

What happens after an emergency call

After an emergency call, the Apple Watch may notify your emergency contacts, if they are configured and if the feature is available. It may also share your location for a period of time, depending on region, settings, and availability. You should know this beforehand. If you do not want a certain person to receive these alerts, do not set that person as an emergency contact.

International emergency calls

Emergency SOS behaviour may vary by country. When travelling, the Apple Watch may try to call the local emergency number, depending on availability and configuration. You should not rely on this blindly without knowing how it works in the country where you are.

If you travel, review:

  • Coverage.
  • Carrier.
  • Apple Watch model.
  • Whether you are carrying the iPhone.
  • Whether Cellular works in that country.
  • Local emergency numbers.

Technology travels with you, but it does not always understand borders, carriers, and rules with the elegance promised in advertisements.

Emergency SOS and Fall Detection

Emergency SOS is related to other safety features, such as Fall Detection. If the Apple Watch detects a hard fall, it may show an alert and allow you to call emergency services. If the person does not respond for a certain period of time, it may try to call automatically under certain conditions. This will be explained in the next module.

For now, it is enough to understand that Emergency SOS is the urgent call feature, while Fall Detection is a feature that may trigger or suggest it after a fall.

Emergency SOS during exercise

Emergency SOS may be relevant during exercise if:

  • You go out alone.
  • You do long routes.
  • You have a risk of falling.
  • You train outdoors.
  • You are not accompanied.
  • You have health problems.
  • You use a Cellular model.
  • But it should not replace planning.
  • Before going out, check battery, coverage, route, and whether you are carrying the iPhone.
  • Do not go out relying only on the idea that the watch will solve any situation.

Emergency SOS at home

It can also be useful at home.

For example:

  • A fall.
  • Sudden illness.
  • Difficulty reaching the iPhone.
  • Living alone.
  • Needing to call quickly.
  • If you are wearing the Apple Watch, it may be more accessible than the phone.
  • This can be especially useful for older people or people with certain health conditions.

Accidental activations

Emergency SOS may be activated accidentally.

For example:

  • By holding down the side button too long.
  • By handling the watch.
  • By pressing it against something.
  • By confusing controls.
  • By trying to turn off the watch.
  • If a countdown appears by mistake, cancel it immediately.

If the call starts and it was not an emergency, explain the situation to the operator if the call connects. Do not simply hang up if the call has already gone through. Emergency services need to know whether it was an error.

How to avoid accidental activations

To reduce mistakes:

  • Know exactly where the side button is.
  • Do not hold it down without a reason.
  • Do not handle the watch nervously.
  • Review Emergency SOS settings.
  • Learn how to cancel if it appears by mistake.
  • Do not practise real emergency calls.
  • Explain to other people that they should not play with this feature.

What to do if you need to use Emergency SOS

If you are in a real emergency:

  • Hold down the side button.
  • Follow the instructions.
  • If Emergency SOS appears, activate it.
  • Or keep holding the button according to the configured behaviour.
  • Pay attention to the call.
  • Speak if you can.
  • If you cannot speak, the call may transmit certain information depending on network, country, and configuration, but you should not depend entirely on that.

If you can, state clearly:

  1. What is happening.
  2. Where you are.
  3. Whether you are alone.
  4. Whether there are injuries.
  5. Whether you need assistance.

After the call

After an emergency call, the Apple Watch may notify emergency contacts, if configured. It may also share your location for a period of time, depending on availability. You should know this in advance. If you do not want a particular person to receive these alerts, do not set that person as an emergency contact.

When to use Emergency SOS

Emergency SOS should be used in real emergency situations.

For example:

  • Serious fall.
  • Chest pain.
  • Significant breathing difficulty.
  • Another person losing consciousness.
  • Accident.
  • Immediate danger.
  • Serious disorientation with risk.
  • Urgent need for assistance.
  • It should not be used for general questions, tests, jokes, non-urgent medical queries, or minor problems.

Alternatives if it is not an emergency

If it is not a real emergency, you can:

  • Call a relative.
  • Call your health centre.
  • Call a non-urgent medical service if one exists in your area.
  • Send your location to someone.
  • Use Messages.
  • Use Siri to call a contact.
  • Ask for help nearby.
  • Emergency SOS should be reserved for urgent situations.

Common mistakes

Confusing the side button with the Digital Crown. Holding down the side button by mistake. Not configuring emergency contacts. Not reviewing Medical ID. Thinking an Apple Watch GPS works the same without the iPhone as a Cellular model.

Going out without the iPhone while relying on calls from a GPS watch.

  • Not checking battery.
  • Not knowing how to cancel an accidental activation.
  • Testing an emergency call without a real reason.
  • Not explaining to the operator if an accidental call has already connected.

Practical advice

First configure Medical ID and emergency contacts.

  • Then review Emergency SOS settings.
  • Learn where the side button is.
  • Learn the difference between pressing once and holding down.
  • Do not make test calls.

Safety is prepared in advance. It is not improvised when your wrist starts vibrating and you do not know whether you have called emergency services or opened Wallet.

Exercise for module 41

  • On the iPhone, open Health.
  • Look for Medical ID.
  • Review your information.
  • Add or update emergency contacts if appropriate.
  • Check that the phone numbers are correct.
  • Then open the Watch app.
  • Go to My Watch.
  • Look for Emergency SOS.
  • Listen to the available options.
  • Do not change anything without understanding it.
  • Physically locate the side button on the Apple Watch.
  • Practise only locating the button, not activating SOS.
  • Press the side button once to open Control Centre if your version works that way.
  • Do not hold it down.
  • Return to the watch face with the Digital Crown.

Summary of module 41

Emergency SOS allows you to contact emergency services from the Apple Watch. It should be used only in real emergencies. It is related to the side button, not the Digital Crown. Holding down the side button may open emergency options. It should not be tested with real calls. Emergency contacts are configured from Medical ID on the iPhone. Medical ID should be kept up to date. An Apple Watch GPS may depend on the iPhone for calls. A Cellular Apple Watch offers more independence if it has an active line and coverage. Battery, connection, and configuration are essential. If an accidental activation connects, you must explain that it was an error.
