Module 42. Fall Detection

Fall Detection is one of the Apple Watch safety features. Its purpose is to detect certain hard falls and offer help if the person may need it. This feature can be especially useful for older people, people with reduced mobility, people who live alone, people who exercise outdoors, or anyone who wants an additional safety layer on the wrist. But it must be understood carefully.

The Apple Watch cannot detect every fall.

  • It may detect some hard falls.
  • It may fail to detect others.
  • It may also be triggered by movements that are not real falls, especially during some sports or sudden movements.

So Fall Detection can help, but it should not be understood as an absolute guarantee.

What Fall Detection does

When the Apple Watch detects what it interprets as a hard fall, it may show an alert on the screen.

  • It may tap the wrist.
  • It may sound an alarm.
  • It may ask whether you are okay.
  • It may offer an option to call emergency services.

If the watch detects that you are moving, it may wait for your response. If it detects that you have been immobile for a period of time, it may start a countdown and try to contact emergency services, depending on configuration, model, connection, country, and availability. This behaviour may vary according to watchOS version and settings.

Which models have Fall Detection

Fall Detection is not necessarily available on every Apple Watch ever released. It depends on the model and system version. Before relying on it, check whether your Apple Watch supports the feature. If the option does not appear, it may be due to model, version, age settings, or configuration. Do not assume that every Apple Watch has it.

Activating Fall Detection

Fall Detection can usually be reviewed from the Watch app on the iPhone.

On the iPhone:

  • Open the Watch app.
  • Go to My Watch.
  • Look for Emergency SOS.
  • Look for Fall Detection.
  • Review whether it is on or off.

There may be options such as:

  • Always on.
  • Only on during workouts.
  • Off.
  • The exact labels may vary depending on version and region.
  • With VoiceOver, listen carefully to each option before changing it.

Always on or only during workouts

Some versions allow Fall Detection to be active all the time or only during workouts. Always on means the watch tries to detect hard falls in everyday life and during activity. Only during workouts means it focuses on exercise sessions. For older people, people at risk of falling, or people who live alone, Always on may be useful. For someone who does high-impact activity and receives false alerts, another setting may be considered. The best option depends on the person. There is no single correct setting for everyone.

Automatic activation by age

In some cases, Fall Detection may be enabled automatically for users above a certain age, depending on Apple’s system behaviour and the data entered in Health. This may vary by region, version, and configuration. It is still advisable to check the setting manually. Do not assume that it is enabled just because the person is older.

What happens after a detected fall

If the Apple Watch detects a hard fall, it may show an alert. The alert may ask whether you are okay.

It may offer options such as:

  • I’m OK.
  • I fell, but I’m OK.
  • I did not fall.
  • Emergency SOS.
  • Call emergency services.
  • The exact wording may vary.
  • With VoiceOver, it is important to listen to the full alert before double tapping.
  • If you are okay, you can indicate that.
  • If you need help, you can use the emergency option.
  • If the fall was not real, you can dismiss the alert.

If you do not respond

If the watch detects that you are not moving for a period of time after a hard fall, it may start a countdown.

  • It may tap your wrist.
  • It may sound an alarm.
  • It may call emergency services.
  • It may notify emergency contacts after the call, depending on configuration and availability.

This is one reason why emergency contacts and Medical ID should be configured properly. If an emergency call connects accidentally, explain that it was a mistake if you can. Do not simply hang up if the call has already gone through.

Emergency contacts

Fall Detection works better as part of a full safety setup. Emergency contacts should be configured in Medical ID from the iPhone.

On the iPhone:

  • Open Health.
  • Open Medical ID.
  • Review emergency contacts.
  • Add or update contacts if needed.
  • Check that phone numbers are correct.
  • Emergency contacts should be people who can respond or help in a real situation.
  • Do not add random contacts just to fill the field. Emergencies are not the place for decorative phone numbers.

Medical ID

Medical ID can include information that may be useful in an emergency.

For example:

  • Medical conditions.
  • Allergies.
  • Medication.
  • Emergency contacts.
  • Blood type, if you choose to include it.
  • Other relevant notes.
  • If Fall Detection leads to an emergency call, having Medical ID configured can be useful.
  • Review this information periodically.
  • A Medical ID with old medication, wrong contacts, or outdated information can create confusion.

Fall Detection and Apple Watch GPS

If your Apple Watch is GPS only, emergency calling may depend on the iPhone being nearby or on other available connection conditions. If you go out without the iPhone and rely on Fall Detection, you must understand this limitation. A GPS watch without the iPhone nearby does not have the same communication independence as a Cellular model.

Fall Detection and Apple Watch Cellular

If your Apple Watch is GPS plus Cellular and has an active mobile plan, it may be able to call emergency services with more independence, provided there is coverage and the feature is available. This can be especially useful for people who go out alone, walk, exercise, or do not always carry the iPhone.

But it still depends on:

  • Battery.
  • Coverage.
  • Carrier.
  • Country or region.
  • Model.
  • Settings.
  • Do not rely on it without testing general communication first in non-emergency situations, such as ordinary calls to trusted contacts.
  • Do not test emergency calls.

Fall Detection during exercise

Fall Detection may be especially useful during exercise.

Examples:

  • Walking outdoors.
  • Running.
  • Hiking.
  • Cycling with support.
  • Training alone.
  • Exercising in a gym.
  • However, some sudden movements can sometimes be interpreted incorrectly.
  • If the watch triggers a false fall alert, respond to the alert and indicate that you are okay.
  • If false alerts happen often during a specific activity, review the Fall Detection setting.

Fall Detection at home

Many falls happen at home. The Apple Watch can be useful if the person is wearing it.

For example:

  • In the bathroom.
  • In the kitchen.
  • In the bedroom.
  • On stairs.
  • While moving around the house.
  • But it only helps if the watch is on the wrist, charged, and configured.
  • A watch left charging on a table cannot detect a fall. Painfully obvious, yes, but apparently still worth saying.

Fall Detection while sleeping

Fall Detection is not mainly a sleep feature. If you fall out of bed or have an incident, behaviour may depend on movement, impact, watch position, and system interpretation. Do not rely on Fall Detection as a complete night safety system. If there is a high risk during sleep or at night, other safety measures may also be needed.

False alerts

Fall Detection may sometimes activate when there has not been a real fall.

This may happen during:

  1. High-impact exercise.
  2. Sudden arm movements.
  3. Dropping the arm strongly.
  4. Certain sports.
  5. Impacts that affect the watch.

If a false alert appears:

  • Do not panic.
  • Listen to the alert.
  • Indicate that you are okay or that you did not fall.
  • Cancel any emergency call if it has not started.
  • If the call connects, explain that it was accidental.
  • False alerts are inconvenient, but they are better than not understanding what the watch is doing.

Falls not detected

The Apple Watch may fail to detect some falls.

This may happen if:

  • The fall is not strong enough.
  • The movement pattern is unusual.
  • The watch is loose.
  • The battery is depleted.
  • The watch is not being worn.
  • The feature is off.
  • The model does not support it.
  • The system does not interpret the movement as a fall.
  • That is why Fall Detection must not be understood as complete protection.
  • It is an additional layer, not a guarantee.

When to enable Fall Detection

It may be especially advisable to review or enable Fall Detection for:

  • Older people.
  • People who live alone.
  • People with balance difficulties.
  • People with mobility problems.
  • People with previous falls.
  • People who go out walking alone.
  • People who exercise outdoors.
  • People with certain health conditions.
  • People who want extra safety.
  • But the decision should consider each person’s real situation.

When to review the setting

Review Fall Detection:

  • When setting up a new Apple Watch.
  • When giving the watch to an older person.
  • After changing Apple Watch model.
  • After a major watchOS update.
  • If there has been a fall.
  • If there have been false alerts.
  • If emergency contacts change.
  • If health information changes.
  • If the person starts walking or exercising alone.

Practical setup for older people

For an older person, it is useful to configure:

  • Fall Detection.
  • Emergency SOS.
  • Medical ID.
  • Emergency contacts.
  • Passcode.
  • Unlock with iPhone if appropriate.
  • Clear notifications.
  • Strong haptics.
  • Simple watch face.
  • Battery routine.
  • A watch full of unused apps is less useful than a simple watch with safety features properly configured.

What the person should know

The user should know:

  • That the watch may detect some hard falls.
  • That it cannot detect every fall.
  • That an alert may appear after a fall.
  • That they must respond if they are okay.
  • That emergency services may be called if they do not respond.
  • That emergency contacts may be notified.
  • That accidental calls must be explained.
  • That the watch needs battery and connection.
  • It is not enough for someone else to configure it. The person wearing it must understand the basic behaviour.

Testing without calling emergency services

  • You should not test Fall Detection by trying to fall.
  • You should not intentionally hit the watch.
  • You should not call emergency services to check the system.

What you can test safely is:

  • Finding the setting.
  • Reviewing whether it is enabled.
  • Checking emergency contacts.
  • Checking Medical ID.
  • Making an ordinary call from the watch to a trusted person.
  • Checking that the watch is charged and connected.
  • That is enough for practice.

What to do after a real fall

If a real fall occurs:

  • Stay still for a moment if moving is painful.
  • Check whether you are injured.
  • If the watch shows an alert, listen to it.
  • If you are okay, indicate it.
  • If you need help, use Emergency SOS.
  • If the watch calls emergency services, explain what happened.
  • If emergency contacts are notified, contact them when possible.
  • If there is pain, dizziness, confusion, head injury, loss of consciousness, or difficulty moving, seek medical attention.
  • Do not ignore a serious fall just because you managed to stand up.
  • Falls can have consequences that are not obvious immediately.

Common mistakes

Assuming all Apple Watches have Fall Detection.

  • Not activating it when it would be useful.
  • Not configuring emergency contacts.
  • Not updating Medical ID.

Going out without the iPhone while using a GPS watch and assuming emergency calls will work.

  • Having the watch with low battery.
  • Taking the watch off at the times when it would be most useful.
  • Ignoring false alerts without reviewing the setting.
  • Thinking Fall Detection detects every fall.
  • Testing the feature by making dangerous movements.

Practical advice

Fall Detection is useful, but only as part of a broader safety setup.

  • Configure it.
  • Understand it.
  • Keep the watch charged.
  • Wear it properly.
  • Review emergency contacts.
  • Do not depend on it as the only measure.

Safety features are best prepared before they are needed. Waiting until after the fall to learn how the alert works is poor planning with bruises.

Exercise for module 42

On the iPhone, open the Watch app.

  • Go to My Watch.
  • Look for Emergency SOS.
  • Find Fall Detection.
  • Listen to the available options with VoiceOver.
  • Check whether it is off, on during workouts, or always on.
  • Choose the setting that fits the user’s situation.
  • Then open the Health app.
  • Open Medical ID.
  • Review emergency contacts.
  • Check that the phone numbers are correct.
  • Review medication, allergies, and relevant health information.
  • Do not make an emergency test call.
  • Do not try to simulate a fall.
  • Only review and configure.

Summary of module 42

Fall Detection can detect some hard falls. It does not detect every fall. It can show an alert, tap the wrist, sound an alarm, and offer Emergency SOS. If the person does not respond and the watch detects immobility, it may try to call emergency services. The feature depends on model, configuration, battery, connection, and region. A GPS watch may depend on the iPhone for calls. A Cellular watch may offer more independence if it has service and coverage.

Emergency contacts and Medical ID should be configured.

  • False alerts can happen.
  • Real falls can also go undetected.
  • Fall Detection is useful support, not an absolute guarantee.

Module 43. Medical ID and emergency contacts

The availability and behaviour of Medical ID and emergency contacts may vary depending on country, region, system version, and configuration. In some places, certain data may be shared automatically with emergency services. In others, Medical ID will mainly serve as information that can be consulted from the device if access from the locked screen is allowed.

The Apple Watch can be useful in an emergency situation, but for it to be more useful, Medical ID and emergency contacts should be configured properly. These data are managed mainly from the iPhone, in the Health app.

Medical ID can include important information so that emergency services or someone assisting you can know basic details about you: medical conditions, allergies, medication, emergency contacts, and other relevant information.

It is not compulsory to complete every field, but it is worth reviewing which information could be useful if one day you need help and cannot explain yourself clearly.

What Medical ID is

Medical ID is a section of the Health app on the iPhone where you can save important emergency information.

It can include:

  • Name.
  • Date of birth.
  • Medical conditions.
  • Allergies.
  • Medications.
  • Blood type.
  • Weight and height.
  • Language.
  • Emergency contacts.
  • Medical notes.
  • Other relevant information.

This information may be available from the iPhone and, depending on configuration, also from the Apple Watch in an emergency situation.

What it is for

Medical ID can help someone assisting you access basic information if something happens.

For example:

  • If you have a serious allergy.
  • If you take important medication.
  • If you have a relevant medical condition.
  • If you use a medical device.
  • If a specific person needs to be called.
  • If there is information that should be known quickly.
  • It does not replace a medical record, but it can provide basic information at a critical moment.

What information should be included

You do not need to put absolutely everything. You should include what could be useful in an emergency.

For example:

  • Important allergies.
  • Medication you take regularly.
  • Relevant medical conditions.
  • Risk of seizures, fainting, epilepsy, diabetes, or other conditions if applicable.
  • Pacemaker or other medical devices, if applicable.
  • Main emergency contact.
  • Alternative emergency contact.
  • Any brief instruction that may help.

Medical ID should be clear. It should not be filled with irrelevant information that makes the important details harder to find.

Allergies

If you have important allergies, it is useful to record them.

For example:

  • Medication.
  • Food.
  • Latex.
  • Insect stings.
  • Other relevant allergens.
  • If an allergy could affect emergency care, it should be included.

Medications

If you take medication regularly, it is useful to record it. Especially if it may be relevant in an emergency.

For example:

  1. Blood thinners.
  2. Heart medication.
  3. Insulin.
  4. Neurological treatments.
  5. Blood pressure medication.
  6. Other important treatments.

There is no need to record an occasional vitamin if it adds nothing relevant, but anything that may influence healthcare should be included.

Medical conditions

Relevant medical conditions may also be included.

For example:

  • Diabetes.
  • Epilepsy.
  • Heart conditions.
  • Respiratory conditions.
  • Neurological conditions.
  • Severe allergies.
  • Risk of fainting.
  • Mobility issues.
  • Other conditions that may affect emergency care.

The goal is not to write a complete medical biography. The goal is to provide the information that could matter if someone needs to assist you quickly.

Medical notes

Medical notes can be useful for brief and clear information.

For example:

  • Blind person. Communicate verbally.
  • Uses a guide dog.
  • Uses a pacemaker.
  • Has severe allergy to a specific medication.
  • Needs medication at specific times.
  • Has difficulty communicating in certain situations.
  • The note should be short.

In an emergency, nobody is going to read a novel on a screen. If the information is important, it should be easy to understand quickly.

Emergency contacts

Emergency contacts are people who may be notified or contacted in an emergency situation. They may be used by Emergency SOS, Medical ID, or other safety features, depending on configuration and availability. Emergency contacts should be chosen carefully.

They should be people who:

  • Can respond.
  • Know you.
  • Understand why they are listed.
  • Have a working phone number.
  • Would know what to do if contacted.
  • Do not choose someone just because they are in your contacts list.

An emergency contact is not a decorative title. It is a person who may receive an important alert when something serious is happening.

Choosing emergency contacts

It is useful to have at least one main contact. It may also be useful to have an alternative contact.

For example:

  • A close relative.
  • A trusted friend.
  • A caregiver.
  • A partner.
  • A neighbour you trust.
  • A person who knows your health situation.
  • If you live alone, this becomes even more important.
  • If you travel or move frequently, choose someone who can actually help or coordinate help.

Keeping contacts up to date

Emergency contacts must be reviewed from time to time.

Check:

  • The phone number is correct.
  • The person is still the right contact.
  • The relationship label is correct.
  • The person knows they are your emergency contact.
  • There is an alternative if the main contact is unavailable.
  • An emergency contact with an old number is not useful.
  • A contact who does not know they have been assigned that role may also be less useful.

How to configure Medical ID

On the iPhone:

  • Open the Health app.
  • Go to your profile or to Medical ID.
  • Choose Edit.
  • Enter or review the relevant information.
  • Add medical conditions if needed.
  • Add allergies if needed.
  • Add medications if needed.
  • Add emergency contacts.
  • Review whether Medical ID can be shown when the device is locked.
  • Save the changes.
  • The exact path may vary depending on iOS version, but Medical ID is managed from the Health app.

Allowing access when locked

Medical ID can be made available from the locked screen, depending on configuration. This may allow another person to consult emergency information without unlocking the iPhone. This can be useful in an emergency. But it also means some health data may be accessible to someone who has physical access to the device. You need to decide what information you want to make available. This is a balance between safety and privacy. For many people, including essential information is useful. But there is no need to include details that are not relevant for emergency assistance.

Medical ID on the Apple Watch

Medical ID may also be accessible from the Apple Watch, depending on configuration. It may appear together with emergency options. This can be useful if the iPhone is not easy to reach but the watch is on the wrist. Again, the information must be clear and up to date.

Medical ID and VoiceOver

With VoiceOver, Medical ID can be configured from the Health app on the iPhone. It is advisable to move slowly through the fields. Review each entry before saving. If you dictate medication names or medical conditions, check that dictation has recognised them correctly. This is not the place for creative spelling. A medication name written incorrectly may be confusing later.

Medical ID and blindness

For a blind person, it may be useful to include a brief note if it could help in an emergency.

For example:

  • Blind person. Please communicate verbally.
  • Blind person and VoiceOver user.
  • Uses a white cane.
  • Uses a guide dog.
  • Needs verbal orientation.
  • These notes should be respectful, brief, and practical.
  • The goal is not to label the person unnecessarily, but to make assistance easier if something happens.

Medical ID and deafblindness or hearing loss

If the person is deafblind or has hearing loss, this may be especially important to include.

For example:

  • Deafblind person. Needs tactile or close communication.
  • Hearing loss. Speak clearly and face the person.
  • Uses hearing aids.
  • Cannot hear spoken instructions well.
  • Needs communication support.
  • In an emergency, communication can be difficult.
  • A clear note may help reduce confusion.

Medical ID and language

If a person travels or lives in a multilingual environment, it may be useful to include a note about preferred language.

For example:

  • Preferred language: English.
  • Preferred language: Spanish.
  • Needs interpreter if possible.
  • This can be useful in international contexts.
  • Emergency information should be understandable for the people likely to assist.

Medical ID and medication

Medication should be written clearly.

If possible, include:

  • Medication name.
  • Dose, if relevant.
  • Frequency, if relevant.
  • Reason, if relevant.
  • But avoid unnecessary complexity.
  • If you take many medications, it may be useful to keep a complete list elsewhere and include the most critical information in Medical ID.

Medical ID and allergies

Allergies should be clear and direct.

For example:

  • Severe allergy to penicillin.
  • Severe allergy to peanuts.
  • Latex allergy.
  • Bee sting allergy.
  • If the allergy is severe, indicate it clearly.
  • If there are no known allergies, you may also indicate that, if you consider it useful.

Medical ID and privacy

Medical ID contains sensitive data.

Before entering information, think about:

  • What is useful in an emergency.
  • What should be visible when locked.
  • What does not need to be included.
  • Who might see it.
  • Whether the data are up to date.
  • Privacy does not mean hiding everything.
  • Safety does not mean exposing everything.
  • The sensible approach is to include what can help in an emergency and avoid irrelevant personal detail.

Emergency contacts and notifications

If Emergency SOS is used, emergency contacts may receive a message, depending on configuration and availability. This may include location information. This is useful, but it should be known beforehand. If you do not want a person to receive that kind of alert, do not add them as an emergency contact. If you do add someone, it is advisable to tell them. A person who receives an emergency alert should not discover at that moment that they had a starring role in your safety setup.

Review after changes

Medical ID should be reviewed when something changes.

For example:

  • New medication.
  • Medication stopped.
  • New allergy.
  • New diagnosis.
  • Change of emergency contact.
  • Change of phone number.
  • Change of address or country.
  • Change of language needs.
  • Change of mobility or communication needs.
  • Outdated information can create confusion.
  • A review every few months may be enough for many people, unless there are frequent medical changes.

Use for older people

For older people, Medical ID and emergency contacts can be especially useful.

It may be worth including:

  • Medication.
  • Allergies.
  • Main conditions.
  • Emergency contacts.
  • Communication needs.
  • Fall risk, if relevant.
  • Relevant notes.
  • The information should be clear and not overloaded.

Use for people who live alone

If a person lives alone, emergency contacts and Medical ID become especially important. The Apple Watch can help call or alert, but the information behind those alerts must be well configured. A safety function without contacts or useful information is weaker.

Use while travelling

When travelling, review:

  • Emergency contacts.
  • International phone numbers.
  • Language notes.
  • Medical conditions.
  • Insurance or assistance information, if relevant.
  • Local emergency numbers.
  • Whether Apple Watch Cellular works in that country, if you rely on it.
  • Emergency behaviour may vary by country.
  • Do not assume it will work exactly the same everywhere.

What not to include

It is not necessary to include:

  • Irrelevant details.
  • Old conditions that no longer matter.
  • Outdated medication.
  • Contacts who cannot help.
  • Long explanations.
  • Private information that has no emergency value.
  • The goal is clarity.
  • Emergency information should be short, useful, and current.

Common mistakes

  • Not configuring Medical ID.
  • Leaving it outdated.
  • Adding medication incorrectly.
  • Not adding allergies.
  • Adding emergency contacts without telling them.
  • Using old phone numbers.
  • Including too much irrelevant information.
  • Not allowing access when locked when it would be useful.
  • Allowing too much private information without thinking.
  • Not reviewing after health changes.

Practical advice

Configure Medical ID from the iPhone, not in a hurry.

  • Use clear language.
  • Add only useful information.
  • Add at least one emergency contact.
  • Review the information after saving it.
  • Tell your emergency contacts that they are listed.
  • Check it again after important changes.

Medical ID is one of those settings that nobody wants to need, but if it is needed, it is better that it does not contain a phone number from three years ago and a medication you stopped taking before humanity developed its latest unnecessary subscription service.

Exercise for module 43

On the iPhone, open the Health app.

  • Go to Medical ID.
  • Choose Edit.
  • Review your name and date of birth.
  • Review medical conditions.
  • Review allergies.
  • Review medications.
  • Add or update emergency contacts.
  • Check that phone numbers are correct.
  • Add a brief communication note if it may help.

For example, if appropriate: blind person, please communicate verbally.

Review whether Medical ID can be shown when the device is locked.

  • Save the changes.
  • Then check that the information appears correctly.
  • Do not include unnecessary details.

Summary of module 43

Medical ID is configured from the Health app on the iPhone. It can include medical conditions, allergies, medications, blood type, notes, and emergency contacts. It may be accessible from the iPhone or Apple Watch in emergency situations, depending on configuration. Emergency contacts may be notified after Emergency SOS, depending on availability and settings. The information should be clear, useful, and up to date. Privacy must be considered. For blind, deafblind, or hard-of-hearing users, a brief communication note may be useful. Emergency contacts should be people who can actually respond. Medical ID should be reviewed whenever important health or contact information changes.

Module 44. Important alerts

The Apple Watch can send different alerts related to health, activity, safety, and the environment. These alerts can be very useful if they are configured properly. They can draw attention to high or low heart rate, irregular rhythm, high noise levels, pending medication, activity, sleep, falls, emergencies, or relevant information. But they can also become annoying if too many are enabled. The goal is not for the watch to alert you about everything. The goal is for it to alert you about what really matters.

Types of important alerts

Among the alerts that the Apple Watch may offer, depending on model, country, and configuration, there may be:

  • High heart rate.
  • Low heart rate.
  • Irregular rhythm.
  • Atrial fibrillation, where applicable.
  • ECG availability or related records.
  • Medication.
  • Sleep.
  • Sleep apnoea, where available.
  • Hypertension, where available.
  • High noise levels.
  • Activity.
  • Stand reminders.
  • Detected workouts.
  • Workout ending reminders.
  • Fall Detection.
  • Emergency SOS.
  • Low battery.
  • Calendar notifications.
  • Reminders.
  • Alarms.
  • Timers.
  • Not all of these are equally important for every person.

Heart rate alerts

Heart rate alerts may indicate that the watch has detected a high or low heart rate under certain conditions. These alerts should be treated with attention. They do not always mean an emergency. But if they are repeated, striking, or accompanied by symptoms, it is advisable to consult healthcare professionals. To configure or review them, the Watch app or Health app on the iPhone is usually used, in sections related to Heart.

Irregular rhythm alerts

Irregular rhythm alerts may appear if the watch detects patterns compatible with certain irregularities.

  • They are not a definitive diagnosis.
  • But they should not be ignored.
  • If they appear, review the information in Health and consult if appropriate.

Medication alerts

Medication alerts help remind you about doses configured in Health.

They can be very useful, but they must be managed accurately.

  • If you took the medication, mark the dose as taken.
  • If at some point you did not take the medication, it is better to leave that reflected. Recording something incorrectly only complicates the follow-up.
  • If you make a mistake, review the record in Health.

Sleep alerts

Sleep alerts can help you maintain a routine. They can remind you of bedtime, activate Sleep mode, alert you with an alarm, or show information when you wake up. They are useful if you want to improve your schedule. If they bother you or do not fit your life, they can be adjusted.

Sleep apnoea alerts

If the feature is available, the Apple Watch can show notifications related to possible signs of sleep apnoea.

  • These alerts are not a diagnosis.
  • If they appear, it is advisable to consult a healthcare professional.
  • If there are symptoms and no alerts appear, consultation is also advisable.

Hypertension alerts

If the feature is available, the Apple Watch may show notifications related to possible hypertension. This does not mean that the watch has measured blood pressure like a blood pressure monitor. They should be understood as a signal to measure with a suitable device and consult if appropriate.

Noise alerts

The Apple Watch can alert you if it detects high noise levels that could affect hearing.

This can be useful in:

  • Streets with heavy traffic.
  • Concerts.
  • Gyms.
  • Events.
  • Construction areas.
  • Work environments.
  • Places with loud music.
  • For a blind person, hearing can also be important for orientation. Protecting hearing is not a minor detail.
  • If you receive frequent high noise alerts, it may be worth reducing exposure, using hearing protection, or moving away from the environment if possible.

Activity alerts

Activity alerts may include:

  • Stand reminders.
  • Ring progress.
  • Completed goals.
  • Achievements.
  • Challenges.
  • Daily summaries.
  • Weekly summaries.
  • Workout reminders.
  • For some people, these alerts are motivating.
  • For others, they are annoying.
  • If they help you move a little more, keep them.
  • If they become pressure or interruption, reduce them.
  • The Apple Watch should encourage activity, not behave like a tiny sports supervisor with too much confidence.

Stand reminders

Stand reminders are meant to encourage you to move during different hours of the day. They may be useful if you spend many hours sitting. But they are not equally suitable for everyone. People with reduced mobility, fatigue, pain, disability, or wheelchair users may need to adapt the configuration. If these reminders do not make sense for your situation, review them.

Detected workout alerts

The Apple Watch may detect that you have started a workout and suggest recording it. For example, it may notice that you are walking and offer to start an Outdoor Walk workout. This can be useful if you forgot to start the workout manually. But it is better not to depend only on automatic detection. If you know you are going to exercise, start the workout yourself.

Workout ending reminders

The watch may also suggest ending a workout if it detects that you have stopped. This is useful when you forget to finish the workout. But it may not always be correct. If the alert appears, listen to it and decide whether you have really finished or whether you are only taking a break.

Fall Detection alerts

If Fall Detection is enabled and the watch detects a hard fall, it may show an alert, tap your wrist, sound an alarm, and offer Emergency SOS.

  • This alert must be treated carefully.
  • If you are okay, indicate it.
  • If you need help, use the emergency option.
  • If it was a false alert, dismiss it properly.
  • Do not ignore this type of alert without understanding what is happening.

Emergency SOS alerts

Emergency SOS is related to emergency calling and safety. If Emergency SOS appears on screen, do not activate it unless there is a real emergency. If it starts accidentally and the call connects, explain that it was an error. Emergency services should not be used for tests or curiosity.

Low battery alerts

Low battery alerts are simple but important. They can warn you that the Apple Watch is running out of battery.

This matters especially if you rely on the watch for:

  • Calls.
  • Emergency SOS.
  • Fall Detection.
  • Medication reminders.
  • Sleep tracking.
  • Workouts.
  • Navigation.
  • Notifications.
  • If the watch battery is low, charge it as soon as possible.
  • A safety feature without battery is a lovely idea and not much else.

Calendar alerts

Calendar alerts can be very useful.

They can notify you of:

  • Appointments.
  • Meetings.
  • Medical visits.
  • Calls.
  • Training sessions.
  • Important events.
  • For a blind person, receiving a vibration on the wrist before an appointment can be very practical.
  • It is advisable to keep calendar alerts enabled if you depend on them.

Reminder alerts

Reminders are useful for tasks.

They can alert you about:

  • Calls.
  • Errands.
  • Medication-related routines, if not configured in Health.
  • Documents to send.
  • Things to check.
  • Places to go.
  • Pending tasks.
  • If you use Reminders seriously, Apple Watch alerts can be very useful.
  • If you create too many reminders, they may become noise.

Alarm and timer alerts

Alarms and timers are among the most useful alerts on the Apple Watch.

They can vibrate on the wrist and help in everyday situations:

  • Cooking.
  • Medication.
  • Waking up.
  • Resting.
  • Exercise.
  • Leaving on time.
  • Checking a task after a period of time.
  • Make sure the haptic feedback is strong enough for you to notice them.

Too many alerts

Too many alerts make the Apple Watch less useful. If every app vibrates, every notification sounds, every achievement appears, every group message interrupts, and every service wants attention, the important alerts get buried. The watch should not become a wrist-shaped notice board. It is better to receive fewer alerts, but more useful ones.

Alerts on the iPhone and on the Apple Watch

Some alerts may appear on the iPhone. Others may appear on the Apple Watch. Some may appear on both, depending on configuration. This can be useful. But excessive duplication should be avoided. If everything alerts on the iPhone and on the watch in a disorganised way, noise is created.

Configuring alerts from the iPhone

Most alerts are reviewed from the iPhone.

The main places are:

  • Watch app.
  • Health app.
  • Fitness app.
  • iPhone Settings.
  • Reminders app.
  • Calendar app.
  • Each type of alert may be in a different place.

Yes, it is absurd that managing alerts requires visiting half the system, but that is how this small theme park of settings is built.

Configuring Apple Watch notifications

In the Watch app:

  • Go to My Watch.
  • Go to Notifications.
  • Review which apps can alert you.
  • Enable the necessary ones.
  • Disable the unnecessary ones.
  • Review Health, Activity, Messages, Phone, Reminders, and Calendar.
  • Do not enable everything by default.
  • Start with the important ones.

Configuring health alerts

In the Health app:

  • Review Heart.
  • Review Sleep.
  • Review Medications.
  • Review Respiratory, if applicable.
  • Review Medical ID.
  • Review other sections according to your needs.
  • Each feature may have its own alerts.

Configuring activity alerts

In the Watch app:

  • Go to My Watch.
  • Find Activity.
  • Review notifications.
  • You can adjust reminders, achievements, challenges, and alerts.
  • If they help you, leave them enabled.
  • If they bother you, reduce them.

Silent Mode and alerts

Silent Mode can prevent sounds, but vibrations may continue. This is useful if you want discreet alerts. For a blind person, it may be practical to use the watch in Silent Mode but with clear vibrations. For a deafblind person or someone with hearing loss, vibration may be essential.

Haptic feedback

Haptic feedback is the vibration or tap the watch makes on your wrist. It should be configured so that it is easy to notice.

In the Watch app:

  • Go to My Watch.
  • Find Sounds and Haptics.
  • Review haptic feedback.
  • Enable Prominent Haptic if it is available and you need it.
  • An alert you cannot feel is like a bright sign in an empty room. Very technological, but useless.

Focus modes

  • Focus modes can filter alerts.
  • They can be useful for sleeping, working, exercising, or resting.
  • But if they are configured badly, they can block important alerts.

Review:

  • Do Not Disturb.
  • Sleep.
  • Work.
  • Exercise.
  • Driving, if applicable.
  • Custom modes.
  • Make sure important calls or alerts are allowed if you need them.

Critical alerts

Some apps or features may have important or critical alerts. These alerts may behave differently from normal notifications. Not every app has this type of alert. If a health or safety app offers critical alerts, read carefully what that means before enabling them. Not everything deserves to bypass Focus modes.

Prioritising alerts

It is useful to divide alerts into three groups. First group: essential.

For example:

  • Important calls.
  • Emergency.
  • Relevant health alerts.
  • Medication.
  • Fall Detection.
  • Calendar alerts for medical appointments.
  • Second group: useful.

For example:

  • Reminders.
  • Activity.
  • Workout detection.
  • Weather.
  • Battery.
  • Third group: optional or unnecessary.

For example:

  • Promotions.
  • Games.
  • Shopping apps.
  • Non-urgent social networks.
  • Repeated news alerts.
  • Apps that interrupt without real value.
  • This division helps decide what should reach the wrist and what should stay on the iPhone.

Privacy of alerts

Alerts may contain private information.

For example:

  • Messages.
  • Medical appointments.
  • Medication.
  • Health notifications.
  • Bank alerts.
  • Personal reminders.
  • If VoiceOver reads them aloud from the watch speaker, other people may hear them.
  • In public places, it may be better to use headphones or adjust notification privacy.

The Apple Watch can be discreet through vibration, but VoiceOver through the speaker is not discreet. It is a small public announcer attached to your wrist, which sounds worse because sometimes it is exactly that.

People who are deafblind or have hearing loss

For deafblind people or people with hearing loss, important alerts must be configured especially carefully.

It is useful to review:

  • Haptic intensity.
  • Prominent Haptic.
  • Medication alerts.
  • Alarms.
  • Timers.
  • Emergency alerts.
  • Important contacts.
  • Calendar alerts.
  • Focus modes.
  • The key is that the person should be able to notice the alert and understand what it means.
  • If all alerts feel the same, it may be difficult to distinguish their importance.

Testing alerts safely

Some alerts can be tested safely.

For example:

  • Timer.
  • Alarm.
  • Reminder.
  • Calendar notification.
  • Find iPhone.
  • A test message from a trusted person.
  • Other alerts should not be tested directly.
  • Do not test Emergency SOS by calling emergency services.
  • Do not try to trigger Fall Detection by falling.
  • Do not create false health situations to see what the watch does.
  • Apparently this needs to be said, because humans and buttons have a long and dramatic relationship.

What to do if an important alert does not arrive

If an important alert does not arrive, check:

  • The Apple Watch is on your wrist.
  • The watch is unlocked.
  • The watch has battery.
  • The iPhone and watch are connected.
  • Airplane Mode is off.
  • The relevant Focus mode is not blocking it.
  • Notifications are enabled.
  • The app is allowed to notify on the watch.
  • Haptic feedback is enabled.
  • Silent Mode is not being misunderstood.
  • The feature is available on your model and in your country.
  • If it is a health alert, check the Health app and feature settings.

What to do if alerts are too frequent

If alerts are too frequent:

  • Open the Watch app.
  • Go to My Watch.
  • Go to Notifications.
  • Review active apps.
  • Disable at least one unnecessary app.
  • Review Activity alerts.
  • Review Health alerts.
  • Review Calendar and Reminders.
  • Review Focus modes.
  • Reduce what is not essential.
  • The goal is not silence.
  • The goal is useful attention.

Common mistakes

  • Enabling all notifications.
  • Not configuring vibrations.
  • Confusing Silent Mode with Do Not Disturb.
  • Forgetting that Focus modes can block alerts.
  • Ignoring important health notifications.
  • Allowing too many apps on the wrist.
  • Not reviewing notification privacy.
  • Not checking battery alerts.
  • Not testing alarms and timers.
  • Not adapting alerts for deafblind users or users with hearing loss.

Practical advice

Configure the Apple Watch so it alerts you about what matters.

A useful first selection may be:

  • Calls.
  • Messages from important people.
  • Calendar.
  • Reminders.
  • Timers.
  • Alarms.
  • Medication, if used.
  • Relevant health alerts.
  • Fall Detection.
  • Battery.
  • Activity, only if it helps.
  • Everything else should be reviewed carefully.

Exercise for module 44

On the iPhone, open the Watch app.

  • Go to My Watch.
  • Go to Notifications.
  • Review the enabled apps.
  • Disable at least one app you do not need on the Apple Watch.
  • Then go to Sounds and Haptics.
  • Check that haptic feedback is enabled.
  • Enable Prominent Haptic if you need it.
  • Then review Activity.
  • Adjust its alerts if there are too many.
  • Then open Health.
  • Review Heart, Sleep, and Medications alerts if you use those features.

Finally, open Control Centre on the Apple Watch and check that you do not have a Focus mode enabled that blocks important alerts.

Summary of module 44

The Apple Watch can send health, activity, safety, battery, calendar, reminder, and app alerts. Not all alerts are equally important. Essential alerts should be prioritised. Vibrations are fundamental for many blind, deafblind, or hard-of-hearing users. Silent Mode is not the same as Do Not Disturb. Focus modes can block important alerts if configured badly. Privacy should be reviewed because VoiceOver may read alerts aloud. Too many alerts reduce the usefulness of the watch. The goal is for the Apple Watch to alert you about what matters, not about everything.

Back to table of contents

Module 45. Sounds, vibrations, and haptic feedback

The Apple Watch can alert you using sound, vibration, or both. For a blind person, this is important because many interactions with the watch do not depend on vision. VoiceOver speaks, the watch vibrates, and some alerts can be received discreetly on the wrist.

For a deafblind person or a person with hearing loss, haptic feedback may be even more important, because vibration may become the main way to notice alerts. That is why sounds and haptics should not be treated as a minor setting. They are part of accessibility.

What haptic feedback is

Haptic feedback is the vibration or tap that the Apple Watch produces on your wrist.

It can be used for:

  • Notifications.
  • Calls.
  • Messages.
  • Alarms.
  • Timers.
  • Reminders.
  • Activity alerts.
  • Navigation.
  • Workout alerts.
  • System confirmations.
  • Some safety features.
  • When the watch taps your wrist, it is trying to get your attention without depending only on sound or vision.
  • This is one of the reasons the Apple Watch can be useful for blind users.

Sound and haptics are not the same

  • Sound is what you hear.
  • Haptics are what you feel on the wrist.
  • You can have both enabled.
  • You can silence sounds and keep haptics.
  • You can increase or reduce the volume.
  • You can make haptics more noticeable.
  • This distinction matters.
  • Silent Mode does not necessarily mean that the watch stops alerting you completely. It may still vibrate.

That is useful in public places, meetings, classes, appointments, or situations where you want discreet alerts.

Where to configure sounds and haptics

On the iPhone:

  1. Open the Watch app.
  2. Go to My Watch.
  3. Find Sounds and Haptics.
  4. Enter that section.

From there, you can usually review:

  • Alert volume.
  • Silent Mode.
  • Haptic alerts.
  • Prominent Haptic.
  • Crown haptics, if available.
  • Other sound and vibration options depending on version.
  • On the Apple Watch, you can also review some settings from Settings, Sounds and Haptics.
  • For a beginner, the iPhone is usually more comfortable.

Alert volume

Alert volume controls how loud the Apple Watch sounds are. If you rely on the watch speaker, make sure the volume is high enough to hear VoiceOver and alerts in your usual environment. If you prefer discreet use, you may reduce the volume or use Silent Mode with haptics. Remember that noisy places can make the watch harder to hear. In those cases, vibrations or headphones may be more useful.

Silent Mode

Silent Mode silences many Apple Watch sounds. It is useful when you do not want the watch to ring or make alert sounds.

You can activate it from:

  • Control Centre on the Apple Watch.
  • Sounds and Haptics settings.
  • With Silent Mode enabled, the watch can still vibrate if haptic alerts are enabled.
  • This can be very practical.
  • For many blind users, Silent Mode with strong haptics is a good everyday configuration.

Haptic alerts

Haptic alerts are the vibrations used to notify you. In Sounds and Haptics, check that haptic alerts are enabled. If they are off, the watch may not vibrate for alerts. That would make many notifications less useful. If you do not notice alerts, this is one of the first settings to review.

Prominent Haptic

Prominent Haptic is an option that adds a stronger or more noticeable vibration before some alerts. This can help people who do not easily notice standard vibrations.

It may be especially useful for:

  • Blind users.
  • Deafblind users.
  • People with hearing loss.
  • People who use Silent Mode.
  • People who miss standard alerts.
  • People who need stronger wrist feedback.
  • If this option is available, it is worth testing it.
  • If you find it too strong or annoying, you can turn it off later.
  • The point is to notice important alerts, not to feel as if the watch is knocking on your wrist with legal urgency.

Crown haptics

Some Apple Watch models and versions allow haptic feedback when turning the Digital Crown.

This can help make scrolling or changing values feel more physical.

  • For some people, this is useful.
  • For others, it is not important.
  • If the option appears, you can test whether it helps you.
  • It is not essential, but it can improve tactile feedback.

Vibration and strap adjustment

To feel vibrations properly, the watch must be positioned correctly. If it is too loose, haptics may feel weaker. If it is too tight, it may be uncomfortable. The watch should be firm, but comfortable.

If you miss alerts, check:

  • Haptic settings.
  • Prominent Haptic.
  • Strap adjustment.
  • Whether the watch is on your wrist.
  • Whether the watch is unlocked.
  • Whether Focus modes are blocking notifications.
  • Whether the alert itself is enabled.
  • Not every missed alert is a settings problem. Sometimes the strap is simply not making good contact.

Testing vibrations

You can test vibrations safely using simple features.

For example:

  • Set a timer for one minute.
  • Create a test reminder.
  • Ask someone to send you a message.
  • Set an alarm a few minutes ahead.
  • Use Find iPhone from the watch.
  • These tests let you check whether you notice the alert.
  • Do not test safety features such as Emergency SOS.
  • Do not try to trigger Fall Detection.
  • There are safer ways to learn whether the watch vibrates than staging a medical drama for a device.

Timers and alarms

Timers and alarms are excellent for testing haptics.

  • Set a timer for one minute.
  • Wait.
  • When it ends, feel the vibration.
  • Stop the timer.
  • If you barely notice it, review haptic settings and strap adjustment.

If you use the Apple Watch as a wake-up alarm, test it first on a day when missing the alarm would not cause a problem.

Messages and calls

  • Calls and messages can use vibration.
  • For calls, the watch may vibrate repeatedly.
  • For messages, it may tap the wrist more briefly.
  • This difference helps identify the type of alert.
  • With use, many people learn to recognise some alerts by the way they feel.
  • Not all haptic patterns are equally clear, but repeated use helps.

Activity alerts

Activity alerts also use haptics.

For example:

  • Stand reminders.
  • Goal completed.
  • Workout reminders.
  • Achievement alerts.
  • If these alerts are not useful, they can be reduced.
  • If you like them, haptics make them easier to notice without sound.

Navigation haptics

In maps or directions, the Apple Watch may use vibrations to indicate turns or alerts, depending on configuration and app behaviour. This can be useful, but it should not be the only navigation method for a blind person.

Haptics can support orientation, but they do not replace mobility skills, accessible navigation apps, a cane, a guide dog, or safe route knowledge.

Workout haptics

During workouts, the Apple Watch may use haptics for:

  • Workout start.
  • Workout pause.
  • Workout end.
  • Goal progress.
  • Heart rate alerts, if configured.
  • Distance or interval alerts, depending on settings.
  • These can be useful if you do not want constant spoken feedback.
  • But if they become too many, they may distract.

Health alerts

Health alerts may also use haptics.

For example:

  • High heart rate.
  • Low heart rate.
  • Irregular rhythm.
  • Medication.
  • Noise.
  • Sleep-related alerts.
  • These alerts should be noticeable.
  • If you depend on them, make sure haptics are enabled and strong enough.

People who are deafblind

For people who are deafblind, haptic feedback may be central.

In these cases, it is important to configure:

  • Haptic alerts.
  • Prominent Haptic.
  • Important notifications only.
  • Timers and alarms.
  • Medication alerts.
  • Emergency-related settings.
  • A simple watch face.
  • Reduced notification noise.
  • The person needs to be able to distinguish important alerts as much as possible.
  • If every notification vibrates, the important ones lose meaning.
  • For deafblind users, it is often better to reduce notifications and keep only essential alerts.

People with hearing loss

For people with hearing loss, haptics can complement or replace sound alerts.

It may be useful to:

  • Use Silent Mode with haptics.
  • Enable Prominent Haptic.
  • Configure strong alarms.
  • Use the watch for calls and messages with visual or tactile alerts.
  • Use headphones or hearing devices if compatible.
  • Review noise alerts.
  • The exact configuration will depend on the person’s hearing, devices, and preferences.

VoiceOver and speaker volume

  • VoiceOver uses sound.
  • If you use VoiceOver from the watch speaker, volume matters.
  • If the volume is too low, it may be hard to understand.
  • If it is too high, people around you may hear private content.
  • You may need different configurations depending on context.
  • At home, speaker volume may be fine.
  • In public, headphones may be better.

Using headphones

Bluetooth headphones can make VoiceOver, calls, Siri, and audio more private and easier to hear. But they can also reduce awareness of the environment.

For blind users outdoors, this is important.

  • Use moderate volume.
  • Keep environmental awareness.
  • Do not block necessary sounds at crossings or in unfamiliar places.

Sound and privacy

If VoiceOver reads notifications aloud, other people may hear them.

This can include:

  • Messages.
  • Medical reminders.
  • Calendar events.
  • Bank alerts.
  • Health notifications.
  • Private reminders.
  • If privacy matters, use headphones, reduce volume, or read on the iPhone in a more controlled way.

The watch speaker is practical, but subtle it is not. It can turn a private message into a small public announcement with impressive lack of shame.

Focus modes and haptics

Focus modes can block notifications before haptics even happen. If a Focus mode silences an app, the watch may not vibrate for it.

If you are missing alerts, check:

  • Do Not Disturb.
  • Sleep.
  • Work.
  • Personal.
  • Exercise.
  • Other Focus modes.
  • Haptics cannot alert you about notifications that the system is blocking.

Silent Mode and Focus are different

  • This is important.
  • Silent Mode affects sounds.
  • Focus modes affect which notifications are allowed.
  • If Silent Mode is on and haptics are on, the watch may still vibrate.
  • If Focus blocks an app, the watch may not alert you at all.
  • Many notification problems come from confusing these two settings.

Low Power Mode

Low Power Mode can affect some Apple Watch functions. If you are not receiving expected alerts or features are reduced, check whether Low Power Mode is active. Battery-saving modes can change behaviour. This may be useful when battery is low, but it can also limit functions you rely on.

When haptics are too strong

Some people may find haptics too noticeable or annoying.

In that case:

  • Turn off Prominent Haptic.
  • Reduce unnecessary notifications.
  • Use fewer activity alerts.
  • Review app notifications.
  • Keep only important haptic alerts.
  • The goal is not maximum vibration.
  • The goal is useful vibration.

When haptics are too weak

If haptics are too weak:

  • Enable Prominent Haptic.
  • Check Haptic Alerts.
  • Tighten the strap slightly.
  • Move the watch slightly above the wrist bone.
  • Check that the watch is not locked.
  • Check notification settings.
  • Test with a timer.
  • If you still do not feel them well, the Apple Watch may not be enough as the only alert system for that person.
  • This is especially important for deafblind users or deep sleepers.

Common mistakes

  • Turning off haptic alerts by mistake.
  • Thinking Silent Mode disables everything.
  • Confusing Silent Mode with Focus.
  • Wearing the watch too loose.
  • Not enabling Prominent Haptic when needed.
  • Keeping too many notifications active.
  • Relying on haptics without testing them.
  • Using headphones outdoors at excessive volume.
  • Forgetting privacy when VoiceOver speaks aloud.
  • Not checking Low Power Mode.

Practical advice

For many blind users, a good starting configuration is:

  • VoiceOver enabled.
  • Alert volume at a comfortable level.
  • Silent Mode according to context.
  • Haptic alerts enabled.
  • Prominent Haptic enabled if standard vibration is weak.
  • Important notifications only.
  • Timers and alarms tested.
  • Medication and health alerts reviewed if used.
  • After a few days, adjust according to real experience.
  • Do not configure sound and haptics based only on theory. The wrist has its own opinion, annoyingly enough.

Exercise for module 45

On the iPhone, open the Watch app.

  • Go to My Watch.
  • Open Sounds and Haptics.
  • Check alert volume.
  • Check whether Silent Mode is on or off.
  • Check that Haptic Alerts are enabled.
  • Enable Prominent Haptic if you want stronger alerts.
  • Put on the Apple Watch properly adjusted.
  • Set a timer for one minute.
  • Wait for the alert.
  • Check whether you clearly feel the vibration.
  • Stop the timer.
  • Then ask someone to send you a test message.
  • Notice whether the vibration is easy to recognise.
  • If it is too weak, adjust the strap or haptic settings.
  • If it is too strong or annoying, reduce unnecessary alerts.

Summary of module 45

The Apple Watch can alert through sound, haptics, or both. Haptic feedback is the vibration or tap on the wrist. For blind, deafblind, or hard-of-hearing users, haptics can be essential. Silent Mode silences sounds but may still allow vibrations. Focus modes can block notifications completely. Prominent Haptic can make alerts more noticeable. The watch must be properly adjusted to feel vibrations well. Timers and alarms are good ways to test haptics safely. Too many alerts reduce usefulness. Sound and VoiceOver may affect privacy in public. The best configuration is the one that makes important alerts noticeable without overwhelming the user.

Back to table of contents

Module 46. Use by people who are deafblind or have hearing loss

The Apple Watch can be useful not only for blind people, but also for people who are deafblind or have hearing loss. In these cases, the configuration must be especially careful. A blind person may rely mainly on VoiceOver, sound, Siri, and haptic feedback.

A person with hearing loss may need stronger vibrations, visual information if they have remaining vision, or audio routed to hearing devices or headphones.

A deafblind person may depend heavily on tactile feedback, simplified notifications, clear routines, and support from the iPhone or other assistive technology. For this reason, the Apple Watch should not be configured in the same way for everyone. The important question is not “what can the watch do?”, but “which channel of information can this person actually perceive?” Sound, vision, touch, vibration, speech, braille, iPhone support, another person’s assistance, or a combination of several.

The Apple Watch and haptic feedback

For people who cannot rely on sight or hearing, haptic feedback becomes especially important.

The watch can tap the wrist for:

  • Calls.
  • Messages.
  • Alarms.
  • Timers.
  • Reminders.
  • Medication.
  • Calendar events.
  • Activity alerts.
  • Workout alerts.
  • Navigation prompts.
  • Some safety alerts.
  • But haptic feedback has limits.
  • Not all vibrations are easy to distinguish.
  • Not every alert has a unique pattern.
  • If too many notifications are enabled, the person may receive many similar vibrations and not know which ones are important.
  • So, in these cases, less is usually better.
  • It is more useful to have fewer, clearer alerts than a wrist that vibrates all day like a tiny nervous appliance.

Configuring strong haptics

From the iPhone:

  • Open the Watch app.
  • Go to My Watch.
  • Go to Sounds and Haptics.
  • Check that Haptic Alerts are enabled.
  • Enable Prominent Haptic if available and useful.
  • Prominent Haptic adds a stronger or more noticeable tap before some alerts.
  • For many deafblind users, this may be important.

After enabling it, test with:

  • Timer.
  • Alarm.
  • Reminder.
  • Incoming call from a trusted person.
  • Message from a trusted person.
  • Do not test emergency features.

Strap adjustment

To feel vibrations properly, the Apple Watch must be correctly adjusted. If it is too loose, vibrations may not be noticeable. If it is too tight, it may be uncomfortable. The watch should be firm and stable, with the back in contact with the skin. This matters especially for users who depend on vibration. A poorly adjusted watch may make the difference between noticing an alert and missing it.

Choosing which alerts should reach the wrist

For deafblind users or users with hearing loss, the notification list should be reduced.

Recommended important alerts may include:

  • Calls from selected contacts.
  • Messages from selected contacts.
  • Alarms.
  • Timers.
  • Medication.
  • Calendar.
  • Reminders.
  • Emergency-related alerts.
  • Battery.
  • Fall Detection, if appropriate.
  • Health alerts, if configured.

It may be advisable to disable:

  • Games.
  • Promotions.
  • Social media notifications.
  • Non-urgent groups.
  • Repeated news alerts.
  • Apps that send frequent low-value notifications.
  • If everything vibrates, nothing stands out.
  • This is especially true when the person cannot easily read or hear every notification immediately.

Using Focus modes carefully

  • Focus modes can help reduce interruptions.
  • But they can also block important alerts.
  • For deafblind users, this is delicate.

Review:

  • Do Not Disturb.
  • Sleep.
  • Work.
  • Personal.
  • Exercise.
  • Custom Focus modes.
  • Make sure important people and apps are allowed.

For example, it may be useful to allow:

  • Emergency contacts.
  • Close relatives.
  • Carers.
  • Medication reminders.
  • Calendar alerts.
  • Important health alerts.
  • Do not activate Focus modes without checking their effects.
  • A Focus mode configured badly can silence exactly the alert the person needs.

Alarms and timers

Alarms and timers can be very useful. For deafblind users, the Apple Watch may act as a tactile alarm on the wrist.

Possible uses:

  • Waking up.
  • Medication.
  • Cooking.
  • Leaving home.
  • Rest breaks.
  • Exercise intervals.
  • Appointments.
  • Daily routines.
  • Before depending on them, test whether the vibration is strong enough.
  • For waking up, do not rely on the watch for the first time on an important day.
  • Test it first when there is no risk.

Medication reminders

Medication reminders can be especially useful if the person can feel the alert and then confirm it with support. However, the person must be able to distinguish the alert and know what action to take.

If not, the Apple Watch may need to be combined with:

  • A caregiver.
  • A second reminder system.
  • A labelled pill organiser.
  • A phone reminder.
  • A vibrating alarm.
  • A braille or tactile routine.
  • The watch can support medication routines, but it does not verify that medication has actually been taken.

Calls

For people with hearing loss, calls may be useful if the audio can be routed to compatible headphones, hearing aids, or other devices. For deafblind users, calls may not be useful unless combined with other communication methods. But call alerts can still be important as a way of knowing that someone is trying to reach them. It may be useful to allow calls only from important contacts, so that vibrations are meaningful.

Messages

Messages can arrive as notifications. For a person with hearing loss and enough vision or VoiceOver access, this may be useful. For a deafblind person, reading the message on the watch may not be practical unless braille or other support is available. In many cases, the iPhone will be more suitable for detailed communication. The Apple Watch may serve mainly as an alert device, not as the main reading device.

VoiceOver and hearing loss

A person with hearing loss may still use VoiceOver if they can hear it through:

  • Watch speaker.
  • Headphones.
  • Hearing aids.
  • Bluetooth audio.
  • Compatible devices.
  • If the speaker is not enough, test headphones or hearing devices.
  • Volume and clarity matter.
  • But outdoors, also consider environmental awareness.

Using headphones

Headphones can help people with hearing loss hear VoiceOver, calls, Siri, or notifications more clearly. However, for blind users, blocking environmental sound may affect orientation and safety. This is especially important outdoors.

If possible, use:

  • Moderate volume.
  • Transparency mode.
  • One ear uncovered, if appropriate.
  • Bone conduction headphones, if useful.
  • A setup that preserves environmental awareness.
  • The best option depends on the person’s hearing, mobility, and environment.

Screen and visual settings

  • Some people with hearing loss may have vision.
  • Some deafblind people may have remaining vision.
  • Some blind people may have light perception or partial vision.

For those users, display settings may matter.

Possible settings:

  • Brightness.
  • Text size.
  • Bold text.
  • Reduced motion.
  • Watch face contrast.
  • Simple watch face.
  • Large complications.
  • Clear layout.
  • For users with low vision and hearing loss, visual clarity and haptic alerts may work together.
  • For totally blind users, visual settings may be less relevant.

Simple watch face

For deafblind users or users with multiple disabilities, the watch face should be simple.

Recommended complications may include:

  • Time.
  • Battery.
  • Timer.
  • Alarms.
  • Medication.
  • Calendar.
  • Activity, if useful.
  • Heart rate, if useful.
  • Too many complications make navigation harder.
  • A simple watch face reduces confusion.

Control Centre

Control Centre can be useful, but it should be learned carefully.

Useful controls may include:

  • Battery.
  • Silent Mode.
  • Focus.
  • Find iPhone.
  • Airplane Mode.
  • Water Lock.
  • For deafblind users, it may be necessary to practise with support so the person understands what each control does.
  • Accidentally enabling Airplane Mode or a Focus mode can stop important alerts.

Find iPhone

Find iPhone may be useful if the person can hear the sound. For a deafblind person, it may be less useful unless another person helps, or unless the sound can be perceived. If the person cannot hear it, locating devices may need other strategies.

Apple Watch as a tactile alert device

For some deafblind people, the Apple Watch may be most useful as a tactile alert device.

Possible uses:

  • Alarm clock.
  • Timer.
  • Medication alert.
  • Reminder device.
  • Call alert from selected people.
  • Calendar alert.
  • Emergency-related alert.
  • Workout or activity prompt.
  • This is a legitimate way to use the watch.
  • Not every user needs to read long notifications on the watch.

Sometimes the most useful function is simply “something important is happening; check the iPhone or ask for support.”

Braille and Apple Watch

Apple Watch has some braille-related possibilities, but they are more advanced and not suitable for every user. Depending on watchOS version, settings, and devices, braille input or output may be available in certain contexts. This will be covered in a later module.

For deafblind users, braille may be especially relevant, but the practical experience depends on:

  • Braille display compatibility.
  • watchOS support.
  • iPhone support.
  • User experience.
  • Language.
  • Configuration.
  • It is not the first thing to configure when starting out.

Assistance from the iPhone

Many settings are easier from the iPhone. For deafblind users, the iPhone may be the main configuration device.

The Apple Watch can then act as:

  • Alert device.
  • Health recorder.
  • Activity recorder.
  • Safety device.
  • Quick control device.
  • The iPhone may be used for reading, reviewing, configuring, and correcting.
  • This distinction can make the experience more manageable.

Training and support

For deafblind users, initial training may need more support.

It is important to teach:

  • How the watch vibrates.
  • What each important alert means.
  • How to stop alarms.
  • How to check battery.
  • How to use emergency functions if appropriate.
  • How to avoid accidental activations.
  • How to use the iPhone for review.
  • How to charge the watch.
  • How to wear it correctly.
  • The goal is not to teach every Apple Watch feature.
  • The goal is to create a reliable daily routine.

Emergency features

Emergency SOS and Fall Detection can be useful, but they must be explained carefully.

A deafblind person must know:

  • What happens if Emergency SOS is activated.
  • That emergency contacts may be notified.
  • That the watch may try to call emergency services.
  • That false activations must be cancelled if possible.
  • That the watch needs battery and connection.
  • For some users, emergency configuration should be done with trusted support.

Fall Detection

Fall Detection may be useful for people with additional mobility risks. But it does not detect every fall. It may also create false alerts. For deafblind users, it is important to understand what kind of vibration or alert may appear and what action to take if possible. If the person cannot respond to the watch alert, emergency contacts and general safety planning become even more important.

Battery routine

For users who depend on alerts, battery is critical. Create a fixed charging routine.

For example:

  • Charge during breakfast.
  • Charge before bed.
  • Charge while showering.
  • Charge during a daily rest period.
  • If the watch is used for sleep, do not leave charging only for the night.
  • The routine must fit the person’s life.
  • A watch without battery is not an accessibility tool. It is jewellery with ambitions.

Avoiding overload

For deafblind users, overload is a real risk. Too many alerts, too many apps, too many watch faces, or too many gestures can make the device unusable.

It is better to start with:

  • One watch face.
  • Few apps.
  • Few alerts.
  • Strong haptics.
  • Important contacts.
  • Timers and alarms.
  • Medication if needed.
  • Battery routine.
  • Then add features gradually.

Suggested basic configuration

A basic configuration for a deafblind or hard-of-hearing user might include:

  • VoiceOver if useful.
  • Haptic Alerts enabled.
  • Prominent Haptic enabled.
  • Silent Mode depending on hearing and context.
  • Few notifications.
  • Important contacts only.
  • Alarms and timers tested.
  • Medication reminders if needed.
  • Simple watch face.
  • Battery complication.
  • Emergency contacts configured.
  • Medical ID updated.
  • Fall Detection reviewed if appropriate.
  • Focus modes checked carefully.
  • This configuration should be adapted to the person.
  • No template replaces individual needs.

What to test first

The first tests should be safe and simple:

  • Timer vibration.
  • Alarm vibration.
  • Reminder vibration.
  • Incoming call from a trusted contact.
  • Message from a trusted contact.
  • Battery check.
  • Charging routine.
  • Finding the Digital Crown.
  • Finding the side button.
  • Do not start with Emergency SOS, Fall Detection, Apple Pay, complex notifications, or advanced health.
  • Start with what the person can actually perceive and use.

Common mistakes

  • Leaving too many notifications enabled.
  • Not testing whether the person feels the vibration.
  • Using a strap that is too loose.
  • Forgetting Prominent Haptic.
  • Blocking alerts with Focus modes.
  • Assuming VoiceOver is useful if the person cannot hear it.
  • Assuming haptics are enough without testing them.
  • Configuring too many apps.
  • Not teaching what each alert means.
  • Depending on emergency features without battery or connection.

Practical advice

For deafblind users or users with hearing loss, the Apple Watch should be configured from real perception, not from the feature list.

First check:

  • Can the person feel the vibration?
  • Can they distinguish important alerts?
  • Can they stop an alarm?
  • Can they check the watch with support?
  • Can they use the iPhone to review information?
  • Can they charge it independently or with help?
  • Only after that should more features be added.

Exercise for module 46

Put the Apple Watch on the person’s wrist.

  • Adjust the strap correctly.
  • Open the Watch app on the iPhone.
  • Go to Sounds and Haptics.
  • Enable Haptic Alerts.
  • Enable Prominent Haptic if useful.
  • Set a timer for one minute.
  • Check whether the person feels the vibration.
  • Create a test reminder.
  • Check whether the alert is noticed.
  • Ask a trusted person to call.
  • Check whether the call vibration is noticed.
  • Review notifications and disable unnecessary apps.
  • Review Focus modes and make sure important alerts are not blocked.
  • Review Medical ID and emergency contacts if the person will use safety features.
  • Do not test Emergency SOS with a real call.

Summary of module 46

The Apple Watch may be useful for people who are deafblind or have hearing loss. Haptic feedback is central in these cases. Prominent Haptic may help make alerts easier to notice. The watch must be properly adjusted to feel vibrations. Too many notifications can make the device confusing. Important alerts should be prioritised. Focus modes must be reviewed carefully so they do not block essential alerts. For some users, the watch will function mainly as a tactile alert device. The iPhone may remain the main device for reading, configuration, and review. Emergency features can be useful, but they must be understood and configured carefully.

Back to table of contents

Module 47. Hand gestures and AssistiveTouch

The Apple Watch includes accessibility features that allow some actions to be performed with hand gestures, without touching the screen directly.

This can be useful for people who have difficulty using the touch screen, people with reduced mobility in one hand, people who use the watch while walking or exercising, and some users who need alternative ways to interact. One of the most important features in this area is AssistiveTouch. AssistiveTouch on Apple Watch is not the same as VoiceOver, although both are accessibility features. VoiceOver reads the screen and allows a blind person to interact with spoken feedback. AssistiveTouch allows certain actions to be controlled through gestures, movement, and alternative interaction methods. Some people may use VoiceOver and AssistiveTouch together, but this requires practice and is not always necessary.

What AssistiveTouch is

AssistiveTouch is an accessibility feature that allows the Apple Watch to recognise certain hand gestures and use them to control the interface.

Depending on model, watchOS version, and configuration, it may allow gestures such as:

  • Pinch.
  • Double pinch.
  • Clench.
  • Double clench.
  • These gestures can be assigned to actions.

For example, they may be used to move forward, go back, select, open a menu, press the Digital Crown, or activate another function. The exact possibilities depend on the version and the device.

Who AssistiveTouch may help

AssistiveTouch may be useful for:

  • People with motor difficulties.
  • People who cannot easily touch the screen.
  • People who have only one hand available.
  • People who find the Digital Crown or side button difficult to use.
  • People who need alternative interaction.
  • People who want to use certain functions while moving.
  • Some blind users, if the gestures are well configured and practised.
  • It may also help in specific situations, but it is not compulsory for everyone.

A blind person who can use the touch screen, VoiceOver gestures, Digital Crown, and side button comfortably may not need AssistiveTouch at all. Accessibility does not mean activating every accessibility feature that exists. That way lies chaos, and probably a watch that reacts to your hand as if you were conducting an invisible orchestra.

Difference between AssistiveTouch and Double Tap

Some newer Apple Watch models include a feature called Double Tap or similar gesture-based control. This allows certain actions by tapping fingers together, depending on model and system version. This should not be confused with VoiceOver’s double tap gesture on the screen. It should also not be confused with AssistiveTouch, although they may seem related.

VoiceOver double tap:

  • A screen gesture.
  • Used to activate the selected item.
  • Performed by tapping the screen twice.

Double Tap gesture:

  • A hand gesture.
  • Performed by tapping fingers together.
  • Used for certain system actions on compatible models.

AssistiveTouch:

An accessibility feature with configurable hand gestures. The terms can be confusing, because Apple and the universe apparently agreed that using similar names for different actions would be character building.

Where to configure AssistiveTouch

AssistiveTouch is usually configured from the Apple Watch accessibility settings or from the Watch app on the iPhone.

From the iPhone:

  1. Open the Watch app.
  2. Go to My Watch.
  3. Go to Accessibility.
  4. Look for AssistiveTouch.
  5. Open it.
  6. Review the available options.

From the Apple Watch:

  • Open Settings.
  • Go to Accessibility.
  • Look for AssistiveTouch.
  • Enter the section.
  • For a beginner, the iPhone is usually more comfortable.

Activating AssistiveTouch

To activate AssistiveTouch:

  • Open the Watch app on the iPhone.
  • Go to My Watch.
  • Go to Accessibility.
  • Enter AssistiveTouch.
  • Turn it on.
  • After enabling it, the system may show explanations or a setup process.
  • Listen carefully with VoiceOver.
  • Do not activate complex gesture assignments without understanding them.

Hand gestures

AssistiveTouch can recognise hand gestures such as:

  • Pinch.
  • Double pinch.
  • Clench.
  • Double clench.
  • The exact gestures available may depend on the model and version.
  • A pinch usually means touching the index finger and thumb together.
  • A double pinch means doing that gesture twice.
  • A clench usually means closing the hand into a fist.
  • A double clench means doing that gesture twice.
  • These gestures must be performed with the hand of the wrist wearing the watch.
  • For example, if the Apple Watch is on the left wrist, the left hand performs the gestures.

Gesture sensitivity
