Gesture recognition may depend on:

  • How the watch is worn.
  • How the hand moves.
  • Strap adjustment.
  • Sensor quality.
  • Speed of the gesture.
  • User mobility.
  • watchOS version.
  • Some people will find gestures easy.
  • Others may find them unreliable.
  • If gestures are not recognised well, AssistiveTouch may become more frustrating than useful.
  • In that case, do not force its use.
  • The goal is accessibility, not turning your hand into a remote control that only works when the planets align.

Assigning actions to gestures

AssistiveTouch may allow different actions to be assigned to each gesture.

Possible actions may include:

  • Move to next item.
  • Move to previous item.
  • Tap.
  • Action Menu.
  • Press Digital Crown.
  • Press side button.
  • Show apps.
  • Open Apple Pay.
  • Scroll.
  • Other system actions depending on version.
  • For a VoiceOver user, it is especially important to avoid assignments that cause confusion.
  • If a gesture triggers an action that the person does not expect, the watch may become harder to control.

Recommended basic approach

For someone starting out, do not enable everything at once.

A sensible approach is:

  • First learn VoiceOver touch gestures.
  • Learn Digital Crown and side button.
  • Learn Control Centre.
  • Learn notifications.
  • Only then test AssistiveTouch if there is a real need.
  • If AssistiveTouch is needed, start with a very simple configuration.

For example:

  • One gesture to move forward.
  • One gesture to activate.
  • One gesture to open the action menu.
  • But the best configuration depends on the person.

Action Menu

AssistiveTouch may include an Action Menu. This menu can give access to actions such as pressing buttons, scrolling, or system controls. It can be useful, but it can also be complex. With VoiceOver, the Action Menu must be explored carefully. It is not advisable to introduce it too early unless the user actually needs it.

Using AssistiveTouch with VoiceOver

AssistiveTouch can be used together with VoiceOver, but this combination requires attention.

  • VoiceOver has its own gestures.
  • AssistiveTouch has hand gestures.
  • If both are active, the user must understand which gesture belongs to which feature.
  • Otherwise, confusion appears quickly.

For example:

  • Swipe right with one finger on the screen moves to the next VoiceOver item.
  • Pinch with the hand may perform an AssistiveTouch action.
  • Double tap on the screen activates the selected VoiceOver item.
  • A hand gesture may also activate something if configured.
  • This can be powerful, but only if the person has enough practice.

When not to use AssistiveTouch

Do not use AssistiveTouch just because it is there.

It may not be necessary if:

  • The person uses VoiceOver comfortably.
  • The person can touch the screen.
  • The person can use the Digital Crown and side button.
  • The gestures are not recognised reliably.
  • The feature causes more confusion than help.
  • The person does not need alternative control.

Accessibility features are tools, not trophies. Activating them all does not make the device more accessible. Sometimes it just creates a small circus on your wrist.

When AssistiveTouch may be very useful

It may be useful if:

  • A person has difficulty touching the screen.
  • A person cannot use the other hand easily.
  • The Digital Crown is hard to press.
  • The side button is hard to locate.
  • There are motor limitations.
  • The person wants to control some actions with the hand wearing the watch.
  • There is a specific routine where gestures help.

For example, someone with one hand occupied may use gestures to answer alerts, move through options, or activate certain actions.

Testing AssistiveTouch safely

AssistiveTouch should be tested in a safe context. Do not test it during a workout, at a street crossing, while paying, or while handling emergency features. Test it sitting down, with the watch unlocked, in a quiet environment. Use simple actions first. If something does not work, turn the feature off and review configuration.

Avoid assigning dangerous actions

Be careful with actions such as:

  • Emergency SOS.
  • Apple Pay.
  • Side button actions.
  • System actions that are easy to trigger accidentally.
  • It is better to avoid assigning sensitive functions to gestures at the beginning.
  • The first goal should be navigation and activation, not launching features that can create real-world consequences.

Using gestures during workouts

Some gesture features may be useful during workouts, depending on model and configuration. For example, answering an alert, controlling audio, or interacting without touching the screen. But during outdoor activity, safety comes first. If a gesture is unreliable, do not depend on it while moving. For blind users outdoors, do not perform gestures that distract you in dangerous areas.

AssistiveTouch and tremor or involuntary movement

If a person has tremor, spasms, or involuntary movements, gesture recognition may behave unpredictably. In that case, AssistiveTouch must be tested carefully. A gesture system that activates unintentionally can be more harmful than useful. It may be better to rely on simpler controls, the iPhone, Siri, or support from another method.

Using AssistiveTouch with deafblind users

For deafblind users, AssistiveTouch may or may not be useful. If the person can feel haptic feedback and understand the gesture response, it might help. But if the person cannot easily confirm what action was performed, it may be confusing. In these cases, it is better to start with simple haptic alerts, timers, alarms, and essential notifications before adding gesture control. Training is essential.

Turning AssistiveTouch off

If AssistiveTouch causes confusion, turn it off.

From the iPhone:

  • Open the Watch app.
  • Go to My Watch.
  • Go to Accessibility.
  • Open AssistiveTouch.
  • Turn it off.
  • There is no shame in turning off a feature that does not help.
  • The best accessibility setting is the one that actually improves use.

Common mistakes

  • Activating AssistiveTouch without needing it.
  • Not understanding the difference between VoiceOver gestures and hand gestures.
  • Assigning too many actions.
  • Assigning sensitive actions.
  • Testing gestures while walking outdoors.
  • Expecting gestures to work perfectly for everyone.
  • Ignoring strap adjustment.
  • Using gestures despite unreliable recognition.
  • Not knowing how to turn the feature off.
  • Confusing Double Tap, VoiceOver double tap, and AssistiveTouch.

Practical advice

If the person can use VoiceOver normally, leave AssistiveTouch for later.

If there is a motor need, configure it slowly.

  • Start with one or two gestures.
  • Test them in a safe place.
  • Do not assign emergency or payment functions at the beginning.
  • If the feature helps, keep it.
  • If it confuses, simplify or turn it off.

Exercise for module 47

On the iPhone, open the Watch app.

  • Go to My Watch.
  • Go to Accessibility.
  • Find AssistiveTouch.
  • Open it.
  • Listen to the description and available options.
  • If you do not need it, do not activate it.

If you want to test it:

  • Turn it on.
  • Review the available hand gestures.
  • Choose a simple action.
  • Test the gesture while sitting down.
  • Check whether the watch recognises it.
  • Try the gesture several times.
  • If it is unreliable or confusing, turn AssistiveTouch off.
  • Do not assign Apple Pay, Emergency SOS, or other sensitive actions during the first test.

Summary of module 47

AssistiveTouch allows some Apple Watch actions to be controlled with hand gestures.

  • It is different from VoiceOver.
  • It may be useful for people with motor difficulties or alternative access needs.
  • Typical gestures may include pinch, double pinch, clench, and double clench.
  • It can be configured from Accessibility in the Watch app or on the Apple Watch.
  • It can be used with VoiceOver, but this requires practice.
  • It should not be activated just because it exists.
  • Sensitive actions should not be assigned at the beginning.
  • If it helps, it can be powerful.
  • If it confuses, it should be simplified or turned off.

Back to table of contents

Module 48. Braille on Apple Watch, as an advanced option

Braille can be part of the Apple Watch accessibility experience, but it should be considered an advanced option. Most blind users will begin with VoiceOver, the touch screen, the Digital Crown, Siri, haptic feedback, notifications, and the Watch app on the iPhone.

Braille may be useful for some users, especially people who already use braille displays, braille input, or braille screen input on Apple devices. It may also be relevant for deafblind users, depending on their devices, configuration, and level of braille use. But it is not the first feature to configure when learning the Apple Watch from scratch. This module introduces the idea so that users know it exists and understand when it may be useful.

Braille and the Apple ecosystem

Apple devices have long included braille support through VoiceOver. On iPhone, iPad, and Mac, VoiceOver can work with braille displays and braille input methods, depending on device, system version, language, and compatibility. The Apple Watch is more limited than the iPhone, because the screen is smaller and the device is designed for quick actions. Even so, some braille-related features may be available depending on the version of watchOS, the connected devices, and Apple’s current support. The exact experience can vary.

That is why this module must be read as a general introduction, not as a promise that every braille feature will be available on every model or in every language.

Who may be interested in braille on Apple Watch

Braille may be especially interesting for:

  • Blind people who already use braille displays.
  • Deafblind people who cannot rely on speech output.
  • Advanced VoiceOver users.
  • People who prefer reading certain information silently.
  • People who use braille for spelling, short text review, or precise information.
  • People who want additional access beyond speech and haptics.
  • For many beginners, however, braille will not be necessary at first.

A person can use the Apple Watch quite well with VoiceOver, gestures, Siri, and haptic feedback without using braille. Braille is not compulsory.

Braille displays

A braille display is an external device that presents text in braille through refreshable cells. On iPhone, braille displays can be paired and used with VoiceOver. On Apple Watch, support may be more limited and may depend on Apple’s current implementation. In many cases, the iPhone will remain the main device for braille use.

That means a deafblind or braille user may use the Apple Watch mainly as an alert device and then check the details on the iPhone with a braille display. This can be a very practical workflow.

For example:

  • The Apple Watch vibrates.
  • The user knows an important notification has arrived.
  • The user checks the full message on the iPhone using a braille display.
  • This avoids forcing the Apple Watch to do tasks that the iPhone handles better.

Braille Screen Input

Braille Screen Input is a feature that allows text to be entered using braille gestures on the screen of some Apple devices. On the iPhone, many blind users use it to write quickly. On the Apple Watch, the small screen may make braille input less comfortable or may limit availability depending on watchOS version. If a braille input option is available, it should be considered an advanced method. For beginners, dictation, Siri, quick replies, and the iPhone will usually be more practical.

Braille for deafblind users

For deafblind users, braille can be crucial. If a person cannot hear VoiceOver and cannot rely on vision, braille may be the main reading channel. In that case, the Apple Watch may be useful in combination with the iPhone and a braille display. The watch can provide tactile alerts on the wrist. The iPhone can provide detailed braille access. This combination may be more realistic than expecting the Apple Watch alone to manage every task.

For a deafblind user, the first configuration should usually focus on:

  1. Strong haptics.
  2. Prominent Haptic.
  3. Important notifications only.
  4. Medication reminders if needed.
  5. Alarms and timers.
  6. Emergency contacts.
  7. Medical ID.
  8. Battery routine.

Then, if braille is part of the user’s system, the iPhone and compatible braille display can be used for detailed reading.

Why the Apple Watch is not ideal for long braille work

The Apple Watch is designed for quick interaction.

It is useful for:

  • Alerts.
  • Short messages.
  • Calls.
  • Timers.
  • Alarms.
  • Health data.
  • Workouts.
  • Quick checks.
  • Simple replies.

It is not ideal for:

  • Long writing.
  • Long reading.
  • Complex editing.
  • Detailed document review.
  • Extensive braille navigation.
  • For those tasks, the iPhone, iPad, Mac, or a braille display connected to a larger device will usually be better.

Trying to turn the Apple Watch into a full braille workstation is possible only in the same sense that eating soup with a fork is possible: technically there is movement, but the method has lost its dignity.

Checking braille options

If you want to review braille-related options, start from the iPhone.

On the iPhone:

  • Open Settings.
  • Go to Accessibility.
  • Go to VoiceOver.
  • Look for Braille.
  • Review connected displays, input options, tables, and commands.
  • This is where most braille configuration is usually managed.

For Apple Watch-specific options, also review:

  • Watch app.
  • My Watch.
  • Accessibility.
  • VoiceOver.
  • Any available braille-related settings, if they appear.
  • If no braille option appears for the watch, it may be because the current system does not provide that feature in the way you expected.

Braille tables and languages

Braille configuration may depend on language.

For example:

  • English contracted braille.
  • English uncontracted braille.
  • Spanish braille.
  • Other language tables.
  • Input and output tables may be configured separately.
  • This is important for users who work in more than one language.
  • If the user receives content in English and Spanish, braille table configuration must be reviewed carefully.
  • Incorrect braille table settings can make reading or writing confusing.

Pairing a braille display

Pairing a braille display is usually done from the iPhone.

General process:

  • Turn on the braille display.
  • Put it in pairing mode if required.
  • On the iPhone, open Settings.
  • Go to Accessibility.
  • Go to VoiceOver.
  • Go to Braille.
  • Search for the display.
  • Select it.
  • Enter a code if required.
  • Follow the instructions.
  • The exact steps depend on the braille display model.
  • It is advisable to consult the display’s own manual.
  • Once paired with the iPhone, the display can be used for iPhone VoiceOver tasks.

Whether and how it can interact with Apple Watch data will depend on the current Apple ecosystem behaviour and available features.

Using the iPhone as the braille centre

For most braille users, the iPhone will be the main braille centre. The Apple Watch can complement it.

A practical workflow could be:

  • Apple Watch receives a notification.
  • The user feels the vibration.
  • If it is important, they open the iPhone.
  • They read the notification with braille.
  • They reply from the iPhone if needed.
  • This is often more comfortable than trying to read or reply from the watch.
  • It also reduces the risk of errors.

Braille and notifications

If the user depends on braille, it is especially important not to overload the Apple Watch with notifications. The watch should vibrate only for important alerts. Then the user can check the content using the iPhone and braille display.

Recommended notifications might include:

  • Calls from important contacts.
  • Messages from important contacts.
  • Calendar.
  • Medication.
  • Alarms.
  • Timers.
  • Emergency-related alerts.
  • Selected reminders.
  • Too many alerts would make the system confusing.

Braille and messages

The Apple Watch can receive message notifications. But for a braille user, especially a deafblind user, reading and replying may be better on the iPhone. The watch can act as the alert. The iPhone can act as the reading and writing device. This is a practical division of work. The watch does what it does best: alert quickly. The iPhone does what it does better: manage text.

Braille and health alerts

Health alerts may also reach the Apple Watch. If the person cannot hear VoiceOver, the vibration may indicate that something needs attention. Then the user can check the Health app on the iPhone with braille.

This may apply to:

  • Medication.
  • Heart alerts.
  • Sleep alerts.
  • Activity.
  • Important reminders.
  • As always, alerts must be configured carefully.

Braille and privacy

Braille can improve privacy. Reading on a braille display is more private than having VoiceOver speak through the speaker.

This can be very useful for:

  • Messages.
  • Medication.
  • Health data.
  • Calendar.
  • Personal reminders.
  • Bank alerts.
  • If privacy is important, the Apple Watch can notify through vibration, and the iPhone with braille can provide private reading.

Braille and Siri

Siri can help with quick actions, but for deafblind users or people who cannot use speech comfortably, Siri may not be the best method. For blind users who hear well, Siri can reduce the need for typing. For deafblind users, braille and haptic workflows may be more appropriate. Again, configuration must follow the person’s real sensory access, not the feature list.

Braille and Apple Watch limitations

It is important to avoid promising more than the Apple Watch can comfortably provide.

Limitations may include:

  • Small screen.
  • Limited typing comfort.
  • Limited app complexity.
  • Dependence on iPhone for many settings.
  • Variable braille support.
  • Differences between watchOS versions.
  • Differences between languages.
  • Differences between braille display models.
  • For advanced braille users, experimentation may be worthwhile.
  • For beginners, it is better to master the basic Apple Watch functions first.

When to introduce braille in training

In a learning process, braille should be introduced after the user already understands:

  • What the Apple Watch is for.
  • How to wear it.
  • How to charge it.
  • How to use VoiceOver or haptic alerts.
  • How notifications work.
  • How to manage essential alerts.
  • How to use the iPhone to configure the watch.
  • Then, if braille is relevant, the workflow can be built around the iPhone and braille display.
  • This order avoids overwhelming the user.

Common mistakes

Trying to configure braille before the basic watch setup is understood.

Expecting the Apple Watch to replace the iPhone for braille use.

  • Not checking language tables.
  • Not checking display compatibility.
  • Allowing too many notifications.
  • Using the watch for long text when the iPhone is better.
  • Assuming all braille features available on iPhone are equally available on Apple Watch.
  • Not reviewing privacy and notification settings.
  • Not considering deafblind users’ actual access needs.

Practical advice

For most users, treat braille on Apple Watch as an advanced support option.

The most practical setup will often be:

  • Apple Watch for haptic alerts.
  • iPhone for reading and writing with braille.
  • Braille display for detailed access.
  • Watch app on iPhone for configuration.
  • Few important notifications.
  • Strong haptics.
  • This combination may offer more reliability than trying to manage everything from the watch alone.

Exercise for module 48

If you use braille:

  • On the iPhone, open Settings.
  • Go to Accessibility.
  • Go to VoiceOver.
  • Go to Braille.
  • Review whether your braille display is paired.
  • Check the input and output braille tables.
  • Then open the Watch app.
  • Go to My Watch.
  • Go to Accessibility.
  • Go to VoiceOver.
  • Review whether any braille-related options appear for Apple Watch.
  • Do not change advanced settings unless you know what they do.

Then create a practical workflow:

  • Receive a test notification on the Apple Watch.
  • Feel the vibration.
  • Open the iPhone.
  • Read the notification with the braille display.
  • Reply from the iPhone if needed.
  • This is often the most useful way to combine Apple Watch and braille.

Summary of module 48

Braille on Apple Watch should be considered an advanced option. Most braille configuration is usually managed from the iPhone. The Apple Watch is not ideal for long braille reading or writing. For many users, the best workflow is Apple Watch for haptic alerts and iPhone with braille display for detailed reading. This can be especially useful for deafblind users. Braille support may vary by model, watchOS version, language, and device compatibility. Do not assume that all iPhone braille features work in the same way on Apple Watch. Braille should be introduced after the basic Apple Watch workflow is understood.

Back to table of contents

Module 49. Maps and basic orientation

The Apple Watch can be used with Maps and other location features to receive route information, directions, and alerts on the wrist. For a blind person, this can be useful in some situations, especially as a complement to the iPhone. The watch can provide haptic alerts, spoken information with VoiceOver, and quick access to directions. But it is essential to be clear about its limits.

The Apple Watch does not replace orientation and mobility skills.

  • It does not replace a white cane.
  • It does not replace a guide dog.
  • It does not replace safe route knowledge.
  • It does not replace specialised accessible navigation apps where they are needed.
  • It can help, but it should be used as a support tool, not as the only source of orientation.

What Maps can do on the Apple Watch

The Maps app can help with:

  • Checking a location.
  • Starting a route.
  • Receiving directions.
  • Following a route started on the iPhone.
  • Receiving haptic alerts for turns, depending on configuration and route.
  • Checking estimated arrival time.
  • Finding nearby places.
  • Using Siri to ask for directions.

The usefulness of these features depends on location accuracy, connection, map data, country, route type, and user situation.

When Maps is useful on the watch

Maps on the Apple Watch can be useful when:

  • You already know the general route.
  • You want extra alerts on your wrist.
  • You are following a route started on the iPhone.
  • You need to check a turn.
  • You want to receive vibration prompts.
  • You want to ask Siri for a nearby place.
  • You are walking with another person and want to monitor the route.
  • You are travelling and want quick route information.

It may be less useful if:

  • The route is completely unknown.
  • The environment is complicated.
  • There is heavy traffic.
  • You need detailed orientation.
  • The map data are poor.
  • You cannot safely check the watch while moving.
  • The route involves complex crossings.
  • In those situations, the iPhone and specialised tools may be more appropriate.

Opening Maps on the Apple Watch

To open Maps:

  • Press the Digital Crown.
  • Find Maps.
  • Double tap.
  • Wait for the app to open.
  • With VoiceOver, move through the available options.
  • Depending on version and location, you may find suggestions, search, nearby places, or route information.

Starting a route from the iPhone

For a blind person, it is often more comfortable to start the route from the iPhone.

On the iPhone:

  • Open Maps.
  • Search for the destination.
  • Choose the correct result.
  • Select directions.
  • Choose walking, public transport, driving, or another mode if available.
  • Start the route.
  • Once the route is active, the Apple Watch may show directions and send alerts.
  • This workflow is usually more accessible than trying to search and configure everything on the small watch screen.

Starting a route from the Apple Watch

You can also start a route from the watch.

One way is using Siri:

  • Give me directions to home.
  • Take me to the nearest pharmacy.
  • Directions to the train station.
  • How do I get to Central Park?
  • The exact result depends on Siri, location, map data, and your contacts or saved places.
  • Before following a route, confirm that the destination is correct.
  • Siri can misunderstand names or choose an unexpected place.

Apparently the universe still believes that “nearby” means exactly what a database thinks it means, which is adorable and occasionally useless.

Using saved places

It can be helpful to have important places saved on the iPhone.

For example:

  • Home.
  • Work.
  • Doctor.
  • Pharmacy.
  • Gym.
  • Relative’s house.
  • Frequent station.
  • Usual bus stop.
  • If these places are saved clearly, Siri and Maps may find them more easily.
  • This is especially useful when using the Apple Watch.

Walking directions

Walking directions can provide turn-by-turn guidance. The Apple Watch may tap your wrist or display instructions when a turn is coming up. This can be useful, but it should not be treated as complete orientation.

A walking route may not always know:

  • Whether a crossing is safe.
  • Whether there are roadworks.
  • Whether pavements are blocked.
  • Whether there are temporary obstacles.
  • Whether a route is comfortable for a blind pedestrian.
  • Whether a crossing has audible signals.
  • Whether the path is accessible.

The map provides route information. It does not understand the full experience of moving as a blind person through the real world.

Haptic alerts during navigation

The Apple Watch may use different vibrations to indicate directions or alerts during navigation. This can help you notice that something is coming up without relying only on speech. However, the meaning of the vibrations may not be obvious at first. It is advisable to practise on known routes.

For example:

  • Start a route to a nearby place you already know.
  • Walk with the iPhone available.
  • Notice when the watch vibrates.
  • Listen to VoiceOver for the instruction.
  • Compare the alert with the real route.
  • This helps you learn how the watch behaves.
  • Do not try to learn haptic navigation for the first time in an unfamiliar and complicated area.

VoiceOver and Maps

With VoiceOver, Maps can read route instructions, buttons, estimated arrival times, and other information.

  • However, map interfaces can be complex.
  • On the Apple Watch, space is limited.
  • For detailed route selection, the iPhone is usually better.

On the watch, it is more practical to:

  1. Receive alerts.
  2. Check the next instruction.
  3. Follow a route already started.
  4. Use Siri for quick requests.

Pausing to check information

If you need to check a route instruction, stop in a safe place.

Do not manipulate the watch while:

  • Crossing a street.
  • Walking near traffic.
  • Going up or down stairs.
  • Moving through crowded spaces.
  • Handling a cane or guide dog in a complex area.
  • Navigating obstacles.
  • The watch can wait.
  • The street will not kindly rearrange itself because you are checking a notification.

Using Maps with a white cane

If you use a white cane, keep cane technique as the primary safety tool. The Apple Watch can support route information, but it does not detect obstacles directly.

Use the watch for:

  1. General direction.
  2. Turn alerts.
  3. Route progress.
  4. Estimated arrival.
  5. Location checks.

But rely on cane skills for:

  1. Obstacles.
  2. Kerbs.
  3. Steps.
  4. Surface changes.
  5. Immediate environment.
  6. Unexpected hazards.

Using Maps with a guide dog

If you use a guide dog, do not let the watch distract from the dog’s work. The Apple Watch may provide route information, but the dog manages obstacle avoidance and route behaviour according to training. If you need to check the watch, stop safely. Avoid giving confusing signals to the dog while you are distracted.

Using Maps with headphones

Headphones can help you hear VoiceOver and route instructions. But outdoors, they must be used carefully. For blind users, environmental sound is important.

If you use headphones:

  • Keep volume moderate.
  • Use transparency mode if available.
  • Avoid blocking traffic sounds.
  • Pause audio content at crossings.
  • Do not let music, podcasts, or directions cover important environmental cues.

Routes in unfamiliar places

In unfamiliar places, the Apple Watch should be used as one part of a broader strategy.

Before going:

  • Review the route on the iPhone.
  • Check the destination.
  • Check public transport if needed.
  • Consider asking for orientation information.
  • Share location if appropriate.
  • Check battery.
  • Carry the iPhone.
  • Know how to call someone if needed.
  • Use accessible navigation tools if you normally use them.
  • The Apple Watch can support, but it should not be the only tool.

Public transport

Maps may provide public transport routes in some countries and cities. Availability varies.

It may include:

  • Bus.
  • Train.
  • Metro.
  • Tram.
  • Walking to stops.
  • Estimated times.
  • Transfers.
  • This can be useful, but public transport accessibility varies greatly.

Maps may not always tell you:

  • Whether a station lift is working.
  • Whether a stop is accessible.
  • Whether the platform is easy to locate.
  • Whether audio announcements are clear.
  • Whether there are temporary changes.

For blind users, it may be necessary to combine Maps with transport apps, official operator information, and personal knowledge.

Weather and routes

Before walking outdoors, check weather. The Apple Watch can show weather information. Rain, wind, heat, cold, or storms can affect safety. For longer routes, this matters. A route that is comfortable in good weather may be much more difficult in heavy rain or heat.

Location accuracy

Location accuracy may vary.

It can be affected by:

  • Tall buildings.
  • Poor GPS signal.
  • Indoor spaces.
  • Underground stations.
  • Battery saving modes.
  • Connection problems.
  • Country or map data.
  • Apple Watch model.
  • If the watch seems to place you incorrectly, do not blindly follow it.
  • Stop, check with the iPhone, and use other references.

Maps and battery

Navigation can use more battery. If you are going to follow a long route, check battery before starting. If you also use Cellular, headphones, workouts, or audio, battery use may increase. For long outings, both iPhone and Apple Watch battery should be considered.

Using Siri for orientation questions

Siri can answer simple location questions.

Examples:

  • Where am I?
  • Take me home.
  • How far is the pharmacy?
  • Directions to the nearest bus stop.
  • How long to walk home?
  • Results depend on Maps, connection, location, and Siri’s understanding.
  • Always confirm the destination before following directions.

Home and work addresses

If you store home and work addresses in your contact card, Siri and Maps may work better.

For example:

  • Take me home.
  • Directions to work.
  • This can be useful.
  • Make sure the addresses are correct.
  • A wrong home address in Contacts can turn a helpful command into a scenic tour of nonsense.

Location sharing during routes

When walking or travelling, you may share your location with a trusted person.

This can be useful if:

  • You are going somewhere unfamiliar.
  • You are travelling alone.
  • You are walking at night.
  • You are exercising outside.
  • You want someone to know your route.
  • Use Find My or Messages, depending on your setup.
  • Share only with people you trust.

Maps and emergency

In an emergency, the Apple Watch may help through Emergency SOS and location features, depending on configuration. But for daily orientation, do not confuse emergency location with navigation. Emergency services may receive or request location in some situations, depending on country and network. This is separate from using Maps for walking.

Common mistakes

Starting a route on the watch without confirming the destination.

  • Checking the watch while crossing.
  • Using headphones too loudly.
  • Relying only on Maps in an unfamiliar place.
  • Not carrying the iPhone when needed.
  • Forgetting battery.
  • Not checking location permissions.
  • Not understanding haptic alerts.
  • Assuming all public transport data are complete.
  • Ignoring real-world obstacles because the route says “continue straight”.

Practical advice

For blind users, the best use of Maps on Apple Watch is usually as a companion to the iPhone.

  • Start routes on the iPhone.
  • Use the watch for alerts and quick checks.
  • Practise on familiar routes.
  • Do not depend only on the watch in unfamiliar areas.
  • Use mobility skills first.
  • Use technology as support.

Exercise for module 49

  • Choose a short and familiar route.
  • On the iPhone, open Maps.
  • Search for the destination.
  • Start walking directions.
  • Put on the Apple Watch.
  • Begin walking.
  • Pay attention to the watch haptic alerts.
  • Stop safely when you want to check an instruction.
  • Use VoiceOver to listen to the next direction.
  • Compare what the watch says with the real route.
  • At the end, stop navigation.

Then try asking Siri from the Apple Watch:

  • Take me home.
  • Cancel if you do not want to start the route.
  • The goal is to learn how Maps and the Apple Watch behave on a safe, known route.

Summary of module 49

Maps on Apple Watch can provide route information and alerts. For blind users, it is usually best used as a companion to the iPhone. The Apple Watch can give haptic prompts during navigation. Routes are not a substitute for orientation and mobility skills. The watch does not detect obstacles or guarantee accessible paths. The iPhone is better for searching and confirming destinations.

Headphones should be used with care outdoors.

  • Location accuracy can vary.
  • Practise first on familiar routes.
  • In unfamiliar places, combine Maps with other tools and safe planning.

Back to table of contents

Module 50. Music, podcasts, and audio

The Apple Watch can be used to control and play audio. It can help with music, podcasts, audiobooks, calls, workout audio, and playback from the iPhone or from the watch itself, depending on the app, model, connection, headphones, and available services.

For a blind person, audio is especially important. The Apple Watch is not only a screen on the wrist. It can also be a small control centre for listening, pausing, resuming, changing tracks, adjusting volume, and managing playback without taking the iPhone out of a pocket or bag.

But it is also important not to confuse everything.

  • Sometimes the audio is playing on the iPhone.
  • Sometimes it is playing on the Apple Watch.
  • Sometimes it goes to Bluetooth headphones.
  • Sometimes it goes to a speaker.
  • Sometimes VoiceOver speaks through one device and the music comes from another.

And then the user wonders where the sound has gone, which is understandable, because the audio ecosystem occasionally behaves like a room full of doors with no labels.

What the Apple Watch can do with audio

The Apple Watch can be used to:

  • Control audio playing on the iPhone.
  • Play music from compatible apps.
  • Play podcasts.
  • Control audiobooks in some apps.
  • Control playback during workouts.
  • Adjust volume.
  • Pause and resume.
  • Skip forward or backward.
  • Select audio output.
  • Use Bluetooth headphones.
  • Store or sync some audio content, depending on app and model.
  • Use Siri to start playback.
  • The exact options depend on the apps you use and the services available in your country.

Audio from the iPhone and audio from the Apple Watch

This distinction is important. Sometimes the Apple Watch is only controlling what is playing on the iPhone. For example, music may be playing from the iPhone, but the watch lets you pause, skip, or adjust volume. Other times, the Apple Watch itself may be the device playing the audio.

For example, if you have downloaded music or podcasts to the watch, or if you use a compatible streaming service from the watch, the sound may come from the watch to Bluetooth headphones. This matters because, if you leave the iPhone at home, audio that depends on the iPhone may not continue.

If you want to listen without the iPhone, you need compatible content available on the watch or a Cellular connection, depending on the app and service.

Using Bluetooth headphones

For listening to music, podcasts, or other audio from the Apple Watch, Bluetooth headphones are usually necessary. The Apple Watch speaker is not intended for playing music or podcasts in the same way as headphones.

To pair headphones:

  • Open Settings on the Apple Watch.
  • Look for Bluetooth.
  • Put the headphones in pairing mode.
  • Select them when they appear.
  • You can also manage some audio devices from the iPhone, depending on the model and Apple ecosystem.
  • If you use AirPods or compatible Apple headphones, pairing may be easier because they can sync through your Apple Account.

Selecting audio output

Sometimes you need to choose where the audio plays.

Possible outputs may include:

  • Apple Watch.
  • iPhone.
  • AirPods.
  • Bluetooth headphones.
  • Bluetooth speaker.
  • Other compatible devices.
  • From playback controls, there may be an AirPlay or audio output button.

With VoiceOver:

  • Find the audio output button.
  • Double tap.
  • Choose the device.
  • Double tap.
  • If you do not hear the audio where you expect, check audio output first.

Music app

The Music app on Apple Watch can control Apple Music or music synced to the watch, depending on subscription, configuration, and availability.

You may be able to:

  • Play music.
  • Pause.
  • Skip tracks.
  • Choose playlists.
  • Use downloaded music.
  • Control iPhone playback.
  • Listen through Bluetooth headphones.
  • If you use Apple Music, the experience may be more complete.
  • If you do not use Apple Music, options may be more limited.

Playing music with Siri

Siri can be useful for music.

Examples:

  • Play music.
  • Play my walking playlist.
  • Play relaxing music.
  • Pause.
  • Next track.
  • Turn the volume up.
  • Turn the volume down.
  • Siri’s behaviour depends on the music service, subscriptions, app compatibility, and country.
  • If it starts the wrong thing, cancel and try again with a clearer command.

Podcasts

The Apple Watch can also be used with podcasts. Depending on configuration, you may listen to episodes synced to the watch or control playback from the iPhone. This can be useful during walks, exercise, housework, or travel.

To use podcasts:

  • Open the Podcasts app on the watch, if available.
  • Choose an episode.
  • Use Bluetooth headphones.
  • Control playback with VoiceOver or Siri.
  • For many people, it is easier to choose the episode on the iPhone and then control playback from the watch.

Audiobooks

Audiobooks may also be accessible from the Apple Watch depending on the app and service. Apple Books may allow some audiobook playback or control, depending on configuration and region. Other audiobook apps may or may not have Apple Watch support. For long audiobooks, the iPhone is usually more comfortable for selection and management.

The watch is useful for quick controls:

  1. Pause.
  2. Resume.
  3. Skip.
  4. Volume.
  5. Checking current playback.

Now Playing

The Apple Watch often includes a Now Playing screen or app. This allows you to control the audio currently playing. It may appear automatically when audio is playing on the iPhone or watch.

With Now Playing, you can usually:

  • Pause.
  • Play.
  • Skip forward.
  • Go back.
  • Adjust volume.
  • Select output.
  • Open related controls.
  • For a blind person, Now Playing can be very useful.
  • If audio starts on the iPhone, the watch can become a remote control on the wrist.

Opening Now Playing

To open Now Playing:

  • Press the Digital Crown.
  • Find Now Playing.
  • Double tap.
  • Or, if it appears automatically, use the screen that opens when audio is playing.

With VoiceOver:

  1. Swipe through the controls.
  2. Find Play or Pause.
  3. Find Next Track.
  4. Find Previous Track or Back.
  5. Find volume.
  6. Find audio output if needed.

Adjusting volume

Volume can often be adjusted with the Digital Crown while in the playback screen.

To do this:

  • Open Now Playing or the audio app.
  • Focus on the playback screen.
  • Turn the Digital Crown slowly.
  • Listen to whether the volume changes.
  • Volume may control the current audio output, such as headphones.
  • If volume does not change as expected, check whether you are controlling the right device.

Play and pause

Play and pause are the most common controls.

With VoiceOver:

  • Find Play or Pause.
  • Double tap.
  • If audio is playing, the button may say Pause.
  • If audio is stopped, it may say Play.
  • This is useful when someone speaks to you, when you reach a crossing, or when you need to hear the environment.

Skipping forward and backward

Audio apps may allow you to skip. For music, this may mean next or previous track. For podcasts and audiobooks, it may mean jumping forward or backward by a number of seconds.

With VoiceOver:

  • Find the relevant button.
  • Listen to the label.
  • Double tap.
  • Be careful with long skips in audiobooks or podcasts.

A careless tap can throw you into another part of the episode, because apparently time travel is now located next to the pause button.

Audio during workouts

Music and podcasts can be used during workouts. This can make walking, cycling, gym sessions, or home exercise more pleasant. But for blind users, especially outdoors, safety matters. Do not use audio at a volume that prevents you from hearing traffic, people, crossings, or environmental cues.

If you use headphones outdoors, consider:

  • Lower volume.
  • Transparency mode.
  • One ear free, if appropriate.
  • Bone conduction headphones, if useful.
  • Pausing audio in complex areas.
  • During workouts, the Apple Watch can control audio without taking out the iPhone.
  • This is very practical, but it should not distract from safe movement.

Downloading music or podcasts to the Apple Watch

Depending on your apps and subscriptions, you may be able to download music or podcasts to the Apple Watch. This allows listening without the iPhone nearby. To manage this, the iPhone is usually more comfortable. From the Watch app or the corresponding music or podcast app, you may find options to sync playlists or episodes to the watch.

The process may require:

  • Apple Watch on charger.
  • iPhone nearby.
  • Wi-Fi.
  • Time to sync.
  • Enough storage on the watch.
  • Not all services allow the same thing.

Apple Watch storage

The Apple Watch has limited storage. If you download too much music, podcasts, or apps, storage may fill up.

To review storage:

  • Open the Watch app on the iPhone.
  • Go to My Watch.
  • Go to General.
  • Look for Storage.
  • There you can check what is taking space.
  • If storage is low, remove content you do not need.

Audio and battery

Audio playback consumes battery.

Battery use increases if:

  • You play from the watch.
  • You use Bluetooth headphones.
  • You stream with Cellular.
  • You also record a workout.
  • You use GPS.
  • You use the screen often.
  • If you go for a long walk with music, Workout, GPS, and Cellular, battery will drop faster.
  • Before depending on the watch for audio and safety features, check battery.

Using audio without the iPhone

If you want to go out without the iPhone and listen from the Apple Watch:

  • You need Bluetooth headphones.
  • You need downloaded content or streaming from the watch.
  • If streaming, you need a Cellular model with active plan or Wi-Fi.
  • You need enough battery.
  • You need the app to support Apple Watch playback.
  • This setup should be tested before relying on it outside.
  • Do not discover in the street that your playlist lives entirely on the iPhone sitting proudly at home.

VoiceOver and audio volume

VoiceOver and media audio may interact. Sometimes VoiceOver may lower media volume temporarily. Sometimes headphones may carry both VoiceOver and music. This can be useful, but if music is too loud, VoiceOver may be harder to understand.

Adjust volume so that:

  • VoiceOver is clear.
  • Environmental sound remains available if needed.
  • Audio content is comfortable.

Privacy

Audio from headphones is private. Audio from the watch speaker is not. VoiceOver may read song titles, podcast names, messages, or controls aloud. If privacy matters, use headphones. Also remember that dictating Siri commands in public is not private. Music and podcasts may be harmless, but messages, reminders, or health notifications are more sensitive.

Using Siri for playback control

Siri can control playback.

Examples:

  • Pause.
  • Play.
  • Next song.
  • Go back.
  • Turn up the volume.
  • Turn down the volume.
  • Play my podcast.
  • Open Music.
  • Open Podcasts.
  • This can be easier than finding controls on the watch screen, especially during exercise.
  • But again, confirm that Siri did what you wanted.

Common problems

  • No sound is heard.
  • Sound comes from the wrong device.
  • Headphones are not connected.
  • The audio is playing on the iPhone, not the watch.
  • The watch has no downloaded content.
  • The app does not support Apple Watch playback.
  • The watch has no connection.
  • Volume is too low.
  • VoiceOver is hard to hear over music.
  • Battery is low.
  • Storage is full.

What to check if no sound is heard

Check:

  • Headphones are connected.
  • Audio output is correct.
  • Volume is high enough.
  • The content is actually playing.
  • The app supports playback on the watch.
  • The watch has connection if streaming.
  • The content is downloaded if offline.
  • The iPhone is nearby if the watch is only controlling iPhone playback.

What to check if VoiceOver is hard to hear

Check:

  • Media volume.
  • VoiceOver volume.
  • Headphones.
  • Environmental noise.
  • Whether audio ducking is affecting playback.
  • Whether the output device is correct.
  • If necessary, pause media audio before using VoiceOver for important tasks.

Audio and navigation

If you are using Maps, VoiceOver, or route instructions, be careful with music and podcasts.

  • Route information should be heard clearly.
  • If you are outdoors, environmental sound also matters.
  • Audio should support the outing, not hide important cues.

Common mistakes

Thinking the watch can play all iPhone audio independently.

Leaving the iPhone at home without downloaded content.

  • Not connecting headphones.
  • Not checking audio output.
  • Using music too loud outdoors.
  • Not checking battery before long listening sessions.
  • Filling the watch storage.
  • Confusing Now Playing with the actual audio app.
  • Using Siri without confirming the result.

Practical advice

At the beginning, use the Apple Watch mainly as a remote control for iPhone audio.

Learn:

  • Pause.
  • Resume.
  • Volume.
  • Next.
  • Previous.
  • Audio output.
  • Then, if you want to listen without the iPhone, configure downloaded content and test it at home.

Exercise for module 50

Start playing music or a podcast on the iPhone.

  • Put on the Apple Watch.
  • Open Now Playing on the Apple Watch.
  • With VoiceOver, find Pause.
  • Double tap.
  • Find Play.
  • Double tap.
  • Find Next or Skip Forward.
  • Double tap if appropriate.
  • Find the volume control.
  • Turn the Digital Crown slowly.
  • Check whether the volume changes.
  • Then connect Bluetooth headphones.
  • Check audio output.
  • If you use podcasts, try starting an episode from the iPhone and controlling it from the watch.
  • If you want to listen without the iPhone, download one episode or playlist to the watch and test it at home first.

Summary of module 50

The Apple Watch can control music, podcasts, audiobooks, and other audio. Sometimes it controls audio from the iPhone. Sometimes the watch itself plays the audio. Bluetooth headphones are usually needed for listening from the watch. Now Playing is useful for controlling current playback. The Digital Crown can often adjust volume. Siri can help control audio. For blind users outdoors, audio volume must not block environmental cues. Downloading content to the watch allows more independence, but it depends on app support, storage, battery, and connection. The Apple Watch is useful as an audio remote control and as a playback device in some situations.

Back to table of contents

Module 51. iPhone camera control from the Apple Watch

The Apple Watch can be used as a remote control for the iPhone camera. This feature can be useful in several situations: taking a photo without holding the iPhone, placing the iPhone somewhere and triggering the shot from the wrist, checking the frame, using the timer, or taking group photos.

For a blind person, this feature can be useful, but with some limitations. The Apple Watch can help activate the camera remotely, but framing and visual composition may still require support, practice, or the use of other accessibility tools.

The Apple Watch does not magically solve photography. It opens the camera, shows what the iPhone sees, and lets you take the photo. It does not tell you whether everyone is smiling, whether someone has been cut out of the frame, or whether the table lamp is now the main character of the picture. Humanity still has work to do there.

What the Camera Remote app is

The Apple Watch includes an app that works as a remote control for the iPhone camera. This app is usually called Camera Remote or Camera, depending on version and language. When you open it on the Apple Watch, it connects to the iPhone camera. The iPhone becomes the camera. The Apple Watch becomes the remote control.

From the watch, you can usually:

  • Open the iPhone camera.
  • Preview what the iPhone sees, if visually accessible.
  • Take a photo.
  • Use a timer.
  • Switch between front and rear camera, depending on options.
  • Control flash or other camera settings, depending on version.
  • Review some basic controls.

Opening Camera Remote

To open it:

  • Place the iPhone where you want to take the photo.
  • Put on the Apple Watch.
  • Press the Digital Crown.
  • Find Camera Remote or Camera.
  • Double tap.
  • Wait for the Apple Watch to connect to the iPhone camera.
  • The iPhone camera may open automatically.
  • Keep the iPhone near enough for the connection to work.

If the iPhone is locked, the system may still open the camera, depending on configuration. If it does not, unlock the iPhone first and try again.

Taking a photo

Once Camera Remote is open:

  • Move through the controls with VoiceOver.
  • Find the shutter button.
  • Double tap.
  • The iPhone will take the photo.
  • If the timer is active, there may be a short countdown before the photo is taken.
  • The exact controls may vary depending on watchOS and iOS version.

Using the timer

The timer is useful because it gives you a few seconds before the photo is taken.

This is especially helpful if you need to:

  • Put your hand down.
  • Move into position.
  • Hold something.
  • Join a group photo.
  • Avoid movement at the moment of pressing.

To use it:

  • Open Camera Remote.
  • Look for the timer option.
  • Turn it on if needed.
  • Then activate the shutter.
  • The iPhone will take the photo after the countdown.
  • For many users, the timer is more practical than taking the photo immediately.

Framing the photo

For sighted users, the Apple Watch screen can show a preview of what the iPhone camera sees. For a blind person, this preview is not directly useful unless there is remaining vision.

However, the feature may still be useful if:

  • The iPhone is placed in a known position.
  • A sighted person helps with framing.
  • The user already knows the environment.
  • The photo does not require precise composition.
  • The user uses other tools to identify objects or people.
  • The person only needs to trigger the shot remotely.

For example, if the iPhone is placed on a stand facing a table, the Apple Watch can trigger the photo without touching the iPhone.

Using the front camera

If the iPhone is using the front camera, it may be easier to take a selfie or record yourself. From the Apple Watch, there may be a control to switch between front and rear camera.

With VoiceOver:

  • Look for options or more controls.
  • Find the camera switch option if available.
  • Double tap.
  • Listen to the confirmation if the system announces it.
  • The label may vary.

If you cannot find the option, it may be easier to set the camera from the iPhone first and then use the Apple Watch as the remote.

Using the rear camera

The rear camera usually offers better quality.

It may be useful for:

  1. Documents.
  2. Objects.
  3. Rooms.
  4. Group photos.
  5. Landscapes.
  6. Products.
  7. Scenes.

For blind users, rear camera use may require more assistance or practice, because framing is harder without visual feedback.

Using a stand or support

This feature becomes much more useful if the iPhone can be placed steadily.

For example:

  • On a tripod.
  • On a phone stand.
  • Against a stable object.
  • On a table.
  • On a shelf.
  • The iPhone should not be placed where it can fall.
  • A remote shutter is very elegant until the iPhone slides off a table with the confidence of an expensive brick.

Using Camera Remote for documents

In theory, you could use the Apple Watch to trigger a photo of a document. In practice, for blind users, this is usually better done with dedicated scanning or OCR apps on the iPhone. The Apple Watch remote can help if the iPhone is fixed in a stable position above a document. But for reading documents, apps designed for scanning, OCR, or accessibility will usually be much better.

Using Camera Remote for video

Depending on version and camera mode, the Apple Watch may offer some control over video recording. If video mode is available, you may be able to start and stop recording. For blind users, this can be useful when recording yourself, recording a demonstration, or creating content. However, framing, audio, lighting, and focus still need attention. If recording video for publication, it is advisable to test first.

VoiceOver and Camera Remote

With VoiceOver on the Apple Watch, you can move through available controls.

Typical controls may include:

  • Shutter.
  • Timer.
  • Options.
  • Camera switch.
  • Flash.
  • Live Photo.
  • Other camera settings.
  • Not all controls appear in all versions.
  • If VoiceOver reads a control that you do not understand, do not activate it immediately.
  • Explore first.
  • Use the iPhone if the watch interface becomes confusing.

Using the iPhone for setup and the watch for shooting

A practical workflow is:

  • Set camera mode on the iPhone.
  • Place the iPhone.
  • Check orientation if needed.
  • Open Camera Remote on the Apple Watch.
  • Use the timer.
  • Activate the shutter from the watch.
  • This way, the watch is used only for the remote action, and the more complex camera setup is done on the iPhone.
  • This is usually easier.

Accessibility limitations

The Camera Remote app may not give enough non-visual information about the scene.

  • It may not describe the frame.
  • It may not identify faces reliably through the watch.
  • It may not tell whether the subject is centred.
  • It may not warn about lighting problems in a way that is useful for blind users.

Therefore, it should be considered a remote control, not a full accessible photography solution. For object recognition, text recognition, scene description, or document reading, other iPhone apps may be more suitable.

Possible uses for blind users

Even with limitations, Camera Remote can be useful for:

  • Starting a selfie from the wrist.
  • Taking a group photo after someone frames the iPhone.
  • Recording a video after placing the iPhone.
  • Taking photos from a fixed position.
  • Avoiding camera shake.
  • Controlling the camera when the iPhone is on a stand.
  • Capturing an image without touching the iPhone.

Practical example: recording a demonstration

If you create tutorials or demonstrations, you may place the iPhone in a fixed position and use the Apple Watch to start recording or take photos.

Before recording:

  • Check the iPhone is stable.
  • Check battery.
  • Check storage.
  • Check camera mode.
  • Check microphone if video is involved.
  • Check that VoiceOver speech will not be recorded unintentionally if that matters.
  • Then use the Apple Watch to start or stop.
  • This can be useful, but it requires testing.

Photos and privacy

Be careful when taking photos or videos.

  • Do not record other people without consent where consent is required.
  • Do not capture private documents unintentionally.
  • Do not photograph payment cards, medical documents, addresses, or personal data without intending to.

The Apple Watch makes it easy to trigger the camera, but the responsibility remains with the user.

Common problems

  • Camera Remote does not connect.
  • The iPhone is too far away.
  • The iPhone is locked or not responding.
  • Bluetooth or Wi-Fi connection is unstable.
  • The wrong camera is active.
  • The photo is not framed properly.
  • The timer is off when it would be useful.
  • VoiceOver reads controls but the user does not know which one to use.
  • The iPhone falls or moves.

What to check if it does not work

Check:

  • The Apple Watch is paired with the iPhone.
  • The iPhone is nearby.
  • The iPhone has battery.
  • The Apple Watch has battery.
  • The iPhone camera can open normally.
  • Bluetooth and Wi-Fi are working.
  • The Camera Remote app is open on the Apple Watch.
  • The iPhone is not blocked by another camera app issue.

Common mistakes

Thinking the Apple Watch takes the photo by itself.

Forgetting that the iPhone is the actual camera.

  • Placing the iPhone unstably.
  • Not using the timer.
  • Expecting the watch to describe the scene.
  • Trying to scan documents with this when a scanning app would be better.
  • Not checking which camera is active.
  • Touching the iPhone after framing and moving it accidentally.
  • Not testing before recording something important.

Practical advice

Use Camera Remote mainly as a remote shutter.

  • For anything that requires careful framing, use help, a stand, or an accessibility app.
  • For documents, use scanning or OCR tools.
  • For videos, test the setup before recording real content.

The feature is useful, but it is not a complete non-visual camera assistant.

Exercise for module 51

Place the iPhone on a stable surface.

Point it toward a simple object or area.

  • Put on the Apple Watch.
  • Open Camera Remote.
  • Wait for it to connect.
  • Move through the controls with VoiceOver.
  • Find the shutter button.
  • Turn on the timer if available.
  • Take a test photo.
  • Then check the photo on the iPhone.
  • If possible, ask a sighted person to describe the framing.
  • Try again after adjusting the iPhone position.
  • Repeat until you understand how the watch triggers the iPhone camera.

Summary of module 51

  • The Apple Watch can control the iPhone camera remotely.
  • The iPhone takes the photo; the watch acts as the remote.
  • The Camera Remote app can trigger photos and may offer timer and camera controls.

For blind users, framing remains the main limitation. The feature is useful when the iPhone is placed on a stable support. The timer can help avoid movement. For documents or text, dedicated scanning or OCR apps are usually better. For video, test framing, audio, and stability before recording important content.

Back to table of contents

Module 52. Weather, climate, and weather alerts

The Apple Watch can show weather information directly on the wrist. This can be useful before leaving home, during walks, before exercising, when travelling, or when planning daily activities.

For a blind person, weather information can be practical because it helps decide what to wear, whether to take an umbrella, whether it is safe to go out, whether there will be wind, heat, cold, rain, or other conditions.

Weather also matters for mobility. A rainy pavement, strong wind, heat, low visibility for companions, or a storm can change the difficulty of a route.

The Apple Watch can provide quick weather information, but it should not be treated as infallible. Forecasts are forecasts, not signed contracts with the sky. The sky, regrettably, has not learned to follow app schedules.

What the Weather app can show

The Weather app on the Apple Watch may show information such as:

  • Current temperature.
  • Weather condition.
  • Chance of rain.
  • Hourly forecast.
  • Daily forecast.
  • High and low temperatures.
  • Wind.
  • UV index.
  • Humidity.
  • Air quality, where available.
  • Rain alerts, where available.
  • Severe weather alerts, where available.
  • The exact data depend on country, region, weather provider, location permissions, and watchOS version.

Opening Weather on the Apple Watch

To open Weather:

  • Press the Digital Crown.
  • Find Weather.
  • Double tap.
  • Wait for the app to open.
  • Use VoiceOver to move through the information.
  • Swipe right or left to hear each item.
  • Turn the Digital Crown if there is more information.

Weather as a complication

Weather can also be placed as a complication on the watch face.

This allows quick access to information such as:

  • Current temperature.
  • Weather condition.
  • Chance of rain.
  • UV index.
  • Air quality.
  • Other available data.
  • For many users, a weather complication is useful.
  • If you often go out walking, exercise outdoors, or depend on weather information, it may be worth adding it to the watch face.
  • However, avoid putting too many complications on the watch face.

Weather with Siri

Siri can answer weather questions from the Apple Watch.

Examples:

  • What’s the weather like?
  • Will it rain today?
  • What’s the temperature?
  • What’s the weather tomorrow?
  • Is it windy?
  • What’s the forecast for this afternoon?
  • What’s the weather in London?
  • This is often faster than opening the app.
  • If you need a quick answer, Siri is practical.
  • If you need to review the full forecast, open the Weather app.

Weather for your current location

To show local weather, the Apple Watch needs location access or a configured location. If location is enabled, it can show weather for where you are. If location is disabled, it may show saved locations or may not update properly.

To review location permissions:

  • On the iPhone, open Settings.
  • Go to Privacy and Security.
  • Go to Location Services.
  • Review Weather permissions.
  • The exact path may vary.

Weather for other cities

The Weather app can also show saved cities.

This is useful if you want to check weather in:

  • A travel destination.
  • A family member’s city.
  • A work location.
  • Another country.
  • A place you visit often.
  • Cities are usually managed more comfortably from the iPhone.
  • Once configured, they may appear on the Apple Watch.

Hourly forecast

The hourly forecast can help you plan the next few hours. It may show whether rain, wind, heat, or temperature changes are expected.

This is useful before:

  • Going for a walk.
  • Exercising outdoors.
  • Travelling.
  • Going to an appointment.
  • Hanging clothes outside, if one insists on participating in the ancient battle between laundry and weather.
  • With VoiceOver, move through the hourly forecast slowly.

Daily forecast

The daily forecast gives a broader view. It can show expected conditions for several days.

This is useful for planning:

  • Exercise.
  • Travel.
  • Medical appointments.
  • Outdoor tasks.
  • Clothing.
  • Routes.
  • But the further ahead the forecast goes, the less precise it may be.

Rain alerts

In some regions, the Weather app or Apple services may send rain alerts. These may notify you if rain is expected soon. This can be very useful for blind users who are about to leave or who are already outside. However, availability varies by country and data source. If you do not receive these alerts, it may be because they are not available in your area or are not configured.

Severe weather alerts

In some countries and regions, the Apple Watch may show severe weather alerts.

These may include warnings for:

  • Storms.
  • Heavy rain.
  • Extreme heat.
  • Strong wind.
  • Snow.
  • Flooding.
  • Other hazards.
  • Availability depends on the country, local weather services, and Apple’s integration.
  • These alerts can be important.
  • If one appears, read it carefully.

Weather and outdoor exercise

Before outdoor exercise, check:

  • Temperature.
  • Rain.
  • Wind.
  • Storm risk.
  • Heat.
  • Cold.
  • UV index, if relevant.
  • Air quality, if available.
  • For blind users, weather can affect orientation and safety.
  • Rain can make surfaces slippery.
  • Wind can make hearing harder.
  • Heavy traffic noise plus rain can reduce sound cues.
  • Heat can cause fatigue or dehydration.
  • Cold can affect hands, mobility, and comfort.
  • The Apple Watch can help you check conditions before starting.

Weather and battery

Weather updates use connection and location. This usually is not a major battery problem, but constant location use and frequent updates can contribute to battery consumption. If battery is low, weather may not update as quickly or some background features may be limited.

Weather and Focus modes

Weather alerts may be affected by notification settings and Focus modes. If you expect important alerts, check that they are allowed. For example, if you are using Do Not Disturb or Sleep Focus, some alerts may be silenced. If severe alerts are important to you, review notification settings.

Weather and accessibility

With VoiceOver, weather information can be read from:

  • Weather app.
  • Weather complication.
  • Siri.
  • Notifications.
  • iPhone Weather app.
  • The iPhone may be more comfortable for detailed forecasts.
  • The Apple Watch is better for quick checks.

Weather and travel

When travelling, weather information can help plan clothing, routes, and safety. Add the destination city before travelling. Check the forecast in advance.

If travelling internationally, remember that units may vary:

  • Celsius or Fahrenheit.
  • Kilometres per hour or miles per hour.
  • Local weather terms.
  • Units can be configured in system settings or Weather settings, depending on version.

Weather units

Some users prefer Celsius. Others use Fahrenheit. Wind may be shown in kilometres per hour, miles per hour, or other units. Make sure the units are understandable for the intended audience. In an international course, it is better not to assume that everyone uses the same units. When explaining, you can mention temperature generally and let each device show local units according to region.

Air quality

In some places, the Weather app may show air quality. This can be useful for people with respiratory conditions, allergies, asthma, or sensitivity to pollution. If air quality is poor, it may be advisable to avoid intense outdoor exercise or consult local recommendations. This data is not available everywhere.

UV index

The UV index may be relevant when spending time outdoors. It can help decide whether sun protection is needed. For blind users, sun exposure still matters, even if visual glare is not the main concern. Skin protection, heat, and hydration are practical issues.

Wind

Wind can matter for blind people because it affects hearing and orientation. Strong wind can make it harder to hear traffic, people, or environmental references. It can also affect walking comfort. Before a long walk, checking wind can be useful.

Rain

Rain affects:

  • Pavement.
  • Traffic noise.
  • Cane feedback.
  • Footwear.
  • Orientation.
  • Public transport.
  • Comfort.
  • If rain is expected, it may be useful to plan extra time, take suitable clothing, or adjust the route.

Heat

Heat can affect:

  • Fatigue.
  • Hydration.
  • Heart rate.
  • Exercise tolerance.
  • Medication sensitivity.
  • Walking comfort.
  • For older people or people with health conditions, heat can be especially important.
  • If extreme heat is expected, avoid unnecessary exertion and follow local health guidance.

Cold

Cold can affect:

  • Hands.
  • Touch sensitivity.
  • Battery.
  • Mobility.
  • Pain.
  • Comfort.
  • If you need to use VoiceOver gestures on the watch outdoors, cold fingers can make it harder.
  • Gloves may also affect touch interaction unless they are compatible.

Weather and Apple Watch Ultra

Some Apple Watch Ultra models include additional outdoor-oriented features, depending on version. These may be useful for hiking, outdoor exercise, and demanding activities. But the basic Weather app remains useful for all models that support it.

Common problems

  • Weather does not update.
  • Location is wrong.
  • The wrong city appears.
  • Forecast is missing.
  • Alerts do not arrive.
  • Siri gives weather for the wrong place.
  • Units are not familiar.
  • The complication is not showing the desired data.

What to check if weather is wrong

Check:

  • Location permissions.
  • Internet connection.
  • Saved cities.
  • Weather app on the iPhone.
  • Whether the Apple Watch is connected.
  • Whether location services are enabled.
  • Whether the correct unit settings are used.
  • Whether you are using the intended weather complication.

Common mistakes

  • Not checking weather before outdoor exercise.
  • Assuming forecasts are always exact.
  • Not reviewing location permissions.
  • Forgetting weather alerts may vary by country.
  • Using a complication that shows temperature but not rain probability when rain is what matters.
  • Ignoring wind for orientation.
  • Using headphones too loudly in rain or wind.
  • Not adapting plans to severe weather alerts.

Practical advice

For blind users, a weather complication can be very useful.

A practical watch face might include:

  • Time.
  • Battery.
  • Weather.
  • Activity or Workout.
  • Timer.
  • Before going out, ask Siri for the weather or open the Weather app.
  • For long walks or exercise, check rain, wind, and temperature, not only the current condition.

Exercise for module 52

  • Open Weather on the Apple Watch.
  • Use VoiceOver to read the current temperature.
  • Find the condition.
  • Look for hourly forecast.
  • Look for chance of rain.
  • Look for daily forecast.

Ask Siri:

  • Will it rain today?
  • Then open the Watch app on the iPhone.
  • Review the watch face complications.
  • Add Weather if it is useful to you.
  • Check whether weather alerts are enabled in the iPhone Weather app, if available in your region.

Summary of module 52

The Apple Watch can show weather information on the wrist. Weather can be checked from the Weather app, a complication, Siri, or notifications. The iPhone is better for detailed forecasts. Weather matters for blind users because it affects mobility, orientation, exercise, and safety. Rain, wind, heat, cold, and severe alerts should be considered before going out. Weather alerts vary by country and availability. Location permissions must be enabled for local weather. Forecasts are useful but not perfect.
