Module 53. Smart home and accessory control

The Apple Watch can control some smart home devices and accessories if they are configured in Apple’s Home app or compatible apps. This can be useful for blind users because it allows quick control from the wrist: turning lights on or off, controlling plugs, checking compatible devices, opening scenes, adjusting thermostats, or activating automations. For some people, this is convenience. For others, it can be accessibility.

A smart home can help reduce dependence on inaccessible physical controls, touch panels, small buttons, or devices that provide no spoken feedback.

Of course, a smart home can also become a spectacular collection of devices that need updates, lose connection, and refuse to obey at the exact moment you are carrying groceries. Technology remains committed to humility training.

What smart home control means

Smart home control means using the Apple Watch to operate devices such as:

  • Lights.
  • Smart plugs.
  • Thermostats.
  • Blinds or shades.
  • Fans.
  • Air conditioners, if compatible.
  • Doorbells.
  • Cameras, where available.
  • Locks, if compatible and safely configured.
  • Sensors.
  • Scenes.
  • Automations.

The exact options depend on the devices installed and whether they are compatible with Apple Home, Matter, or other systems that support Apple Watch control.

Apple Home app

Apple’s Home app is the central place for HomeKit and compatible smart home devices. Devices are usually configured first from the iPhone. Once configured, some of them can be controlled from the Apple Watch. The Apple Watch may have a Home app that lets you access rooms, accessories, and scenes.

Opening Home on the Apple Watch

To open Home:

  • Press the Digital Crown.
  • Find Home.
  • Double tap.
  • Wait for the app to open.
  • Move through accessories and scenes with VoiceOver.
  • If you have many devices, navigation may be long.
  • That is why good organisation from the iPhone is important.

Using Siri for smart home control

Siri is often the easiest way to control smart home devices from the Apple Watch.

Examples:

  • Turn on the living room light.
  • Turn off the bedroom light.
  • Turn on the fan.
  • Set the thermostat to twenty-two degrees.
  • Open the blinds.
  • Close the blinds.
  • Turn off all lights.
  • Run the good night scene.
  • Turn on the kitchen plug.
  • The command must match the names configured in the Home app.
  • If devices have confusing names, Siri will also be confused. Fair enough, really.

Naming devices clearly

Device names matter a lot. A blind user should be able to say a device name naturally.

Good names:

  1. Living room light.
  2. Kitchen light.
  3. Bedroom lamp.
  4. Desk plug.
  5. Hallway light.
  6. Fan.
  7. Thermostat.
  8. Bedroom blind.

Less useful names:

  • Light one.
  • Device two.
  • Plug final version.
  • Lamp test.
  • IKEA outlet 3.
  • The names may seem harmless when setting up, but later Siri has to understand them.
  • Clear names make the whole system easier.

Rooms

The Home app allows devices to be organised by rooms.

For example:

  1. Living room.
  2. Kitchen.
  3. Bedroom.
  4. Bathroom.
  5. Hallway.
  6. Office.
  7. This helps with Siri commands.

Examples:

  • Turn off the lights in the bedroom.
  • Turn on the kitchen light.
  • Turn off everything in the living room.
  • For blind users, clear room organisation reduces confusion.

Scenes

Scenes are groups of actions.

For example:

  • Good morning.
  • Good night.
  • Leaving home.
  • Arriving home.
  • Reading.
  • Exercise.
  • Relax.
  • A scene can turn several devices on or off at once.

Example:

  • Good night could turn off lights, lower blinds, reduce thermostat, and turn off a plug.
  • On the Apple Watch, scenes can be activated from the Home app or with Siri.
  • Scenes can be especially useful because they reduce the number of steps.

Smart plugs

Smart plugs can be useful for controlling appliances or lamps. But they must be used safely. Do not connect devices that should not be controlled this way. Avoid using smart plugs with appliances that can be dangerous if turned on remotely or accidentally. For example, be very careful with heaters, irons, cooking appliances, or anything that generates heat. Convenience is not worth setting up a domestic disaster with Wi-Fi.

Lights

Lights are one of the most common smart home devices.

For blind users, lights may still be useful:

  • For people with remaining vision.
  • For visitors.
  • For family members.
  • For safety.
  • For video calls or recording.
  • For signalling presence.
  • For people with combined visual and hearing needs.
  • Voice and watch control can be easier than inaccessible switches.

Thermostats and climate

Compatible thermostats can be controlled from the Apple Watch or Siri. This can be useful for adjusting temperature without finding a wall panel.

Examples:

  • Set the thermostat to twenty-one degrees.
  • Increase the temperature.
  • Turn off heating.
  • Set cooling to twenty-four degrees.
  • Availability depends on device compatibility.

Blinds and shades

Smart blinds or shades can also be controlled if compatible. For a blind user, this can be useful because physical blind controls may be hard to locate or operate.

Examples:

  • Open the bedroom blinds.
  • Close all blinds.
  • Open the living room shade halfway.
  • Safety and correct naming are important.

Locks and doors

Some smart locks can be controlled from Apple devices. This area requires special caution. A lock is not like a lamp.

Before using the Apple Watch for locks, consider:

  • Security.
  • Who has access.
  • Accidental activation.
  • Voice commands.
  • Notifications.
  • Battery.
  • Manual backup method.
  • Reliability.
  • Do not configure locks casually.
  • Make sure you understand exactly how they work.

Cameras and doorbells

Some smart cameras and doorbells may send notifications to the Apple Watch. The watch may alert you when someone rings the doorbell or when motion is detected. For a blind user, the notification may be useful, but reviewing video content may not be very accessible. The iPhone may be better for audio, two-way communication, or other controls, depending on the device.

Smart home notifications

The Apple Watch can receive smart home notifications.

Examples:

  • Doorbell rang.
  • Motion detected.
  • Door opened.
  • Sensor triggered.
  • Smoke or alarm alert, depending on compatible system.
  • These alerts can be important.
  • But if there are too many motion alerts or low-value notifications, they become noise.
  • Configure only the important alerts.

Home hubs

For some Home features to work remotely, Apple may require a home hub, such as Apple TV, HomePod, or another compatible device, depending on the setup. This matters if you want to control devices when you are away from home. Local control and remote control may not behave the same. If a device works at home but not away from home, check home hub configuration, internet connection, and device compatibility.

Matter and compatibility

Matter is a smart home standard supported by many newer devices. Some Matter devices can work with Apple Home, depending on setup. However, compatibility should be checked before buying.

Do not assume every smart device works well with Apple Watch or Apple Home.

  • The label on the box matters.
  • So does user experience.
  • So does accessibility.
  • Because apparently “smart” on a box still does not always mean “usable by humans.”

Using Home complications

Some watch faces may allow Home or specific shortcuts as complications. This can make frequent actions faster.

For example:

  • Open Home.
  • Run a scene.
  • Control a favourite accessory.
  • Availability depends on watchOS version and Home configuration.
  • For a blind user, Siri may still be faster for many actions.

Using automations

Automations can trigger actions automatically.

Examples:

  • Turn on a light at sunset.
  • Turn off devices when leaving home.
  • Turn on heating before arriving.
  • Run good night scene at a certain time.
  • Turn on a hallway light when motion is detected.
  • Automations are usually configured from the iPhone.
  • The Apple Watch can benefit from them, but the detailed setup is better on the iPhone.
  • Automations should be reviewed carefully.
  • A badly configured automation can be annoying or unsafe.

Accessibility benefits

Smart home control can help blind users by:

  • Reducing dependence on inaccessible controls.
  • Allowing voice control through Siri.
  • Providing wrist notifications.
  • Controlling lights for others.
  • Managing devices from one place.
  • Creating routines with scenes.
  • Avoiding physical search for switches or remotes.
  • Making some home tasks easier.
  • However, the setup must be stable and understandable.
  • A badly configured smart home creates more problems than it solves.

Security and privacy

Smart home devices can involve security and privacy.

Review:

  • Who has access to the home.
  • Which devices have microphones or cameras.
  • Which automations exist.
  • Whether remote access is enabled.
  • Whether devices are updated.
  • Whether passwords and accounts are secure.
  • Which notifications are enabled.
  • For locks, cameras, and sensors, be especially cautious.

Common problems

Siri does not understand the device name.

  • The device does not respond.
  • The accessory is offline.
  • The Apple Watch is not connected.
  • The iPhone or home hub has connection problems.
  • The device is not compatible.
  • The Home app is poorly organised.
  • The wrong room name is used.
  • The automation does the wrong thing.

Notifications are too frequent.

What to check if a device does not respond

Check:

  • The accessory has power.
  • Wi-Fi or network is working.
  • The accessory works from the iPhone.
  • The Apple Watch is connected.
  • Siri understood the command.
  • The device name is correct.
  • The room name is correct.
  • The Home app is working.
  • The home hub is online if remote control is needed.

Common mistakes

Buying devices without checking Apple Home compatibility.

  • Giving devices unclear names.
  • Creating too many scenes.
  • Creating automations without testing.
  • Allowing too many notifications.
  • Using smart plugs with risky appliances.
  • Depending on smart locks without understanding backup options.
  • Expecting all camera features to be accessible on the watch.
  • Not reviewing who has access to the home.

Practical advice

Start small.

A good first smart home setup for an Apple Watch user could be:

  • One lamp.
  • One smart plug.
  • One simple scene.
  • Clear names.
  • Siri tested from the watch.
  • Notifications limited.
  • Once that works well, add more devices.
  • Do not begin by automating the entire house unless you enjoy debugging your living room.

Exercise for module 53

On the iPhone, open the Home app.

  • Review your devices.
  • Check that names are clear.
  • Check that rooms are correctly assigned.
  • Create or review one simple scene, such as Good Night.
  • Put on the Apple Watch.
  • Ask Siri to turn one device on or off.
  • Check whether it responds.
  • Open the Home app on the Apple Watch.
  • Find the same device.
  • Control it with VoiceOver.
  • Then review notifications and turn off any that are not useful.

Summary of module 53

The Apple Watch can control compatible smart home devices. Most setup is done from the Home app on the iPhone. Siri is often the easiest way to control devices from the watch. Clear device names and room names are essential. Scenes can group several actions. Smart plugs, lights, thermostats, blinds, sensors, locks, cameras, and other accessories may be controlled if compatible. Locks, cameras, and plugs for risky appliances require special caution. Notifications should be useful, not excessive. A small, reliable smart home setup is better than a large confusing one.

Module 54. Battery, charging, and daily battery life

Battery management is part of using the Apple Watch well. The Apple Watch is a small computer on your wrist. It records health data, receives notifications, connects to the iPhone, uses sensors, plays sounds, vibrates, manages workouts, uses GPS, and sometimes connects to a mobile network. All of that uses battery.

Unlike a traditional watch, the Apple Watch needs to be charged frequently. This is not a fault. It is the price of asking a wrist device to do the work of a phone, a pedometer, a heart sensor, an alarm clock, and a tiny notification clerk.

Why battery matters

Battery matters because, without it, many important features stop working.

If the Apple Watch has no battery, it cannot:

  • Show the time.
  • Receive notifications.
  • Track workouts.
  • Record heart rate.
  • Record sleep.
  • Vibrate for alarms.
  • Alert you about medication.
  • Use Emergency SOS.
  • Use Fall Detection.
  • Help find the iPhone.
  • Make calls.
  • Track location.
  • For users who rely on the watch for accessibility or safety, charging is not optional. It is part of the routine.

Checking battery from Control Centre

The quickest way to check battery is from Control Centre.

On the Apple Watch:

  • Return to the watch face.
  • Press the side button once to open Control Centre, on recent versions.
  • Find the battery percentage with VoiceOver.
  • Listen to the value.
  • If your watchOS version opens Control Centre differently, use the method that applies to your device.

Battery complication

You can also add battery as a complication on the watch face. This is very useful. With a battery complication, you can check the remaining battery without opening Control Centre. For many blind users, battery is one of the most useful complications. If you use sleep tracking, workouts, or safety features, having battery visible on the watch face is recommended.

Charging the Apple Watch

The Apple Watch charges using its magnetic charging cable or a compatible charging base.

To charge it:

  • Connect the charger to power.
  • Place the circular magnetic charging base on a stable surface.
  • Place the back of the Apple Watch on the charger.
  • Let the magnet align the watch.
  • Check that charging has started.
  • If VoiceOver is active or the watch has battery, you may hear or feel a confirmation.
  • If the battery is very low, it may take a few minutes to show signs of life.

Correct placement on the charger

  • The back of the watch must rest on the circular charger.
  • The screen usually faces upward.
  • The magnet should hold it in place.

If the watch is not aligned, it may not charge.

If it does not charge:

  • Lift it.
  • Place it again.
  • Check the cable.
  • Check the power adapter.
  • Check the socket.
  • Check whether the charger is compatible.

Do not assume the watch is broken until the charger and power source have been checked. Humanity has declared many devices dead while the problem was a plug. A tragic tradition.

Fast charging

Some Apple Watch models support fast charging. This can be useful if you use the watch for sleep and cannot leave it charging all night.

Fast charging may require:

  • A compatible Apple Watch model.
  • A compatible fast charging cable.
  • A suitable power adapter.
  • If one of these is missing, charging may be slower.

Fast charging is useful for short charging routines:

  1. While showering.
  2. During breakfast.
  3. Before bed.
  4. While resting.
  5. Not every model supports it.

Charging routine

A fixed charging routine is very important.

Possible routines:

  • Charge while showering.
  • Charge during breakfast.
  • Charge before going to bed.
  • Charge while sitting at the computer.
  • Charge during a daily rest period.
  • Charge after exercise.
  • If you do not track sleep, charging overnight may be simple.
  • If you do track sleep, you need another routine.

Using the watch for sleep

If you sleep with the Apple Watch, battery planning becomes more important. Before going to bed, check whether there is enough battery for the night. If battery is low, charge it before sleeping. When you wake up, you may charge it again for a while.

A practical sleep routine could be:

  • Charge before bed.
  • Wear during sleep.
  • Charge while showering or having breakfast.
  • This depends on the model and use.

Workouts and battery

Workouts use more battery than normal use.

Battery drain increases with:

  • GPS.
  • Heart rate tracking.
  • Cellular.
  • Music or podcasts.
  • Long sessions.
  • Navigation.
  • Screen use.
  • If you are going for a long workout or walk, check battery first.
  • If you use the watch for safety, do not start a long outdoor session with very low battery.

Cellular and battery

A Cellular Apple Watch uses more battery when it connects to the mobile network. This is especially noticeable when the iPhone is not nearby. Calls, streaming, messages, and data over Cellular can reduce battery faster. If you go out without the iPhone, check battery before leaving. If you are going for a long outing, consider taking the iPhone too, especially if battery is limited.

GPS and battery

Outdoor workouts and navigation can use GPS.

  • GPS uses battery.
  • If you use Maps and Workout at the same time, battery use may increase.
  • This is normal.
  • For long routes, battery should be checked in advance.

Audio and battery

Music, podcasts, audiobooks, and Bluetooth headphones use battery. Streaming from the watch uses more battery than playing downloaded content. Streaming over Cellular uses even more. If you want to listen during a long walk, plan battery accordingly.

Notifications and battery

Frequent notifications also use battery. Each alert can wake the screen, vibrate, make sound, or communicate with the iPhone. If the watch receives too many notifications, battery may drain faster. Reducing unnecessary notifications can help both attention and battery.

Always-On display

Some Apple Watch models have an Always-On display. For totally blind users, this may not be necessary. Turning it off may help conserve battery. If you have remaining vision and use the display visually, you may prefer to keep it on.

To review this:

  • Open the Watch app on the iPhone.
  • Go to Display and Brightness.
  • Look for Always On, if available.
  • Turn it on or off according to need.
  • The exact path may vary.

Wake on Wrist Raise

Wake on Wrist Raise turns the screen on when you raise your wrist. This can be useful, but it may also use battery. For VoiceOver users, the usefulness depends on how they interact with the watch. If the screen wakes too often or battery is poor, review the setting.

Low Power Mode

The Apple Watch includes Low Power Mode. It helps extend battery life by reducing or limiting some functions. This can be useful when battery is low. But it may affect certain features.

Depending on model and version, Low Power Mode may reduce:

  • Background measurements.
  • Always-On display.
  • Some notifications.
  • Heart rate frequency.
  • Workout features.
  • Other background activity.
  • Do not use Low Power Mode without understanding what it changes, especially if you rely on health, safety, or workout features.

When to use Low Power Mode

Low Power Mode may be useful:

  • When battery is low.
  • During a long day away from home.
  • During travel.
  • During a long workout where extended battery matters.
  • When you only need basic functions.
  • But if you rely on alerts, health monitoring, or safety features, understand the limitations first.

Battery Health

The Apple Watch battery ages over time.

  • Battery capacity decreases with use.
  • Older watches may last less than when they were new.
  • You can review battery health from settings, depending on watchOS version.

On the Apple Watch:

  • Open Settings.
  • Look for Battery.
  • Look for Battery Health, if available.
  • There you may see maximum capacity or related information.
  • If battery health is very low, daily battery life may be noticeably worse.

Optimised charging

Apple Watch may include optimised charging features. These help reduce battery ageing by learning charging routines and managing how the battery charges. This can be useful. If you notice the watch does not charge to full immediately, it may be because of optimised charging behaviour. You can review battery settings if needed.

What uses the most battery

Battery drain can increase with:

  • Long workouts.
  • GPS.
  • Cellular.
  • Streaming audio.
  • Frequent notifications.
  • Always-On display.
  • High brightness.
  • Many background apps.
  • Poor signal.
  • Navigation.
  • Calls.
  • Old battery.
  • Understanding this helps identify why the watch is draining quickly.

What to do if battery drains too fast

Check:

  • Battery Health.
  • Notifications.
  • Always-On display.
  • Brightness.
  • Cellular use.
  • Workout use.
  • Audio streaming.
  • Background apps.
  • watchOS updates.
  • Connection with iPhone.
  • Whether the watch is searching for signal often.
  • If battery suddenly becomes much worse after an update, observe for a day or two. Sometimes devices reindex or adjust after updates.
  • If the problem continues, review settings or contact Apple Support.

Charging problems

If the watch does not charge:

  • Check the charger is connected.
  • Check the power adapter.
  • Check the socket.
  • Clean the back of the watch gently if needed.
  • Check the charger surface.
  • Remove protective films if any remain.
  • Try another compatible charger.
  • Restart the watch if it has enough battery and the issue continues.
  • If nothing works, seek technical support.
  • Never use damaged chargers.

Battery and safety

For people who rely on the Apple Watch for Emergency SOS, Fall Detection, medication, or important alerts, battery is part of safety. A low battery warning should not be ignored. If you are going out alone, especially outdoors, check battery first. A watch at five percent is not a safety plan. It is a countdown with straps.

Common mistakes

  • Forgetting to charge before sleeping.
  • Starting a long workout with low battery.
  • Using Cellular all day and expecting the same battery life.
  • Leaving too many notifications active.
  • Not checking battery health on older watches.
  • Not realising Low Power Mode changes behaviour.
  • Using incompatible or unreliable chargers.
  • Thinking charging overnight is possible while also tracking sleep.
  • Not creating a charging routine.
  • Depending on the watch for safety without checking battery.

Practical advice

Create a fixed charging routine. Add battery as a complication.

Check battery before:

  • Leaving home.
  • Sleeping.
  • Starting a workout.
  • Travelling.
  • Going out without the iPhone.
  • If the watch is used by an older person, make charging part of the daily routine and keep the charger in a predictable place.

Exercise for module 54

Open Control Centre on the Apple Watch.

  • Find the battery percentage.
  • Listen to it with VoiceOver.
  • Then open the Watch app on the iPhone.
  • Review your current watch face.
  • Add Battery as a complication if it is useful.
  • Place the Apple Watch on its charger.
  • Check that charging begins.
  • After a few minutes, check the battery again.

Then review your routine:

  • When will you charge it if you do not track sleep?
  • When will you charge it if you do track sleep?
  • Choose a fixed daily charging moment.

Summary of module 54

The Apple Watch needs frequent charging. Battery matters for notifications, health, workouts, sleep, safety, and accessibility. Battery can be checked from Control Centre or with a complication. Some models support fast charging. Sleep tracking requires a charging routine outside the night. Workouts, GPS, Cellular, streaming, and frequent notifications use more battery. Low Power Mode can extend battery life but may limit features. Battery health decreases over time. A reliable charging routine is essential, especially for users who depend on the watch for alerts or safety.

Module 55. watchOS updates

watchOS is the operating system of the Apple Watch. Like the iPhone, the Apple Watch receives software updates. These updates may add features, fix errors, improve security, change settings, modify app behaviour, or adjust accessibility.

For a blind person using VoiceOver, updates are important because they may improve the experience, but they may also change gestures, menus, labels, or behaviour. That is why updates should be done carefully. Not with fear. Not with blind enthusiasm either.

A new update can bring useful improvements, but it can also move buttons around because apparently software designers wake up some mornings convinced that everyone needed a small treasure hunt.

Why updates matter

watchOS updates can include:

  • Security fixes.
  • Accessibility improvements.
  • New features.
  • Bug fixes.
  • Health feature updates.
  • Workout improvements.
  • Battery optimisations.
  • Compatibility changes.
  • New watch faces.
  • Changes to apps.
  • Changes to notifications.
  • Changes in Control Centre or buttons.
  • Updating can be important for safety and compatibility.
  • But it is also sensible to know what version you are installing and whether there are known problems.

Relationship between iOS and watchOS

The Apple Watch depends on the iPhone. To update the Apple Watch, the iPhone usually needs to be compatible and updated. Sometimes a new watchOS version requires a certain iOS version. If the iPhone is not updated, the Apple Watch update may not appear or may not install. Before updating the watch, check the iPhone.

Checking for updates

From the iPhone:

  • Open the Watch app.
  • Go to My Watch.
  • Go to General.
  • Go to Software Update.
  • The system will check whether an update is available.
  • You can also check from the Apple Watch settings, but the iPhone is usually more comfortable with VoiceOver.

Requirements for updating

To update the Apple Watch, you usually need:

  • Apple Watch charged.
  • Apple Watch on its charger.
  • iPhone nearby.
  • iPhone connected to Wi-Fi.
  • iPhone with enough battery or connected to power.
  • Apple Watch with enough battery.
  • Enough time.
  • Stable connection.
  • The exact requirements may vary, but in practice it is best to place both devices charging and near each other.
  • Do not start an update with low battery.
  • Do not start it if you need the watch immediately.
  • Do not start it while leaving home.
  • Updates are not famous for respecting your schedule.

Automatic updates

The Apple Watch may offer automatic updates. This means the system can install updates automatically, usually when conditions are suitable. This can be convenient. But some users prefer manual control, especially if they rely heavily on accessibility.

For VoiceOver users, it may be useful to wait briefly and check whether other users report accessibility problems before installing a major update. Security updates are important, so this does not mean ignoring updates indefinitely. It means updating thoughtfully.

Minor updates and major updates

Not all updates are the same. A minor update may fix bugs or security issues. A major update may change more things. For example, a new watchOS version may introduce interface changes, new features, or changes in gestures. Major updates deserve more attention. Minor security updates may be more urgent.

What to do before updating

Before updating:

  • Check that the iPhone is working well.
  • Check that VoiceOver works properly on the iPhone.
  • Check battery on both devices.
  • Place the watch on the charger.
  • Make sure you know your Apple Watch passcode.
  • Make sure you have time.
  • If the watch is critical for medication, alarms, or safety, avoid updating right before you need those features.
  • If possible, update at a moment when you can solve problems calmly if something changes.

Reading about known issues

For major updates, it may be useful to check reliable sources or communities before installing. Especially communities of blind users, VoiceOver users, Apple accessibility groups, or official Apple information.

This can help detect:

  1. VoiceOver bugs.
  2. Battery problems.
  3. Changed gestures.
  4. Broken apps.
  5. Health feature changes.
  6. Notification issues.
  7. Braille issues.

This course itself cannot know future update behaviour. Updates change over time, because software companies apparently enjoy keeping humans and manuals equally unstable.

During the update

During the update:

  • Keep the Apple Watch on the charger.
  • Keep the iPhone nearby.
  • Do not restart devices unless instructed.
  • Do not remove the watch from the charger.
  • Do not interrupt the process.
  • Wait until the update completes.
  • The watch may restart.
  • The process may take time.
  • VoiceOver may not speak during some parts of the update.
  • That can be normal.

If the update seems slow

Updates can take a long time.

This depends on:

  • Size of update.
  • Wi-Fi speed.
  • Apple servers.
  • Battery.
  • Device model.
  • Available storage.
  • Do not assume it has failed just because it takes a while.
  • But if it remains stuck for a very long time, you may need to check Apple guidance or technical support.

After updating

After the update:

  • Unlock the Apple Watch.
  • Check that VoiceOver works.
  • Check the watch face.
  • Check Control Centre.
  • Check notifications.
  • Check battery behaviour.
  • Check important apps.
  • Check health features you use.
  • Check alarms and timers.
  • Check the accessibility shortcut.
  • If anything changed, review settings.
  • Do not assume everything remains exactly where it was.

Checking VoiceOver after update

This is important.

After updating:

  • Check that VoiceOver is still on.
  • Check speech rate.
  • Check volume.
  • Check the accessibility shortcut.
  • Check whether gestures behave normally.
  • Check whether the Digital Crown and side button behave as expected.
  • If VoiceOver has changed, use the Watch app on the iPhone to correct settings.

Checking notifications after update

Updates may affect notifications or settings.

Check:

  • Calls.
  • Messages.
  • Medication reminders.
  • Alarms.
  • Timers.
  • Health alerts.
  • Calendar.
  • Important app notifications.
  • If an alert is important, test it safely.
  • For example, create a test timer or reminder.

Checking battery after update

Sometimes battery behaves differently after an update. It may temporarily drain faster during the first hours or day. If battery drain continues, review settings, restart devices, and check whether others report the same issue. Do not panic after the first hour. Do not ignore a persistent problem either.

Checking apps after update

Some apps may need updates after watchOS changes. Open the Watch app and App Store if needed.

Check whether important apps still work:

  • Workout.
  • Heart Rate.
  • Sleep.
  • Medications.
  • Messages.
  • Phone.
  • Wallet.
  • Home.
  • Weather.
  • Any third-party app you use.
  • If something does not work, check for app updates.

If the update fails

If an update fails:

  • Check Wi-Fi.
  • Check battery.
  • Check charger.
  • Keep devices near each other.
  • Restart the iPhone and Apple Watch if appropriate.
  • Try again later.
  • Check available storage.
  • Seek Apple support if the issue persists.
  • Do not erase the Apple Watch unless you understand the consequences.

Storage and updates

Updates may require free space. If there is not enough space, the system may ask you to remove apps or content.

To free space:

  • Remove unused apps.
  • Remove downloaded music or podcasts.
  • Remove unnecessary content.
  • Use the Watch app on the iPhone to review storage.
  • Storage problems are more likely on older or lower-capacity models.

Updating an older Apple Watch

Older Apple Watch models may not support the latest watchOS. At some point, Apple stops providing major updates for older models. This does not mean the watch immediately stops working.

But over time:

  • New apps may not be compatible.
  • Some features may not appear.
  • Security updates may stop.
  • Battery may be worse.
  • Performance may be lower.
  • If you are using an older watch, check compatibility before following instructions written for newer versions.

Updating when using the watch for safety

If the Apple Watch is used by an older person or for safety, choose update timing carefully.

  • Do not update just before bedtime if the watch is used for sleep or falls.
  • Do not update before a walk if it is used for Emergency SOS.
  • Do not update before medication reminders if they are critical.

Update when another support is available or when the device is not urgently needed.

Accessibility and updates

Accessibility behaviour can change in updates.

This may include:

  • VoiceOver gestures.
  • Labels.
  • Button behaviour.
  • Braille support.
  • Siri behaviour.
  • Notifications.
  • Watch face elements.
  • Control Centre access.
  • For this reason, after a major update, take time to review the basics.
  • Do not assume that the course instructions will match every future version exactly.
  • If labels differ, look for the equivalent option in the same area.
  • Should you update immediately?
  • For security reasons, updates should not be ignored for long.

But for major updates, especially if accessibility is essential, it may be reasonable to wait a short time and check user reports. This is a practical balance. Do not install blindly the moment an update appears if you depend heavily on the watch and cannot handle possible changes. Do not postpone forever either.

The sensible approach is:

  1. Read.
  2. Check.
  3. Prepare.
  4. Update.
  5. Review.

Common mistakes

  • Updating with low battery.
  • Updating away from Wi-Fi.
  • Removing the watch from the charger.
  • Starting an update before leaving home.
  • Not checking VoiceOver afterwards.
  • Not testing important alerts afterwards.
  • Ignoring major accessibility reports.
  • Never updating at all.
  • Updating an older watch without checking compatibility.
  • Panicking if the update takes a while.

Practical advice

For most users, the iPhone is the best place to manage Apple Watch updates.

  • Keep the iPhone updated.
  • Keep the watch charged.
  • Update at a sensible time.
  • After updating, check the features you rely on.
  • For accessibility users, major updates deserve a little more attention.

Exercise for module 55

On the iPhone, open the Watch app.

  • Go to My Watch.
  • Go to General.
  • Open Software Update.
  • Check whether an update is available.
  • Do not install it immediately unless you are ready.
  • Check battery on the iPhone.
  • Check battery on the Apple Watch.
  • Place the watch on the charger.
  • If you decide to update, keep the iPhone nearby and connected to Wi-Fi.

After the update, check:

  1. VoiceOver.
  2. Accessibility shortcut.
  3. Notifications.
  4. Alarms.
  5. Timers.
  6. Battery.
  7. Important apps.

Summary of module 55

watchOS is the operating system of the Apple Watch.

Updates can bring security fixes, features, accessibility changes, and bug fixes.

  • The iPhone usually manages Apple Watch updates.
  • The watch should be charged and on its charger during updates.
  • The iPhone should be nearby, connected to Wi-Fi, and have enough battery.

Major updates may change menus, gestures, or behaviour. After updating, check VoiceOver, notifications, battery, and important apps. Older Apple Watch models may not support the latest versions. Updates should be done carefully, especially when the watch is used for safety, health, or accessibility.

Module 56. Storage and installed apps

The Apple Watch has limited internal storage. That storage is used for apps, watchOS, music, podcasts, photos, data, updates, and other system files.

Most users do not need to think about storage every day, but it becomes important when the watch is full, when updates cannot be installed, when music or podcasts do not sync, or when the Apple Watch becomes cluttered with apps that are not really used.

For a blind person using VoiceOver, storage is also related to simplicity. A watch with too many apps can be harder to navigate. A shorter and cleaner app list is usually more comfortable.

What storage is used for

Apple Watch storage can be used by:

  • watchOS.
  • System data.
  • Installed apps.
  • Music.
  • Podcasts.
  • Audiobooks.
  • Photos.
  • Maps or offline data, depending on version and configuration.
  • Health and activity data.
  • Temporary files.
  • Updates.
  • The exact categories may vary depending on model and watchOS version.

Checking storage from the iPhone

The easiest way to check storage is usually from the Watch app on the iPhone.

On the iPhone:

  • Open the Watch app.
  • Go to My Watch.
  • Go to General.
  • Look for Storage.
  • Open Storage.
  • With VoiceOver, move through the information.
  • You should be able to hear how much storage is used and what types of content are taking up space.

Checking storage from the Apple Watch

You may also be able to check storage from the Apple Watch.

On the Apple Watch:

  • Open Settings.
  • Go to General.
  • Look for Storage.
  • Open it.
  • With VoiceOver, move through the information.
  • For most users, the iPhone will be more comfortable.

What happens when storage is full

If the Apple Watch storage is full or nearly full, several problems may appear.

For example:

  • Updates may not install.
  • Apps may not install.
  • Music may not sync.
  • Podcasts may not download.
  • The watch may feel less tidy.
  • Storage warnings may appear.
  • Some features may not have enough space for temporary files.
  • If an update fails because there is not enough space, you may need to remove apps or downloaded content.

Apps and storage

Apps take up space. Some apps are very small. Others use more storage. Apps may also store data. If you installed many apps during the initial setup, you may have more than you need. For blind users, it is often better to keep only the apps that are actually useful on the watch. The iPhone can handle the rest. The Apple Watch does not need to become a museum of apps you opened once and then abandoned, as humanity does with admirable consistency.

Removing apps from the Apple Watch

To remove apps from the Apple Watch, the easiest method is usually from the iPhone.

On the iPhone:

  • Open the Watch app.
  • Go to My Watch.
  • Move down to the list of installed apps.
  • Open the app you want to remove.
  • Turn off the option to show it on Apple Watch, if available.
  • Or use the available uninstall option.
  • The exact wording may vary depending on app and system version.
  • Removing the watch version does not always remove the iPhone app.
  • It usually removes only the Apple Watch app.

Removing apps directly from the watch

Apps can also be removed from the Apple Watch itself, depending on app view and version. If you use List View, the process may vary. With VoiceOver, it is usually more comfortable to manage apps from the iPhone. This avoids accidental deletions and makes it easier to review what is installed.

Which apps to keep

A useful basic app selection may include:

  • Settings.
  • Phone.
  • Messages.
  • Calendar.
  • Reminders.
  • Timers.
  • Alarms.
  • Workout.
  • Activity.
  • Heart Rate.
  • Weather.
  • Find Devices.
  • Wallet, if used.
  • Home, if used.
  • Medications, if used.
  • Sleep, if used.
  • This does not mean that every user needs all of them.
  • The best app list is the one that reflects real use.

Which apps can be removed or avoided

You may remove or avoid installing apps that:

  • You never open.
  • Duplicate iPhone functions you prefer to use on the phone.
  • Are not accessible enough.
  • Send too many notifications.
  • Use storage without value.
  • Are uncomfortable on the small screen.
  • Were installed automatically during setup.
  • There is no obligation to keep an app just because it has an Apple Watch version.

Music and storage

Music can take up a lot of storage. If you download playlists or albums to the Apple Watch, they remain stored on the watch.

This is useful if you want to listen without the iPhone.

  • But it uses space.
  • If storage is low, review downloaded music.
  • You can remove playlists or albums you no longer need.

Podcasts and storage

Podcasts can also use a lot of storage. Episodes may sync automatically. If you subscribe to many podcasts, the watch may download episodes you do not actually listen to from the watch. Review podcast sync settings from the iPhone. Remove old episodes if needed. A podcast episode sitting on your watch for six months without being heard is not culture. It is digital luggage.

Photos and storage

The Apple Watch can sync photos from the iPhone. This may be useful for people with remaining vision, for watch faces, or for sharing images quickly. For a totally blind user, syncing many photos may not be necessary. If storage is low, review whether photos are being synced.

From the Watch app on the iPhone:

  • Go to My Watch.
  • Look for Photos.
  • Review sync settings.
  • Reduce or disable photo syncing if you do not need it.

Downloaded maps or offline content

Depending on watchOS version and apps used, some maps or offline content may use storage. This can be useful for routes or outdoor activities, but it may also occupy space. If storage is low and you use navigation or outdoor apps, review whether offline data are stored.

System data

Some storage is used by system data. This cannot always be removed manually. watchOS needs space to work. If system data seems very high and the watch has problems, restarting the watch or updating may help, but do not erase the watch without understanding the consequences.

Storage and updates

Updates may need free space.

If watchOS says there is not enough storage:

  • Remove unused apps.
  • Remove downloaded music.
  • Remove podcasts.
  • Remove photos if not needed.
  • Restart the Apple Watch.
  • Try the update again.
  • If the problem persists, check Apple guidance or support.
  • Do not erase the watch as the first step unless there is no other option.

Storage and accessibility

For a VoiceOver user, removing unnecessary apps is not only about storage. It also makes navigation easier.

A shorter app list means:

  • Fewer swipes.
  • Less confusion.
  • Faster access.
  • Fewer notifications.
  • Less clutter.
  • This is an accessibility improvement.
  • Simple organisation often helps more than adding more features.

Automatic app installation

The Watch app may include an option to automatically install Apple Watch versions of iPhone apps. If this is enabled, apps may appear on the watch automatically. For a beginner, it may be better to disable automatic installation and install apps manually. That way, only useful apps appear.

To review this:

  • Open the Watch app on the iPhone.
  • Go to My Watch.
  • Go to General.
  • Look for Automatic App Install or a similar option.
  • Turn it off if you prefer manual control.
  • The exact wording may vary.

Managing app notifications

Removing an app is one option. Another is keeping the app installed but disabling notifications. If an app is useful occasionally but does not deserve wrist alerts, keep the app and turn off its notifications.

From the Watch app:

  1. Go to Notifications.
  2. Review the app.
  3. Disable alerts if appropriate.
  4. This helps reduce interruptions.

Organising with List View

As mentioned earlier, List View is usually more comfortable with VoiceOver than Grid View. If you have many apps, List View makes navigation more predictable.

To review:

  • Open the Watch app on the iPhone.
  • Look for App View, if available.
  • Choose List View.
  • Or review this from Apple Watch Settings.

App Store on Apple Watch

The Apple Watch has access to apps through the App Store. However, searching, reading descriptions, and reviewing apps is usually more comfortable on the iPhone.

Before installing a watch app, ask:

  • Will I really use this on the watch?
  • Is it accessible with VoiceOver?
  • Does it add something useful?
  • Will it send too many notifications?
  • Can the iPhone do this better?
  • This avoids filling the watch with apps that later become digital clutter.

Third-party apps

Some third-party Apple Watch apps are very useful.

  • Others are not worth installing.
  • Accessibility varies.
  • Some apps work well with VoiceOver.
  • Others have unlabeled buttons, confusing layouts, or limited functions.
  • If an app is not accessible enough, do not waste too much time with it.
  • Use the iPhone version or another app if needed.

What to do before deleting an app

Before deleting an app, consider:

  • Do I use it on the watch?
  • Does it store data?
  • Does removing it affect notifications?
  • Can I reinstall it later?
  • Is the iPhone app still available?
  • Does it contain important information?
  • Most watch apps can be reinstalled later, but it is still useful to check.

Resetting the Apple Watch because of storage

If storage is badly stuck, some users erase and re-pair the watch. This can solve certain problems, but it is more drastic. Do not do it casually.

Before erasing:

  • Check backups.
  • Check pairing.
  • Check Apple Account.
  • Check passcode.
  • Check Activation Lock.
  • Check whether health and activity data are syncing.
  • Check whether you know how to pair again.
  • For most storage problems, removing apps and content is enough.

Common mistakes

  • Installing every available app.
  • Leaving automatic app installation on without wanting it.
  • Downloading many podcasts.
  • Syncing photos unnecessarily.
  • Not checking storage before updates.
  • Deleting apps without knowing what they do.
  • Using Grid View with too many apps.
  • Keeping apps only because they exist.
  • Ignoring inaccessible apps instead of removing them.
  • Trying to fix storage by erasing the watch too quickly.

Practical advice

  • Keep the Apple Watch simple.
  • Review installed apps once in a while.
  • Remove what you do not use.
  • Use the iPhone for complex tasks.
  • Keep only the watch apps that provide quick, practical value.

A clean Apple Watch is easier to use, easier to update, and less likely to become a tiny wrist drawer full of digital junk.

Exercise for module 56

On the iPhone, open the Watch app.

  • Go to My Watch.
  • Go to General.
  • Open Storage.
  • Listen to how much storage is used.
  • Review which apps or content use the most space.
  • Return to My Watch.
  • Review installed apps.
  • Choose one app you do not use on the watch.
  • Remove it from the Apple Watch if appropriate.
  • Then review Music, Podcasts, and Photos settings.
  • Check whether unnecessary content is synced.
  • Finally, make sure the app view is set to List View if that is more comfortable with VoiceOver.

Summary of module 56

The Apple Watch has limited storage. Storage is used by watchOS, apps, music, podcasts, photos, data, and updates. Storage can be checked from the Watch app on the iPhone or from Apple Watch settings. If storage is full, updates and downloads may fail. Removing unused apps improves both storage and accessibility. Music, podcasts, and photos can take up a lot of space. Automatic app installation may fill the watch with unnecessary apps. List View is usually more comfortable with VoiceOver. A simple app list makes the Apple Watch easier to use.

Module 57. Finding the Apple Watch, locking it, and lost mode

Just as the Apple Watch can help find the iPhone, the iPhone can help find the Apple Watch. This is important because the watch is small, light, and easy to leave on a charger, under clothes, in a bag, on a table, beside the bed, or in some other location selected by domestic chaos with its usual precision. The Find My system can help locate the Apple Watch, make it play a sound, mark it as lost, or protect it if it disappears. For blind users, this can be very useful, especially if the watch has been placed somewhere nearby and cannot be found by touch.

What Find My can do

Find My can help you:

  • Locate the Apple Watch on a map.
  • Make the Apple Watch play a sound.
  • Mark the watch as lost.
  • Protect the device with Activation Lock.
  • Check its last known location, depending on conditions.
  • Locate other Apple devices linked to your Apple Account.
  • Share or check location with trusted people, if configured.
  • The available options depend on battery, connection, model, location settings, and Find My configuration.

Requirements

To use Find My with Apple Watch, you need:

  • Find My enabled.
  • The Apple Watch linked to your Apple Account.
  • The Apple Watch paired correctly.
  • Location services enabled where needed.
  • Battery on the watch.
  • Connection or recent location information.
  • If the watch is turned off, out of battery, or disconnected, Find My may show the last known location rather than live location.

Finding the Apple Watch from the iPhone

On the iPhone:

  • Open the Find My app.
  • Go to Devices.
  • Find your Apple Watch in the list.
  • Open it.
  • Listen to the available options with VoiceOver.

You may find:

  1. Play Sound.
  2. Directions.
  3. Mark as Lost.
  4. Notify When Found.
  5. Erase This Device.
  6. The exact options may vary.

Making the Apple Watch play a sound

If the Apple Watch is nearby, Play Sound is often the most useful option.

To use it:

  • Open Find My on the iPhone.
  • Choose the Apple Watch.
  • Select Play Sound.
  • The watch should make a sound.
  • Follow the sound to find it.

This is useful if the watch is:

  • Under clothes.
  • In a bag.
  • On a table.
  • Beside the bed.
  • In another room.
  • On its charger.
  • The sound may continue for a while or until dismissed.
  • If you are deaf or hard of hearing, this may be less useful unless someone else can help locate the sound.

Finding it by touch

If the watch is nearby but you cannot hear it well, search methodically.

Common places:

  • Charger.
  • Bedside table.
  • Bathroom.
  • Desk.
  • Kitchen counter.
  • Bag.
  • Coat pocket.
  • Under clothes.
  • Near the iPhone charger.
  • Gym bag.
  • The Find My sound can help narrow the area.
  • If someone else is with you, ask them to listen for the sound.

Directions to the watch

If the Apple Watch is not nearby, Find My may offer directions.

This can open Maps and guide you toward the device’s location, if available.

  • For blind users, use this carefully.
  • If the watch appears in an unfamiliar place, plan the route safely.
  • Do not rely only on the watch’s location if the situation is unclear.

Last known location

If the Apple Watch has no battery or is offline, Find My may show its last known location. This can still be useful. For example, it may indicate that the watch was last seen at home, at work, at the gym, or in a shop. But it may not be the current location. The watch may have moved, or the location may be approximate.

Mark as Lost

If you cannot find the Apple Watch, you can mark it as lost. This may lock the device and help protect your information.

From Find My:

  • Choose the Apple Watch.
  • Find Mark as Lost or Lost Mode.
  • Follow the instructions.
  • You may be able to add a phone number or message so someone who finds it can contact you.
  • The exact steps may vary.
  • This option should be used when you believe the watch is lost, not just because it is probably under a cushion.

Activation Lock

Activation Lock helps prevent another person from using your Apple Watch if it is lost or stolen. It is linked to your Apple Account. This is why a used Apple Watch must be removed from the previous owner’s account before being sold or given away. If Activation Lock is active, another person cannot simply erase the watch and use it normally without the correct account credentials. This is useful for security. It is also the reason buying second-hand devices without checking them can become a magnificent lesson in regret.

Erasing the Apple Watch remotely

Find My may offer an option to erase the Apple Watch. This should be a last resort. If you erase it remotely, data on the watch are removed, but Activation Lock may still protect it.

Before erasing, consider:

  • Is it truly lost or stolen?
  • Could it still be nearby?
  • Do you have recent backups?
  • Do you understand what will happen?
  • Would marking it as lost be better first?
  • Do not erase casually.

Locking the Apple Watch

The Apple Watch normally locks when removed from the wrist, if wrist detection and passcode are enabled.

That is why using a passcode is important.

  • If someone finds your watch, they should not be able to access it easily.
  • If you use Apple Pay, passcode protection is required.
  • If the watch is lost, use Find My to protect it further.

What to do if the watch is lost at home

If you think it is at home:

  • Open Find My on the iPhone.
  • Make the watch play a sound.
  • Check the charger.
  • Check the usual places.
  • Check clothes and bags.
  • Check under cushions or bedding.
  • If the sound cannot be heard, move through the house slowly and repeat Play Sound if needed.

Most “lost” watches at home are not lost. They are simply participating in the ancient ritual of hiding in plain sight.

What to do if it is lost outside

If the watch appears outside:

  • Check its last location.
  • Consider whether you left it somewhere known.
  • Call the place if possible.
  • Use Directions if safe.
  • Mark as Lost if you cannot retrieve it quickly.
  • Do not go alone to an unsafe place.
  • Do not confront anyone if theft is suspected.
  • Protect the device through Find My.

What to do if it is stolen

If you believe it has been stolen:

  • Mark it as Lost.
  • Do not remove it from your Apple Account immediately unless you understand the consequences.
  • Contact local authorities if appropriate.
  • Do not meet unknown people alone to recover it.
  • Review Apple Pay and cards.
  • Contact your bank if needed.
  • Keep the device protected by Activation Lock.
  • Removing the device from your account can reduce protection, so do not do that casually.

Apple Pay and lost Apple Watch

If the Apple Watch has cards configured in Wallet and is lost, Apple Pay should be protected by the passcode and wrist detection.

Even so, if you are concerned:

  • Use Find My.
  • Mark the watch as lost.
  • Review Wallet and Apple Pay on the iPhone.
  • Contact your bank if needed.
  • Security is better handled early.

Find My and battery

If the Apple Watch battery is dead, live location will not work. You may still see last known location. This is another reason battery matters. If you often leave the watch with low battery, Find My becomes less useful.

Finding an Apple Watch used by a family member

If the watch is set up for a family member, location options may depend on Family Setup, permissions, region, and account settings. Use the Find My app and family sharing settings as configured. Do not assume every watch appears in every account.

Find My and privacy

Location is sensitive information. Only share location with trusted people. Review who can see your location. If the Apple Watch is used by an older person or a child, location sharing should be configured with consent and clarity. Safety does not mean ignoring privacy.

Common problems

  • The watch does not appear in Find My.
  • The watch has no battery.
  • The watch is offline.
  • Location is outdated.
  • Play Sound does not work.
  • The wrong watch appears.
  • Find My was not enabled.
  • The watch was removed from the account.
  • The watch is still linked to someone else’s account.

What to check if the watch does not appear

Check:

  • The Apple Watch is paired.
  • You are using the correct Apple Account.
  • Find My is enabled.
  • The watch has battery.
  • The iPhone is connected.
  • The watch has not been removed from the account.
  • Family setup or account configuration if it is not your watch.

Common mistakes

  • Not enabling Find My.
  • Not using a passcode.
  • Removing a lost watch from the Apple Account too quickly.
  • Forgetting that last known location may not be current.
  • Assuming Play Sound works without battery.
  • Buying a used watch still linked to another account.
  • Not marking the watch as lost when it really is lost.
  • Going alone to retrieve a device from an unsafe place.
  • Not reviewing cards after loss.

Practical advice

Make sure Find My is enabled before there is a problem.

  • Use a passcode.
  • Know how to make the watch play a sound from the iPhone.
  • If the watch is truly lost, use Lost Mode.
  • If it may be stolen, protect the device and avoid risky recovery attempts.

Exercise for module 57

  • On the iPhone, open Find My.
  • Go to Devices.
  • Find your Apple Watch.
  • Open it.
  • Listen to the available options.
  • Use Play Sound while the watch is nearby.
  • Locate the watch by sound.
  • Stop the sound if needed.
  • Review whether Mark as Lost appears, but do not activate it unless you actually need it.
  • Check that the watch has a passcode enabled.
  • Then return to the Watch app and review Passcode settings.

Summary of module 57

The iPhone can help find the Apple Watch through Find My. You can make the watch play a sound if it is nearby. Find My can show location or last known location. Lost Mode can protect the watch if it is lost.

Activation Lock helps prevent another person from using the watch.

  • A passcode is important for security.
  • If the watch has no battery, Find My may be limited.
  • If theft is suspected, protect the device and avoid unsafe recovery attempts.
  • Find My should be configured before you need it.

Module 58. Buying a new, used, or refurbished Apple Watch

Before buying an Apple Watch, it is useful to understand the differences between new, used, and refurbished devices. This matters because the Apple Watch is not just a watch. It is linked to an Apple Account, can contain health data, may have Activation Lock, depends on battery condition, and may include or exclude features depending on model, region, and generation.

Buying badly can lead to problems: a watch that cannot be paired, a battery that barely lasts, a model without the health feature you expected, or a Cellular version that does not work with your carrier.

Because apparently the human species decided that buying a watch should now require checking accounts, sensors, carriers, battery chemistry, and regional health approvals. Very efficient, naturally.

New Apple Watch

A new Apple Watch is bought from Apple or an authorised seller as a new device.

Advantages:

  • It should not be linked to another account.
  • It should have full warranty according to local law and seller conditions.
  • Battery should be new.
  • Accessories should be included according to the package.
  • Activation Lock should not be a problem.
  • You know exactly what model you are buying.
  • It should be eligible for current support depending on model.

Disadvantages:

  • It is usually more expensive.
  • Some models or bands may cost more.
  • Not all features may be available in every country, even when new.
  • For users who want the least complicated purchase, a new Apple Watch is usually the safest choice.

Used Apple Watch

A used Apple Watch has belonged to another person. It may be cheaper, but it requires careful checking.

The main risks are:

  • Activation Lock.
  • Poor battery health.
  • Physical damage.
  • Unknown repair history.
  • Missing charger.
  • Wrong model.
  • Incompatible Cellular version.
  • No warranty or limited warranty.
  • Health features not available on that model.
  • Water damage.
  • Scratched screen.
  • Buttons or Digital Crown problems.
  • A used Apple Watch can be a good purchase, but only if properly checked.

Activation Lock

This is the most important issue in a used Apple Watch. If the watch is still linked to the previous owner’s Apple Account, you may not be able to use it. Erasing the watch is not enough. Resetting it is not enough. The previous owner must remove it from their account. Before buying, the seller should unpair the Apple Watch from their iPhone and remove it from Find My. When setting it up, it should not ask for the previous owner’s Apple Account. If it asks for someone else’s Apple Account, do not buy it or return it. There is no clever trick that turns a locked watch into a good purchase. There are only headaches wearing a strap.

How to check a used Apple Watch before buying

If possible, check:

  • It turns on.
  • The screen works.
  • VoiceOver can be activated or settings can be reached.
  • Digital Crown works.
  • Side button works.
  • Charger works.
  • Battery charges.
  • Watch is erased and ready for setup.
  • It does not ask for another person’s Apple Account.
  • Serial number and model match what is advertised.
  • The case is not damaged.
  • Sensors are not cracked or damaged.
  • Strap attachment works.
  • Battery health is acceptable.
  • Cellular model is compatible with your carrier if you need Cellular.
  • If you cannot check these things, the risk is higher.

Refurbished Apple Watch

A refurbished Apple Watch may mean different things depending on the seller. Apple’s official refurbished products usually go through Apple’s own process, include a new battery and outer shell in many cases, and come with Apple warranty, depending on country and availability. Refurbished products from other sellers may vary greatly. Some are carefully restored. Others are simply used devices cleaned and resold. The word refurbished is not magical. It can mean “professionally restored” or “we wiped it with a cloth and became optimistic.”

Official refurbished from Apple

If available in your country or region, Apple’s official refurbished store is usually safer than random second-hand sales.

Advantages may include:

  • Apple inspection.
  • Warranty.
  • Clear model information.
  • Battery and outer shell handling according to Apple’s refurbished policy.
  • Lower price than new.
  • Less risk of Activation Lock.

Disadvantages:

  1. Availability varies.
  2. Selection may be limited.
  3. Price may still be high.
  4. Older models may be offered.

Refurbished from other shops

If buying refurbished from another shop, check:

  • Warranty.
  • Return policy.
  • Battery health.
  • Activation Lock status.
  • What refurbished means for that seller.
  • Whether charger is included.
  • Whether the watch has been tested.
  • Whether the model is clearly identified.
  • Whether it is compatible with your iPhone.
  • Whether health features are available.
  • Do not rely only on the word refurbished.
  • Ask for details.

Checking compatibility with iPhone

Apple Watch requires an iPhone. Before buying, check that the Apple Watch model is compatible with your iPhone and iOS version. Newer Apple Watch models may require newer iPhones. Older iPhones may not work with newer Apple Watch models. Older watches may not support newer watchOS features. If the iPhone is too old, pairing may fail or be limited. This is especially important when buying used.

GPS or GPS plus Cellular

Apple Watch models may be GPS or GPS plus Cellular.

GPS model:

  • Usually depends on nearby iPhone for calls and mobile connection.
  • Often cheaper.
  • Enough for many users.

GPS plus Cellular:

  • Can have mobile service if activated with a compatible carrier.
  • Can make calls and use data without the iPhone in more situations.
  • Usually more expensive.
  • Requires compatible carrier and plan.
  • Uses more battery when using mobile data.
  • Before paying extra for Cellular, check whether your carrier supports Apple Watch service in your country.

Carrier compatibility

A Cellular Apple Watch requires carrier support.

  • Not all carriers support Apple Watch.
  • Not all plans include it.
  • It may cost extra.
  • It may depend on country or region.

If you buy a Cellular Apple Watch and your carrier does not support it, the watch can still work as a GPS model, but you will not get Cellular independence. Check this before buying.

Model and health features

Not all Apple Watch models have the same health features.

Depending on model and region, features may include or exclude:

  • ECG.
  • Blood oxygen.
  • Wrist temperature.
  • Sleep apnoea notifications.
  • Hypertension-related notifications.
  • Advanced sensors.
  • Fall Detection.
  • Crash Detection.
  • Other features.
  • If you want a specific feature, check that the exact model supports it in your country.

Do not rely on general phrases such as “Apple Watch has ECG.”

Ask:

  • Which Apple Watch model?
  • Which country?
  • Which watchOS version?
  • Is the feature available here?

Battery health

Battery health matters a lot in used or refurbished watches. An older battery may last much less.

To check battery health, if the watch can be accessed:

  • Open Settings.
  • Go to Battery.
  • Look for Battery Health, if available.
  • Check maximum capacity.
  • If battery health is low, the watch may need service or may not last all day.
  • This affects sleep tracking, workouts, and safety features.

Physical condition

Check:

  • Screen scratches.
  • Cracks.
  • Digital Crown movement.
  • Side button.
  • Back sensors.
  • Charging contact.
  • Strap slots.
  • Speaker.
  • Microphone.
  • Water damage signs.
  • Case damage.

A scratched screen may not matter much to a totally blind user, but cracks, sensor damage, button problems, or charging problems matter.

Water resistance

Apple Watch water resistance can decrease over time. A used watch may have been exposed to water, impacts, repairs, or wear. Do not assume an old used watch has the same water resistance as when it was new. If swimming or water use matters, be especially cautious.

Straps and sizes

Apple Watch comes in different case sizes. Bands must match compatible sizes.

Before buying:

  • Check case size.
  • Check strap compatibility.
  • Check wrist comfort.
  • Check whether the strap is easy to put on by touch.
  • For blind users, the strap should be practical, not just attractive.
  • A beautiful strap that is difficult to fasten is just a small daily punishment with branding.

Which model to choose

The right model depends on needs.

Basic use:

  1. Notifications.
  2. Calls.
  3. Messages.
  4. Timers.
  5. Activity.
  6. Basic workouts.
  7. Heart rate.

More advanced health:

  1. ECG.
  2. Sleep features.
  3. Temperature.
  4. Other sensors.

Outdoor use:

  1. Better battery.
  2. GPS.
  3. Cellular if needed.
  4. Durability.

Older person or safety use:

  • Fall Detection.
  • Emergency SOS.
  • Good battery.
  • Simple setup.
  • Strong haptics.
  • For a beginner, the newest model is not always necessary.
  • But buying too old a model may limit updates and features.

Buying from a private seller

If buying from a private seller:

  • Meet in a safe place.
  • Check the watch before paying.
  • Ask the seller to unpair it.
  • Make sure it does not ask for their Apple Account.
  • Check serial and model.
  • Check charging.
  • Check battery health if possible.
  • Do not accept excuses about Activation Lock.
  • If the seller says “you can unlock it later”, walk away from the purchase.
  • “Later” is where bad purchases go to die.

Buying online

Buying used online has more risk.

Check:

  • Seller reputation.
  • Return policy.
  • Clear photos.
  • Exact model.
  • Battery health if stated.
  • Activation Lock guarantee.
  • Warranty.
  • Payment protection.
  • Avoid deals that are too good to be true.
  • They often are.

Accessories

Check whether the watch includes:

  • Charging cable.
  • Strap.
  • Original box, if relevant.
  • Documentation, if relevant.
  • Power adapter may or may not be included depending on model and seller.
  • Make sure you have a compatible charger.

Software support

Older Apple Watch models may stop receiving major watchOS updates.

This affects:

  • New features.
  • Security updates.
  • App compatibility.
  • Health features.
  • Future support.
  • Before buying an older model, check whether it still supports current watchOS or whether it fits your needs anyway.
  • The cheapest watch may not be the best value if it is already near the end of support.

For blind users

For a blind user, consider:

  • VoiceOver support.
  • Haptic strength.
  • Battery life.
  • Ease of using Digital Crown and side button.
  • Useful health features.
  • Compatibility with current iPhone.
  • Simple app navigation.
  • Good strap.
  • Charging routine.
  • Do not buy based only on appearance.
  • The visual design may matter less than tactile controls, battery, and supported features.

For older people

For older people, consider:

  • Fall Detection.
  • Emergency SOS.
  • Battery life.
  • Clear haptics.
  • Simple watch face.
  • Comfortable strap.
  • Cellular if they go out without iPhone.
  • Medical ID and emergency contacts.
  • Ease of charging.
  • Support from family or caregiver.
  • The watch must be configured simply.
  • Too many apps and alerts can confuse.

Questions to ask before buying

  • Which exact model is it?
  • What size is it?
  • Is it GPS or Cellular?
  • Is it compatible with my iPhone?
  • Is Activation Lock removed?
  • What is battery health?
  • Does it include charger?
  • Does it have warranty?
  • Has it been repaired?
  • Does it have water damage?
  • Are the buttons working?
  • Is the screen damaged?
  • Does it support the health features I need?
  • Is Cellular supported by my carrier?

Common mistakes

  • Buying a used watch still linked to another account.
  • Buying Cellular without checking carrier support.
  • Buying too old a model.

Assuming every Apple Watch has the same health features.

  • Ignoring battery health.
  • Not checking iPhone compatibility.
  • Not checking charger.
  • Choosing a strap that is difficult to use.
  • Trusting the word refurbished without details.
  • Buying for a safety use without checking Emergency SOS and Fall Detection support.

Practical advice

  • If the budget allows, buying new or officially refurbished is usually safer.
  • If buying used, check Activation Lock before paying.
  • If buying for health or safety, do not choose only by price.
  • If buying for a blind user, prioritise comfort, battery, VoiceOver, haptics, and support.

The best Apple Watch is not always the newest or most expensive one. It is the one that actually fits the user’s needs and works reliably.

Exercise for module 58

Before buying an Apple Watch, create a checklist:

  • Exact model.
  • Size.
  • GPS or Cellular.
  • iPhone compatibility.
  • watchOS support.
  • Battery health.
  • Activation Lock removed.
  • Charger included.
  • Warranty or return policy.
  • Health features needed.
  • Carrier support if Cellular.
  • Physical condition.
  • Strap comfort.
  • VoiceOver and accessibility needs.
  • Use this checklist before paying.
  • If buying used, do not complete the purchase until the watch can be paired or at least shown as free from Activation Lock.

Summary of module 58

A new Apple Watch is usually the safest purchase. A used Apple Watch may be cheaper but must be checked carefully. Activation Lock is the most important risk in second-hand watches. Refurbished quality depends greatly on the seller.

Official Apple refurbished products are usually safer where available.

  • Battery health matters.
  • GPS and Cellular models are not the same.
  • Cellular requires carrier support.
  • Not all models have the same health features.
  • The watch must be compatible with the iPhone.
  • For blind users, practical use matters more than appearance.
