Module 59. Resetting, unpairing, and changing iPhone

At some point, you may need to reset the Apple Watch, unpair it from the iPhone, or pair it with a new iPhone.

This can happen for several reasons:

  • You bought a new iPhone.
  • You are selling or giving away the Apple Watch.
  • The watch has serious problems.
  • You want to start over.
  • The watch belongs to another person.
  • You need to remove your data.
  • You are changing Apple Account or setup.

These processes must be done carefully, because the Apple Watch is linked to your Apple Account, health data, backup, Activation Lock, Wallet cards, and iPhone. Unpairing is not the same as simply erasing without understanding what happens.

What unpairing means

Unpairing means disconnecting the Apple Watch from the iPhone it is paired with. When you unpair correctly from the Watch app on the iPhone, the system usually creates a backup of the Apple Watch and removes it from the iPhone. It may also remove Activation Lock if the correct Apple Account credentials are provided. This is the recommended method if you still have the iPhone.

When to unpair

You should unpair when:

  • You are going to sell the Apple Watch.
  • You are giving it to someone else.
  • You are pairing it with a different iPhone.
  • You need to solve certain serious problems.
  • You want to erase it properly.
  • You are returning it.
  • You no longer want to use it.
  • If you are only restarting because something minor failed, unpairing is not usually necessary.
  • Restart first.
  • Unpair only when appropriate.

Unpairing from the iPhone

To unpair from the iPhone:

  • Keep the Apple Watch and iPhone close together.
  • Open the Watch app on the iPhone.
  • Go to My Watch.
  • Open All Watches if it appears.
  • Choose the Apple Watch.
  • Find the information button or watch details.
  • Choose Unpair Apple Watch.
  • Follow the instructions.
  • Enter the Apple Account password if asked.
  • Wait for the process to complete.
  • The exact labels may vary depending on iOS version.
  • With VoiceOver, listen carefully before confirming.
  • Do not interrupt the process.

Backup during unpairing

When unpairing correctly, the iPhone usually creates a backup of the Apple Watch. This backup may later be used to restore the watch. The backup can include settings, app layout, watch faces, and other data. Some items may not be included, such as certain cards in Wallet, Bluetooth pairings, or security-related items. Health and activity data are handled through the iPhone and iCloud Health settings, depending on configuration. Before unpairing, it is useful to make sure the iPhone itself is backed up.

Activation Lock

Activation Lock protects the Apple Watch if it is lost or stolen. If you are selling or giving away the Apple Watch, Activation Lock must be removed. Unpairing from the iPhone with the correct Apple Account usually removes Activation Lock. If you simply erase the watch without removing it from your account, the next person may not be able to use it. This is why used Apple Watch purchases can become a small tragedy in aluminium and glass.

Erasing the Apple Watch from settings

You can erase the Apple Watch from the watch itself.

On the Apple Watch:

  • Open Settings.
  • Go to General.
  • Look for Reset.
  • Choose Erase All Content and Settings.
  • Follow the instructions.
  • However, if you erase it this way without unpairing properly, Activation Lock may remain.
  • If you are keeping the watch and pairing again yourself, that may be manageable.
  • If you are giving or selling the watch, unpairing from the iPhone is usually better.

Erasing from Find My

You may also erase the Apple Watch remotely from Find My if it is lost or stolen. This is a different situation. Remote erase should be used carefully. It may protect your information, but Activation Lock may still remain. Do not use remote erase for ordinary setup changes unless you understand what you are doing.

Changing to a new iPhone

If you get a new iPhone, there are usually ways to transfer or restore your Apple Watch setup. The exact process depends on iOS, watchOS, backups, and whether both iPhones are available.

A general approach:

  • Back up the old iPhone.
  • Set up the new iPhone.
  • Make sure you use the same Apple Account.
  • During setup, the system may offer to transfer the Apple Watch.
  • Follow the instructions.
  • Keep Apple Watch and iPhone nearby.
  • If needed, unpair from the old iPhone and pair with the new one.
  • The process may vary.
  • If the old iPhone is still available, it is usually easier.

If the old iPhone is lost or broken

If the old iPhone is not available, pairing the Apple Watch with a new iPhone may be more complicated. You may need to erase the Apple Watch and pair it again. Activation Lock may require your Apple Account password. Health and activity data restoration depends on backups and iCloud settings.

Before erasing, make sure you know:

  • Apple Account email.
  • Apple Account password.
  • Apple Watch passcode, if needed.
  • Whether iCloud Health sync was enabled.
  • Whether the iPhone backup is available.

Setting up as new or restoring from backup

When pairing again, you may be offered:

  • Set Up as New Apple Watch.
  • Restore from Backup.
  • If you want to recover settings, choose a backup.
  • If you want a clean start, choose setup as new.
  • For a beginner, restoring may save work.
  • But if the previous setup was confusing, setting up as new may be cleaner.

Before selling or giving away the watch

Before selling or giving away:

  • Unpair from the iPhone.
  • Remove Activation Lock.
  • Erase content.
  • Remove Wallet cards from the watch.
  • Remove from Find My if needed through proper unpairing.
  • Clean the watch physically.
  • Include charger and strap if agreed.
  • Make sure it no longer appears linked to your account.
  • Do not hand over a watch that still asks for your Apple Account.
  • That is not a gift. It is a future support call with a strap.

Before buying a second-hand watch

Ask the seller to:

  • Unpair it from their iPhone.
  • Remove Activation Lock.
  • Erase all content.
  • Show that it starts setup without asking for their Apple Account.
  • If possible, begin pairing enough to confirm it is not locked.
  • If the watch asks for someone else’s Apple Account, do not proceed.

Reset for troubleshooting

Sometimes people reset too quickly.

Before erasing the Apple Watch because something does not work, try:

  • Restarting the Apple Watch.
  • Restarting the iPhone.
  • Checking connection.
  • Checking Wi-Fi and Bluetooth.
  • Checking battery.
  • Checking settings.
  • Updating iOS and watchOS.
  • Checking the Watch app.
  • Removing and reinstalling a problematic app.
  • Only consider unpairing or resetting if simpler steps fail.

Backing up the iPhone

Because Apple Watch backups are linked to the iPhone, keeping the iPhone backed up is important. Use iCloud Backup or computer backup, depending on your setup. If you rely on health data, check Health data sync and backup settings. Health data are sensitive and may require encrypted backups in some computer backup cases.

Wallet and Apple Pay after reset

After unpairing or resetting, cards in Wallet may need to be added again. Apple Pay cards are not always restored automatically for security reasons.

After pairing again:

  • Open the Watch app.
  • Go to Wallet and Apple Pay.
  • Add cards again if needed.
  • Verify with the bank if required.
  • Do not assume payment will work immediately after restoring.

Passcode after reset

After resetting or pairing, you will likely need to configure a passcode again. If you use Apple Pay, a passcode is required. If you use the watch for privacy or safety, a passcode is strongly recommended.

Data that may be lost

Depending on backup and sync settings, some data may not return exactly as before.

Possible affected areas:

  • Unsynced activity.
  • Settings changed recently.
  • Downloaded music or podcasts.
  • Wallet cards.
  • Bluetooth pairings.
  • Some app data.
  • Watch faces, depending on backup.
  • Before resetting, make sure important data are synced or backed up where possible.

When to contact Apple Support

Contact Apple Support if:

  • The watch cannot be unpaired.
  • Activation Lock behaves unexpectedly.
  • The watch will not erase.
  • Pairing repeatedly fails.
  • You cannot access your Apple Account.
  • The watch is stuck during setup.
  • The watch fails after update or reset.
  • Do not try random steps with account or activation issues.
  • That usually makes the mess more decorated, not more solved.

Common mistakes

Erasing the watch instead of unpairing it before selling.

  • Forgetting Activation Lock.
  • Not knowing the Apple Account password.
  • Resetting without backing up the iPhone.
  • Assuming Wallet cards will remain.
  • Changing iPhone without checking watch transfer.
  • Buying a used locked watch.
  • Resetting as the first troubleshooting step.
  • Interrupting the unpairing process.
  • Giving away a watch still linked to your account.

Practical advice

  • If you still have the iPhone, unpair from the Watch app.
  • If selling or giving away, make sure Activation Lock is removed.
  • If changing iPhone, back up first.
  • If troubleshooting, restart and check settings before resetting.
  • If buying used, never accept a watch that still asks for the previous owner’s Apple Account.

Exercise for module 59

Do not reset your Apple Watch just for practice. Instead, review where the options are.

On the iPhone:

  • Open the Watch app.
  • Go to My Watch.
  • Find All Watches if it appears.
  • Locate your Apple Watch information.
  • Find where Unpair Apple Watch would be, but do not activate it.
  • Then open Find My.
  • Check that the Apple Watch appears under Devices.
  • Then open the Watch app again.
  • Review Wallet and Apple Pay if you use cards.
  • Review Passcode.
  • Review your Apple Account information.
  • The goal is to know where the settings are without erasing anything.

Summary of module 59

Unpairing disconnects the Apple Watch from the iPhone. Unpairing from the Watch app usually creates a backup and removes Activation Lock if done correctly. Erasing the watch from settings is not always enough before selling or giving it away. Activation Lock must be removed before another person can use the watch. Changing to a new iPhone requires backup, transfer, or pairing again. Wallet cards may need to be added again after reset. Do not reset as the first troubleshooting step. Before selling, giving away, or buying used, check account lock carefully.

Module 60. Common problems and basic troubleshooting

Even when the Apple Watch is well configured, problems can appear. The watch may stop speaking, fail to receive notifications, lose connection with the iPhone, stop vibrating, drain battery quickly, fail to charge, not record sleep, not start workouts properly, or behave strangely after an update. This module gathers common problems and first steps to solve them.

The idea is not to turn every user into a technician. The idea is to know what to check before panicking, resetting the watch, or declaring that the device has developed a personality disorder.

General rule: check the simple things first

Before doing anything drastic, check:

  • Battery.
  • Connection.
  • Whether the watch is on the wrist.
  • Whether it is unlocked.
  • Wi-Fi and Bluetooth.
  • Airplane Mode.
  • Focus modes.
  • Silent Mode.
  • Volume.
  • Haptic settings.
  • watchOS and iOS updates.
  • Whether the iPhone is nearby.
  • Whether the feature is available on your model.
  • Many problems come from one of these points.

VoiceOver does not speak

If VoiceOver does not speak:

  • Check whether VoiceOver is turned on.
  • Triple-click the Digital Crown if the accessibility shortcut is configured.
  • Use Siri if available and say: turn on VoiceOver.
  • Open the Watch app on the iPhone.
  • Go to Accessibility.
  • Go to VoiceOver.
  • Turn VoiceOver on.
  • Check volume.
  • Check whether audio is going to headphones.
  • Check whether the watch is muted or volume is too low.
  • If VoiceOver is on but silent, audio output or volume may be the issue.

The watch does not vibrate

If the Apple Watch does not vibrate:

  • Open the Watch app on the iPhone.
  • Go to Sounds and Haptics.
  • Check Haptic Alerts.
  • Enable Prominent Haptic if needed.
  • Check that the watch is on the wrist.
  • Check strap adjustment.
  • Check Focus modes.
  • Check notifications.
  • Test with a timer.
  • If the timer vibrates but messages do not, the issue may be notification settings.
  • If nothing vibrates, haptic settings or hardware may need review.

Notifications do not arrive

If notifications do not arrive:

  • Check that the watch is on your wrist.
  • Check that it is unlocked.
  • Check connection with the iPhone.
  • Check Bluetooth.
  • Check Wi-Fi.
  • Check Airplane Mode.
  • Check Focus modes.
  • Check Notification settings in the Watch app.
  • Check notification settings on the iPhone.
  • Check whether the iPhone is active. If you are using the iPhone, some notifications may appear there instead.
  • Check that the app supports Apple Watch notifications.
  • Do not forget Focus modes. They are responsible for many “mysterious” silences, because apparently one setting can impersonate a broken device rather convincingly.

Calls do not arrive

If calls do not arrive on the Apple Watch:

  • Check that the watch is connected.
  • Check that the iPhone is nearby if the watch is GPS.
  • Check Cellular service if using a Cellular model.
  • Check Airplane Mode.
  • Check Focus modes.
  • Check Phone notifications.
  • Check Bluetooth.
  • Check whether the watch is locked.
  • Check whether the iPhone receives the call.
  • If the iPhone itself does not receive the call, the problem is not the watch.

Messages do not arrive

If messages do not arrive:

  • Check Messages notifications in the Watch app.
  • Check Messages notifications on the iPhone.
  • Check Focus modes.
  • Check connection.
  • Check whether you are using the iPhone at that moment.
  • Check the app type. Not all messaging apps behave the same on Apple Watch.
  • For third-party apps, check whether they support replies or only notifications.

The watch is disconnected from the iPhone

If the Apple Watch loses connection:

  • Bring the devices close together.
  • Check Bluetooth on the iPhone.
  • Check Wi-Fi.
  • Check Airplane Mode on both devices.
  • Restart the Apple Watch.
  • Restart the iPhone.
  • Check whether the watch is paired.
  • Open the Watch app.
  • Check if the Apple Watch appears connected.
  • If it repeatedly disconnects, review updates or possible pairing problems.

The watch does not charge

If the watch does not charge:

  • Check the charger is connected to power.
  • Check the power adapter.
  • Check the wall socket.
  • Place the watch again on the magnetic charger.
  • Make sure the back touches the charger.
  • Remove any protective film.
  • Check that the charger surface is clean.
  • Try another compatible charger if available.
  • Try another power adapter.
  • Wait a few minutes if the battery is completely empty.
  • If nothing works, technical support may be needed.

The watch turns off quickly

If battery drains quickly:

  • Check battery health.
  • Check recent updates.
  • Check Always-On display.
  • Check brightness.
  • Check notifications.
  • Check Cellular use.
  • Check workouts and GPS.
  • Check audio streaming.
  • Check background apps.
  • Restart the watch.
  • Restart the iPhone.
  • Observe whether the problem continues for more than a day after an update.
  • If battery health is low, service may be needed.

The watch is slow

If the Apple Watch feels slow:

  • Restart it.
  • Check available storage.
  • Remove unused apps.
  • Update watchOS if appropriate.
  • Check battery health.
  • Close or avoid unnecessary apps.
  • If it is an older model, performance may be limited by age.
  • Older devices do not become faster with optimism. Tragic, but measurable.

The Digital Crown does not respond well

If the Digital Crown does not respond:

  • Check whether it is physically stuck.
  • Turn it gently.
  • Check whether debris or moisture may be present.
  • Restart the watch.
  • Check whether the issue happens everywhere or only in one app.
  • If the Digital Crown is physically damaged, technical support may be needed.
  • Do not force it.

The side button does not respond well

If the side button does not respond:

  • Check whether it is stuck.
  • Press it gently.
  • Restart the watch.
  • Check whether the function has changed with watchOS version.
  • Check whether you are pressing once, twice, or holding it down.
  • If it is physically damaged, seek support.
  • Do not press repeatedly with force.

VoiceOver gestures do not work well

If gestures do not work well:

  • Check that VoiceOver is on.
  • Use smaller gestures.
  • Do not swipe too hard.
  • Clean the screen.
  • Dry the screen if wet.
  • Check whether Water Lock is on.
  • Check whether the watch is responding slowly.
  • Restart if needed.
  • The Apple Watch screen is small, so gestures need precision.

Water Lock is on and the screen does not respond

If Water Lock is enabled, the screen may not respond normally. To turn it off, follow the watch instructions. Usually, you need to press and hold or turn the Digital Crown, depending on watchOS version. Listen to VoiceOver instructions if available. If Water Lock was activated by mistake, unlock it carefully and continue.

The watch does not record sleep

If sleep is not recorded:

  • Check that you wore the watch.
  • Check battery.
  • Check Sleep tracking settings.
  • Check sleep schedule.
  • Check that the watch was unlocked.
  • Check strap adjustment.
  • Check Health app data.
  • Check whether the watch was too loose.
  • Remember that some sleep data may require several nights.
  • If only one night failed, observe before changing everything.

Heart rate is not recorded well

If heart rate readings fail:

  • Adjust the strap.
  • Place the watch slightly above the wrist bone.
  • Clean the sensors.
  • Keep your arm still for manual readings.
  • Use a suitable strap during workouts.
  • Check whether tattoos or poor contact affect the sensor area.
  • Check battery.
  • If readings continue to fail, review support options.

Workout was not recorded correctly

If a workout is missing or wrong:

  • Check whether you started the workout.
  • Check whether you chose the correct type.
  • Check whether the watch had battery.
  • Check whether location was enabled for outdoor workouts.
  • Check whether you ended the workout properly.
  • Check Fitness on the iPhone.
  • Check whether data synced.
  • If you forgot to start the workout, some activity may still be recorded, but not as a complete workout.

Workout is still running

If the workout continues after you finished:

  • Open the Workout app.
  • Find the active workout screen.
  • Find End.
  • Double tap.
  • Confirm if needed.
  • Listen to the summary.
  • Find Done.
  • Leaving the app is not enough.
  • You need to end the workout.

Weather does not update

If weather does not update:

  • Check connection.
  • Check location permissions.
  • Open Weather on the iPhone.
  • Check the correct city.
  • Check whether the Apple Watch is connected.
  • Check Focus or Low Power Mode if relevant.
  • Restart if needed.

Siri does not work

If Siri does not respond:

  • Check Siri settings in the Watch app.
  • Check connection.
  • Check microphone.
  • Check whether Siri is enabled.
  • Check language.
  • Check whether you are invoking Siri correctly.
  • Try holding the Digital Crown.
  • Try a simple command.
  • If Siri misunderstands often, use shorter commands.

Apple Pay does not work

If Apple Pay fails:

  • Check the card is added to the Apple Watch.
  • Check passcode is enabled.
  • Check the watch is unlocked and on your wrist.
  • Double-press the side button, not the Digital Crown.
  • Check the terminal supports contactless payments.
  • Check with your bank if the card is blocked.
  • Check whether the card needs verification.
  • Check whether Wallet opens correctly.

Do not wait until you are in a crowded queue to discover which button opens Wallet. The queue will not become more patient because accessibility is involved.

The watch asks for a passcode too often

If the watch asks for passcode frequently:

  • Check strap fit.
  • Check wrist detection.
  • Check whether the watch is too loose.
  • Check whether it is being removed from the wrist.
  • Check tattoos or sensor contact.
  • If the watch thinks it has been removed, it may lock.

The watch is locked and you forgot the passcode

If you forgot the Apple Watch passcode, you may need to erase it and pair again. This can be done through the Watch app or recovery steps, depending on situation. You will need the Apple Account to remove Activation Lock if required. Before erasing, understand that data may depend on backups. If unsure, consult Apple Support.

The watch is asking for another person’s Apple Account

This is Activation Lock. It means the watch is still linked to another account. You need the previous owner to remove it from their account. Erasing alone will not solve it. If you bought it used and cannot contact the previous owner, the watch may not be usable. There is no legitimate shortcut around this.

The watch does not update

If watchOS update fails:

  • Check iPhone Wi-Fi.
  • Check Apple Watch battery.
  • Place watch on charger.
  • Keep iPhone nearby.
  • Check storage.
  • Restart iPhone and watch.
  • Try again later.
  • Remove unused apps or content if storage is low.
  • Do not interrupt the update.

The watch is too cluttered

If navigation is confusing:

  • Switch to List View.
  • Remove unused apps.
  • Reduce notifications.
  • Use a simple watch face.
  • Keep only useful complications.
  • Use Siri for common tasks.
  • Configure the Watch app from the iPhone.
  • The Apple Watch becomes easier when it is not overloaded.

The problem appeared after an update

If something changed after an update:

  • Check settings.
  • Review VoiceOver.
  • Review notifications.
  • Review Control Centre behaviour.
  • Check accessibility shortcut.
  • Check app updates.
  • Restart both devices.
  • Look for reports from other users if needed.
  • Some changes are intentional.
  • Others may be bugs.

The iPhone is often the rescue tool

If the Apple Watch becomes hard to use, go to the iPhone.

From the Watch app, you can manage:

  • VoiceOver.
  • Notifications.
  • Sounds and Haptics.
  • Passcode.
  • Apps.
  • Watch faces.
  • Siri.
  • General settings.
  • Software updates.
  • Accessibility.
  • The iPhone screen is larger and often easier with VoiceOver.

When to restart

Restarting can help with many temporary problems.

Restart the Apple Watch if:

  • It behaves strangely.
  • Apps do not open.
  • Connection seems stuck.
  • VoiceOver behaves oddly.
  • Battery display seems wrong.
  • Some controls do not respond.
  • Also restart the iPhone if the problem involves connection, notifications, pairing, or syncing.

Restarting is not magic, but sometimes it clears temporary confusion. A rare case where turning something off and on again deserves its reputation.

When to unpair and pair again

Unpairing and pairing again is more drastic.

Consider it if:

  • Connection problems persist.
  • Settings are badly corrupted.
  • Major syncing problems continue.
  • Apple Support recommends it.
  • You are changing iPhone.
  • You are selling or giving away the watch.
  • Do not unpair as the first step for minor issues.

When to contact Apple Support

Contact Apple Support or an authorised service provider if:

  • The watch does not charge with known good chargers.
  • Buttons are physically damaged.
  • Screen is damaged.
  • Sensors fail repeatedly.
  • Battery health is poor.
  • Activation Lock issues are unclear.
  • Pairing repeatedly fails.
  • The watch is stuck during update.
  • Serious hardware problems appear.

Common troubleshooting mistakes

  • Resetting too quickly.
  • Ignoring Focus modes.
  • Forgetting Airplane Mode.
  • Not checking battery.
  • Not checking whether the watch is locked.
  • Not using the iPhone Watch app to fix settings.
  • Assuming every missing feature is a VoiceOver problem.
  • Not checking model or country availability.
  • Forgetting that GPS and Cellular models behave differently.
  • Trying random button combinations.

Practical advice

When something fails, use this order:

  • Check battery.
  • Check connection.
  • Check lock status.
  • Check Focus and Airplane Mode.
  • Check the relevant setting.
  • Test with a simple action.
  • Restart watch and iPhone.
  • Check updates.
  • Use the Watch app from the iPhone.
  • Only then consider unpairing or support.

Exercise for module 60

  • Choose one simple troubleshooting practice.
  • For example, notifications.
  • On the iPhone, open the Watch app.
  • Go to Notifications.
  • Check Messages or Reminders.
  • Make sure notifications are enabled.
  • Create a test reminder for a few minutes later.
  • Put on the Apple Watch.
  • Check that it is unlocked.
  • Wait for the reminder.
  • If it arrives, confirm that notifications work.
  • If it does not arrive, check Focus, connection, and notification settings.
  • Then set a one-minute timer to test haptics.
  • This teaches a basic troubleshooting method without changing dangerous settings.

Summary of module 60

Many Apple Watch problems can be solved by checking simple settings first. Battery, connection, lock status, Focus modes, Airplane Mode, notifications, volume, and haptics are common causes. The iPhone Watch app is often the easiest way to fix settings. VoiceOver can be turned on from the iPhone if needed. Notifications depend on watch status, iPhone status, app settings, and Focus modes. Charging problems should be checked with cable, adapter, socket, and placement. Storage problems can affect updates. Unpairing should not be the first solution for minor problems. If hardware, Activation Lock, or repeated pairing issues appear, contact Apple Support.

Back to table of contents

Module 61. Practical setup for a blind beginner

A person who is starting to use the Apple Watch with VoiceOver does not need to configure everything on the first day.

Trying to configure every feature at once is one of the best ways to make the watch feel confusing.

  • The best approach is progressive setup.
  • First, make the watch accessible.
  • Then, make it comfortable.
  • Then, make it useful.
  • Then, add more features only when they are truly needed.

First goal: make VoiceOver reliable

The user should be able to:

  • Turn VoiceOver on.
  • Understand what VoiceOver says.
  • Move through items.
  • Activate buttons.
  • Return to the watch face.
  • Use the Digital Crown.
  • Use the side button without confusing it with the Digital Crown.
  • Open the Watch app on the iPhone.
  • Use the iPhone to change Apple Watch settings.
  • Before configuring advanced health, workouts, or Apple Pay, the user should be able to perform these basic actions.

Second goal: configure the accessibility shortcut

The accessibility shortcut can allow VoiceOver to be turned on or off with a triple-click of the Digital Crown.

On the iPhone:

  • Open the Watch app.
  • Go to My Watch.
  • Go to Accessibility.
  • Find Accessibility Shortcut.
  • Select VoiceOver.
  • After that, triple-clicking the Digital Crown should control VoiceOver.
  • Explain that the same shortcut can also turn VoiceOver off.

Third goal: choose a simple watch face

A beginner should use a simple watch face.

Useful complications may include:

  • Battery.
  • Weather.
  • Timer.
  • Calendar or Reminders.
  • Activity, if useful.
  • Do not start with a watch face full of information.
  • The main goal is to understand the screen, not to decorate it with complications.

Fourth goal: use List View

The app view should usually be set to List View. List View is easier with VoiceOver because apps are arranged in order. Grid View may be attractive visually, but it can be less practical for a blind beginner.

Fifth goal: reduce notifications

A beginner should not receive every notification on the watch.

Start with only the most useful:

  • Phone.
  • Messages.
  • Calendar.
  • Reminders.
  • Timers.
  • Alarms.
  • Medication, if used.
  • Important health alerts, if configured.
  • Battery.
  • Disable promotions, games, social networks, news apps, and non-urgent alerts at first.

Sixth goal: configure haptics

Haptics are essential.

From the Watch app on the iPhone:

  • Go to Sounds and Haptics.
  • Enable Haptic Alerts.
  • Enable Prominent Haptic if needed.
  • Adjust volume.
  • Test with a timer.
  • An alert that cannot be felt or heard is not an alert. It is merely a failed ambition with a watch strap.

Seventh goal: learn the Digital Crown and side button

The user should physically identify:

  • Digital Crown.
  • Side button.
  • The Digital Crown is round and can be turned.
  • The side button is elongated and does not turn.

The user should practise pressing the Digital Crown once, turning the Digital Crown, pressing the side button once, and returning to the watch face. The user should not practise holding down the side button without understanding Emergency SOS.

Eighth goal: learn Control Centre

Control Centre gives access to useful quick controls.

The user should learn to:

  • Open Control Centre.
  • Check battery.
  • Turn Silent Mode on or off.
  • Find the button to make the iPhone play a sound.
  • Check Airplane Mode.
  • Check Focus modes.
  • Finding the iPhone from the watch is one of the first features worth mastering.

Ninth goal: configure passcode and unlock

The Apple Watch should have a passcode. This protects the device and is required for some features such as Apple Pay. The user should understand that the watch may lock when removed from the wrist and that the passcode unlocks it.

Tenth goal: learn timers and alarms

Timers and alarms are very useful and easy to test. The user should learn to set a timer with Siri, stop a timer, set an alarm, stop an alarm, feel the vibration, and use the Timers app. This is a safe practice area.

Eleventh goal: learn calls and messages

Once the basics are understood, calls and messages can be practised with a trusted person. The user should learn how an incoming call feels, how VoiceOver announces the caller, how to answer, how to decline, how to hang up, how to read a message, and how to reply with dictation or quick replies.

Twelfth goal: configure emergency basics

After basic use is understood, configure Medical ID, emergency contacts, Emergency SOS review, and Fall Detection if appropriate. The user should know that Emergency SOS is not for testing and that emergency contacts may be notified.

Thirteenth goal: configure health gradually

Health features should be added gradually. Start with heart rate, activity, sleep if desired, and medication if needed. Then add ECG, irregular rhythm notifications, blood oxygen, sleep apnoea notifications, cycle tracking, or other model-specific features where available.

Suggested first-day setup

For the first day, configure only:

  • VoiceOver.
  • Speech rate.
  • Accessibility shortcut.
  • Simple watch face.
  • Battery complication.
  • List View.
  • Haptic Alerts.
  • Prominent Haptic if needed.
  • Passcode.
  • Basic notifications.
  • Find iPhone from Control Centre.
  • Timer test.
  • That is enough for one day.

Common mistakes with beginners

  • Configuring too much at once.
  • Leaving all notifications enabled.
  • Using a complicated watch face.
  • Using Grid View.
  • Not configuring the accessibility shortcut.
  • Not testing haptics.
  • Not explaining the side button.
  • Activating Apple Pay too early.
  • Not creating a charging routine.
  • Teaching health features before basic navigation.

Practical advice

Start simple. The Apple Watch becomes useful when the user controls it. Not when every possible feature is activated. A well-configured simple watch is better than a complete setup that nobody understands.

Exercise for module 61

Configure the Apple Watch for a beginner using this order:

  • Turn on VoiceOver.
  • Adjust speech rate.
  • Configure the accessibility shortcut.
  • Choose a simple watch face.
  • Add battery as a complication.
  • Set apps to List View.
  • Enable haptic alerts.
  • Test a timer.
  • Open Control Centre.
  • Find the battery percentage.
  • Make the iPhone play a sound.
  • Open the app list.
  • Open Timers.
  • Return to the watch face.
  • Answer a test call.
  • Read a test message.
  • Charge the watch at the same time each day.
  • Do not configure advanced features until these actions are comfortable.

Summary of module 61

A blind beginner should not configure everything at once.

VoiceOver, haptics, accessibility shortcut, simple watch face, and List View come first.

  • Notifications should be reduced.
  • Battery and charging routines are essential.
  • Timers and alarms are good first practice features.
  • Calls and messages should be practised with a trusted person.
  • Health, workouts, Apple Pay, and safety features should be added gradually.
  • A simple, understandable Apple Watch is more useful than an overloaded one.

Back to table of contents

Module 62. Recommended setup for older people

The Apple Watch can be especially useful for older people. It can help with time, reminders, medication, calls, emergency contacts, fall detection, activity, heart rate, sleep, and safety. But the setup should be simple. The goal is not to give an older person every possible feature. The goal is to configure the watch so it is useful, understandable, and not overwhelming.

Main priorities

For older people, the most useful priorities are usually:

  • Clear time access.
  • Strong haptics.
  • Calls.
  • Important messages.
  • Medication reminders, if needed.
  • Calendar or appointments.
  • Alarms and timers.
  • Medical ID.
  • Emergency contacts.
  • Fall Detection, if appropriate.
  • Emergency SOS.
  • Heart rate alerts, if appropriate.
  • Battery routine.
  • Simple watch face.
  • Everything else can be secondary.

Simple watch face

Choose a simple watch face with few elements.

Useful complications may include:

  • Battery.
  • Date.
  • Weather.
  • Timer or Alarms.
  • Medication, if used.
  • Calendar.
  • Heart Rate, if useful.
  • Avoid complicated watch faces and too many complications.

Haptics and volume

For older people, alerts must be noticeable.

From the Watch app:

  • Go to Sounds and Haptics.
  • Set a comfortable alert volume.
  • Enable Haptic Alerts.
  • Enable Prominent Haptic if needed.
  • Test with a timer.
  • If the person has hearing loss, haptics may be more important than sound.
  • If the person has reduced tactile sensitivity, standard vibrations may not be enough.

Notifications

Limit notifications.

Recommended alerts:

  • Phone.
  • Messages from important contacts.
  • Calendar.
  • Reminders.
  • Medication.
  • Alarms.
  • Timers.
  • Health alerts.
  • Emergency-related alerts.
  • Battery.
  • Avoid games, promotions, social networks, repeated news alerts, shopping apps, and non-urgent notifications.
  • Too many notifications can make the person ignore all of them.

Calls

Calls are often one of the most useful features. The person should learn how the watch alerts for a call, how to answer, how to decline, how to hang up, and how to call a favourite contact. Favourite contacts should be configured on the iPhone.

Messages

Messages may be useful, but replying from the watch may be harder for some older users.

Keep it simple:

  1. Read message.
  2. Use quick reply.
  3. Use dictation only if comfortable.
  4. Use iPhone for longer replies.

Medication reminders

If the person takes medication regularly, medication reminders may be useful. Configure them from the Health app on the iPhone. Check medication names, times, frequency, notifications, whether the person can feel or hear the reminder, and whether they understand how to mark it as taken. The watch records what the person marks. It cannot verify that the medicine was actually taken.

Medical ID and emergency contacts

Medical ID is important for older people. Configure relevant medical conditions, medication, allergies, emergency contacts, and brief communication notes if useful. Emergency contacts should be people who can respond. Check phone numbers and make sure the person listed knows they are an emergency contact.

Fall Detection

Fall Detection may be important for older people. Review whether the Apple Watch model supports it, whether it is enabled, whether it is set to always on or workouts only, emergency contacts, Medical ID, and battery routine. The person should know that the watch may show an alert after a detected fall. They should also know that the watch does not detect every fall.

Emergency SOS

Emergency SOS should be explained carefully. The person should know that it is for real emergencies, that it is activated through the side button, and that it should not be tested with real calls. A GPS watch may need the iPhone nearby. A Cellular watch may work more independently if configured and with coverage.

Activity reminders

Activity reminders may help some older people move during the day.

  • But they may not suit everyone.
  • Consider mobility, pain, fatigue, balance, wheelchair use, and medical advice.
  • If Stand reminders are useful, keep them.
  • If they are annoying or inappropriate, adjust them.

Battery routine

A charging routine is essential. For older people, the charger should be in a fixed place.

The routine should be simple:

  • Charge during breakfast.
  • Charge while showering.
  • Charge before bed.
  • Charge during a daily rest.
  • If sleep tracking is used, choose a daytime charging moment.
  • Add Battery as a complication.

Cellular or GPS model

For older people who go out without the iPhone, a Cellular model may be useful. It can allow calls and emergency communication with more independence. But it requires compatible carrier, active plan, coverage, battery, and correct setup. If the person always carries the iPhone, a GPS model may be enough.

Training the person

The person should practise checking time, answering a call, ending a call, stopping a timer, stopping an alarm, finding the iPhone, checking battery, charging the watch, recognising important vibrations, and responding to a fall alert if possible. Do not explain everything in one session. Repeat and simplify.

Privacy

Older people have the same right to privacy as anyone else. Health data, location, medication, and activity are personal. If location sharing or health sharing is configured, it should be done with understanding and consent where possible. Safety does not mean taking control away from the person.

Common mistakes

  • Giving the person too many notifications.
  • Not testing haptics.
  • Not setting up Medical ID.
  • Not checking emergency contacts.
  • Not explaining Emergency SOS.
  • Assuming Fall Detection detects every fall.
  • Not creating a charging routine.
  • Using a complicated watch face.
  • Not practising basic actions.

Exercise for module 62

Configure an Apple Watch for an older user using this order:

  • Simple watch face.
  • Battery complication.
  • Strong haptics.
  • Important notifications only.
  • Favourite contacts.
  • Medical ID.
  • Emergency contacts.
  • Fall Detection reviewed.
  • Emergency SOS explained.
  • Medication reminders if needed.
  • Calendar alerts if needed.
  • Timer and alarm tested.
  • Find iPhone tested.
  • Charging routine created.

Then practise with the person:

  • Answer a call.
  • End a call.
  • Stop an alarm.
  • Check battery.
  • Charge the watch.
  • Do not move to advanced features until these are comfortable.

Summary of module 62

The Apple Watch can be very useful for older people. The setup should be simple and practical. Important areas include calls, medication, calendar, haptics, safety, Medical ID, emergency contacts, and battery. Fall Detection may help, but it does not detect every fall.

Emergency SOS must be explained and not tested with real calls.

  • Notifications should be limited.
  • Battery routine is essential.
  • Privacy must be respected.
  • A simple and well-understood watch is more useful than a complex configuration full of features.

Back to table of contents

Module 63. Recommended setup for a blind advanced user

A blind advanced user may want more from the Apple Watch than basic notifications, calls, and timers. They may want to use workouts, health features, automation, Apple Pay, maps, audio, smart home, braille workflows, shortcuts, and deeper integration with the iPhone. The Apple Watch can support many advanced workflows. But advanced does not mean chaotic. A well-configured advanced setup is organised. It has the right complications, the right notifications, useful apps, strong haptics, and clear routines.

Main priorities for advanced users

An advanced blind user may care about:

  • Fast access to frequent apps.
  • Optimised watch faces.
  • Multiple watch faces for contexts.
  • Workout metrics.
  • Health alerts.
  • Apple Pay.
  • Siri.
  • Shortcuts.
  • Audio control.
  • Navigation support.
  • Smart home control.
  • Medication.
  • Sleep.
  • Focus modes.
  • Braille workflows.
  • Battery optimisation.
  • Privacy.

Multiple watch faces

Advanced users may benefit from several watch faces.

For example:

  • Daily watch face.
  • Workout watch face.
  • Health watch face.
  • Sleep watch face.
  • Travel watch face.
  • Minimal watch face.
  • Each one can have different complications.

Complication strategy

Complications should be chosen by use, not by curiosity. Good complications save time. Bad complications create noise.

Ask:

  • Do I use this every day?
  • Do I need it on my wrist?
  • Is it faster than Siri?
  • Does VoiceOver read it clearly?
  • Does it clutter the watch face?
  • For advanced users, complications can be very powerful if selected carefully.

Notifications strategy

Advanced users should be strict with notifications.

The more apps installed, the more important filtering becomes.

  • Allow only high-value wrist alerts.
  • Move medium-value alerts to the iPhone.
  • Disable low-value alerts.
  • Use Focus modes intelligently.
  • Allow important contacts.
  • Keep health and safety alerts visible.

Focus modes

Focus modes can be useful for advanced setups.

Examples:

  • Work Focus.
  • Sleep Focus.
  • Exercise Focus.
  • Recording Focus.
  • Travel Focus.
  • Do Not Disturb.
  • Each can allow different apps and contacts.
  • Focus modes require careful setup.

One badly configured Focus mode can make important alerts disappear with the elegance of a bureaucrat losing a form.

Siri for advanced workflows

Siri can be used for fast actions:

  • Start workouts.
  • Set reminders.
  • Open apps.
  • Send messages.
  • Control smart home.
  • Start timers.
  • Check weather.
  • Start navigation.
  • Play audio.
  • Run some shortcuts, depending on compatibility.
  • The clearer the command, the better.

Shortcuts

Some Shortcuts may be available from the Apple Watch. This depends on the shortcut, permissions, apps, and whether it supports Apple Watch. Shortcuts can automate actions such as starting routines, logging information, sending messages, controlling smart home devices, creating notes, starting timers, changing Focus modes, or opening useful workflows. Not every iPhone shortcut is practical on the watch. A shortcut designed for a large screen may be awkward on the wrist. Shortcut names should be clear so Siri can understand them and VoiceOver can read them easily.

Apple Pay

Advanced users may use Apple Pay often.

Recommended setup:

  • Correct default card.
  • Passcode enabled.
  • Know how to change cards.
  • Confirm payment amount.
  • Use side button, not Digital Crown.
  • Carry backup payment at first.
  • Payment is not an area for guessing.

Maps and navigation

Advanced users may use the Apple Watch as a companion to iPhone navigation.

Recommended workflow:

  • Plan route on iPhone.
  • Start route on iPhone.
  • Use watch for haptic prompts.
  • Check instructions only when stopped.
  • Use headphones carefully.
  • Use specialised navigation apps if needed.
  • Share location when appropriate.
  • The Apple Watch should complement orientation, not replace it.

Audio workflows

Advanced users may use the watch to control music, podcasts, audiobooks, workout audio, VoiceOver, calls, playback from iPhone, and playback from watch. Know the audio output, use Now Playing, download content if going without iPhone, check battery, and keep environmental awareness outdoors.

Smart home workflows

Advanced users may control Home accessories.

Recommended setup:

  • Clear device names.
  • Clear room names.
  • Useful scenes.
  • Few but powerful automations.
  • Watch complications or Siri commands for frequent actions.
  • Avoid risky devices on smart plugs.
  • Review privacy and access.

Braille workflows

Advanced braille users may combine Apple Watch haptic alerts, iPhone braille display, VoiceOver, and selected notifications.

  • The watch alerts.
  • The iPhone provides detailed braille reading.
  • This is especially useful for deafblind users or those who prefer silent reading.

Health workflows

Advanced users may monitor heart rate, workout trends, sleep, medication, ECG, irregular rhythm, blood oxygen, sleep apnoea where available, cycle tracking if relevant, and mobility.

  • Use trends.
  • Use alerts.
  • Use the Health app on the iPhone for detail.

Do not turn health data into a full-time hobby unless there is a medical reason.

Battery optimisation

Advanced users often use many features, so battery planning matters. Review Always-On display, notifications, Cellular, GPS, audio, workout duration, sleep tracking, Low Power Mode, charging routine, and battery complication.

Storage management

Advanced users may install more apps and download more content. Review storage regularly. Remove unused apps, old podcasts, unused music, unneeded photos, and old offline content.

Privacy

Advanced setups often involve more data. Review privacy for Health, Location, Home, Siri, Shortcuts, notifications, Wallet, apps, and location sharing. Do not grant broad permissions without need.

Common mistakes by advanced users

  • Installing too many apps.
  • Creating too many watch faces.
  • Overusing complications.
  • Trusting automations without testing.
  • Letting notifications multiply.
  • Using health data obsessively.
  • Relying on Cellular without checking battery.
  • Not reviewing privacy.
  • Forgetting that simplicity still matters.
  • Treating the watch as a tiny iPhone.

Exercise for module 63

Create three watch faces:

  • Daily.
  • Workout.
  • Sleep.
  • For each one, choose only the complications that match that context.
  • Then review notifications and disable at least five low-value alerts.
  • Review Focus modes and create or adjust Exercise Focus.
  • Choose one shortcut that makes sense on the watch and test it.
  • Add Battery as a complication if missing.
  • Review storage and remove unused apps or downloaded content.
  • The goal is to create an advanced setup that remains organised.

Summary of module 63

Advanced users can make strong use of Apple Watch features. Multiple watch faces can support different contexts. Complications should be chosen carefully.

Focus modes, Siri, Shortcuts, Home, Wallet, audio, and workouts can create powerful workflows.

  • Advanced use requires strict notification control.
  • Battery, storage, and privacy must be reviewed.
  • The Apple Watch should complement the iPhone, not replace it for every task.
  • A good advanced setup is organised, tested, and simple where simplicity helps.

Back to table of contents

Module 64. Final review of the complete Apple Watch workflow

After reviewing setup, gestures, apps, notifications, health, workouts, safety, audio, maps, smart home, battery, updates, and troubleshooting, it is useful to bring everything together into a complete workflow. The Apple Watch should not be understood as a collection of isolated features. It is a companion device linked to the iPhone.

For a blind person, it can provide quick access, haptic alerts, VoiceOver interaction, health recording, workouts, calls, reminders, safety features, and everyday controls.

  • But its usefulness depends on configuration.
  • A badly configured Apple Watch may become confusing.
  • A well-configured Apple Watch can become a practical tool.

The complete daily workflow

A typical daily workflow might be:

  • Put on the watch.
  • Unlock it.
  • Check battery.
  • Check the watch face.
  • Receive important notifications.
  • Use timers and reminders.
  • Answer calls if needed.
  • Reply to short messages.
  • Check weather before going out.
  • Record workouts.
  • Use Siri for quick actions.
  • Use the watch to find the iPhone.
  • Review health or activity on the iPhone later.
  • Charge the watch at the planned time.
  • The watch accompanies the day.
  • It should not dominate it.

Morning routine

In the morning:

  • Stop the alarm if the watch was used for sleep.
  • Check battery.
  • Review sleep data if desired.
  • Charge the watch if needed.
  • Check calendar or reminders.
  • Check weather.
  • Put the watch on properly.
  • Make sure it is unlocked.
  • If the watch is used for medication, check morning reminders.

Before leaving home

Before leaving home:

  • Check Apple Watch battery.
  • Check iPhone battery.
  • Check weather.
  • Check whether you need the iPhone.
  • Check whether Cellular works if going without iPhone.
  • Check that important notifications are not blocked by Focus.
  • Check that the watch is unlocked.
  • If going to an unfamiliar place, check route.
  • If exercising, start the correct workout.
  • If the watch is used for safety, do not leave with low battery.

During exercise

During exercise:

  • Start the correct workout.
  • Check essential data only.
  • Use headphones carefully.
  • Pause if needed.
  • Resume if continuing.
  • End the workout properly.
  • Review the summary.
  • Check details later on the iPhone.
  • Safety comes before data.
  • No activity ring is worth a fall, a collision, or getting disoriented.

At night

At night:

  • Charge the watch if not using sleep tracking.
  • Or check battery before sleeping if using sleep tracking.
  • Enable Sleep Focus if configured.
  • Make sure important contacts can reach you if needed.
  • Use haptic alarm if desired.
  • Wear the watch comfortably.
  • Review sleep data in the morning, not obsessively at midnight.

The Apple Watch and the iPhone together

The Apple Watch is not independent in every sense. The iPhone remains central for initial setup, Watch app, Health app, Fitness app, detailed review, accessibility settings, app management, updates, pairing, backups, Wallet setup, and advanced configuration. The watch is excellent for quick access. The iPhone is better for detailed control.

What the Apple Watch is best at

The Apple Watch is best at:

  • Immediate alerts.
  • Haptic notifications.
  • Quick calls.
  • Short replies.
  • Timers and alarms.
  • Activity recording.
  • Workout recording.
  • Heart rate.
  • Safety alerts.
  • Finding the iPhone.
  • Apple Pay.
  • Quick Siri actions.
  • Audio control.
  • Weather checks.

What the Apple Watch is not best at

The Apple Watch is not ideal for:

  • Long writing.
  • Long reading.
  • Complex editing.
  • Detailed health analysis.
  • Detailed maps review.
  • Complex app setup.
  • Large documents.
  • Long email handling.
  • Deep troubleshooting.
  • Those tasks are usually better on the iPhone, iPad, Mac, or another device.

The most important habits

The best Apple Watch habits are:

  • Charge it daily.
  • Keep notifications under control.
  • Use a simple watch face.
  • Check battery before going out.
  • End workouts properly.
  • Review health data on the iPhone.
  • Keep Medical ID updated.
  • Know how Emergency SOS works.
  • Do not test emergency calls.
  • Use the iPhone for complex settings.
  • Keep VoiceOver comfortable.
  • Use haptics deliberately.

For blind users

For blind users, the most important configuration areas are VoiceOver, speech rate, volume, accessibility shortcut, haptics, simple watch face, List View, notifications, battery, Siri, and the iPhone Watch app. These determine whether the watch feels accessible.

For deafblind or hard-of-hearing users

For deafblind or hard-of-hearing users, prioritise Haptic Alerts, Prominent Haptic, few important notifications, alarms and timers, medication alerts, battery, simple workflow, iPhone support, braille display workflow if used, and emergency contacts.

For older users

For older users, prioritise calls, emergency contacts, Medical ID, Fall Detection, medication, calendar, strong haptics, battery routine, simple watch face, and limited notifications.

For advanced users

For advanced users, focus on contextual watch faces, Shortcuts, Focus modes, workouts, health trends, audio, Maps, Wallet, Home, battery optimisation, and privacy review.

When to simplify

Simplify when the user gets lost often, notifications are overwhelming, battery drains too fast, apps are hard to find, the watch face is cluttered, the user ignores alerts, settings are confusing, or the person depends on the watch for safety. Simplicity is not a downgrade. It is often the most advanced accessibility decision.

Exercise for module 64

Review your complete Apple Watch setup:

  • Check VoiceOver.
  • Check accessibility shortcut.
  • Check watch face.
  • Check complications.
  • Check app view.
  • Check notifications.
  • Check haptics.
  • Check Control Centre.
  • Check battery routine.
  • Check Find iPhone.
  • Check calls.
  • Check messages.
  • Check timers.
  • Check alarms.
  • Check Medical ID.
  • Check emergency contacts.
  • Check Fall Detection if used.
  • Check workouts if used.
  • Check sleep if used.
  • Check medication if used.
  • Check Apple Pay if used.
  • Check Maps, audio, Home, installed apps, storage, and watchOS update status if relevant.
  • Remove at least one unnecessary notification or app.
  • Simplify one part of the setup.
  • The goal is not to add more.
  • The goal is to make the watch easier and more useful.

Summary of module 64

The Apple Watch works best as a companion to the iPhone. For blind users, VoiceOver, haptics, notifications, and simple navigation are central. The watch is excellent for quick alerts, calls, timers, workouts, health recording, and safety features. The iPhone is better for detailed configuration and review.

Notifications should be limited to what matters.

  • Battery routine is essential.
  • Medical ID and emergency contacts should be kept updated.
  • Advanced features should be added only when the basics are mastered.
  • A simple and reliable setup is usually better than a complicated one.

Back to table of contents

Module 65. Closing and final recommendations

The Apple Watch can be a very useful device for blind people, deafblind people, people with hearing loss, older people, and anyone who wants a practical companion on the wrist. But its value does not come from the number of features it includes. Its value comes from how well it is configured for the person who is going to use it.

A well-configured Apple Watch can help with notifications, calls, messages, timers, alarms, reminders, workouts, health data, sleep, medication, safety, finding the iPhone, weather, audio, Apple Pay, smart home control, and many other tasks.

A poorly configured Apple Watch can become a source of interruptions, confusion, battery problems, accidental activations, and unnecessary frustration. The difference is not only the device. The difference is the setup, the training, and the daily routine.

The Apple Watch is not an iPhone on the wrist

This is one of the most important ideas in the whole course. The Apple Watch is not meant to replace the iPhone. It complements it.

The iPhone remains better for:

  • Long reading.
  • Long writing.
  • Detailed configuration.
  • Reviewing Health data.
  • Reviewing Fitness data.
  • Managing apps.
  • Writing messages.
  • Reading long emails.
  • Planning routes.
  • Editing settings.
  • Solving problems.

The Apple Watch is better for:

  • Quick alerts.
  • Haptic notifications.
  • Short actions.
  • Timers.
  • Alarms.
  • Calls.
  • Short replies.
  • Workouts.
  • Heart rate.
  • Weather checks.
  • Apple Pay.
  • Finding the iPhone.
  • Safety features.
  • Quick Siri commands.
  • The best experience comes from using each device for what it does best.

VoiceOver makes the Apple Watch usable

VoiceOver is the main accessibility feature that allows a blind person to use the Apple Watch. With VoiceOver, the user can hear the screen, move through elements, activate buttons, read notifications, use apps, check health data, answer calls, reply to messages, and interact with many system features. But VoiceOver must be configured comfortably. Speech rate should not be too fast at the beginning.

Volume should be appropriate.

  • The accessibility shortcut should be configured.
  • The user should learn the basic gestures.
  • The Digital Crown and side button must be clearly identified.

A blind user should not begin with advanced features before understanding the basics of VoiceOver on the watch.

Haptic feedback is not optional for many users

For many users, haptic feedback is one of the most important parts of the Apple Watch.

A vibration on the wrist can announce:

  • A call.
  • A message.
  • A reminder.
  • A timer.
  • An alarm.
  • A medication reminder.
  • A calendar event.
  • A health alert.
  • A workout notification.
  • An emergency-related alert.
  • For blind users, haptics can complement VoiceOver.
  • For deafblind users or users with hearing loss, haptics may be essential.
  • For older users, haptics can make alarms and reminders easier to notice.
  • That is why haptic alerts should be tested, not assumed.
  • The watch must fit properly.
  • Prominent Haptic may be useful.
  • Notifications must be limited.
  • A vibration that cannot be felt is not useful.
  • A wrist that vibrates for everything is not useful either.

Notifications should be chosen carefully

The Apple Watch should not receive every notification from the iPhone. This is one of the main mistakes. At first, the user may think that more notifications mean more usefulness. In practice, too many notifications make the watch annoying.

Recommended important notifications may include:

  • Phone.
  • Messages from important people.
  • Calendar.
  • Reminders.
  • Timers.
  • Alarms.
  • Medication.
  • Health alerts.
  • Battery.
  • Emergency-related alerts.
  • Workout alerts, if used.
  • Everything else should be reviewed.

Social media, promotions, games, shopping apps, repeated news alerts, and non-urgent group messages usually do not need to be on the wrist. The Apple Watch should interrupt only when interruption makes sense.

Battery routine is part of accessibility

The Apple Watch needs battery. This sounds obvious, but it matters. If the watch is used for alarms, medication, Emergency SOS, Fall Detection, calls, workouts, or sleep, charging becomes part of the accessibility setup. The user needs a routine.

For example:

  • Charge during breakfast.
  • Charge while showering.
  • Charge before going to bed.
  • Charge during a daily rest period.
  • Charge when sitting at the computer.
  • If the watch is used for sleep tracking, charging overnight will not work.

Battery should be checked before leaving home, before exercise, before sleep, and before relying on safety features. A watch without battery is not a safety device. It is a small silent object with very little ambition left.

Health features are useful, but limited

The Apple Watch can record and show valuable health information.

It can help with:

  • Heart rate.
  • High and low heart rate alerts.
  • Irregular rhythm notifications, where available.
  • ECG, where available.
  • Blood oxygen, where available.
  • Sleep.
  • Sleep apnoea notifications, where available.
  • Medication reminders.
  • Activity.
  • Workouts.
  • Mobility data.
  • Noise alerts.
  • Other health-related information.
  • But the Apple Watch does not replace healthcare professionals.
  • It does not diagnose every condition.
  • It does not rule out problems if no alert appears.
  • It does not replace medical tests.
  • It does not replace emergency care.
  • If there are symptoms, symptoms matter.
  • If there are repeated alerts, they deserve attention.
  • If a feature is not available, it may be because of model, country, age, version, or configuration.
  • Health data should be used as support, not as absolute truth.

Safety features must be understood before they are needed

Emergency SOS, Fall Detection, Medical ID, emergency contacts, and location features can be very useful. But they must be configured before an emergency occurs.

The user should know:

  • Where the side button is.
  • That the side button is not the Digital Crown.
  • What happens when Emergency SOS is activated.
  • That emergency calls should not be tested without a real emergency.
  • That Fall Detection does not detect every fall.
  • That false alerts can happen.
  • That emergency contacts may be notified.
  • That Medical ID should be accurate.
  • That battery and connection matter.
  • Safety features are useful only when the user understands them.
  • A feature that surprises the user in an emergency may create confusion.

The Apple Watch must be adapted to each person

There is no single ideal setup.

A blind beginner may need:

  • Simple watch face.
  • VoiceOver.
  • Slow speech rate.
  • List View.
  • Few notifications.
  • Strong haptics.
  • Battery complication.
  • Timers and alarms.
  • Find iPhone.
  • Basic calls and messages.

An older person may need:

  • Simple watch face.
  • Strong haptics.
  • Calls.
  • Medication.
  • Medical ID.
  • Emergency contacts.
  • Fall Detection.
  • Calendar alerts.
  • Battery routine.

A deafblind user may need:

  • Haptic alerts.
  • Prominent Haptic.
  • Very few notifications.
  • Tactile routines.
  • iPhone support.
  • Braille display workflow if used.
  • Medication and alarms.
  • Emergency contacts.

An advanced blind user may want:

  • Multiple watch faces.
  • Focus modes.
  • Shortcuts.
  • Workouts.
  • Health trends.
  • Apple Pay.
  • Maps.
  • Audio.
  • Smart home.
  • Braille workflows.
  • Automation.
  • The setup should follow the user’s real needs, not the device’s feature list.

Start small and grow gradually

The best way to learn the Apple Watch is progressive.

First:

  1. VoiceOver.
  2. Gestures.
  3. Digital Crown.
  4. Side button.
  5. Watch face.
  6. Control Centre.
  7. Battery.
  8. Haptics.

Then:

  1. Timers.
  2. Alarms.
  3. Calls.
  4. Messages.
  5. Reminders.
  6. Calendar.
  7. Find iPhone.

Then:

  1. Activity.
  2. Workouts.
  3. Heart rate.
  4. Weather.
  5. Sleep.
  6. Medication.

Then:

  • Safety.
  • Apple Pay.
  • Maps.
  • Audio.
  • Smart home.
  • Shortcuts.
  • Advanced health.
  • Trying to learn everything at once creates overload.
  • The Apple Watch is easier when each function is added after the previous one is understood.

The iPhone is the control centre

Many important Apple Watch settings are easier from the iPhone.

The Watch app allows you to manage:

  • Watch faces.
  • Apps.
  • Notifications.
  • VoiceOver.
  • Accessibility.
  • Sounds and haptics.
  • Passcode.
  • Wallet.
  • Siri.
  • General settings.
  • Software updates.

The Health app allows you to manage:

  1. Medical ID.
  2. Health data.
  3. Heart information.
  4. Sleep.
  5. Medication.
  6. Cycle tracking.
  7. Permissions.
  8. Trends.

The Fitness app allows you to review:

  • Activity.
  • Workouts.
  • Awards.
  • Trends.
  • Exercise history.
  • The Apple Watch is on the wrist, but the iPhone remains essential.
  • When in doubt, check the iPhone.

Keep the watch simple

Even for advanced users, simplicity is useful.

  • A clear watch face is better than a crowded one.
  • A short app list is better than a long one.
  • A few important notifications are better than constant alerts.
  • A clear battery routine is better than improvising.
  • A simple emergency setup is better than a complicated one.

Simplicity is not a lack of skill. It is good design. And, against all odds, good design occasionally survives contact with real users.

Review the configuration from time to time

The Apple Watch setup should not remain untouched forever. It is useful to review it periodically.

Every few weeks or months, check:

  • Notifications.
  • Battery.
  • Watch face.
  • Apps.
  • Complications.
  • Medical ID.
  • Emergency contacts.
  • Medication.
  • Health alerts.
  • Focus modes.
  • Storage.
  • Updates.
  • Privacy permissions.
  • Remove what is not used.
  • Adjust what is annoying.
  • Add only what is truly needed.
  • The best configuration is the one that continues to fit the user’s life.

Do not ignore privacy

The Apple Watch can handle sensitive information.

It may show or record:

  • Messages.
  • Calls.
  • Location.
  • Health data.
  • Medication.
  • Sleep.
  • Heart rate.
  • Cycle data.
  • Payments.
  • Home devices.
  • Calendar events.
  • Reminders.
  • This information should be protected.

Review:

  • Passcode.
  • Wrist detection.
  • Notification previews.
  • Health permissions.
  • Location sharing.
  • Home access.
  • Wallet.
  • Apps with Health access.
  • Emergency information visible when locked.
  • Accessibility and privacy should go together.
  • Do not solve one problem by creating another.

Know when the Apple Watch is not enough

The Apple Watch is useful, but it is not always the right tool. Use the iPhone, iPad, Mac, braille display, specialist app, mobility aid, healthcare professional, or human support when needed. The Apple Watch should not be forced into tasks it does not handle well.

Examples:

  • Long writing.
  • Detailed document reading.
  • Complex navigation.
  • Medical diagnosis.
  • Emergency assessment.
  • Complex troubleshooting.
  • Heavy app configuration.
  • Long braille work.
  • In those cases, another tool may be better.
  • The intelligent use of technology includes knowing when not to use a device.

Final practical recommendations

  • Keep VoiceOver comfortable.
  • Use List View.
  • Use a simple watch face.
  • Add Battery as a complication.
  • Keep notifications limited.
  • Enable haptic alerts.
  • Test alarms and timers.
  • Learn Control Centre.
  • Learn to find the iPhone.
  • Configure Medical ID.
  • Add emergency contacts.
  • Review Fall Detection if appropriate.
  • Do not test Emergency SOS with a real call.
  • Use the iPhone for detailed setup.
  • Use Health and Fitness for reviewing data.
  • Create a charging routine.
  • Review updates carefully.
  • Do not buy used without checking Activation Lock.
  • Add advanced features gradually.

Final exercise

Take one day to review the full Apple Watch setup. Do not add new features first. Review what already exists.

Check:

  • VoiceOver.
  • Speech rate.
  • Accessibility shortcut.
  • Watch face.
  • Complications.
  • Battery.
  • Haptics.
  • Notifications.
  • Control Centre.
  • Find iPhone.
  • Calls.
  • Messages.
  • Timers.
  • Alarms.
  • Reminders.
  • Calendar.
  • Medical ID.
  • Emergency contacts.
  • Fall Detection.
  • Health alerts.
  • Workout setup.
  • Sleep setup.
  • Medication setup.
  • Apple Pay, if used.
  • Maps, if used.
  • Audio, if used.
  • Home, if used.
  • Installed apps.
  • Storage.
  • watchOS update status.
  • Then remove or simplify at least three things that are not helping.
  • A good final review is not about adding more.
  • It is about making the Apple Watch more reliable, more understandable, and more useful.

Final summary

The Apple Watch can be a valuable accessibility tool for blind users. It can also help deafblind users, people with hearing loss, older people, and users with specific health or safety needs.

Its main strengths are quick access, haptic alerts, VoiceOver, timers, notifications, calls, health recording, workouts, safety features, and integration with the iPhone.

Its main limitations are the small screen, battery dependence, limited suitability for long tasks, variable feature availability, and the need for careful configuration. The Apple Watch works best when it is simple, well organised, and adapted to the user. The iPhone remains essential for setup and detailed review.

Health and safety features are useful, but they have limits.

  • Notifications should be controlled.
  • Battery routine is essential.
  • The best Apple Watch is not the one with the most features activated.
  • It is the one that the user can understand, trust, and use every day.
