Appendix 1. Quick reference of essential gestures with VoiceOver

This appendix gathers the most important gestures and controls for using the Apple Watch with VoiceOver. It is not meant to replace the full course. It is a quick reference to review when the user needs to remember a gesture, a button, or a basic action.

The Apple Watch is small, and VoiceOver use requires precision. At first, it is normal to confuse gestures, press the wrong button, or get lost between the watch face, the app list, Control Centre, and notifications. That is not failure.

It is simply what happens when a device the size of a biscuit tries to behave like a computer, a phone, a health assistant, and a tiny wrist secretary.

Physical controls

The Apple Watch has two main physical controls:

  1. Digital Crown.
  2. Side button.

Digital Crown

The Digital Crown is the round button. It can be pressed. It can be turned.

It is used for actions such as:

  • Returning to the watch face.
  • Opening the app list.
  • Scrolling in some lists.
  • Adjusting values.
  • Using some accessibility shortcuts.
  • Interacting with some apps.
  • With VoiceOver, the Digital Crown is very important.

Side button

  • The side button is elongated.
  • It is near the Digital Crown.
  • It is not round.

It is used for actions such as:

  • Opening Control Centre in recent versions of watchOS.
  • Opening Wallet with a double press.
  • Accessing emergency options if held down, depending on configuration.
  • Activating some system functions.
  • Do not confuse the side button with the Digital Crown.
  • This is especially important for Apple Pay and Emergency SOS.

Basic VoiceOver gestures

Touch the screen

Touching an item lets VoiceOver say what is under your finger. This is useful for exploring the screen.

Swipe right

Moves to the next item. This is one of the most important gestures.

Swipe left

Moves to the previous item. This lets you go back through screen elements.

Double tap

  • Activates the selected item.
  • If VoiceOver is focused on a button, double tap activates that button.
  • If VoiceOver is focused on a switch, double tap changes its state.

Double tap and hold

May open extra actions or allow some controls to be adjusted, depending on the item. Use this carefully.

Swipe up or down

May change the value of adjustable controls, depending on the VoiceOver rotor or selected element. On Apple Watch, behaviour may vary by context.

Two-finger double tap

In some contexts, this can start or stop an action. Depending on app and system settings, it may be useful for calls, audio, timers, or other actions. The behaviour can vary, so do not depend on it until you have tested it in your version.

Digital Crown with VoiceOver

Turning the Digital Crown can scroll through lists or adjust values.

Examples:

  1. Moving through the app list.
  2. Scrolling through settings.
  3. Adjusting time or values.
  4. Moving through long screens.
  5. Turn it slowly.
  6. Listen after each movement.

Opening the app list

From the watch face:

  • Press the Digital Crown once.
  • The app list opens.
  • If you use List View, move through apps with swipes or by turning the Digital Crown.

Returning to the watch face

  • Press the Digital Crown.
  • Depending on where you are, you may need to press it once or more than once.
  • Listen to what VoiceOver says so you know where you are.

Opening Control Centre

In recent versions of watchOS:

  • Press the side button once.
  • Control Centre opens.
  • There you can check battery, Silent Mode, Focus modes, Find iPhone, Airplane Mode, and other controls.
  • If your watchOS version behaves differently, use the method available on that version.

Opening Wallet

To open Wallet for Apple Pay:

  • Double-press the side button.
  • This is two quick presses of the side button.
  • Not the Digital Crown.
  • The watch must be unlocked and on your wrist.

Using Emergency SOS

Emergency SOS may be activated by holding down the side button, depending on configuration. Do not practise Emergency SOS with a real call. Do not hold the side button down casually. If emergency options appear by mistake, cancel safely. If a call connects by mistake, explain that it was accidental.

Finding the iPhone

From Control Centre:

  • Press the side button once.
  • Move through controls with VoiceOver.
  • Find the button to make the iPhone play a sound.
  • Double tap.
  • The iPhone will play a sound if nearby and connected.
  • This is one of the most useful features to learn early.

Checking battery

From Control Centre:

  • Press the side button once.
  • Move through the controls.
  • Find the battery percentage.
  • Listen to the value.
  • You can also add Battery as a complication on the watch face.

Answering a call

When a call arrives:

  1. Listen to VoiceOver.
  2. Find Answer.
  3. Double tap.

To reject it:

  1. Find Decline.
  2. Double tap.

To end the call:

  1. Find End or Hang Up.
  2. Double tap.

Reading a notification

When a notification arrives:

  • Touch the screen or raise the wrist if needed.
  • Listen to VoiceOver.
  • Swipe through the notification.
  • Find available actions.
  • Possible actions may include Reply, Dismiss, Open, or Clear.

Replying to a message

From the notification:

  • Find Reply.
  • Double tap.
  • Choose dictation, quick reply, emoji, or another method.
  • Review the text if dictated.
  • Find Send.
  • Double tap.
  • For long or delicate messages, use the iPhone.

Using Siri

Depending on configuration, Siri can be activated by:

  • Saying Siri or Hey Siri.
  • Holding down the Digital Crown.
  • Raising your wrist and speaking, if enabled.

Siri can be used for:

  • Calls.
  • Messages.
  • Timers.
  • Alarms.
  • Reminders.
  • Weather.
  • Opening apps.
  • Starting workouts.
  • Short commands work best.

Starting a timer with Siri

Activate Siri.

Say:

  • Set a timer for five minutes.
  • Listen to confirmation.
  • When the timer ends, find Stop and double tap.

Starting a workout with Siri

Activate Siri.

Say:

  • Start an outdoor walk workout.
  • Listen to confirmation.
  • When finished, make sure you end the workout from the Workout app.
  • Do not simply leave the app.

Ending a workout

On the workout screen:

  • Find End or Finish.
  • Double tap.
  • Confirm if required.
  • Listen to the summary.
  • Find Done, OK, or Close.
  • Double tap.
  • This saves the workout.

Common gesture mistakes

Confusing the Digital Crown with the side button. Pressing and holding the side button by mistake.

Double-pressing the Digital Crown instead of the side button for Wallet.

  • Swiping too quickly without listening.
  • Trying to manipulate the watch while walking in unsafe places.
  • Leaving a workout screen without ending the workout.
  • Not checking whether a button is on or off before double tapping.

Practical gesture advice

  • Practise gestures while seated.
  • Use a simple watch face.
  • Use List View.
  • Keep notifications limited.
  • Learn one action at a time.

Practise with harmless features first:

  • Timer.
  • Weather.
  • Battery.
  • Find iPhone.
  • Messages from a trusted person.
  • Do not practise with emergency calls, Apple Pay, or important health settings until the basics are understood.

Summary of appendix 1

The Digital Crown is round and can be pressed or turned. The side button is elongated and is used for Control Centre, Wallet, and emergency options.

With VoiceOver, swipe right and left to move.

  • Double tap activates the selected item.
  • Control Centre is essential for battery, Silent Mode, Focus, and Find iPhone.
  • Wallet uses a double press of the side button.
  • Emergency SOS should not be tested with real calls.

The most useful beginner actions are checking battery, finding the iPhone, using timers, answering calls, and reading notifications.

Back to table of contents

Appendix 2. Quick checklist for configuring an Apple Watch with VoiceOver

This appendix provides a practical checklist for configuring an Apple Watch for a blind user. It can be used by the person themselves, by a trainer, by a family member, or by someone helping with setup. The order matters. Do not configure advanced features before the basics are working.

Step 1. Check compatibility

Before setup, check:

  • The Apple Watch model.
  • The iPhone model.
  • The iOS version.
  • The watchOS version.
  • Whether the watch is new, used, or refurbished.
  • Whether Activation Lock is removed if it is used.
  • Whether the charger is available.
  • Whether the battery charges properly.
  • Do not proceed with a used watch that asks for another person’s Apple Account.

Step 2. Pair the Apple Watch

Use the Watch app on the iPhone.

  • Keep both devices close.
  • Follow the pairing instructions.
  • Use the same Apple Account where appropriate.
  • Choose whether to restore from backup or set up as new.
  • For a beginner, setting up as new may sometimes be cleaner.
  • For a user replacing a watch, restoring from backup may be convenient.

Step 3. Turn on VoiceOver

From the iPhone Watch app:

  • Go to My Watch.
  • Go to Accessibility.
  • Go to VoiceOver.
  • Turn VoiceOver on.
  • Adjust speech rate.
  • Adjust volume if needed.
  • Check that the user can hear VoiceOver comfortably.

Step 4. Configure the accessibility shortcut

From the Watch app:

  • Go to Accessibility.
  • Find Accessibility Shortcut.
  • Choose VoiceOver.
  • Now triple-clicking the Digital Crown can turn VoiceOver on or off.
  • Explain this carefully.
  • The user must know that the same shortcut can also turn VoiceOver off.

Step 5. Choose a simple watch face

Use a simple face.

Recommended complications:

  • Battery.
  • Weather.
  • Timer.
  • Calendar or Reminders.
  • Activity or Workout if useful.
  • Avoid crowded faces.
  • The user should easily return to the watch face and understand what is there.

Step 6. Set List View

For VoiceOver users, List View is usually easier.

From the Watch app or Apple Watch settings:

  • Find App View.
  • Choose List View.
  • This makes app navigation more predictable.

Step 7. Configure haptics

From the Watch app:

  • Go to Sounds and Haptics.
  • Enable Haptic Alerts.
  • Enable Prominent Haptic if needed.
  • Set alert volume.
  • Test with a timer.
  • If the user cannot feel the timer, adjust the strap or haptic settings.

Step 8. Configure passcode

  • Set a passcode.
  • This protects the watch.
  • It is also required for Apple Pay.

Explain:

  • The watch may lock when removed.
  • The passcode unlocks it.
  • Unlock with iPhone may help, if available and appropriate.
  • If the watch asks for the passcode too often, check strap fit and wrist detection.

Step 9. Reduce notifications

Start with only essential notifications.

Recommended at first:

  • Phone.
  • Messages.
  • Calendar.
  • Reminders.
  • Timers.
  • Alarms.
  • Medication, if used.
  • Health alerts, if configured.
  • Battery.

Disable or postpone:

  • Games.
  • Shopping.
  • Promotions.
  • Social networks.
  • News alerts.
  • Non-urgent apps.
  • The watch should not vibrate constantly.

Step 10. Learn Control Centre

Teach the user to open Control Centre.

In recent watchOS versions:

  • Press the side button once.
  • Practise:
  • Checking battery.
  • Finding Silent Mode.
  • Checking Focus.
  • Finding Airplane Mode.
  • Making the iPhone play a sound.
  • This is essential.

Step 11. Test Find iPhone

From Control Centre:

  • Find the button to make the iPhone play a sound.
  • Double tap.
  • Confirm that the iPhone sounds.
  • This is one of the most practical everyday features.

Step 12. Test a timer

  • Use Siri or the Timers app.
  • Set a one-minute timer.
  • Wait.
  • Feel the vibration.
  • Stop the timer.
  • This confirms VoiceOver, haptics, and basic interaction.

Step 13. Test an alarm

Set an alarm a few minutes ahead.

  • Wait for the alert.
  • Stop the alarm.
  • Check whether the user notices the vibration and understands how to stop it.

Step 14. Practise calls

With a trusted person:

  • Make a test call to the Apple Watch.
  • Listen to VoiceOver.
  • Answer.
  • Speak briefly.
  • End the call.
  • Then call from the Apple Watch using Siri or the Phone app.

Step 15. Practise messages

  • Send a test message.
  • Read it on the Apple Watch.
  • Reply with a quick reply.
  • Reply with dictation if appropriate.
  • Review before sending.
  • For long replies, use the iPhone.

Step 16. Configure Medical ID

From the Health app on the iPhone:

  1. Open Medical ID.
  2. Add relevant medical conditions.
  3. Add allergies.
  4. Add medication.
  5. Add emergency contacts.
  6. Add communication notes if useful.

For example:

  • Blind person. Please communicate verbally.
  • Keep the information brief and useful.

Step 17. Configure emergency contacts

  • Choose contacts who can respond.
  • Check phone numbers.
  • Tell them they are emergency contacts.
  • Review whether they may receive alerts after Emergency SOS.
  • Do not add random contacts.
  • Emergency contacts should be meaningful.

Step 18. Review Emergency SOS

From the Watch app:

  • Go to Emergency SOS.
  • Review options.
  • Explain the side button.
  • Explain that Emergency SOS is for real emergencies only.
  • Do not test with a real call.
  • Make sure the user knows how to avoid accidental activation.

Step 19. Review Fall Detection if appropriate

If the model supports it:

  • Go to Emergency SOS or relevant setting.
  • Find Fall Detection.
  • Choose the suitable option.
  • For older people or people at risk, Always On may be useful.
  • Explain that Fall Detection does not detect every fall.
  • Explain that false alerts can happen.

Step 20. Configure health features gradually

Do not activate everything at once.

Start with:

  1. Heart rate.
  2. Activity.
  3. Medication if needed.
  4. Sleep if wanted.

Then review advanced features if available:

  • ECG.
  • Irregular rhythm.
  • Blood oxygen.
  • Sleep apnoea notifications.
  • Other model-specific features.
  • Explain limits clearly.
  • The watch does not replace medical care.

Step 21. Configure workouts if needed

Start with one workout:

  1. Outdoor Walk.
  2. Indoor Walk.

Teach:

  • Start.
  • Pause.
  • Resume.
  • End.
  • Review summary.
  • Review Fitness on the iPhone.
  • Do not introduce too many workout types at once.

Step 22. Configure Apple Pay only when ready

Only configure Apple Pay when the user understands:

  • Side button.
  • Passcode.
  • Wallet.
  • Default card.
  • Payment process.
  • Amount confirmation.
  • Apple Pay uses a double press of the side button.
  • Not the Digital Crown.
  • Do not introduce Apple Pay before basic button control is reliable.

Step 23. Configure weather

Add Weather as a complication if useful.

Teach:

  • Open Weather.
  • Ask Siri for weather.
  • Check rain.
  • Check wind.
  • Check temperature.
  • This is practical before going out.

Step 24. Configure battery routine

Choose a charging time.

For example:

  • During breakfast.
  • While showering.
  • Before bed.
  • During rest.
  • Add Battery complication.
  • Explain that safety and alerts depend on battery.

Step 25. Remove unnecessary apps

  • Review installed apps.
  • Remove those not needed.
  • Keep the app list short.
  • This improves both storage and accessibility.

Step 26. Test the complete basic workflow

The user should be able to:

  • Check time.
  • Check battery.
  • Open app list.
  • Open Control Centre.
  • Find iPhone.
  • Set a timer.
  • Stop a timer.
  • Answer a call.
  • End a call.
  • Read a message.
  • Charge the watch.
  • Return to the watch face.
  • Only after this should advanced features be introduced.

Final configuration checklist

  • VoiceOver enabled.
  • Speech rate comfortable.
  • Accessibility shortcut configured.
  • Simple watch face.
  • Battery complication.
  • List View.
  • Haptic Alerts enabled.
  • Prominent Haptic tested if needed.
  • Passcode configured.
  • Notifications reduced.
  • Control Centre understood.
  • Find iPhone tested.
  • Timer tested.
  • Alarm tested.
  • Calls practised.
  • Messages practised.
  • Medical ID configured.
  • Emergency contacts configured.
  • Emergency SOS explained.
  • Fall Detection reviewed if appropriate.
  • Battery routine created.
  • Unnecessary apps removed.

Summary of appendix 2

Apple Watch setup should be done in order. VoiceOver, haptics, watch face, List View, passcode, and notifications come first. Timers, calls, messages, Control Centre, and Find iPhone should be practised early. Medical ID and emergency contacts should be configured before safety features are relied upon. Health, workouts, Apple Pay, and advanced features should be introduced gradually. A simple, tested setup is better than a complete but confusing setup.

Back to table of contents

Appendix 3. Quick checklist before leaving home with the Apple Watch

This appendix is designed as a practical checklist before leaving home. It is especially useful for blind users, older people, people who exercise outdoors, people who use the Apple Watch for safety, and anyone who depends on the watch for calls, alerts, medication, routes, or communication. The Apple Watch can be very helpful outside the home, but only if it is charged, connected, unlocked, properly configured, and worn correctly.

A watch left on the charger, without battery, locked, disconnected, or silenced by a Focus mode is not exactly a masterpiece of assistive technology. It is just a small expensive object quietly failing at its job.

Before putting on the Apple Watch

  • Check that the watch is charged.
  • Check that the strap is attached correctly.
  • Check that the watch is clean and dry.
  • Check that the back sensors are not covered.
  • Check that the charger is not still attached.

Put the Apple Watch on the wrist where you normally wear it.

  • Adjust the strap firmly, but comfortably.
  • The watch should not move around loosely.
  • It should not hurt or press too much either.

Check that the Apple Watch is unlocked

After putting it on, check whether the watch asks for the passcode.

  • If it asks for the passcode, enter it.
  • If the watch remains locked, notifications, Apple Pay, and some features may not work as expected.
  • If the watch keeps locking during the day, check strap fit and wrist detection.

Check battery

Before leaving home, check battery.

You can do this from:

  • Battery complication on the watch face.
  • Control Centre.
  • Ask Siri, if supported.
  • If the battery is low, charge the watch before leaving if possible.

This is especially important if you will use:

  • Workouts.
  • Maps.
  • Calls.
  • Cellular.
  • Music or podcasts.
  • Fall Detection.
  • Emergency SOS.
  • Medication reminders.
  • Sleep later that night.
  • A low battery is not just inconvenient. It may affect safety features.

Check iPhone battery

If you carry the iPhone, check its battery too. This matters especially if your Apple Watch is GPS only. A GPS Apple Watch depends on the iPhone for many communication functions outside Wi-Fi. If both the iPhone and watch are low on battery, consider charging before leaving or carrying a power bank if the outing is long.

Check connection

If you are leaving with the iPhone:

  • Make sure the iPhone is with you.
  • Make sure Bluetooth is enabled.
  • Make sure the Apple Watch is connected.

If you are leaving without the iPhone:

  • Make sure you understand what your Apple Watch can do without it.
  • If it is a GPS model, many communication features may be limited.
  • If it is a Cellular model, check that the mobile plan is active and that there is likely to be coverage.
  • Do not assume every Apple Watch works independently outside the home.
  • The difference between GPS and Cellular matters.

Check Airplane Mode

Make sure Airplane Mode is not enabled by mistake. Open Control Centre and check the Airplane Mode button. If Airplane Mode is on, some connections may be disabled. Turn it off if you need calls, messages, location, or data.

Check Focus modes

Check whether a Focus mode is active.

This can include:

  • Do Not Disturb.
  • Sleep.
  • Work.
  • Personal.
  • Exercise.
  • Driving.
  • A custom Focus mode.
  • If a Focus mode is active, some notifications may be blocked.

Before leaving, make sure important calls, messages, medication reminders, calendar alerts, or safety-related notifications are not being silenced. Focus modes are useful, but when badly configured they can impersonate a broken watch with remarkable dedication.

Check Silent Mode

Silent Mode may be fine if haptics are enabled. If you rely on sound, make sure Silent Mode is not on. If you rely on haptics, make sure Haptic Alerts are enabled and the strap is adjusted properly. For many blind users, Silent Mode with strong haptics is a good combination. But the user must know which mode is active.

Check haptics

Before a long outing, it may be useful to test haptics quickly with a timer or reminder if you are unsure.

This is especially important for:

  • Deafblind users.
  • Users with hearing loss.
  • Older people.
  • People who miss standard vibrations.
  • People using medication reminders.
  • If haptics are weak, enable Prominent Haptic if available or adjust the strap.

Check notifications

Make sure important notifications are enabled.

For example:

  • Phone.
  • Messages from important contacts.
  • Calendar.
  • Reminders.
  • Medication.
  • Alarms.
  • Timers.
  • Health alerts.
  • Battery.
  • Emergency-related alerts.
  • Do not enable every app before leaving.
  • Useful notifications are not the same as many notifications.

Check weather

Before going out, check weather.

Use:

  • Weather complication.
  • Weather app.
  • Siri.
  • iPhone Weather app.

Check:

  • Temperature.
  • Rain.
  • Wind.
  • Storm warnings.
  • Extreme heat.
  • Cold.
  • Air quality, if relevant.
  • UV index, if relevant.

For blind users, wind and rain are especially important because they can affect hearing, cane use, orientation, and safety.

Check route if needed

If you are going to an unfamiliar place, check the route before leaving. Use the iPhone for detailed route planning.

If you will use the Apple Watch for Maps:

  • Start the route from the iPhone if easier.
  • Use the watch for haptic prompts.
  • Do not manipulate the watch while crossing streets.
  • Use headphones carefully.
  • The Apple Watch can support orientation, but it does not replace mobility skills, a cane, a guide dog, or accessible navigation tools.

Check headphones

If you will use headphones:

  • Check they are charged.
  • Check they are connected.
  • Check audio output.
  • Check volume.
  • Check whether transparency or ambient mode is useful.
  • If you are blind and outdoors, do not block environmental sound completely.
  • Hearing may be part of orientation and safety.

Check Wallet or payment method

If you plan to pay with Apple Watch:

  • Check that Wallet is configured.
  • Check that the correct default card is selected.
  • Check that the watch is unlocked.
  • Remember that Apple Pay uses a double press of the side button.
  • Carry another payment method if needed.
  • Especially when learning, do not depend only on Apple Pay.
  • The day a terminal fails is always the day humans form a queue behind you with Olympic impatience.

Check medication reminders

If you use medication reminders:

  • Check that today’s reminders are configured.
  • Check that Focus modes are not blocking them.
  • Check that the Apple Watch is on your wrist.
  • Check battery.
  • If medication is important, do not rely only on the Apple Watch unless the routine is already well tested.

Check emergency setup

Before outings, especially if you go alone, it is useful to have configured:

  • Medical ID.
  • Emergency contacts.
  • Emergency SOS.
  • Fall Detection if appropriate.
  • Location sharing if needed.
  • Make sure emergency contacts are correct.
  • Make sure the watch has enough battery and connection.
  • Do not test Emergency SOS by calling emergency services.

Check workout if you are going to exercise

If you are going out to walk, run, cycle, or train:

  • Choose the correct workout type.
  • Check battery.
  • Check whether you need the iPhone.
  • Check route and weather.
  • Check headphones.
  • Start the workout when ready.
  • Pause and resume if needed.
  • End the workout properly when finished.
  • Do not simply leave the Workout app.
  • Leaving the screen is not the same as ending the workout.

Check if you need the iPhone

Do not leave the iPhone at home automatically.

Ask:

  • Is my watch GPS only?
  • Do I need calls?
  • Do I need navigation?
  • Do I need accessible apps on the iPhone?
  • Do I need battery backup?
  • Do I need to write messages?
  • Do I need documents or tickets?
  • Do I need transport apps?
  • For many blind users, carrying the iPhone remains advisable.
  • The Apple Watch is a companion, not a complete replacement.

Check identification and essentials

Depending on the outing, you may also need:

  • Keys.
  • Identification.
  • Physical payment card.
  • Transport card.
  • Medication.
  • Water.
  • Headphones.
  • Cane or guide dog equipment.
  • Charger or power bank.
  • The Apple Watch helps, but it does not replace all physical essentials.
  • Technology still has not solved the ancient problem of humans forgetting keys. A scandal, really.

Quick leaving-home checklist

  • Apple Watch on wrist.
  • Apple Watch unlocked.
  • Battery checked.
  • iPhone battery checked.
  • iPhone carried if needed.
  • Connection checked.
  • Airplane Mode off.
  • Focus mode reviewed.
  • Silent Mode understood.
  • Haptics working.
  • Weather checked.
  • Route checked if needed.
  • Headphones checked if used.
  • Wallet checked if used.
  • Medication reminders active if needed.
  • Emergency contacts configured.
  • Medical ID configured.
  • Workout ready if exercising.
  • Physical essentials taken.

What to do if something is not ready

  • If the watch battery is low, charge it.
  • If the iPhone battery is low, charge it.
  • If Focus mode is blocking alerts, change it.
  • If the route is unclear, review it on the iPhone.
  • If the weather is unsafe, reconsider the outing.
  • If the watch is locked and you cannot unlock it, do not rely on it.
  • If Cellular is not working and you are leaving without iPhone, reconsider.
  • If something affects safety, solve it before leaving.

Common mistakes before leaving home

  • Leaving the watch on the charger.
  • Leaving with low battery.
  • Forgetting the iPhone with a GPS watch.
  • Having Airplane Mode enabled.
  • Having Sleep Focus still active.
  • Using headphones too loud outdoors.
  • Starting a route without checking destination.
  • Starting a workout and forgetting to end it.
  • Relying on Apple Pay without backup.
  • Going out alone without checking emergency setup.

Practical advice

Create a simple personal routine before leaving.

For example:

  • Watch on.
  • Unlocked.
  • Battery.
  • iPhone.
  • Weather.
  • Keys.
  • This short sequence can prevent many problems.

Users who rely on safety features should add:

  1. Medical ID.
  2. Emergency contacts.
  3. Connection.
  4. Battery.

Exercise for appendix 3

Before your next outing, follow this checklist:

  • Put on the Apple Watch.
  • Unlock it.
  • Check battery.
  • Open Control Centre.
  • Check Airplane Mode.
  • Check Focus.
  • Check Silent Mode.
  • Make the iPhone play a sound if you want to confirm connection.
  • Check weather.
  • Check whether you need the iPhone.
  • If going for a walk, start the correct workout.
  • When you return, end the workout if one was started.
  • Review what worked and what you forgot.
  • Adjust your personal checklist accordingly.

Summary of appendix 3

Before leaving home, the Apple Watch should be on the wrist, unlocked, charged, and connected as needed. Battery matters for accessibility and safety. Focus modes and Airplane Mode can block important functions. Weather and route should be checked before outdoor activity. GPS and Cellular models do not behave the same away from the iPhone. Headphones should be used carefully outdoors. Medication, emergency contacts, Medical ID, and safety features should be reviewed if they matter to the user. A short leaving-home routine makes the Apple Watch much more reliable.

Back to table of contents

Appendix 4. Glossary of important Apple Watch terms

This glossary explains common Apple Watch terms in plain language. It is designed for users who are learning the device with VoiceOver or who need to understand the meaning of words that appear in settings, apps, and instructions.

Apple Watch

Apple’s smartwatch. It works together with the iPhone and can show notifications, calls, messages, health data, workouts, alarms, timers, weather, Wallet, apps, and other functions.

Apple Watch GPS

Apple Watch model without its own mobile data connection. It usually depends on the iPhone for calls, messages, and data when away from Wi-Fi.

Apple Watch GPS plus Cellular

Apple Watch model that can use a mobile plan, if supported by the carrier. It can work more independently from the iPhone for calls, messages, and data, provided service and coverage are available.

Activation Lock

Security feature linked to the Apple Account. It prevents another person from using the Apple Watch if it is lost, stolen, or still linked to the previous owner. Very important when buying used.

Activity

The app and system that records daily movement, exercise minutes, and stand or movement goals.

Activity rings

  • Visual representation of daily goals.
  • The main rings are Move, Exercise, and Stand.
  • VoiceOver can read the information even if the rings are not seen.

Airplane Mode

Mode that disables wireless connections. If enabled, it may affect calls, messages, data, and connection with the iPhone.

Always-On display

Feature on some models that keeps the screen visible even when the wrist is lowered. For totally blind users, it may not be necessary and may use more battery.

Apple Account

The account used for Apple services, iCloud, Find My, App Store, and Activation Lock. Formerly often referred to as Apple ID.

Apple Pay

Apple’s contactless payment system. On Apple Watch, it is usually opened by double-pressing the side button.

App View

The way Apple Watch shows installed apps. It can be Grid View or List View. List View is usually easier with VoiceOver.

AssistiveTouch

Accessibility feature that allows some Apple Watch actions to be controlled with hand gestures. It is different from VoiceOver.

Battery complication

A watch face element that shows Apple Watch battery percentage. Very useful for quick checking.

Blood Oxygen

Health feature available on some models and regions. It estimates blood oxygen from the wrist. It does not replace a medical pulse oximeter.

Bluetooth

Wireless technology used to connect the Apple Watch with the iPhone, headphones, and other accessories.

Braille display

External device that shows text in refreshable braille cells. Mainly used with iPhone, iPad, Mac, and VoiceOver. Its relationship with Apple Watch depends on system support and workflow.

Cellular

Mobile network capability. On Apple Watch, Cellular means the watch can use a mobile plan if supported.

Complication

A small item on the watch face that shows information or opens an app. Examples: battery, weather, timer, activity, calendar.

Control Centre

Quick settings area on the Apple Watch. It allows access to battery, Silent Mode, Focus, Airplane Mode, Find iPhone, and other controls. On recent watchOS versions, it opens by pressing the side button once.

Crown haptics

Tactile feedback when turning the Digital Crown on some models.

Digital Crown

The round physical control on the side of the Apple Watch. It can be pressed and turned. It is different from the side button.

Double tap

With VoiceOver, double tap means tapping the screen twice to activate the selected item. It should not be confused with the hand gesture called Double Tap on some newer models.

Double Tap gesture

Hand gesture available on some newer models for certain actions. It is performed by tapping fingers together. It is not the same as VoiceOver double tap.

ECG

Electrocardiogram feature available on some models and in some countries. It records a single-lead ECG from the wrist. It does not replace a clinical ECG.

Emergency contacts

People listed in Medical ID who may be contacted or notified in emergency situations, depending on settings and availability.

Emergency SOS

Safety feature that can call emergency services from the Apple Watch. It is for real emergencies and should not be tested with real calls.

Fall Detection

Safety feature that can detect some hard falls and offer emergency help. It does not detect every fall.

Find Devices

App or feature used to locate Apple devices linked to the Apple Account.

Find iPhone

Control on the Apple Watch that makes the iPhone play a sound if it is nearby and connected.

Find My

Apple system for locating devices, people, and some items. Used for lost devices, location sharing, and Activation Lock.

Focus

  • System feature that filters notifications.
  • Examples include Do Not Disturb, Sleep, Work, Exercise, and custom modes.
  • Focus modes can block alerts if configured badly.

GPS

Satellite positioning system used for location and outdoor workouts. On Apple Watch, GPS also refers to models without Cellular.

Grid View

App view where apps are shown as a grid of icons. It may be less comfortable with VoiceOver than List View.

Haptic feedback

Vibration or tap felt on the wrist. Used for alerts, notifications, timers, alarms, and other events.

Health app

iPhone app where health data are reviewed and managed. It includes heart, sleep, medication, Medical ID, permissions, and many other categories.

Heart Rate app

Apple Watch app that measures and shows heart rate.

Irregular rhythm notifications

Health feature that may notify about patterns compatible with certain irregular heart rhythms, depending on model and region. It is not a diagnosis.

List View

App view where apps appear in a list. Usually easier with VoiceOver.

Low Power Mode

Mode that reduces some functions to extend battery life. It may affect background activity or some features depending on version.

Medical ID

Emergency health information stored in the Health app. It can include medication, allergies, conditions, and emergency contacts.

Move ring

Activity ring that measures active calories.

Noise

Feature that can alert about high environmental sound levels on compatible models.

Now Playing

App or screen that controls current audio playback. Useful for music, podcasts, audiobooks, and iPhone audio control.

Passcode

Numeric code used to unlock the Apple Watch. Required for Apple Pay and important for privacy.

Prominent Haptic

Setting that makes some haptic alerts stronger or more noticeable. Useful for users who miss standard vibrations.

Side button

The elongated physical button near the Digital Crown. Used for Control Centre, Wallet, and emergency options depending on action and version.

Silent Mode

Mode that silences many sounds but can still allow vibrations. Not the same as Focus.

Siri

Apple’s voice assistant. On Apple Watch, Siri can make calls, send messages, create timers, start workouts, open apps, and more.

Sleep Focus

Focus mode designed to reduce interruptions during sleep.

Sleep tracking

Feature that records sleep duration and related data when wearing the Apple Watch at night.

Stand ring

Activity ring that encourages movement during different hours of the day. For wheelchair users, it may be adapted.

Timer

Countdown alert. Useful for cooking, medication routines, exercise, and daily tasks.

VoiceOver

Apple’s screen reader. It reads the Apple Watch screen aloud and allows blind users to interact through gestures.

Wallet

Apple app for payment cards, passes, tickets, and other compatible items.

watchOS

Operating system of the Apple Watch.

Watch app

iPhone app used to configure the Apple Watch.

Workout

App used to record specific exercise sessions.

Wrist Detection

Feature that detects whether the Apple Watch is being worn. It affects locking, Apple Pay, and some health features.

Summary of appendix 4

Apple Watch has many specific terms. The most important for blind users are VoiceOver, Digital Crown, side button, Control Centre, haptics, complications, notifications, Watch app, Health app, Fitness app, and Emergency SOS. Understanding the vocabulary makes settings and instructions easier to follow.

Back to table of contents

Appendix 5. Frequent problems and quick solutions

This appendix gathers common Apple Watch problems and gives quick solutions. It is intended as a practical reference for users who need to check something quickly without reading the full troubleshooting module. The order is important.

Always check the simple things first: battery, connection, lock status, Focus modes, Airplane Mode, notifications, volume, haptics, and whether the feature is available on that model. Many problems that look serious are caused by one small setting. Technology likes drama, but most failures begin with something boring.

Problem: VoiceOver does not speak

Possible causes:

  • VoiceOver is off.
  • Volume is too low.
  • Audio is going to headphones.
  • The watch is muted or sound settings are low.
  • The watch is locked or not responding.

What to do:

  • Triple-click the Digital Crown if the accessibility shortcut is configured.
  • Ask Siri to turn on VoiceOver, if Siri is available.
  • Open the Watch app on the iPhone.
  • Go to Accessibility.
  • Go to VoiceOver.
  • Turn it on.
  • Check volume.
  • Check audio output.
  • Restart the watch if needed.

Problem: I turned VoiceOver off by mistake

What to do:

  • Triple-click the Digital Crown if the shortcut is configured.
  • If that does not work, use the Watch app on the iPhone.
  • Open Watch.
  • Go to My Watch.
  • Go to Accessibility.
  • Go to VoiceOver.
  • Turn VoiceOver on.

If Siri is available, you can also try:

  • Turn on VoiceOver.
  • Problem: The Apple Watch does not vibrate

Possible causes:

  • Haptic Alerts are off.
  • Prominent Haptic is off or not needed.
  • The strap is too loose.
  • The watch is locked.
  • Notifications are blocked.
  • Focus mode is active.

What to do:

  • Open the Watch app on the iPhone.
  • Go to Sounds and Haptics.
  • Enable Haptic Alerts.
  • Enable Prominent Haptic if needed.
  • Adjust the strap.
  • Set a one-minute timer to test vibration.
  • Check Focus modes.
  • Check notification settings.

Problem: Notifications do not arrive

Possible causes:

  • The watch is locked.
  • The watch is not on the wrist.
  • Focus mode is active.
  • Airplane Mode is on.
  • Notifications are disabled.
  • The iPhone is being used.
  • The app does not support Apple Watch notifications.

What to do:

  • Check that the watch is on your wrist.
  • Unlock the watch.
  • Check Control Centre.
  • Turn off Airplane Mode if needed.
  • Check Focus modes.
  • Open the Watch app.
  • Go to Notifications.
  • Review the app.
  • Check the same app’s notification settings on the iPhone.

Problem: Calls do not arrive on the Apple Watch

Possible causes:

  • The watch is disconnected.
  • The iPhone is not nearby, if using a GPS model.
  • Cellular is not active, if relying on Cellular.
  • Focus mode is blocking calls.
  • Phone notifications are disabled.
  • The watch is locked.

What to do:

  • Check connection.
  • Check Bluetooth on the iPhone.
  • Check whether the iPhone receives the call.
  • Check Focus modes.
  • Check Phone notifications in the Watch app.
  • If using Cellular, check mobile plan and coverage.
  • If using GPS, keep the iPhone nearby.

Problem: Messages do not arrive

Possible causes:

  • Messages notifications are disabled.
  • Focus mode is active.
  • The watch is disconnected.
  • The app does not support full Apple Watch interaction.
  • The iPhone is being used.

What to do:

  • Open the Watch app.
  • Go to Notifications.
  • Review Messages.
  • Check iPhone Settings, Notifications, Messages.
  • Check Focus modes.
  • Check connection.
  • Remember that other messaging apps may behave differently from Apple Messages.

Problem: The Apple Watch is disconnected from the iPhone

Possible causes:

  1. Bluetooth is off.
  2. Wi-Fi is off.
  3. Airplane Mode is active.
  4. Devices are too far apart.
  5. One device needs restarting.
  6. Pairing has a problem.

What to do:

  • Bring the iPhone and Apple Watch close together.
  • Check Bluetooth on the iPhone.
  • Check Wi-Fi.
  • Check Airplane Mode on both devices.
  • Restart the Apple Watch.
  • Restart the iPhone.
  • Open the Watch app and check whether the watch appears connected.

Problem: The Apple Watch does not charge

Possible causes:

  • The charger is not connected.
  • The power adapter is faulty.
  • The socket is not working.
  • The watch is not aligned with the magnetic charger.
  • The charger is dirty or damaged.
  • The battery is fully depleted.

What to do:

  • Check the cable.
  • Check the power adapter.
  • Try another socket.
  • Place the watch again on the charger.
  • Wait a few minutes if the battery is completely empty.
  • Try another compatible charger if available.
  • If nothing works, contact Apple Support or an authorised service provider.

Problem: Battery drains too quickly

Possible causes:

  • Old battery.
  • Cellular use.
  • GPS.
  • Long workouts.
  • Audio streaming.
  • Too many notifications.
  • Always-On display.
  • High brightness.
  • Recent update.
  • Background activity.

What to do:

  • Check Battery Health.
  • Review notifications.
  • Reduce unnecessary alerts.
  • Check Always-On display.
  • Check Cellular use.
  • Check downloaded or streaming audio.
  • Restart the watch.
  • Restart the iPhone.
  • Observe after updates.
  • If battery health is poor, service may be needed.

Problem: The watch asks for the passcode too often

Possible causes:

  • The watch is too loose.
  • Wrist Detection is not working well.
  • The watch thinks it has been removed.
  • Sensor contact is poor.

What to do:

  • Adjust the strap.
  • Wear the watch slightly above the wrist bone.
  • Check Wrist Detection settings.
  • Check whether tattoos or poor contact affect the sensors.
  • If it continues, review settings or contact support.

Problem: Apple Pay does not work

Possible causes:

  • The card is not added to the Apple Watch.
  • The watch is locked.
  • Passcode is not enabled.
  • The wrong button is being pressed.
  • The terminal does not accept contactless payment.
  • The bank requires verification.
  • The card is blocked.

What to do:

  • Check Wallet and Apple Pay in the Watch app.
  • Make sure the card is added to the Apple Watch.
  • Unlock the watch.
  • Double-press the side button.
  • Do not use the Digital Crown.
  • Confirm that the shop accepts contactless payments.
  • Check with your bank if needed.

Problem: Siri does not respond

Possible causes:

  1. Siri is disabled.
  2. No connection.
  3. Microphone issue.
  4. Wrong invocation method.
  5. Language or settings problem.

What to do:

  1. Open the Watch app.
  2. Go to Siri.
  3. Review enabled methods.
  4. Try holding the Digital Crown.
  5. Use a short command.
  6. Check connection.
  7. Restart if needed.

Problem: Siri misunderstands commands

What to do:

  1. Use shorter phrases.
  2. Speak clearly.
  3. Avoid background noise.
  4. Use exact contact names.
  5. Rename confusing contacts.
  6. Break the action into steps.

Instead of saying a long message at once, say:

  • Send a message to Anna.
  • Then dictate the message when Siri asks.

Problem: The workout did not record correctly

Possible causes:

  1. Workout was not started.
  2. Wrong workout type.
  3. Battery ran out.
  4. Location was disabled.
  5. The watch was loose.
  6. Workout was not ended properly.
  7. Data did not sync yet.

What to do:

  • Check Fitness on the iPhone.
  • Check whether the workout appears.
  • Start workouts manually next time.
  • Choose the correct workout type.
  • Check battery before starting.
  • End the workout properly.
  • For outdoor workouts, check location permissions.

Problem: Workout is still running after finishing

What to do:

  • Open the Workout app.
  • Return to the active workout screen.
  • Find End or Finish.
  • Double tap.
  • Confirm if required.
  • Listen to the summary.
  • Find Done, OK, or Close.
  • Double tap.
  • Do not just press the Digital Crown and leave.

Problem: Sleep was not recorded

Possible causes:

  1. The watch was not worn.
  2. Battery ran out.
  3. Sleep tracking is not enabled.
  4. Sleep schedule is not configured.
  5. The watch was too loose.
  6. The watch was locked.
  7. Not enough nights of data.

What to do:

  • Check battery before sleeping.
  • Wear the watch properly.
  • Check Sleep settings in Health.
  • Check Sleep settings in the Watch app.
  • Review data in Health.
  • Repeat for several nights before drawing conclusions.

Problem: Medication reminder did not appear

Possible causes:

  • Medication schedule is wrong.
  • Notification is disabled.
  • Focus mode blocked it.
  • The watch was locked or not worn.
  • Battery was low.

What to do:

  • Open Health on the iPhone.
  • Go to Medications.
  • Check schedule.
  • Check notifications.
  • Check Focus modes.
  • Check Apple Watch notification settings.
  • Test with a harmless reminder if needed.

Problem: Weather does not update

Possible causes:

  1. Location permission is disabled.
  2. No connection.
  3. Wrong city selected.
  4. Watch is disconnected.
  5. Weather service issue.

What to do:

  1. Open Weather on the iPhone.
  2. Check location permissions.
  3. Check Apple Watch connection.
  4. Check saved locations.
  5. Ask Siri for weather.
  6. Restart if needed.

Problem: Maps gives confusing directions

Possible causes:

  1. Wrong destination.
  2. Poor location accuracy.
  3. Map data problem.
  4. Route type wrong.
  5. GPS signal weak.

What to do:

  • Confirm destination on the iPhone.
  • Use the iPhone for route setup.
  • Stop in a safe place before checking.
  • Do not follow uncertain directions blindly.
  • Use mobility skills and other navigation tools.

Problem: The iPhone cannot be found from the watch

Possible causes:

  • iPhone is too far away.
  • Devices are disconnected.
  • iPhone has no battery.
  • Bluetooth or Wi-Fi issue.

What to do:

  • Open Control Centre on the Apple Watch.
  • Use Find iPhone.
  • If no sound plays, check connection.
  • Search common places.
  • Use Find My from another device if needed.

Problem: The Apple Watch cannot be found from the iPhone

What to do:

  • Open Find My on the iPhone.
  • Go to Devices.
  • Choose the Apple Watch.
  • Use Play Sound if nearby.
  • Check last known location.
  • Use Mark as Lost if truly lost.
  • Remember that no battery means limited location information.

Problem: ECG does not appear

Possible causes:

  • Model does not support ECG.
  • Country or region does not support it.
  • Health setup is incomplete.
  • Age requirement not met.
  • System not updated.

What to do:

  • Check Apple Watch model.
  • Check country availability.
  • Open Health on the iPhone.
  • Go to Heart.
  • Look for ECG setup.
  • Update iPhone and Apple Watch if appropriate.
  • Do not assume it is a VoiceOver problem.

Problem: Blood Oxygen does not appear

Possible causes:

  • Model does not support it.
  • Feature not available in country or region.
  • Specific restrictions affect the device.
  • System version issue.

What to do:

  • Check model.
  • Check region availability.
  • Open the app list on the Apple Watch.
  • Search for Blood Oxygen.
  • Check Health on iPhone.
  • If unavailable, do not keep searching for a button that is not there.

Problem: Fall Detection does not appear

Possible causes:

  1. Model does not support it.
  2. System version issue.
  3. Setting is in Emergency SOS.
  4. Age or configuration affects availability.

What to do:

  1. Open Watch app on iPhone.
  2. Go to Emergency SOS.
  3. Look for Fall Detection.
  4. Check model compatibility.
  5. Update if appropriate.

Problem: Emergency SOS appears by mistake

What to do:

  • Do not panic.
  • Listen to VoiceOver.
  • Cancel if the call has not started.
  • If the call connects, explain clearly that it was accidental.
  • Do not hang up without explanation if emergency services have answered.

Problem: The watch is asking for another person’s Apple Account

Cause:

  • Activation Lock is active.
  • What to do:
  • Ask the previous owner to remove the Apple Watch from their Apple Account.
  • Do not buy or keep the watch if this cannot be done.
  • Erasing the watch will not solve Activation Lock.
  • There is no legitimate shortcut.

Problem: watchOS update does not install

Possible causes:

  • Battery too low.
  • Watch not on charger.
  • iPhone not near.
  • No Wi-Fi.
  • Not enough storage.
  • Temporary server problem.

What to do:

  • Put the watch on charger.
  • Keep iPhone nearby.
  • Connect iPhone to Wi-Fi.
  • Check battery.
  • Check storage.
  • Remove unused apps or downloaded content.
  • Restart both devices.
  • Try again later.

Problem: The app list is confusing

What to do:

  • Use List View.
  • Remove unused apps.
  • Reduce installed apps.
  • Use Siri to open frequent apps.
  • Use simple watch faces.
  • Manage apps from the iPhone Watch app.

Problem: There are too many notifications

What to do:

  • Open Watch app on iPhone.
  • Go to Notifications.
  • Disable unnecessary apps.
  • Review Activity notifications.
  • Review Messages groups.
  • Review Focus modes.
  • Keep only important alerts on the wrist.

Problem: VoiceOver is too fast

What to do:

  • Open Watch app on iPhone.
  • Go to Accessibility.
  • Go to VoiceOver.
  • Adjust speech rate.
  • Test on the watch.
  • Choose comfort over speed, especially for beginners.

Problem: VoiceOver is too quiet

What to do:

  • Check watch volume.
  • Check Sounds and Haptics.
  • Check whether audio is going to headphones.
  • Check VoiceOver volume if available.
  • Use headphones if needed.
  • Avoid reading private content aloud in public.

Problem: The watch feels overwhelming

What to do:

  • Simplify the watch face.
  • Use List View.
  • Remove unused apps.
  • Reduce notifications.
  • Keep only essential complications.
  • Focus on timers, calls, messages, battery, and Find iPhone first.
  • Add advanced features later.

Common quick troubleshooting order

  • Check battery.
  • Check lock status.
  • Check connection.
  • Check Airplane Mode.
  • Check Focus modes.
  • Check Silent Mode.
  • Check haptics.
  • Check notification settings.
  • Check the iPhone Watch app.
  • Restart Apple Watch.
  • Restart iPhone.
  • Check updates.
  • Only then consider unpairing or support.

Summary of appendix 5

Most Apple Watch problems should be checked step by step. Battery, connection, Focus modes, Airplane Mode, lock status, notifications, haptics, and volume are common causes. The iPhone Watch app is often the easiest place to fix settings. Do not reset the watch as the first solution. Activation Lock requires the previous owner’s account removal. Emergency SOS should not be tested with real calls. When hardware, account, charging, or repeated pairing problems appear, contact Apple Support or an authorised service provider.

Back to table of contents

Appendix 6. Suggested watch faces and complications for different users

The Apple Watch face is the starting point of the whole experience. For a sighted user, the watch face is mainly visual. For a blind user with VoiceOver, the watch face is also a structured place where information can be read and apps can be opened quickly. That is why choosing a good watch face matters. A crowded watch face can make the Apple Watch harder to use. A simple watch face can make it much easier. The goal is not to create the most decorative face.

The goal is to create a face that answers practical questions quickly.

  • What time is it?
  • How much battery is left?
  • Do I have an appointment?
  • Will it rain?
  • Can I start a timer?
  • Can I start a workout?
  • Can I access medication reminders?
  • Can I reach the feature I use most?

That is the point. Not visual drama. Not digital jewellery. Usefulness. A rare concept, but still legal.

What a complication is

A complication is a small element on the watch face. It can show information or open an app.

Examples:

  • Battery.
  • Weather.
  • Timer.
  • Calendar.
  • Activity.
  • Heart Rate.
  • Workout.
  • Alarms.
  • Medication.
  • Reminders.
  • Home.
  • Maps.
  • Wallet.
  • Not all complications are available on all watch faces.
  • Not all apps provide complications.
  • Some complications are more useful with VoiceOver than others.

General rule for VoiceOver users

  • Use fewer complications.
  • Choose the ones that are truly useful.
  • Check whether VoiceOver reads them clearly.
  • Do not add a complication just because it exists.
  • A good watch face for VoiceOver should be predictable.
  • The user should know what appears on it and in what order.

Recommended face for a blind beginner

A beginner should start with a simple face.

Suggested complications:

  • Battery.
  • Weather.
  • Timer.
  • Calendar or Reminders.
  • Optional: Activity.
  • Why these?
  • Battery tells whether the watch can be trusted during the day.
  • Weather helps before leaving home.
  • Timer is useful and easy to practise.
  • Calendar or Reminders help with appointments and tasks.
  • Activity can be useful if the user is starting to monitor movement.

Avoid:

  1. Too many health metrics.
  2. Too many third-party apps.
  3. Decorative complications.
  4. Complex faces.

Recommended face for an older person

Suggested complications:

  • Battery.
  • Date.
  • Timer or Alarms.
  • Medication, if used.
  • Calendar.
  • Heart Rate, if useful.
  • Weather.
  • Why these?
  • Battery supports daily reliability.
  • Date helps orientation.
  • Timer and alarms support routines.
  • Medication supports treatment schedules.
  • Calendar supports appointments.
  • Heart Rate may be useful if the person checks it.
  • Weather helps before going out.
  • Keep the face simple.
  • For older users, fewer elements are usually better.

Recommended face for a deafblind user

Suggested complications:

  • Battery.
  • Timer.
  • Alarms.
  • Medication, if used.
  • Calendar or Reminders.
  • Optional: Activity or Heart Rate if useful.
  • The most important part is not visual layout.
  • It is haptic alerts and simplicity.
  • The watch face should not have too many elements.
  • The user may use the watch mainly as a tactile alert device and the iPhone for detailed review.

Recommended face for workouts

Suggested complications:

  • Workout.
  • Battery.
  • Heart Rate.
  • Activity.
  • Weather.
  • Timer.
  • Why these?
  • Workout opens the Workout app quickly.
  • Battery matters before exercise.
  • Heart Rate helps with quick checks.
  • Activity shows progress.
  • Weather matters outdoors.
  • Timer helps with intervals or rests.
  • This face can be used only during exercise.

Recommended face for health monitoring

Suggested complications:

  • Heart Rate.
  • Medication.
  • Sleep.
  • Activity.
  • Battery.
  • ECG, if available.
  • Blood Oxygen, if available and useful.
  • Use this face only if the user understands the data.
  • Do not overload a beginner with health complications.
  • Health information can help, but too much constant checking can create anxiety.

Recommended face for travel

Suggested complications:

  • Battery.
  • Weather.
  • Calendar.
  • Maps.
  • Wallet.
  • World Clock, if useful.
  • Find Devices.
  • Reminders.
  • Why these?
  • Travel requires battery, route, tickets, weather, time, and appointments.
  • Wallet can be useful for cards or passes.
  • Find Devices helps with Apple devices.
  • This face can be useful in airports, stations, hotels, or unfamiliar cities.

Recommended face for daily productivity

Suggested complications:

  • Calendar.
  • Reminders.
  • Timer.
  • Battery.
  • Weather.
  • Messages or Phone, if useful.
  • Shortcuts, if used.
  • This is useful for users who use the watch for tasks and scheduling.
  • Keep it practical.

Recommended face for smart home users

Suggested complications:

  • Home.
  • Battery.
  • Timer.
  • Weather.
  • Shortcuts, if used.
  • Calendar or Reminders.
  • This can help control devices or scenes quickly.
  • However, many smart home tasks may be faster with Siri.

Recommended face for sleep

Suggested complications:

  • Time.
  • Alarm.
  • Battery.
  • Sleep.
  • Nothing else may be needed.
  • A sleep face should be minimal.
  • At night, the user does not need a crowded dashboard.

Recommended face for Apple Pay users

Apple Pay is usually opened by double-pressing the side button, so a Wallet complication may not be necessary. But if the user wants quick access to Wallet or passes, a Wallet complication may be useful.

Suggested complications:

  • Battery.
  • Wallet.
  • Calendar.
  • Weather.
  • Timer.
  • The key is knowing that payment uses the side button.

Recommended face for people who often lose the iPhone

There is not always a direct Find iPhone complication, depending on version and face. But the user should know how to open Control Centre quickly.

Suggested complications:

  • Battery.
  • Timer.
  • Weather.
  • Calendar.
  • Maybe Find Devices, if available.

The real skill is:

  1. Open Control Centre.
  2. Find iPhone.
  3. Make it play a sound.

Choosing between one face and several faces

Beginners should start with one face.

Advanced users may use several:

  • Daily face.
  • Workout face.
  • Sleep face.
  • Travel face.
  • Health face.
  • This can be useful if the user understands how to switch between faces.
  • But too many faces can create confusion.
  • For many people, one well-designed face is enough.

How to choose complications

Ask these questions:

  • Do I use this every day?
  • Is it faster from the watch face than from Siri?
  • Does VoiceOver read it clearly?
  • Does it help before leaving home?
  • Does it help with health, safety, or routine?
  • Can I remove something less useful?
  • If the answer is no, do not add it.

Complications that are often useful

  • Battery.
  • Weather.
  • Timer.
  • Calendar.
  • Reminders.
  • Workout.
  • Activity.
  • Heart Rate.
  • Medication.
  • Alarms.
  • Sleep.
  • Maps.
  • Wallet.
  • Home.
  • Shortcuts.

Complications that may be less useful for some blind users

  • Decorative photo complications.
  • Visual-only complications.
  • Complications with unclear VoiceOver labels.
  • Apps that are better used on the iPhone.
  • Complications for apps rarely used.
  • This depends on the user.
  • A complication is useful only if it saves time.

How to change watch faces from the iPhone

The iPhone is usually the easiest place.

  • Open the Watch app.
  • Go to Face Gallery or My Faces.
  • Choose a face.
  • Add complications.
  • Review the layout.
  • Set it as current watch face.
  • With VoiceOver, move through options carefully.

Changing complications

From the Watch app:

  • Choose the watch face.
  • Find complications.
  • Select each position.
  • Choose the desired complication.
  • Save or set the face.
  • The exact layout depends on the face.
  • Not all faces offer the same number or type of complications.

Changing from the Apple Watch

It may also be possible to edit the face from the Apple Watch itself. However, for VoiceOver users, this can be more complex. For beginners, use the iPhone.

Testing a watch face

After creating a watch face:

  • Put on the watch.
  • Return to the watch face.
  • Swipe through the items with VoiceOver.
  • Listen to each complication.
  • Check whether the order makes sense.
  • Open each important complication.
  • Return to the watch face.
  • If it feels confusing, simplify.
  • A watch face is only good if it works in real use.

When to simplify the face

Simplify if:

  • VoiceOver takes too long to read everything.
  • The user forgets what each item does.
  • Battery is hard to find.
  • Important items are buried.
  • The user opens the wrong app often.
  • The face feels cluttered.
  • The user is a beginner.
  • Remove complications until only useful ones remain.

Common mistakes

  • Adding too many complications.
  • Choosing a face because it looks nice but is awkward with VoiceOver.
  • Using visual complications that do not help.
  • Not adding Battery.
  • Not testing with VoiceOver.
  • Creating too many watch faces.
  • Using a workout face as the daily face when it has too much information.
  • Using a health face that encourages constant checking.

Practical advice

  • Start with a simple face.
  • Add Battery.
  • Add Weather.
  • Add Timer.
  • Add Calendar or Reminders.
  • Add one personal priority.
  • Then stop.
  • Use the watch for a few days.
  • Only add more if something is truly missing.

Exercise for appendix 6

Open the Watch app on the iPhone. Choose your current watch face. Review every complication.

Ask:

  • Do I use this?
  • Does VoiceOver read it clearly?
  • Does it help me daily?
  • Remove one unnecessary complication.
  • Add Battery if it is not already present.
  • Add Timer if you use timers often.
  • Add Weather if you go out frequently.
  • Save the face.
  • Then check it on the Apple Watch with VoiceOver.

Summary of appendix 6

The watch face should be practical, not crowded. Complications provide quick access to information or apps. For VoiceOver users, fewer complications are usually better. Battery is one of the most useful complications. Weather, Timer, Calendar, Reminders, Workout, Heart Rate, Medication, and Activity may be useful depending on the person. Beginners should use one simple face. Advanced users may create different faces for daily use, workouts, sleep, travel, or health. Every watch face should be tested with VoiceOver.

Back to table of contents

Appendix 7. Quick checklist to print or review before starting

This appendix brings together a short checklist. It is designed to be used before starting with a new Apple Watch, after restoring it, or when helping another blind person configure it. You do not need to activate everything. The important thing is to check that the essentials are ready.

Block 1

Before pairing

  • Apple Watch charged.
  • iPhone charged.
  • iPhone updated.
  • Bluetooth enabled on the iPhone.
  • Wi-Fi or mobile data working.
  • Apple Account active.
  • Apple Watch near the iPhone.
  • Enough time for setup.
  • Band prepared.
  • Charger located.
  • If the watch is used, check that it does not have Activation Lock.

Block 2

During pairing

Open the Watch app on the iPhone.

  • Start pairing.
  • Choose Set Up for Myself or for someone else, as appropriate.
  • Follow the iPhone instructions.
  • Turn on VoiceOver if needed.
  • Choose wrist.
  • Choose Digital Crown orientation.
  • Create passcode.
  • Accept only options you understand.
  • Do not activate everything without reviewing it.

Block 3

Basic accessibility

  • VoiceOver enabled.
  • Speech rate adjusted.
  • Volume suitable.
  • Accessibility Shortcut configured with VoiceOver.
  • Triple-click on the Digital Crown understood.
  • App view set to List View, if more comfortable.
  • Haptic feedback enabled.
  • Prominent Haptic enabled if needed.
  • Silent Mode understood.
  • Do Not Disturb or Focus understood.

Block 4

Physical controls

  • Digital Crown located.
  • Side button located.
  • Press Digital Crown to go back or open apps.
  • Turn Digital Crown to scroll.
  • Press side button once for Control Centre, where applicable.
  • Double-press side button for Wallet, if used.
  • Hold down side button only when you know what you are doing.
  • Do not confuse Digital Crown with side button.

Block 5

Initial watch face

  • Choose a simple watch face.
  • Add Battery complication.
  • Add Weather complication if used.
  • Add Workout complication if exercise will be used.
  • Add Timer if used often.
  • Avoid too many complications.
  • Check that VoiceOver reads the watch face elements well.

Block 6

Control Centre

  • Know how to open Control Centre.
  • Locate battery.
  • Locate Silent Mode.
  • Locate Find iPhone.
  • Locate Airplane Mode.
  • Locate Focus.
  • Locate Wi-Fi if it appears.
  • Know how to return to the watch face.
  • Test making the iPhone play a sound.

Block 7

Notifications

  • Phone reviewed.
  • Messages reviewed.
  • Calendar reviewed.
  • Reminders reviewed.
  • Alarms and timers checked.
  • Health reviewed if alerts are used.
  • Medication reviewed if used.
  • Social media limited.
  • Promotions disabled.
  • Unnecessary apps not allowed to send alerts to the watch.

Block 8

Communication

  • Test call completed.
  • Answering a call tested.
  • Ending a call tested.
  • Test message completed.
  • Reading a message tested.
  • Short message reply tested.
  • Dictation reviewed before sending.
  • Siri tested with a simple command.
  • Timer with Siri tested.

Block 9

Basic routines

  1. Timer created and stopped.
  2. Alarm created and stopped.
  3. Reminder created and completed.
  4. Find iPhone tested.
  5. Weather checked.
  6. Battery checked.
  7. Charging tested.

Block 10

Activity and workout

  • Activity opened.
  • Move, Exercise, and Stand listened to.
  • Fitness opened on the iPhone.
  • Workout opened.
  • Short test workout started.
  • Pause tested.
  • Resume tested.
  • End tested.
  • Summary listened to.
  • Workout reviewed in Fitness.

Block 11

Health

  • Personal data reviewed in Health.
  • Age reviewed.
  • Height reviewed.
  • Weight reviewed.
  • Heart rate located.
  • Sleep configured only if it will be used.
  • Medication configured only if appropriate.
  • Advanced features reviewed according to model.
  • Do not interpret data as a diagnosis.
  • Do not activate features without understanding them.

Block 12

Safety

  • Medical ID created or reviewed.
  • Important allergies added if appropriate.
  • Relevant medication added if appropriate.
  • Important medical conditions added if appropriate.
  • Communication note added if useful.
  • Emergency contacts added.
  • Contact numbers reviewed.
  • Emergency SOS located.
  • Fall Detection reviewed if appropriate.
  • Do not make test calls to emergency services.

Block 13

Apple Pay and Wallet

  • Watch passcode enabled.
  • Wallet reviewed.
  • Card added to Apple Watch if payment will be used.
  • Default card checked.
  • Double-pressing the side button practised at home.
  • First purchase planned in a quiet environment.
  • Alternative payment method prepared.

Block 14

Sleep and battery

Decide whether the Apple Watch will be worn during sleep. If sleep is used, configure it from Health.

Haptic alarm tested before relying on it.

  • Charging routine defined.
  • Battery checked before sleeping.
  • Battery checked before leaving home.
  • Charger located.
  • Low Power Mode understood, but not used without understanding it.

Block 15

Maps, audio, and other features

Maps tested with a known route if it will be used.

Do not use Maps as a substitute for orientation and mobility.

  • Now Playing tested.
  • Bluetooth headphones tested.
  • Suitable outdoor volume checked.
  • Home reviewed only if accessories are configured.
  • Camera Remote tested only as a remote control, not as visual description.

Block 16

Privacy

  • Health permissions reviewed.
  • Location permissions reviewed.
  • Apps with data access reviewed.
  • Private notifications reviewed.
  • Location sharing reviewed.
  • Activity sharing reviewed if used.
  • Health sharing reviewed if used.
  • Do not grant permissions without a reason.

Block 17

Updates and maintenance

  • watchOS version reviewed.
  • Automatic updates reviewed.
  • Do not update at a bad time.
  • Unnecessary apps removed or not installed.
  • Find My checked.
  • Apple Watch appears in Find My.
  • Backup and unpairing understood before selling or giving away.

Block 18

Final test of basic independence

The user can:

  • Check the time.
  • Return to the watch face.
  • Open the app list.
  • Open Control Centre.
  • Check battery.
  • Make the iPhone play a sound.
  • Answer a call.
  • End a call.
  • Read a notification.
  • Reply to a short message.
  • Create a timer.
  • Stop a timer.
  • Use Siri for a simple command.
  • Start and end a workout.
  • Charge the watch.
  • Know how to ask for help if something fails.

Ultra-quick ten-point checklist

  • VoiceOver enabled.
  • VoiceOver shortcut configured.
  • Battery visible.
  • Vibrations checked.
  • Notifications limited.
  • Calls tested.
  • Timer tested.
  • Workout tested.
  • Medical ID and contacts reviewed.
  • Charging routine defined.

Final advice for this appendix

If these ten points are correct, the Apple Watch already has a reasonable basis for use. More features can be added gradually afterwards. There is no need to turn the first day into a complete relocation to the wrist ecosystem. The watch should start by helping, not by examining the user.
