Appendix 8. Recommended learning plan for the first month

This appendix proposes a gradual learning plan for the first month of using the Apple Watch with VoiceOver. It is designed for blind users who are starting from scratch or who have used the watch very little. It can also help trainers, relatives, or support people who want to teach the Apple Watch without overwhelming the user. The goal is not to learn every feature in thirty days. The goal is to build a solid base. If the user understands the basics well, the rest can be added later.

If everything is taught too quickly, the Apple Watch becomes a confusing device full of gestures, sounds, vibrations, alerts, buttons, menus, and settings. A wonderful little storm on the wrist, because apparently one screen was not enough for modern life.

General rule for the first month

Learn in layers. Do not add a new layer until the previous one is reasonably comfortable.

The order should be:

  • Accessibility.
  • Physical controls.
  • Basic navigation.
  • Notifications.
  • Timers and alarms.
  • Calls and messages.
  • Battery and charging.
  • Health basics.
  • Workouts.
  • Safety.
  • Optional advanced features.
  • This order helps the user understand the watch gradually.

Week 1

Basic control and confidence

The first week should focus only on the essential handling of the Apple Watch.

Main goals:

  • Understand the physical controls.
  • Use VoiceOver.
  • Return to the watch face.
  • Open the app list.
  • Open Control Centre.
  • Check battery.
  • Use Find iPhone.
  • Use timers and alarms.
  • Charge the watch.
  • Nothing more is required in the first week.

Day 1

First contact

Tasks:

  • Put on the Apple Watch.
  • Unlock it.
  • Listen to the watch face with VoiceOver.
  • Locate the Digital Crown.
  • Locate the side button.
  • Press the Digital Crown.
  • Return to the watch face.
  • Open the app list.
  • Return again to the watch face.
  • The user should learn where they are.
  • There is no need to explore every app.

Day 2

VoiceOver gestures

Practise:

  • Swipe right.
  • Swipe left.
  • Double tap.
  • Touch exploration.
  • Turning the Digital Crown.
  • Returning with the Digital Crown.
  • Use a simple screen, such as the watch face or app list.
  • Do not practise in complicated apps.

Day 3

Control Centre

Practise:

  • Open Control Centre.
  • Find battery.
  • Find Silent Mode.
  • Find Focus.
  • Find Airplane Mode.
  • Find the button to make the iPhone play a sound.
  • Return to the watch face.
  • This day is important because Control Centre solves many daily situations.

Day 4

Find iPhone

Practise:

  • Place the iPhone nearby.
  • Open Control Centre.
  • Find the button to make the iPhone play a sound.
  • Activate it.
  • Locate the iPhone by sound.
  • Repeat several times.
  • This feature is easy and very useful.
  • It gives the user a quick practical success, which is rare enough in technology to be celebrated quietly.

Day 5

Timers

Practise:

  • Set a timer with Siri.
  • Set a timer from the Timers app.
  • Stop the timer.
  • Feel the vibration.
  • Listen to the alert.
  • Set different short timers.
  • Timers are excellent for learning without risk.

Day 6

Alarms

Practise:

  • Create an alarm a few minutes ahead.
  • Wait for the alert.
  • Stop the alarm.
  • Review how it feels on the wrist.
  • Try again if necessary.
  • Do not use an important wake-up alarm as the first test.

Day 7

Charging and daily routine

Practise:

  • Check battery.
  • Place the watch on the charger.
  • Confirm that it charges.
  • Remove it from the charger.
  • Put it on again.
  • Unlock it.
  • Choose a daily charging time.

At the end of week 1, the user should be able to:

  • Use basic gestures.
  • Identify Digital Crown and side button.
  • Open Control Centre.
  • Check battery.
  • Find the iPhone.
  • Use timers and alarms.
  • Charge the watch.

Week 2

Communication and notifications

The second week should focus on calls, messages, reminders, calendar, and notification control.

Main goals:

  1. Answer calls.
  2. End calls.
  3. Read messages.
  4. Reply briefly.
  5. Use reminders.
  6. Check calendar alerts.
  7. Understand notifications.
  8. Reduce unnecessary alerts.

Day 8

Incoming calls

With a trusted person:

  • Receive a test call.
  • Listen to VoiceOver.
  • Find Answer.
  • Double tap.
  • Speak.
  • Find End.
  • Double tap.
  • Repeat until the user is comfortable.

Day 9

Outgoing calls

Practise:

  • Call a trusted contact with Siri.
  • Call from the Phone app if appropriate.
  • End the call.
  • Check volume.
  • If Siri misunderstands names, review contact names on the iPhone.

Day 10

Messages

Practise:

  • Receive a test message.
  • Read it with VoiceOver.
  • Find Reply.
  • Use a quick reply.
  • Send.
  • Then try dictation if appropriate.
  • For long replies, use the iPhone.

Day 11

Reminders

Practise:

  • Create a reminder with Siri.
  • Example:
  • Remind me to check the Apple Watch in ten minutes.
  • Wait for the alert.
  • Open it.
  • Mark it as completed if appropriate.
  • Review it on the iPhone.

Day 12

Calendar

Practise:

  • Create a test calendar event on the iPhone.
  • Set an alert.
  • Wait for the Apple Watch notification.
  • Read it.
  • Dismiss it.
  • This helps the user understand appointment alerts.

Day 13

Notification review

Open the Watch app on the iPhone.

  • Go to Notifications.
  • Review enabled apps.
  • Disable unnecessary alerts.
  • Keep only important ones.
  • The goal is to avoid overload.
  • A watch that vibrates for every app is not a helpful assistant. It is a tiny attention thief with a strap.

Day 14

Review of week 2

The user should practise:

  1. Answering a call.
  2. Ending a call.
  3. Reading a message.
  4. Replying briefly.
  5. Creating a reminder.
  6. Receiving a calendar alert.
  7. Checking notifications.

At the end of week 2, the user should be able to communicate in basic situations and understand the most common alerts.

Week 3

Health, activity, and workouts

The third week introduces health and activity features. Do not introduce every health feature. Start with basic activity, heart rate, and one simple workout.

Main goals:

  • Open Activity.
  • Understand Move, Exercise, and Stand.
  • Open Heart Rate.
  • Start and end a workout.
  • Review Fitness on the iPhone.
  • Understand that health data are guidance, not diagnosis.

Day 15

Activity app

Open Activity on the Apple Watch.

Listen to:

  • Move.
  • Exercise.
  • Stand.
  • Steps, if available.
  • Distance, if available.
  • Do not worry about goals yet.
  • The first step is understanding what the watch shows.

Day 16

Fitness app on iPhone

  • Open Fitness on the iPhone.
  • Review daily activity.
  • Look for workouts, if any exist.
  • Compare what is easier on the watch and what is better on the iPhone.
  • The user should understand that the iPhone is better for detailed review.

Day 17

Heart Rate app

Open Heart Rate on the Apple Watch.

  • Keep the arm still.
  • Listen to the current heart rate.
  • Then open Health on the iPhone and review the Heart section.

Explain clearly:

  • This is useful information.
  • It is not a diagnosis.
  • Symptoms matter more than the watch.

Day 18

First workout

Choose a simple workout.

Recommended:

  • Indoor Walk.
  • Outdoor Walk.
  • Start an open goal workout.
  • Walk for a few minutes.
  • End the workout.
  • Listen to the summary.
  • This day is only for learning the process.

Day 19

Pause and resume workout

  • Start another short workout.
  • Pause it.
  • Resume it.
  • End it.
  • Review the summary.
  • The user should understand that leaving the app is not the same as ending the workout.

Day 20

Review workout in Fitness

  • Open Fitness on the iPhone.
  • Find the workout.
  • Review duration, distance, heart rate, and calories if available.
  • Do not focus on performance.
  • Focus on understanding where the data are.

Day 21

Health limits

Review the main health idea:

  • Apple Watch records information.
  • It can show alerts.
  • It can help observe trends.
  • It does not replace healthcare professionals.
  • It does not rule out problems if no alert appears.
  • If symptoms appear, seek help.

At the end of week 3, the user should be able to:

  1. Check Activity.
  2. Check Heart Rate.
  3. Start a simple workout.
  4. Pause and resume.
  5. End correctly.
  6. Review workouts on the iPhone.
  7. Understand health limits.

Week 4

Safety, personalisation, and optional features

The fourth week introduces safety and personalisation.

Main goals:

  • Configure Medical ID.
  • Add emergency contacts.
  • Review Emergency SOS.
  • Review Fall Detection if appropriate.
  • Choose a better watch face.
  • Review battery routine.
  • Introduce optional features only if useful.

Day 22

Medical ID

Open Health on the iPhone. Review Medical ID.

Add relevant information:

  1. Medical conditions.
  2. Allergies.
  3. Medication.
  4. Emergency contacts.
  5. Communication note if useful.

For example:

  • Blind person. Please communicate verbally.
  • Keep it short and practical.

Day 23

Emergency contacts

  • Review emergency contacts.
  • Check phone numbers.
  • Choose people who can respond.
  • Tell them they are emergency contacts.
  • Do not add contacts who cannot help.

Day 24

Emergency SOS

  1. Open the Watch app.
  2. Go to Emergency SOS.
  3. Review settings.

Explain:

  • It uses the side button.
  • It is for real emergencies.
  • It should not be tested with real calls.
  • A GPS watch may need the iPhone nearby.
  • A Cellular watch may work more independently if configured.

Day 25

Fall Detection

If appropriate, review Fall Detection.

Explain:

  • It can detect some hard falls.
  • It does not detect every fall.
  • False alerts can happen.
  • It depends on battery, model, and connection.
  • It should not be tested by falling.

Day 26

Watch face review

Review the watch face.

Ask:

  • Is Battery visible?
  • Is Weather useful?
  • Is Timer useful?
  • Are there too many complications?
  • Does VoiceOver read it clearly?
  • Simplify if needed.

Day 27

Apps and storage

  • Review installed apps.
  • Remove unused apps.
  • Use List View.
  • Keep the app list short.
  • This makes the watch easier to use.

Day 28

Optional features

Choose only one optional feature to introduce.

Possible options:

  • Apple Pay.
  • Sleep.
  • Medication.
  • Maps.
  • Audio.
  • Home.
  • Shortcuts.
  • Do not introduce all at once.
  • Pick the one that matters most to the user.

Day 29

Full workflow practice

Practise a complete day simulation:

  • Check battery.
  • Open Control Centre.
  • Find iPhone.
  • Set timer.
  • Answer call.
  • Read message.
  • Check weather.
  • Start short workout.
  • End workout.
  • Review Fitness.
  • Check reminder.
  • Charge watch.

Day 30

Final review

Review:

  • VoiceOver.
  • Haptics.
  • Notifications.
  • Battery.
  • Watch face.
  • Control Centre.
  • Calls.
  • Messages.
  • Timers.
  • Alarms.
  • Activity.
  • Workout.
  • Medical ID.
  • Emergency contacts.
  • Safety features.
  • Remove anything confusing.
  • Add nothing unless necessary.

At the end of the first month

The user should be able to:

  • Use the watch face.
  • Use VoiceOver gestures.
  • Open apps.
  • Open Control Centre.
  • Check battery.
  • Find iPhone.
  • Use timers and alarms.
  • Answer calls.
  • Read and reply to short messages.
  • Use reminders.
  • Check weather.
  • Start and end a workout.
  • Check heart rate.
  • Charge the watch.
  • Understand Medical ID and emergency contacts.
  • Understand Emergency SOS and Fall Detection.
  • Understand that advanced features can be added later.

What not to do in the first month

  • Do not overload notifications.
  • Do not install many apps.
  • Do not configure every health feature at once.
  • Do not use Apple Pay before the side button is understood.
  • Do not rely on Emergency SOS without understanding it.
  • Do not start with complex workouts.
  • Do not force sleep tracking if charging is not organised.
  • Do not expect the user to remember everything after one explanation.
  • Do not confuse teaching with dumping information.

Technology training is not a race. And if it were, most settings menus would be disqualified for cruelty.

Suggested pace for trainers

If teaching another person:

  • Use short sessions.
  • Repeat actions.
  • Practise with real tasks.
  • Avoid long theoretical explanations.
  • Let the person do the gestures.
  • Do not take the watch away to fix everything yourself.
  • Explain what you change.
  • Leave written or recorded notes if useful.
  • Review after a few days.
  • The goal is independence.
  • If the trainer does everything, the user learns dependence, which is an impressively unhelpful outcome.

Suggested pace for self-learning

If learning alone:

  • Do one new thing per day.
  • Practise it several times.
  • Do not change many settings at once.
  • Keep the iPhone nearby.
  • Use Siri when useful.
  • Use the Watch app for corrections.
  • Take notes of what works.
  • Undo what confuses you.
  • When something fails, check simple settings first.
  • Do not reset the watch at the first problem.

When to move to advanced features

Move to advanced features when the user can already:

  • Return to the watch face.
  • Open Control Centre.
  • Check battery.
  • Open apps.
  • Use timers.
  • Answer calls.
  • Read notifications.
  • Charge the watch.
  • Use the iPhone Watch app.
  • Once these basics are comfortable, advanced features are much easier.

Summary of appendix 8

The first month should be progressive.

  • Week 1 focuses on VoiceOver, controls, battery, Control Centre, Find iPhone, timers, alarms, and charging.
  • Week 2 focuses on calls, messages, reminders, calendar, and notifications.
  • Week 3 focuses on Activity, Heart Rate, workouts, and Fitness.
  • Week 4 focuses on safety, Medical ID, emergency contacts, Fall Detection, watch faces, apps, and optional features.

The Apple Watch should be learned in layers. A gradual setup creates confidence. Trying to configure everything at once creates confusion.

Back to table of contents

Appendix 9. Quick guide for relatives, trainers, and support people

This appendix is intended for people who help a blind user, deafblind user, older person, or person with hearing loss configure and learn the Apple Watch. The goal is not to take control of the device. The goal is to help the person understand it and use it with as much independence as possible. This distinction matters. Helping is not the same as doing everything for the person.

If you configure the watch quickly, activate many features, explain very little, and then leave, the person may have a device full of options they do not understand. That is not support. That is leaving a technological puzzle on someone’s wrist and hoping for the best, which is a bold strategy and usually a terrible one.

Start with the person, not with the device

Before configuring anything, ask what the person actually needs.

Useful questions:

  • Does the person want to receive calls?
  • Does the person want to answer messages?
  • Does the person need medication reminders?
  • Does the person go out alone?
  • Does the person want Fall Detection?
  • Does the person want to track activity?
  • Does the person want to use sleep tracking?
  • Does the person hear VoiceOver well?
  • Does the person feel vibrations clearly?
  • Does the person use braille?
  • Does the person have hearing loss?
  • Does the person use a cane, guide dog, or other mobility support?
  • Does the person carry the iPhone when leaving home?
  • The configuration should be based on the answers.
  • Do not configure the Apple Watch as if every person had the same needs.

Respect the user’s pace

  • The Apple Watch has many functions.
  • That does not mean they must all be explained in one session.
  • For a beginner, one session should focus on a few actions only.

For example:

  • Put on the watch.
  • Unlock it.
  • Hear VoiceOver.
  • Press the Digital Crown.
  • Open Control Centre.
  • Check battery.
  • Find the iPhone.
  • Set and stop a timer.
  • Charge the watch.
  • That may already be enough for the first day.

Trying to teach calls, messages, workouts, Apple Pay, sleep, ECG, Fall Detection, Maps, Wallet, Home, and Shortcuts in the same session is not training. It is a data storm with straps.

Let the person touch the watch

Do not keep the watch in your hands while explaining everything.

The person who will use it must physically practise:

  • Finding the Digital Crown.
  • Finding the side button.
  • Swiping.
  • Double tapping.
  • Turning the Digital Crown.
  • Opening Control Centre.
  • Returning to the watch face.
  • Stopping an alert.
  • The helper may guide, but the user must do the actions.
  • Muscle memory matters.

Explain what you change

Do not silently change settings. Say what you are changing and why.

For example:

  • I am enabling Prominent Haptic so the vibration is easier to feel.
  • I am disabling notifications from this app so the watch does not vibrate unnecessarily.
  • I am adding Battery to the watch face so you can check it quickly.
  • I am setting List View because it is usually easier with VoiceOver.
  • This helps the person understand the setup.
  • If something later behaves differently, they will know why.

Do not activate everything

Avoid the temptation to activate every health and accessibility feature.

Do not enable:

  • Every notification.
  • Every health alert.
  • Every Focus mode.
  • Every app.
  • Every complication.
  • Every smart home control.
  • Every advanced gesture.
  • The best setup is usually selective.
  • Start with the essentials.
  • Add more later.

Configure VoiceOver carefully

If the user is blind, VoiceOver should be configured comfortably.

Check:

  • VoiceOver on.
  • Speech rate.
  • Volume.
  • Accessibility shortcut.
  • Speaking rate not too fast.
  • Voice clear enough.
  • The user should be able to understand VoiceOver without effort.
  • Do not set speech rate to your own preference.
  • Use the user’s pace.

Configure haptics carefully

Haptics are essential for many users.

Check:

  • Haptic Alerts on.
  • Prominent Haptic if needed.
  • Strap properly adjusted.
  • Timer test completed.
  • Alarm test completed.
  • Call vibration tested.
  • For deafblind users or people with hearing loss, this is especially important.
  • Never assume the person feels the vibration.
  • Test it.

Reduce notifications

This is one of the most useful things a support person can do.

At first, keep only:

  • Phone.
  • Important messages.
  • Calendar.
  • Reminders.
  • Timers.
  • Alarms.
  • Medication, if used.
  • Important health alerts.
  • Battery.
  • Emergency-related alerts.
  • Disable unnecessary apps.
  • A watch that vibrates every few minutes will soon be ignored.

When everything is urgent, nothing is urgent. A discovery that notification systems continue to resist with heroic stubbornness.

Use clear names

If configuring contacts, smart home devices, reminders, or shortcuts, use clear names.

Good names:

  1. Call Maria.
  2. Medication at nine.
  3. Living room light.
  4. Good night.
  5. Start walking routine.

Bad names:

  • Test.
  • Shortcut 2.
  • Lamp old.
  • Reminder thing.
  • Scene final.
  • Clear names help Siri, VoiceOver, and memory.

Test with real situations

Training should include realistic examples.

Examples:

  • Receive a call from a trusted person.
  • Read a message.
  • Set a timer.
  • Make the iPhone play a sound.
  • Check battery.
  • Start a short workout.
  • Stop an alarm.
  • These practical tasks matter more than explaining menus for half an hour.

Do not use emergency services for practice

Never test Emergency SOS with a real emergency call.

  • Do not intentionally trigger Fall Detection.
  • Do not simulate dangerous situations.
  • You can review settings.
  • You can explain the side button.
  • You can configure emergency contacts.
  • You can check Medical ID.
  • But do not call emergency services unless there is a real emergency.

Respect privacy

If helping someone configure the Apple Watch, you may see sensitive information.

This may include:

  • Messages.
  • Contacts.
  • Medication.
  • Health data.
  • Location.
  • Calendar.
  • Payments.
  • Emergency contacts.
  • Medical conditions.
  • Do not read private information aloud unnecessarily.
  • Do not browse health data out of curiosity.
  • Do not configure location sharing without consent.
  • Do not add yourself as an emergency contact unless the person agrees and it makes sense.
  • Support does not cancel privacy.
  • Especially with older people, do not confuse safety with control.

Configure Medical ID with care

Medical ID should be useful, not overloaded.

Help the person add:

  1. Relevant conditions.
  2. Important allergies.
  3. Medication.
  4. Emergency contacts.
  5. Communication notes.

For a blind person, a note may be useful:

  • Blind person. Please communicate verbally.
  • For a deafblind person, a different note may be useful:
  • Deafblind person. Needs tactile or close communication support.
  • Use clear, short wording.

Review emergency contacts

Emergency contacts must be people who can respond.

Check:

  • Correct phone numbers.
  • Relationship.
  • Backup contact.
  • The person knows they are listed.
  • Do not add contacts without telling them.
  • Do not add people who cannot help.

Teach battery routine

The user should know when and how to charge the Apple Watch.

Help establish a routine:

  • Charge during breakfast.
  • Charge while showering.
  • Charge before bed.
  • Charge during a daily rest period.
  • If sleep tracking is used, charging overnight is not possible.
  • Add Battery to the watch face.
  • Teach how to check battery from Control Centre.

Use the iPhone as the configuration tool

Many settings are easier from the iPhone.

Teach the user where to find:

  • Watch app.
  • Health app.
  • Fitness app.
  • Find My.
  • Settings.
  • The Apple Watch is small.
  • The iPhone is better for setup and review.
  • A support person should not make the user depend only on the watch for complex configuration.

Write down the basic workflow

For many users, a short written or audio note can help.

It may include:

  • How to check battery.
  • How to find the iPhone.
  • How to stop a timer.
  • How to answer a call.
  • How to charge the watch.
  • How to open Control Centre.
  • How to return to the watch face.
  • How to ask for help.
  • Keep the instructions short.
  • A three-page explanation for stopping a timer is not support. It is punishment with headings.

Avoid changing too many things later

If the person is already used to a setup, do not change it casually.

Changing watch face, notifications, gestures, Focus modes, or app layout may confuse the user.

  • Before changing something, explain it.
  • After changing it, practise.
  • Make sure the person agrees.

Be careful with Focus modes

Focus modes can block alerts. If you configure Focus modes, check that important calls and reminders are still allowed.

This is especially important for:

  • Medication.
  • Emergency contacts.
  • Older users.
  • People who live alone.
  • Sleep mode.
  • Do Not Disturb.
  • A badly configured Focus mode can make the watch seem broken.

Teach what not to do

The user should know:

  • Do not hold the side button casually.
  • Do not test Emergency SOS.
  • Do not ignore low battery.
  • Do not rely on Apple Pay without understanding the side button.
  • Do not leave a workout running.
  • Do not change health settings randomly.
  • Do not remove pairing without understanding it.
  • Do not buy a used watch with Activation Lock.
  • Knowing what not to do prevents many problems.

For older users

When helping an older person:

  • Simplify.
  • Use few notifications.
  • Use a simple face.
  • Use strong haptics.
  • Configure emergency contacts.
  • Configure Medical ID.
  • Review Fall Detection.
  • Create a charging routine.
  • Practise calls.
  • Practise alarms.
  • Do not overload with apps.
  • The person should understand the watch, not simply wear it.

For deafblind users

When helping a deafblind user:

  • Test haptics first.
  • Use Prominent Haptic if useful.
  • Keep notifications very limited.
  • Use alarms and timers carefully.
  • Use the iPhone and braille display if part of the user’s workflow.
  • Do not rely on speech if the person cannot hear it.
  • Do not assume vibration is enough without testing.
  • Create clear routines.

For advanced blind users

With advanced users, do not oversimplify unnecessarily. Respect their experience. Help only where needed.

Advanced users may want:

  • Shortcuts.
  • Focus modes.
  • Smart home.
  • Multiple watch faces.
  • Workout metrics.
  • Braille workflows.
  • Automation.
  • Privacy settings.
  • Still, the setup should remain organised.
  • Advanced does not mean cluttered.

Common mistakes by helpers

  • Doing everything too quickly.
  • Activating too many features.
  • Not explaining changes.
  • Ignoring the user’s preferences.
  • Leaving all notifications enabled.
  • Not testing haptics.
  • Not configuring Medical ID.
  • Not teaching charging.
  • Confusing the side button and Digital Crown.
  • Using emergency features for practice.
  • Taking over instead of teaching.

Practical advice for support people

  • Configure less.
  • Explain more.
  • Practise slowly.
  • Test real tasks.
  • Respect privacy.
  • Write down essentials.
  • Return after a few days to adjust.
  • The first setup is not final.
  • The best support is the kind that makes the person need less support later.

Exercise for appendix 9

If you are helping someone configure an Apple Watch, use this session plan:

  • First thirty minutes:
  • VoiceOver.
  • Haptics.
  • Digital Crown.
  • Side button.
  • Watch face.
  • Battery.
  • Control Centre.
  • Find iPhone.
  • Timer.

Second session:

  1. Calls.
  2. Messages.
  3. Reminders.
  4. Calendar.
  5. Notifications.

Third session:

  1. Medical ID.
  2. Emergency contacts.
  3. Fall Detection.
  4. Emergency SOS explanation.

Fourth session:

  • Activity.
  • Workout.
  • Health.
  • Optional features.
  • Do not combine all sessions into one unless the user is already experienced.

Summary of appendix 9

A support person should help the user understand the Apple Watch, not take control of it.

  • Start with the person’s needs.
  • Configure VoiceOver, haptics, simple watch face, List View, notifications, battery, and basic actions first.
  • Do not activate everything.
  • Respect privacy.
  • Practise real tasks.
  • Avoid emergency tests.
  • For older, deafblind, or beginner users, simplicity is essential.
  • For advanced users, organisation remains important.
  • Good support creates independence.

Back to table of contents

Appendix 10. Final quick reference by user profile

This appendix summarises the most recommended Apple Watch configuration depending on the type of user.

  • It is not a rigid rule.
  • It is a practical guide.
  • Each person may need adjustments.

The same Apple Watch can be very different depending on who wears it, how they perceive information, whether they use VoiceOver, whether they hear haptics, whether they go out alone, whether they take medication, or whether they use the watch mainly for calls, health, activity, or safety. One device, many possible setups. A shocking idea, apparently, given how often technology is configured as if all humans were copied from the same template.

Profile 1

Blind beginner

Main goal:

  • Make the Apple Watch understandable and manageable.
  • Recommended priorities:
  • VoiceOver.
  • Comfortable speech rate.
  • Accessibility shortcut.
  • Simple watch face.
  • Battery complication.
  • List View.
  • Haptic Alerts.
  • Prominent Haptic if needed.
  • Reduced notifications.
  • Control Centre.
  • Find iPhone.
  • Timers.
  • Alarms.
  • Calls.
  • Messages.
  • Charging routine.

Recommended first complications:

  1. Battery.
  2. Weather.
  3. Timer.
  4. Calendar or Reminders.
  5. Activity only if useful.

Recommended notifications:

  1. Phone.
  2. Messages from important contacts.
  3. Calendar.
  4. Reminders.
  5. Timers.
  6. Alarms.
  7. Battery.

Avoid at first:

  1. Apple Pay.
  2. Advanced health.
  3. Shortcuts.
  4. Multiple watch faces.
  5. Many apps.
  6. Complex Focus modes.
  7. Smart home.
  8. Advanced workouts.

First skills to learn:

  • Return to watch face.
  • Open app list.
  • Open Control Centre.
  • Check battery.
  • Find iPhone.
  • Set timer.
  • Stop timer.
  • Answer call.
  • End call.
  • Read notification.
  • Charge watch.

Profile 2

Blind intermediate user

Main goal:

  • Use the Apple Watch as a practical daily companion.
  • Recommended priorities:
  • More refined notifications.
  • Calendar.
  • Reminders.
  • Weather.
  • Activity.
  • Workout.
  • Heart Rate.
  • Siri.
  • Audio control.
  • Find Devices.
  • Medical ID.
  • Emergency contacts.
  • Basic Apple Pay if ready.

Recommended complications:

  1. Battery.
  2. Weather.
  3. Timer.
  4. Calendar.
  5. Workout.
  6. Heart Rate or Activity.

Recommended additions:

  • Outdoor Walk.
  • Indoor Walk.
  • Fitness review on iPhone.
  • Heart Rate app.
  • Weather complication.
  • Apple Pay with default card.
  • Maps only on familiar routes at first.

Avoid:

  • Too many apps.
  • Too many health alerts.
  • Unclear shortcuts.
  • Using the watch for long writing.
  • Depending on Maps alone.

Profile 3

Blind advanced user

Main goal:

  • Create a powerful but organised Apple Watch workflow.
  • Recommended priorities:
  • Multiple contextual watch faces.
  • Focus modes.
  • Shortcuts.
  • Workout metrics.
  • Health trends.
  • Audio.
  • Wallet.
  • Maps with iPhone support.
  • Home control.
  • Siri commands.
  • Privacy review.
  • Storage management.

Recommended watch faces:

  1. Daily.
  2. Workout.
  3. Sleep.
  4. Travel.
  5. Health.

Recommended complications:

  • Battery.
  • Weather.
  • Workout.
  • Timer.
  • Calendar.
  • Reminders.
  • Heart Rate.
  • Medication if used.
  • Wallet if useful.
  • Home or Shortcuts if used.

Recommended advanced tools:

  1. Shortcuts.
  2. Focus modes.
  3. Home scenes.
  4. Downloaded audio.
  5. Workout views.
  6. Health trends.
  7. Find My.
  8. Braille workflow if relevant.

Warnings:

  • Do not overload notifications.
  • Do not create too many watch faces.
  • Review battery often.
  • Review privacy permissions.
  • Keep emergency setup simple.

Profile 4

Older blind user

Main goal:

  • Safety, communication, reminders, and simplicity.
  • Recommended priorities:
  • Simple watch face.
  • Strong haptics.
  • Phone.
  • Important messages.
  • Medication reminders if needed.
  • Calendar.
  • Alarms.
  • Timers.
  • Medical ID.
  • Emergency contacts.
  • Fall Detection.
  • Emergency SOS explanation.
  • Battery routine.

Recommended complications:

  1. Battery.
  2. Date.
  3. Medication if used.
  4. Timer or Alarms.
  5. Calendar.
  6. Weather.
  7. Heart Rate if useful.

Recommended notifications:

  • Phone.
  • Important contacts.
  • Calendar.
  • Medication.
  • Alarms.
  • Timers.
  • Health alerts if appropriate.
  • Battery.
  • Emergency-related alerts.

Avoid:

  1. Too many apps.
  2. Social alerts.
  3. Complex Focus modes.
  4. Unnecessary complications.
  5. Advanced features without explanation.

Important teaching:

  • How to answer a call.
  • How to end a call.
  • How to stop an alarm.
  • How to charge.
  • How to check battery.
  • What Fall Detection can and cannot do.
  • Emergency SOS is not for testing.

Profile 5

Deafblind user

Main goal:

  • Tactile alerts, simplicity, and iPhone or braille support.
  • Recommended priorities:
  • Haptic Alerts.
  • Prominent Haptic.
  • Very limited notifications.
  • Timer.
  • Alarms.
  • Medication if needed.
  • Calendar.
  • Important calls or messages.
  • Battery complication.
  • Simple watch face.
  • Medical ID.
  • Emergency contacts.
  • iPhone support.
  • Braille display workflow if used.

Recommended complications:

  1. Battery.
  2. Timer.
  3. Alarms.
  4. Medication.
  5. Calendar or Reminders.

Recommended notifications:

  1. Medication.
  2. Alarms.
  3. Timers.
  4. Emergency contacts.
  5. Calendar.
  6. Important calls.
  7. Important messages.
  8. Battery.

Avoid:

  • Too many vibrations.
  • Complex app navigation.
  • Relying on VoiceOver speech if not heard.
  • Unclear haptic patterns.
  • Advanced gestures too early.

Recommended workflow:

  • Apple Watch alerts by vibration.
  • User checks details on iPhone.
  • Braille display used for detailed reading if applicable.
  • Support person helps configure essentials.

Profile 6

User with hearing loss

Main goal:

  • Strong tactile alerts and clear audio routing if useful.
  • Recommended priorities:
  • Haptic Alerts.
  • Prominent Haptic.
  • Volume adjusted.
  • Headphones or hearing device support.
  • Important calls.
  • Messages.
  • Alarms.
  • Timers.
  • Medication.
  • Calendar.
  • Battery.

Recommended settings:

  1. Silent Mode according to preference.
  2. Strong haptics.
  3. Reduced notifications.
  4. Important contacts allowed.
  5. Focus modes checked carefully.

Recommended tests:

  1. Timer vibration.
  2. Alarm vibration.
  3. Incoming call vibration.
  4. Message vibration.
  5. Headphone audio.
  6. VoiceOver volume if used.

Profile 7

User mainly interested in health

Main goal:

  • Record and review health data without turning the watch into a source of anxiety.
  • Recommended priorities:
  • Heart Rate.
  • High and low heart rate notifications if appropriate.
  • Irregular rhythm notifications if available.
  • ECG if available.
  • Sleep.
  • Medication if needed.
  • Activity.
  • Workouts.
  • Health app on iPhone.
  • Medical ID.
  • Emergency contacts.

Recommended complications:

  1. Battery.
  2. Heart Rate.
  3. Medication.
  4. Sleep.
  5. Activity.
  6. Workout.

Warnings:

  • Health data are not diagnosis.
  • No alert does not mean no problem.
  • Symptoms matter.
  • Review trends, not only isolated numbers.
  • Consult healthcare professionals when needed.

Profile 8

User mainly interested in exercise

Main goal:

  • Record workouts safely and review progress.
  • Recommended priorities:
  • Workout app.
  • Activity.
  • Heart Rate.
  • Weather.
  • Battery.
  • Fitness app on iPhone.
  • Headphone safety.
  • Outdoor safety.
  • Correct workout types.

Recommended complications:

  1. Workout.
  2. Battery.
  3. Weather.
  4. Heart Rate.
  5. Activity.
  6. Timer.

Recommended first workouts:

  1. Outdoor Walk.
  2. Indoor Walk.
  3. Strength Training.
  4. Functional Training.
  5. Stationary bike.

Important skills:

  1. Start workout.
  2. Pause.
  3. Resume.
  4. End.
  5. Review summary.
  6. Review Fitness on iPhone.
  7. Check battery before exercise.
  8. Use headphones carefully outdoors.

Profile 9

User mainly interested in safety

Main goal:

  • Emergency readiness, reliable alerts, and battery.
  • Recommended priorities:
  • Medical ID.
  • Emergency contacts.
  • Emergency SOS.
  • Fall Detection if appropriate.
  • Battery.
  • Haptics.
  • Phone.
  • Location sharing if appropriate.
  • Find My.
  • Passcode.

Recommended complications:

  1. Battery.
  2. Phone or contacts if available.
  3. Weather.
  4. Timer.
  5. Medication if relevant.

Important checks:

  1. GPS or Cellular model.
  2. Whether iPhone is carried.
  3. Battery before leaving.
  4. Emergency contacts updated.
  5. Medical ID updated.
  6. Fall Detection enabled if useful.
  7. Emergency SOS understood.

Warnings:

  • Do not test Emergency SOS with real calls.
  • Fall Detection does not detect every fall.
  • GPS model may need iPhone nearby.

Profile 10

User mainly interested in independence outside home

Main goal:

  • Communication, location support, battery, and practical alerts.
  • Recommended priorities:
  • Battery.
  • iPhone connection.
  • Cellular if available and needed.
  • Phone.
  • Messages.
  • Weather.
  • Maps with iPhone support.
  • Find Devices.
  • Find iPhone.
  • Wallet if used.
  • Emergency contacts.
  • Medical ID.

Recommended complications:

  1. Battery.
  2. Weather.
  3. Maps.
  4. Wallet.
  5. Calendar.
  6. Workout if walking.

Recommended habits before leaving:

  • Check watch battery.
  • Check iPhone battery.
  • Check weather.
  • Check Focus modes.
  • Check connection.
  • Carry iPhone if needed.
  • Check payment method.
  • Check route.
  • Keep headphones at safe volume.

Profile 11

User mainly interested in smart home

Main goal:

  • Control home devices quickly and accessibly.
  • Recommended priorities:
  • Home app.
  • Clear device names.
  • Clear room names.
  • Siri.
  • Useful scenes.
  • Few important notifications.
  • Safety with plugs and locks.

Recommended complications:

  1. Home.
  2. Shortcuts if used.
  3. Battery.
  4. Timer.
  5. Weather.

Recommended Siri commands:

  • Turn on the living room light.
  • Turn off all lights.
  • Run good night scene.
  • Turn on the fan.
  • Set thermostat to twenty-two degrees.

Warnings:

  • Do not use smart plugs with risky appliances without caution.
  • Be careful with locks.
  • Review who has access to the home.
  • Keep device names clear.

Profile 12

User who mainly wants Apple Pay and Wallet

Main goal:

  • Safe and reliable payment from the wrist.
  • Recommended priorities:
  • Passcode.
  • Wallet.
  • Default card.
  • Side button.
  • Amount confirmation.
  • Backup payment method.

Recommended complications:

  • Battery.
  • Wallet, if passes are used.
  • Calendar.
  • Weather.

Important learning:

  • Apple Pay opens with double-press of the side button.
  • Not the Digital Crown.
  • The watch must be unlocked.
  • The card must be added to the Apple Watch.
  • Ask the cashier to confirm the amount if needed.
  • Carry backup payment until confident.

Common configuration mistakes across profiles

  • Too many notifications.
  • Too many apps.
  • Complicated watch face.
  • No battery complication.
  • No charging routine.
  • Haptics not tested.
  • Medical ID not updated.
  • Emergency contacts missing.
  • Apple Pay configured before button control is clear.
  • Health features activated without explanation.
  • Focus modes blocking important alerts.
  • Used watch bought without checking Activation Lock.

Best universal configuration

For most users, a solid basic setup includes:

  • VoiceOver, if blind.
  • Haptic Alerts.
  • Prominent Haptic if needed.
  • Simple watch face.
  • Battery complication.
  • List View.
  • Phone notifications.
  • Messages from important contacts.
  • Calendar.
  • Reminders.
  • Timers.
  • Alarms.
  • Weather.
  • Find iPhone.
  • Medical ID.
  • Emergency contacts.
  • Charging routine.
  • This foundation can then be adapted.

Final summary of appendix 10

The Apple Watch should be configured according to user profile. Blind beginners need simplicity and basic control. Older users need safety, reminders, calls, and clear routines. Deafblind users need strong haptics and carefully limited alerts. Advanced users can use more features, but still need organisation. Health users should understand the limits of the data. Exercise users should prioritise correct workouts and safety. Safety users should configure Medical ID, emergency contacts, Emergency SOS, Fall Detection, and battery routines. There is no single perfect setup. The best setup is the one that matches the person’s real needs and can be used reliably every day.

Back to table of contents

Appendix 11. Final checklist before publishing or sharing the course

This appendix is intended for the person preparing this course for publication, distribution, printing, conversion to HTML, conversion to Word, translation, or sharing with other users. After a course of this size, it is not enough to check whether the text is complete.

It is also necessary to check structure, consistency, accessibility, tone, terminology, internal links, headings, examples, and references to countries or regions. A long document can be good and still become uncomfortable to use if the structure is poor. And if a document is aimed at blind users, structure is not decoration. Structure is access. A beautiful document with bad headings is still a maze wearing clean shoes.

General review

Before publishing, check:

  • The course has a clear title.
  • The introduction is present.
  • The table of contents is complete.
  • All modules are included.
  • All appendices are included.
  • The order is logical.
  • There are no duplicated modules.
  • There are no missing module numbers.
  • The closing section is present.
  • The language is consistent.
  • The tone is consistent.
  • The content does not assume one country unless necessary.

Heading structure

Headings should be clear and hierarchical. The main title should be the highest-level heading. Modules should use the same heading level.

Appendices should use the same heading level as modules or a clearly defined appendix heading level.

  • Subsections should use lower-level headings.
  • Do not use headings only for visual style.
  • A heading should describe the section that follows.
  • For screen reader users, headings are navigation points.
  • If headings are wrong, navigation becomes worse.

Table of contents

The table of contents should include:

  • Introduction.
  • All modules.
  • All appendices.
  • Closing section, if separate.
  • Links should point to the correct sections if the format allows it.
  • If the document is in Word, the table of contents should use real headings or internal links.
  • If the document is in HTML, the table of contents should use internal anchor links.
  • If the document is in plain text, the table of contents should still be clean and readable.

Return links

If the document is converted to HTML or Word with internal navigation, it is useful to include a return link after each module.

For example:

  • Back to table of contents.
  • This helps users return to the index without navigating manually through the whole document.
  • For long documents, this is not a luxury.
  • It is basic mercy.

Module numbering

Check that modules are numbered correctly. There should be no jumps unless intentional. Check:

Module 1. Module 2. Module 3. And so on until the final module. If a module number is missing, find out whether the module is absent or whether the numbering is wrong. If two modules have the same number, correct it.

Appendix numbering

Check that appendices are numbered correctly. For example:

Appendix 1. Appendix 2. Appendix 3. And so on. Appendices should appear after the main course, unless there is a clear reason to place them elsewhere.

Consistency of terms

Use consistent terms throughout the document.

For example:

  • Apple Watch.
  • iPhone.
  • VoiceOver.
  • Digital Crown.
  • Side button.
  • Control Centre.
  • Watch app.
  • Health app.
  • Fitness app.
  • Find My.
  • Emergency SOS.
  • Fall Detection.
  • Medical ID.
  • Wallet.
  • Apple Pay.
  • Do not change terms unnecessarily.
  • If a term is official, keep it stable.
  • Consistency helps users recognise features.

Digital Crown and side button

Check carefully that the Digital Crown and the side button are not confused.

This is especially important in sections about:

  • Control Centre.
  • Wallet.
  • Apple Pay.
  • Emergency SOS.
  • Power options.
  • App list.
  • VoiceOver shortcut.
  • The Digital Crown is round.
  • The side button is elongated.
  • Wallet usually opens with a double press of the side button.
  • Emergency SOS is related to holding down the side button.
  • VoiceOver shortcut may use triple-click of the Digital Crown, depending on configuration.
  • This distinction should be correct throughout the course.

Country and region references

The course should be suitable for international readers.

Avoid assuming:

  • One emergency number.
  • One payment system.
  • One health feature availability.
  • One transport system.
  • One language variant.
  • One measurement unit.
  • One carrier.
  • One bank.
  • One climate.
  • One country’s public services.

Instead, use expressions such as:

  1. Depending on country or region.
  2. Where available.
  3. If supported by your carrier.
  4. If available on your model.
  5. If available in your country.
  6. According to local emergency services.

This is especially important for:

  • Emergency SOS.
  • Apple Pay.
  • Wallet.
  • ECG.
  • Blood oxygen.
  • Sleep apnoea notifications.
  • Irregular rhythm notifications.
  • Hypertension-related features.
  • Cellular.
  • Public transport.
  • Weather alerts.

Health feature availability

Apple Watch health features vary by model and country. Check that the document does not imply that every Apple Watch has every feature.

Use caution with:

  • ECG.
  • Blood oxygen.
  • Wrist temperature.
  • Sleep apnoea notifications.
  • Irregular rhythm notifications.
  • AFib History.
  • Hypertension-related notifications.
  • Fall Detection.
  • Crash Detection, if mentioned.
  • Cycle tracking features.

The wording should make clear that availability may depend on model, watchOS version, iPhone version, country, age, and configuration.

Medical disclaimers

Health sections should not overpromise.

Check that the course says clearly:

  • The Apple Watch does not replace healthcare professionals.
  • The Apple Watch does not replace medical tests.
  • The absence of alerts does not guarantee absence of problems.
  • Symptoms should be taken seriously.
  • Emergency symptoms require medical help.
  • Medication should not be changed based only on watch data.
  • Health alerts should be discussed with professionals when appropriate.
  • This is important.
  • Health content must be useful, but not reckless.

Apple Pay and payments

Check that Apple Pay sections are careful.

They should explain:

  • Apple Pay depends on country, bank, card, issuer, and shop.
  • The card must be added to the Apple Watch.
  • Passcode is required.
  • Payment usually uses double-press of the side button.
  • The side button is not the Digital Crown.
  • The amount should be confirmed before paying if the user cannot see the terminal.
  • A backup payment method is advisable at first.
  • Do not present Apple Pay as universally available.

Emergency content

Check that emergency sections are precise.

They should explain:

  • Emergency SOS is for real emergencies.
  • It should not be tested with real calls.
  • Emergency numbers vary by country.
  • Apple Watch may call the appropriate local emergency service depending on configuration and availability.
  • A GPS model may need the iPhone nearby.
  • A Cellular model may work more independently if service and coverage are available.
  • Fall Detection does not detect every fall.
  • False alerts can happen.
  • Medical ID and emergency contacts should be configured.
  • If an accidental emergency call connects, the user should explain that it was a mistake.

Accessibility tone

The tone should be practical and respectful.

  • Avoid speaking to blind users as if they were children.
  • Avoid excessive drama.
  • Avoid overpromising.
  • Avoid making the Apple Watch sound magical.
  • Avoid making accessibility sound like charity.

The course should explain what works, what may work, what depends on context, and what has limits. That is more useful than polished enthusiasm, which has injured enough manuals already.

VoiceOver clarity

Check that VoiceOver instructions are clear.

When giving steps, make sure they include:

  1. Where to start.
  2. Which app to open.
  3. Which control to find.
  4. What VoiceOver may announce.
  5. What action to perform.
  6. What to expect.
  7. What may vary by version.

Avoid vague instructions such as:

  • Go there and activate it.
  • Use the button.
  • Press the thing.
  • That sort of wording belongs in nightmares and badly written support chats.

Plain language

  • The course should use plain language.
  • It can be detailed without being obscure.
  • Avoid unnecessary technical terms.
  • When a technical term is needed, explain it.

For example:

  • Haptic feedback means vibration or taps on the wrist.
  • A complication is an element on the watch face.
  • Activation Lock is a security feature linked to the Apple Account.
  • The reader should not need to be a technician.

Examples

Examples should be practical.

Good examples:

  • Set a one-minute timer.
  • Answer a test call from a trusted person.
  • Start a short Indoor Walk workout.
  • Check battery from Control Centre.
  • Make the iPhone play a sound.
  • Review Medical ID.
  • Avoid examples that create risk.

Do not ask the user to:

  • Test Emergency SOS.
  • Simulate a fall.
  • Use Apple Pay before understanding the side button.
  • Change medication based on a reminder.
  • Rely on Maps in an unfamiliar area without preparation.
  • Safety examples must be safe.

Exercises

Check that each exercise is realistic. Exercises should help the user practise without risk.

Good exercises:

  1. Explore settings without changing them.
  2. Set a test timer.
  3. Review a feature.
  4. Start a short test workout.
  5. Check Medical ID.
  6. Review notifications.

Bad exercises:

  • Make an emergency call.
  • Trigger a fall alert.
  • Make a payment during first practice.
  • Change health thresholds without guidance.
  • Erase or reset the watch for practice.
  • If an exercise involves a sensitive feature, it should say not to activate it unless needed.

Summaries

Each module should have a short summary. Summaries help users review without rereading the whole module.

Check that summaries:

  • Do not introduce new information.
  • Reflect the module content.
  • Are concise.
  • Mention key warnings if needed.
  • For long courses, summaries are very helpful for screen reader users.

Internal consistency

Check that earlier and later modules do not contradict each other.

For example:

  • If one module says to use List View, later modules should not assume Grid View unless explaining both.
  • If one module says not to test Emergency SOS, later exercises should not suggest testing it.
  • If one module says Apple Pay depends on country and bank, later sections should not imply universal availability.
  • If one module says the iPhone is better for detailed review, later modules should not force all review on the watch.
  • Contradictions in a course are not charming. They are trip hazards made of text.

Length and readability

This course is long. That is acceptable if the structure is good.

For readability:

  • Use clear sections.
  • Use short paragraphs.
  • Avoid huge blocks.
  • Keep examples separated.
  • Keep summaries.
  • Use internal links if possible.
  • If publishing as HTML, headings and links are essential.
  • If publishing as Word, use real heading styles.
  • If publishing as plain text, preserve clear module labels.

Accessibility of the final format

If the course is converted to Word:

  • Use real headings.
  • Use a generated or linked table of contents.
  • Use meaningful internal links.
  • Avoid text boxes for essential content.
  • Avoid images for text.
  • Check reading order.

If the course is converted to HTML:

  • Use proper heading hierarchy.
  • Use anchor links.
  • Use meaningful link text.
  • Use paragraphs, not visual-only layout.
  • Do not rely on colour alone.
  • Make return links usable.

If the course is converted to PDF:

  • Check that it is tagged.
  • Check heading structure if possible.
  • Check reading order.
  • Avoid scanned image-only PDFs.
  • PDF can be accessible, but only if created properly.
  • An image-only PDF for blind users is not a document. It is a locked door pretending to be paper.

Links

If links are included, use meaningful link text.

Good:

  1. Apple Watch user guide.
  2. Apple accessibility support.
  3. Back to table of contents.

Bad:

  • Click here.
  • More.
  • This link.
  • Raw long URLs.
  • For screen reader users, link text should say where it goes.
  • If the document is for Tony’s usual distribution style, links may be adapted to accessible phrasing according to the publishing format.

Language review

Before final publication, check:

  • Spelling.
  • Grammar.
  • Repeated phrases.
  • Incorrect module numbers.
  • Inconsistent capitalisation.
  • Wrong terms.
  • Unnatural translated expressions.
  • Regional expressions that may confuse international readers.
  • Overly robotic sentences.
  • Tone changes between modules.
  • A translation can be accurate but still sound unnatural.

The final English version should sound like a natural training document, not like a Spanish document wearing an English coat.

Global English

For English distribution, use clear international English. Avoid expressions that only make sense in one country unless explained.

For example, avoid assuming:

  • A specific emergency number.
  • A specific supermarket payment terminal behaviour.
  • A specific health system.
  • A specific carrier.
  • A specific transport card.
  • Use global wording.

This makes the course more useful for users in the United States, United Kingdom, Canada, Ireland, Australia, India, Singapore, South Africa, and other English-speaking or English-using contexts.

Apple terminology in English

Use Apple’s English terms when possible.

Examples:

  • Apple Watch.
  • iPhone.
  • VoiceOver.
  • Digital Crown.
  • Side button.
  • Control Centre.
  • Watch app.
  • Health app.
  • Fitness app.
  • Find My.
  • Medical ID.
  • Emergency SOS.
  • Fall Detection.
  • Wallet.
  • Apple Pay.
  • Low Power Mode.
  • Silent Mode.
  • Focus.
  • Haptic Alerts.
  • Prominent Haptic.
  • Keeping official terms helps users find settings.

Version differences

The course should mention that some steps may vary by watchOS and iOS version. This is important because Apple changes menus. When possible, use stable paths.

For example:

  • Open the Watch app on the iPhone.
  • Go to My Watch.
  • Go to Accessibility.
  • This is more robust than overdescribing every screen in a way that may change later.
  • However, steps should still be practical.

Final technical check

Before sharing:

  • Open the file with a screen reader if possible.
  • Navigate by headings.
  • Test the table of contents links.
  • Test return links.
  • Search for “Module”.
  • Search for “Appendix”.
  • Check that every module appears.
  • Check that no untranslated Spanish remains in the English version.
  • Check that no editing notes remain.
  • Check that no duplicate chunks appear.
  • Check that the final file name is clear.
  • Check that metadata or comments do not contain irrelevant draft information.

Final file names

Use clear file names.

For example:

  • Apple Watch with VoiceOver. Complete Course.
  • Apple Watch with VoiceOver. Practical Guide.
  • Canal TifloAcosta. Apple Watch with VoiceOver.

Avoid unclear file names such as:

  • Final final corrected version 3.
  • New document.
  • Watch course English fixed really now.
  • Humanity has suffered enough from file names that look like emotional breakdowns.

Recommended final title

A clear English title could be:

  • Apple Watch with VoiceOver. Complete Practical Course for Blind Users
  • Another possible title:
  • Apple Watch with VoiceOver. A Complete Practical Guide for Blind and Low Vision Users

If the course also explicitly includes deafblind people, hearing loss, and older users, a broader title could be:

  • Apple Watch with VoiceOver. Complete Practical Guide for Blind, Deafblind, and Older Users
  • Choose the title according to the final intended audience.

Final publication check

Before publishing, confirm:

  • The title matches the content.
  • The course audience is clear.
  • The introduction explains the purpose.
  • The table of contents works.
  • All modules and appendices are included.
  • The tone is consistent.
  • Health and safety warnings are appropriate.
  • Country-specific references have been globalised.
  • Apple terms are correct.
  • The file is accessible.
  • The final version has been reviewed.

Exercise for appendix 11

Before publishing, do this review:

  • Navigate the document only by headings.
  • Check whether the structure makes sense.
  • Open the table of contents.
  • Activate several links.
  • Return to the table of contents from several modules.
  • Search for the word “112”.
  • Search for the word “Spain”.
  • Search for the word “emergency number”.
  • Search for untranslated Spanish words.
  • Search for repeated module numbers.
  • Search for “Digital Crown” and “side button” to confirm they are used correctly.
  • Review one health module.
  • Review one safety module.
  • Review one practical appendix.
  • If everything is consistent, the course is ready for final formatting.

Summary of appendix 11

A complete course must be reviewed for structure, consistency, accessibility, terminology, tone, and safety.

Headings and table of contents are essential.

  • Country-specific references should be globalised.
  • Health and safety features must not be overpromised.
  • Apple terminology should be consistent.
  • The final document should be accessible in Word, HTML, or the chosen format.
  • Internal links should work.
  • Return links help navigation.
  • The English version should sound natural, not like a literal translation.
  • Final review is not decoration. It is part of making the course usable.

Back to table of contents

Appendix 12. Suggested final structure for Word or HTML

This appendix proposes a final structure for preparing the course in Word, HTML, or another accessible format. The aim is to make the document easy to navigate with a screen reader, easy to publish, easy to update, and comfortable to read. A course can have excellent content and still be difficult to use if the structure is bad. For blind users, structure is not an aesthetic matter. It is how the document is travelled.

A document without proper headings is not long-form training. It is a corridor with no doors and no signs. Admirable if you enjoy suffering, but not especially educational.

Recommended document title

The final document should begin with a clear title.

Suggested title:

  • Apple Watch with VoiceOver. Complete Practical Course for Blind Users
  • Alternative title:
  • Apple Watch with VoiceOver. Complete Practical Guide for Blind and Low Vision Users

Broader title:

  • Apple Watch with VoiceOver. Complete Practical Guide for Blind, Deafblind, and Older Users
  • Choose the title according to the final audience.
  • If the course includes significant content for deafblind users, users with hearing loss, and older users, the broader title may be more accurate.

Initial presentation

After the title, include a short presentation.

It should explain:

  • What the course is.
  • Who it is intended for.
  • That it is aimed mainly at VoiceOver users.
  • That some features depend on Apple Watch model, watchOS version, iPhone, country, region, carrier, and configuration.
  • That health features do not replace medical care.
  • That safety features do not replace caution.
  • That the course is practical and progressive.
  • The introduction should be clear and direct.
  • It should not sound like advertising.

Recommended initial sections

A possible opening structure:

  • Title.
  • Presentation.
  • Who this course is for.
  • Important note about models, versions, and countries.
  • Important note about health and safety.
  • How to use this course.
  • Table of contents.
  • Then the modules begin.
  • This order helps the reader understand the scope before entering the practical content.

Table of contents

The table of contents should include every module and appendix.

  • In Word, it should be generated from heading styles whenever possible.
  • In HTML, it should use internal links.
  • In plain text, it should still be clean and ordered.

The table of contents should be near the beginning. A long course without a table of contents is technically a document, yes. In the same way a drawer full of loose cables is technically storage.

Heading levels in Word

If the document is in Word, use real heading styles.

Recommended structure:

  • Title of course as Heading 1 or document title style.
  • Main opening sections as Heading 1 or Heading 2, depending on layout.
  • Each module title as Heading 1.
  • Major sections inside modules as Heading 2.
  • Subsections inside those sections as Heading 3 if needed.
  • Appendices as Heading 1.
  • Subsections inside appendices as Heading 2.
  • Do not use bold text manually as a substitute for headings.
  • Screen readers can navigate real headings.
  • They cannot reliably navigate visual decoration.

Heading levels in HTML

If the document is in HTML, use proper heading tags.

Recommended structure:

  • h1 for the course title.
  • h2 for introduction sections, if needed.
  • h2 for each module title, or h1 for modules if the title is separate.
  • h3 for major sections inside each module.
  • h4 only if necessary.

A common structure could be:

  • h1: Apple Watch with VoiceOver. Complete Practical Course for Blind Users.
  • h2: Presentation.
  • h2: Table of contents.
  • h2: Module 1. Title.
  • h3: First section inside module.
  • h3: Exercise.
  • h3: Summary.
  • h2: Module 2. Title.
  • And so on.
  • The key is consistency.
  • Do not jump randomly from h2 to h5 because it looks nice.
  • HTML is not a mood board.

Module structure

Each module should follow a similar structure. Recommended pattern:

Module title.

  • Introductory explanation.
  • Practical development.
  • Warnings or limitations.
  • Step-by-step instructions where needed.
  • Common mistakes.
  • Practical advice.
  • Exercise.
  • Summary.
  • Back to table of contents.
  • Not every module needs exactly the same number of subsections, but the general rhythm should remain consistent.

Exercises

Exercises should be easy to find.

Use a clear heading:

  • Exercise for module 1.
  • Exercise for module 2.
  • Exercise for module 3.
  • And so on.
  • This allows users to search or navigate directly to exercises.
  • Exercises should not be hidden inside long paragraphs.

Summaries

Summaries should also be easy to find.

Use a clear heading:

  • Summary of module 1.
  • Summary of module 2.
  • Summary of module 3.
  • Summaries help users review the course later.
  • They also help trainers quickly locate the key points.

Back to table of contents links

At the end of each module and appendix, include:

  • Back to table of contents.
  • In HTML, this should be an internal link.
  • In Word, it can be an internal hyperlink.
  • In plain text, it can remain as text.
  • For long documents, this helps navigation enormously.
  • A return link is not decoration.
  • It is a handrail.

Internal anchors in HTML

For HTML, each module and appendix should have a unique anchor.

Examples:

  • module-1
  • module-2

module-3

appendix-1

appendix-2

appendix-3

Avoid spaces, accents, and strange characters in anchor names. Use simple lowercase names. Table of contents links should point to these anchors. Example link text:

Module 1. What the Apple Watch is. Module 2. Apple Watch models. Appendix 1. Quick reference of essential gestures with VoiceOver. The link text should be meaningful.

Avoid link text such as:

  • Click here.
  • More.
  • Link.
  • That is not helpful for screen reader users.

Word internal links

In Word, internal links can point to headings or bookmarks. If using heading styles, Word can generate a table of contents. For screen reader users, real headings are usually the most important element. If adding manual return links, make sure they are real links and not only blue underlined text.

Plain text version

If a plain text version is created, structure still matters.

  • Use clear module labels.
  • Use blank lines between sections.
  • Do not use excessive symbols.
  • Do not rely on indentation for meaning.
  • Do not insert decorative separators.
  • A plain text version can be very accessible if it is clean and consistent.

Avoid visual clutter

Avoid:

  • Decorative lines.
  • Repeated symbols.
  • Complex tables.
  • Text boxes.
  • Images of text.
  • Overuse of icons.
  • Unnecessary emojis.
  • Complicated indentation.
  • For screen reader users, these elements can become noise.
  • The course should be clean.

Tables

Use tables only when they truly help. Many screen reader users can read tables, but complex tables can be tiring. If a list or paragraphs work better, use them.

If a table is used, it should have clear headers.

  • In HTML, use proper table markup.
  • In Word, use real tables with header rows where appropriate.
  • Do not create tables with spaces or tabs.

Images

If the course includes images, every meaningful image should have alternative text. However, for this course, images are not essential. If screenshots are included, they should not replace written instructions. A blind user should be able to follow the course without seeing the images. Screenshots may help sighted helpers, but the text must stand on its own.

Links to Apple documentation

If official Apple documentation links are included, use meaningful link text.

For example:

  • Apple Watch User Guide.
  • Apple accessibility support.
  • Apple Watch safety features.
  • Do not paste long raw URLs inside the main text unless necessary.
  • Raw URLs are uncomfortable for screen reader users.
  • Also, official links may vary by country and language.
  • If the document is meant for international readers, choose global or English Apple pages where appropriate.

Language and tone

The final document should sound natural in English.

  • Avoid literal Spanish structures.
  • Avoid overly formal wording if it makes the text stiff.
  • Avoid marketing tone.
  • Avoid exaggerated claims.

The style should be:

  1. Practical.
  2. Clear.
  3. Direct.
  4. Respectful.
  5. Detailed.
  6. Readable.

The document should sound like a training course written by someone who understands accessibility, not like a brochure that escaped from a product launch.

Terminology consistency in English

Use the same English terms throughout:

  • Digital Crown.
  • Side button.
  • Control Centre.
  • Watch app.
  • Health app.
  • Fitness app.
  • VoiceOver.
  • Haptic Alerts.
  • Prominent Haptic.
  • Silent Mode.
  • Focus.
  • Emergency SOS.
  • Medical ID.
  • Fall Detection.
  • Find My.
  • Apple Account.
  • Apple Pay.
  • Wallet.
  • Workout.
  • Do not alternate between unofficial translations or invented names.

Regional spelling

If the target audience is international, choose one spelling convention and keep it consistent.

British English terms may include:

  1. Centre.
  2. Organisation.
  3. Practise as a verb.

American English terms may include:

  1. Center.
  2. Organization.
  3. Practice as verb and noun.

The course has used English forms such as Control Centre because Apple often uses that term in many English regions. What matters most is consistency. If distributing mainly in the United States, some Apple interface terms may appear as Control Center. If distributing globally, users may encounter different regional spelling depending on their device language. This can be noted once if necessary.

Measurement units

  • Avoid assuming one measurement system.
  • Temperature may appear as Celsius or Fahrenheit.
  • Distance may appear as kilometres or miles.
  • Weight may appear as kilograms or pounds.
  • The user’s device settings usually determine units.
  • In the text, avoid forcing one unless needed.
  • When giving examples, keep them general or mention that units may vary by region.

Emergency numbers

Do not mention only one emergency number as universal.

Use wording such as:

  • Emergency services.
  • Local emergency number.
  • Emergency services in your country or region.
  • If examples are needed, explain that numbers vary by country.
  • This is critical for an international course.

Health warnings

Health warnings should be included in relevant modules, but not repeated in a way that makes the course unreadable. The general introduction should include a clear health disclaimer. Health modules should include specific cautions. The closing should remind users that Apple Watch health data are guidance, not diagnosis. The wording should be serious but not frightening.

Safety warnings

Safety warnings should be included in modules about:

  • Exercise.
  • Maps.
  • Emergency SOS.
  • Fall Detection.
  • Apple Pay.
  • Smart home.
  • Buying used.
  • Resetting.
  • Battery.
  • The point is to prevent mistakes, not to scare the reader away from the watch.

Document metadata

If preparing a Word or PDF file, review metadata before sharing.

Metadata may include:

  • Author name.
  • Company.
  • Comments.
  • Revision history.
  • Previous file names.
  • Hidden notes.
  • Remove anything that should not be published.
  • This is especially important when files have gone through several drafts.

File naming

Choose clear file names.

Examples:

  • Apple Watch with VoiceOver. Complete Practical Course.docx
  • Apple Watch with VoiceOver. Complete Practical Course.html

Version control

If you maintain several versions, use clear version names.

For example:

  • Version 1.0.
  • Version 1.1.
  • Spanish version.
  • English version.
  • HTML version.
  • Word version.
  • Archive older versions.
  • Do not mix drafts with final files.
  • If a course is shared with many users, a clear version helps avoid confusion.

Accessibility testing

Before distribution, test with at least one screen reader if possible.

For Word:

  • Test with NVDA, JAWS, or VoiceOver on Mac if available.
  • Check headings.
  • Check table of contents.
  • Check links.
  • Check reading order.

For HTML:

  • Test with a browser and screen reader.
  • Check heading navigation.
  • Check links.
  • Check return links.
  • Check mobile reading if relevant.

For PDF:

  • Check whether text is selectable.
  • Check whether headings and reading order are preserved.
  • Avoid scanned PDFs.
  • If the PDF is not accessible, provide Word or HTML as the main format.

HTML recommended structure

A good HTML version should include:

  • Language attribute.
  • Title tag.
  • Main h1.
  • Introductory sections.
  • Table of contents with links.
  • Each module as a section.
  • Each appendix as a section.
  • Headings.
  • Paragraphs.
  • Meaningful links.
  • Back to table of contents links.
  • No unnecessary visual clutter.
  • No text inside images.
  • Good HTML is often one of the best formats for screen reader users.

Word recommended structure

A good Word version should include:

  • Real document title.
  • Heading styles.
  • Linked table of contents.
  • Internal links or bookmarks if used.
  • Clear paragraphs.
  • No text boxes for essential content.
  • No images of text.
  • Accessible lists if lists are used.
  • Meaningful link text.
  • Word can be a good format if structured properly.

PDF caution

PDF should be handled carefully. PDF may be useful for printing or fixed layout. But for blind users, Word or HTML often provides a better reading experience unless the PDF is properly tagged and accessible. If distributing PDF, also provide HTML or Word if possible. Do not make PDF the only accessible option unless it has been tested.

Checklist before creating final files

Before converting:

Text complete. Module numbering checked.

Appendix numbering checked.

  • Headings assigned.
  • Table of contents created.
  • Return links added.
  • Terminology checked.
  • Country references globalised.
  • Health warnings reviewed.
  • Safety warnings reviewed.
  • Spanish leftovers removed from English version.
  • Links checked.
  • File name chosen.
  • Metadata reviewed.
  • Accessibility tested.

Final publication formats

Recommended final formats:

  • HTML for online reading.
  • DOCX for editing and offline reading.
  • Accessible PDF only if properly generated.
  • Plain text as an optional lightweight version if desired.
  • If distributing to blind users, HTML and DOCX are usually very practical.

Final quality check

Read one full module from beginning to end.

  • Navigate by headings.
  • Jump from table of contents to a module.
  • Use Back to table of contents.
  • Search for a term such as Emergency SOS.
  • Search for Digital Crown.
  • Search for Apple Pay.
  • Search for Medical ID.
  • Check that results make sense.
  • This helps detect structural issues.

Final summary of appendix 12

The final course should have a clear title, introduction, table of contents, modules, appendices, summaries, exercises, and return links.

  • Word should use real heading styles.
  • HTML should use proper heading hierarchy and internal links.
  • PDF should only be used if accessible.
  • The document should avoid visual clutter, raw URLs, text boxes, and images of text.
  • Apple terminology should remain consistent.
  • Country-specific content should be globalised.
  • Health and safety warnings should be clear.
  • The final file should be tested with a screen reader.
  • Good structure is part of accessibility.

Final note

This completes the translated course material for Apple Watch with VoiceOver. The purpose of this course is not to make every person use every Apple Watch feature. The purpose is to help each user understand the device, configure it sensibly, and decide which features genuinely improve daily use.

For blind users, the Apple Watch can be useful when it provides quick access to information, discreet haptic alerts, VoiceOver support, calls, messages, timers, alarms, reminders, workouts, health records, safety features, weather, audio control, Apple Pay, smart home access, and practical interaction with the iPhone.

For deafblind users or users with hearing loss, the most important value may be in haptic alerts, simple routines, selected notifications, alarms, medication reminders, emergency contacts, and support from the iPhone or a braille display.

For older users, the Apple Watch may be useful for calls, medication, appointments, Fall Detection, Emergency SOS, Medical ID, heart alerts, battery routines, and a simple, predictable daily setup.

For advanced users, the Apple Watch can become a powerful companion through multiple watch faces, Focus modes, Shortcuts, workouts, health trends, audio, Wallet, Maps, smart home control, braille workflows, and carefully selected notifications.

But in every case, the principle is the same:

  • The Apple Watch should adapt to the person.
  • The person should not have to adapt their whole life to the watch.
  • A useful Apple Watch is not the one with the most features activated.
  • It is the one that the user understands, controls, and can rely on.
  • If a feature helps, keep it.
  • If a feature confuses, simplify it.
  • If a notification interrupts without value, remove it.
  • If a setting is not understood, review it before depending on it.
  • If a health alert appears, treat it with attention.
  • If symptoms appear, seek proper help.
  • If a safety feature is configured, learn how it behaves before it is needed.
  • If the watch is used for independence, battery, haptics, connection, and emergency contacts matter.
  • The Apple Watch can be a practical accessibility tool.
  • It can also become a small source of noise if configured without judgement.
  • The difference is in the setup, the learning process, and the way it is used every day.

Canal TifloAcosta offers this course as a practical guide for users, families, trainers, and support people who want to approach the Apple Watch with VoiceOver from a clear, realistic, and accessible perspective. Technology should not be a maze. It should be a tool.

And when it is configured well, understood properly, and used with common sense, the Apple Watch can be one more useful piece in the daily autonomy of blind people and other users with accessibility needs. End of course material.
